explanation.summary: DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy (cross placenta; lack of fetal safety data) and in breastfeeding (cross into breast milk). Warfarin is teratogenic in trimester 1 (warfarin embryopathy) and crosses placenta throughout, so avoided except in mechanical heart valves where risk-benefit favours its use. LMWH (enoxaparin or dalteparin) does NOT cross placenta or transfer into breast milk and is the AU first-line for any pregnant patient requiring anticoagulation. Dose: prophylactic 40 mg SC daily (60-80 mg if BMI elevated) for VTE prophylaxis; therapeutic 1 mg/kg BD for treatment or extended prophylaxis for prior idiopathic events. Continue at least 6 weeks postpartum (peak postpartum VTE window). Switch back to DOAC postpartum only if breastfeeding ceased.
key_points: DOACs contraindicated in pregnancy AND breastfeeding (AU)
Warfarin avoided in pregnancy except mechanical heart valves
LMWH: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD therapeutic, 40 mg daily prophylactic
Continue at least 6 weeks postpartum (peak risk)
DOAC can resume postpartum only if not breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Anti-Xa monitoring of enoxaparin is recommended in pregnancy at booking, mid-pregnancy, and term, because volume of distribution and renal clearance change with gestation. Target 4-hour post-dose anti-Xa 0.5-1.0 IU/mL on BD dosing.

options.rationale: DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) are contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding in Australia due to lack of fetal safety data and likely teratogenicity (placental transfer demonstrated). Continuation is wrong. Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy; AMH.

AU practice (RANZCOG): switch any pregnant patient on warfarin or DOAC to LMWH at confirmation of pregnancy. Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BD (or weight-based) is preferred for prior idiopathic PE with extended prophylaxis indication (her recurrence risk justifies therapeutic dose). Continue through pregnancy and at least 6 weeks postpartum. Switch back to DOAC postpartum only if breastfeeding ceased (DOACs are NOT BF-compatible). Renal function and anti-Xa monitoring in select patients. Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy; ANZSBT.

Warfarin is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy: nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses) in T1 and crosses placenta throughout pregnancy. AU practice avoids warfarin in pregnancy except in mechanical heart valves where benefit outweighs risk. Source: RANZCOG.
Stopping anticoagulation in someone with prior idiopathic PE on extended prophylaxis is unsafe - pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state and VTE risk approaches 5-10x baseline. Source: RANZCOG.
Aspirin is not adequate VTE prophylaxis or treatment in a patient with prior idiopathic PE; LMWH is required. Source: RANZCOG.

explanation.summary: Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is a serology + clinical syndrome distinct from idiopathic SLE: ANA positive with the ANTI-HISTONE antibody, anti-dsDNA NEGATIVE, complement normal, renal and CNS involvement rare, resolves within weeks-months of stopping the culprit drug. Antihypertensive precipitants: methyldopa, hydralazine. Antiarrhythmic: procainamide (highest risk - up to 30 percent over time). Antimicrobial: isoniazid. Antipsychotic: chlorpromazine. Biologic: anti-TNF (e.g. infliximab, etanercept). In pregnancy, methyldopa was historically first-line antihypertensive but is now often second-line behind labetalol or nifedipine due to side-effect profile including DILE and depression.
key_points: DILE antibody pattern: ANA + anti-HISTONE positive, anti-dsDNA NEGATIVE, complement normal
Pregnancy antihypertensive DILE precipitant: methyldopa
Highest-risk DILE drug overall: procainamide
Resolution: 2-12 weeks after stopping the drug
Switch first-line AU pregnancy AHT: labetalol or nifedipine
explanation.pearls: When a new symptom cluster appears 4-8 weeks after a new drug start, always ask: 'Could this be drug-induced?' Anti-histone is the highest-yield serology to request when DILE is suspected.

options.rationale: CCBs are not implicated in drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE). Their side-effect profile is ankle oedema, headache, gingival hyperplasia, reflex tachycardia. Source: AMH.

ANTIBODY PATTERN: ANA homogeneous + anti-histone strongly positive + anti-dsDNA negative + normal complement = drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE), distinct from SLE. The distinguishing feature is anti-histone (positive in >95 percent of DILE) and absence of dsDNA + normal complement. Methyldopa is a well-recognised DILE precipitant and is the most common antihypertensive used in pregnancy in Australia. Stop methyldopa; switch to labetalol or nifedipine; symptoms typically resolve over 2-12 weeks. Other DILE precipitants: procainamide (highest risk), hydralazine (second), isoniazid, quinidine, chlorpromazine, anti-TNF. Source: RANZCOG; AMH; ACR DILE.
Beta-blockers are not implicated in DILE. Labetalol's pregnancy-specific side effects are neonatal hypoglycaemia and bradycardia. Source: AMH.
Thiazides are not typical DILE precipitants. Also avoided in pregnancy due to fluid balance concerns. Source: AMH.
ACEIs are contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios) and are not associated with DILE. Source: AMH.

explanation.summary: Each constraint independently excludes one option. ACEi angioedema history rules out perindopril. Severe asthma rules out atenolol. CKD-3a and gout rule out thiazide. Postpartum status rules out methyldopa. Only nifedipine MR satisfies all constraints. The pattern-matching skill is to enumerate constraints and cross off rather than match a single feature.
key_points: Postpartum HTN first-line: nifedipine MR or labetalol
ACEi angioedema cross-reacts within class (enalapril -> perindopril)
Thiazides reduce milk supply early postpartum
Methyldopa associated with postnatal depression - avoid
Severe asthma with prior ICU is relative contraindication to beta-blockade
explanation.pearls: Postpartum BP often peaks at days 3-6 due to fluid mobilisation; review at days 3-5 and 7-10 is standard. Persistent HTN beyond 12 weeks needs investigation for secondary causes.

options.rationale: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are recommended in the postpartum period by SOMANZ and RANZCOG, are compatible with breastfeeding (negligible milk transfer), do not exacerbate asthma, do not require renal dose adjustment at eGFR 48, and avoid the cross-reactive angioedema risk of ACEi/ARBs.
Thiazides reduce milk supply in the first weeks postpartum, raise urate (problematic with her gout), and have reduced efficacy at eGFR <45. (Source: SOMANZ).

ACE inhibitors are otherwise breastfeeding-compatible but are contraindicated in this woman due to documented enalapril-induced angioedema; cross-reactivity between ACEi members is high. (Source: AMH).

Cardioselective beta-blocker but still relatively contraindicated in severe asthma with prior ICU admission; atenolol also concentrates in breast milk more than labetalol or metoprolol. (Source: AMH).
Methyldopa is used antenatally but is not recommended postpartum due to its sedative effect and association with postnatal depression. (Source: SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: Australian methotrexate eligibility requires ALL of: beta-hCG <5000 IU/L, adnexal mass <35 mm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant free fluid (>50 mL by some criteria; any free fluid lowers success), reliable follow-up, normal renal/hepatic function, no breastfeeding, no immune compromise. Even when the number is below 5000, a rapidly rising trend and any free fluid shift the risk calculus toward surgery. Eligibility is a checklist of criteria, not a single number.
key_points: MTX threshold: beta-hCG <5000 IU/L AND <35 mm mass AND no FH AND no significant fluid
Rising hCG predicts MTX failure even below the 5000 cutoff
Salpingectomy preferred over salpingotomy when contralateral tube normal
Anti-D 250 IU IM if Rh negative regardless of management
Day 4 and day 7 hCG required if MTX given
explanation.pearls: ASUM consensus: discriminatory zone for intrauterine pregnancy on TVUS is beta-hCG 1500-2000 IU/L. Empty uterus above this level with no adnexal pathology raises concern for ectopic or a complete miscarriage.

options.rationale: RANZCOG and ASUM criteria for methotrexate eligibility require beta-hCG <5000 IU/L AND adnexal mass <35 mm AND no fetal cardiac activity AND no significant free fluid AND patient able to comply with follow-up. Her beta-hCG of 4800 is below 5000 but the rising trend (>50% over 48 hours indicating active trophoblast) combined with 12 mL free fluid in Douglas reduces methotrexate success and increases rupture risk. Surgery is the safer pathway, particularly as she has completed her family.
Free fluid in Douglas plus a rapidly rising beta-hCG reduce methotrexate efficacy below acceptable thresholds despite the beta-hCG number itself being below 5000. (Source: RANZCOG).
Expectant management requires falling beta-hCG and an asymptomatic patient; her hCG is rising and she is symptomatic. (Source: RANZCOG).

Salpingotomy is offered when contralateral tube is damaged and future fertility is desired; she has a normal contralateral tube and has completed her family. Salpingectomy is preferred to reduce persistent trophoblast risk. (Source: RANZCOG).
Delays definitive management in a symptomatic patient with confirmed ectopic features; rupture risk is unacceptable. (Source: RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Anti-Ro and anti-La are IgG autoantibodies present in Sjogren syndrome, SLE, and isolated asymptomatic seropositivity. They cross the placenta from approximately 16 weeks gestation and can bind to the fetal AV node, producing inflammatory damage and progressive heart block. First-degree block may respond to maternal dexamethasone or fluorinated steroids; second-degree is sometimes reversible; third-degree is irreversible and may require fetal/neonatal pacing. Weekly fetal echo with PR-interval (mechanical) assessment 16-26 weeks is the AU surveillance standard for anti-Ro positive pregnancies. Neonatal lupus erythematosus (skin rash, hepatitis, cytopenias) is the postnatal counterpart and resolves as maternal IgG is cleared (~6 months).
key_points: Anti-Ro/SSA + anti-La/SSB cross placenta from ~16 weeks
Surveillance window: 16-26 weeks for congenital heart block
Continue hydroxychloroquine in pregnancy (compatible, reduces CHB risk)
First-degree block may respond to maternal dexamethasone
Recurrence risk of CHB in subsequent affected pregnancy ~15-20 percent
explanation.pearls: Hydroxychloroquine is associated with reduced incidence of congenital heart block in anti-Ro positive pregnancies (PATCH trial); continuation through pregnancy is supported by RANZCOG.

options.rationale: Uterine artery Doppler is for placental insufficiency / preeclampsia risk stratification and is non-specific for this serology pattern. The dominant fetal risk in anti-Ro positive pregnancies is congenital heart block, not placental insufficiency. Source: RANZCOG.

The discriminator is the anti-Ro (SSA) titre. Anti-Ro IgG crosses the placenta and binds fetal cardiac conduction tissue, producing congenital heart block (CHB) - irreversible once third-degree. Window of highest risk is 16-26 weeks gestation. AU practice: weekly fetal echo with PR-interval measurement; first-degree block may be reversible with maternal dexamethasone. Risk in first anti-Ro pregnancy ~1-2 percent; recurrence in subsequent affected pregnancy ~15-20 percent. Source: RANZCOG; AHA Fetal Cardiology Statement; ACR Reproductive Health Guideline.
Complement monitoring is used in SLE for flare surveillance but is non-specific for Sjogren and does not address the fetal risk. Source: ACR.

Aspirin prophylaxis is appropriate per general preeclampsia risk algorithm but is not the most important step specific to this antibody pattern. It does not prevent congenital heart block. Source: RANZCOG.
Fetal MRI is not part of routine surveillance for anti-Ro positive pregnancies and the antibodies do not cause CNS malformation. Source: RANZCOG.

explanation.summary: MgSO4 for fetal neuroprotection acts via voltage-gated calcium channel modulation, NMDA receptor antagonism, and free-radical scavenging in the immature periventricular white matter, which is particularly vulnerable to hypoxic-ischaemic and inflammatory injury before 30 weeks gestation. Australian practice: indicated when birth is anticipated within 24 hours and gestation is <30 weeks (some units extend to 32 weeks). Maternal magnesium toxicity is monitored by patellar reflexes (loss at >3.5 mmol/L), respiratory rate, and urine output. Calcium gluconate IV is the antidote.
key_points: AU indication: anticipated birth <30 weeks within 24 hours
Dose: 4 g IV over 20 min loading, then 1 g/h
NNT ~63 to prevent one case of cerebral palsy
Monitor patellar reflexes hourly; RR; urine output
Calcium gluconate IV reverses toxicity
explanation.pearls: Same drug, different indication, different mechanism: eclampsia prophylaxis (maternal cortex), fetal neuroprotection (periventricular white matter), severe asthma (bronchodilation), torsades (membrane stabilisation).

sources.label: Australian Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Neuroprotection Guideline

options.rationale: Eclampsia prophylaxis is indeed a magnesium indication but acts via maternal cortical neuronal stabilisation, not fetal periventricular white-matter protection. The mechanism described targets the immature fetal brain specifically. Source: RANZCOG.

Magnesium has been used historically as a tocolytic but is no longer recommended in Australia (no benefit over placebo). The mechanism described is neuroprotective, not myometrial. Source: RANZCOG Preterm Labour Guidance.

Australian Antenatal Magnesium sulfate for Neuroprotection Clinical Practice Guideline (2010, reaffirmed) recommends IV magnesium sulfate for women at <30 weeks gestation with anticipated birth within 24 hours, to reduce cerebral palsy risk in surviving infants. Mechanism is calcium-channel modulation + glutamate/NMDA attenuation + free-radical scavenging at the developing periventricular white matter (which is highly vulnerable to hypoxic injury). NNT ~63 to prevent one case of CP. Loading 4 g IV over 20 min then 1 g/h until birth or 24 h. Source: Australian Antenatal Magnesium sulfate Neuroprotection Guideline; RANZCOG.
source_refs: Australian Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Neuroprotection Guideline

options.rationale: Magnesium has class effect at ion channels but is not used as primary SVT therapy; mechanism described is neuro-specific. Source: AHA.
IV magnesium has a role in severe asthma via smooth muscle relaxation, but the mechanism described targets fetal periventricular tissue, not adult bronchial smooth muscle. Source: TSANZ.

explanation.summary: Puerperal fever (>38 degrees within 14 days postpartum) requires systematic differential by timing and physical findings: day 1-2 favours atelectasis or wound; day 2-10 favours endometritis (especially post-caesarean); day 7-14 favours wound infection, mastitis, DVT/PE; any time UTI, catheter-related infection. Endometritis incidence is ~3 percent of vaginal births but ~5-10x higher with caesarean even after prophylaxis. Triple antibiotic regimen (ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole) covers polymicrobial flora typical of endometritis (anaerobes, group B strep, E coli, enterococcus, gardnerella). Resolution typically within 48 hours; persistent fever suggests abscess, retained products, or pelvic vein thrombophlebitis - imaging indicated.
key_points: Puerperal fever day 2-10: endometritis top of differential
Caesarean increases risk 5-10x vs vaginal even with prophylaxis
AU triple therapy: ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole
Persistent fever despite 48h appropriate antibiotics: imaging for abscess
Postpartum VTE risk persists 6 weeks; high index of suspicion
explanation.pearls: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis is the diagnosis of exclusion in persistent puerperal fever with normal imaging - empirical heparin produces dramatic defervescence within 48 hours and confirms diagnosis.

options.rationale: Wound is dry without erythema or discharge; wound infections typically present day 4-7 with localised signs that are absent here. Source: RANZCOG; eTG Antibiotic.

Time of onset favours endometritis, which is the most common cause of puerperal sepsis at day 2-10 post-caesarean (risk 5-10x vaginal birth even with prophylaxis). Diagnostic constellation: fever >38, uterine tenderness, raised WCC + CRP, lochia may or may not be offensive (often subtle), other foci negative (wound, urine, chest, DVT). Treatment: gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily + ampicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly + metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly (or as per local NSW Health antibiotic stewardship). Source: RANZCOG Postnatal Infections; eTG Antibiotic; NSW Health Maternity Sepsis.
Mastitis would typically present with breast pain, erythema and induration; chest findings absent. Source: ABA; eTG.

DVT presents with calf swelling, tenderness, asymmetry; calf exam negative. DVT also less commonly causes fever this high. Pulmonary embolism would present with tachycardia + dyspnoea + hypoxia. Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy.
Urinalysis is negative; catheter was removed day 2 (48 hours before symptom onset). Possible but less likely than endometritis given the timing and uterine tenderness. Source: eTG Antibiotic.

explanation.summary: Preconception care in pregestational diabetes is central to reducing congenital malformations, miscarriage and stillbirth. Key elements include high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily for at least 3 months preconception, optimisation of HbA1c below 6.5 percent (or as close as safely achievable), cessation of teratogenic medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, statins, certain antihypertensives), screening for diabetic complications (retinopathy, nephropathy), and contraception until ready. Multidisciplinary care involving diabetes-in-pregnancy specialists is recommended.
key_points: Folic acid 5 mg daily for high-risk women including diabetes
HbA1c target below 6.5 percent before conception if safely achievable
Cease ACE inhibitors, ARBs and statins before conception
Screen for retinopathy and nephropathy before pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Risk of major congenital malformation rises with HbA1c: approximately 2 percent at HbA1c 6 percent, 5 percent at 8 percent, 12 percent at 10 percent.

options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and statins are teratogenic and ceased before conception; folic acid 5 mg daily reduces neural tube defects in high-risk women; tight glycaemic control reduces malformation and stillbirth risk. (Source: ADIPS Preconception Care Guidelines)

Perindopril and atorvastatin are teratogenic and must be ceased; folic acid 5 mg daily is required for high-risk women; HbA1c target is below 6.5 percent if achievable safely. (Source: ADIPS Preconception Care Guidelines)
Continuing ACE inhibitor and statin to conception risks fetal exposure during organogenesis; both should be ceased preconception. (Source: ADIPS Preconception Care Guidelines)
Type 1 diabetes requires insulin; gliclazide is not used in pregnancy; metformin is added in selected cases of T2DM, not T1DM. (Source: ADIPS Preconception Care Guidelines)
Microalbuminuria does not preclude pregnancy but warrants nephrology input; deferring without active counselling is not appropriate. (Source: ADIPS Preconception Care Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but life-threatening late-third-trimester emergency, characterised by maternal hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy with low fibrinogen, hyperammonaemia, mildly elevated transaminases and acute kidney injury. The Swansea criteria support diagnosis. Distinguishing features from HELLP include hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy out of proportion to platelet count, and absence of marked haemolysis. Treatment is urgent delivery, correction of hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy, and tertiary supportive care. Many patients improve rapidly after delivery; some require ICU and rarely liver transplantation.
key_points: Hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and AKI distinguish AFLP from HELLP
Urgent delivery is the only definitive treatment
Caesarean is often preferred due to coagulopathy and CTG abnormalities
Tertiary multidisciplinary care including HDU and ICU
explanation.pearls: LCHAD deficiency in the fetus is associated with AFLP; postpartum genetic screening of the neonate is offered.

sources.label: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: AFLP is a maternal emergency requiring urgent delivery regardless of gestation beyond 34 weeks; awaiting steroid effect or observing risks rapid maternal decompensation. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy requires urgent delivery, correction of hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy, and tertiary multidisciplinary care; survival depends on prompt delivery and supportive care. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Magnesium is for eclampsia prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia, not AFLP; vaginal delivery is acceptable in stable AFLP but delivery should be expedited not deferred; coagulopathy may favour caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: NAC is used in paracetamol-induced liver failure with debated benefit in AFLP; observation alone delays delivery and risks fetal and maternal death. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Liver biopsy in coagulopathic peripartum patients is dangerous and unnecessary; AFLP is a clinical and biochemical diagnosis with Swansea criteria; delivery should not wait for histology. (Source: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency. Ultrasound features include an enlarged oedematous ovary, ovarian mass or cyst, and abnormal or absent Doppler flow (venous flow is lost before arterial). Diagnosis is supported by clinical picture and imaging but normal Doppler does not exclude torsion. Treatment is urgent laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation, even if the ovary appears dusky or congested. Cystectomy may be performed in the same procedure if a clear lead point is present. Oophorectomy is reserved for postmenopausal women or clearly necrotic ovary.
key_points: Torsion is a clinical and ultrasound diagnosis; treat urgently
Detorsion with ovarian conservation is preferred even if dusky
Venous flow lost before arterial; normal Doppler does not exclude torsion
Oophorectomy reserved for postmenopausal or necrotic ovary
explanation.pearls: Recurrent torsion can occur; oophoropexy may be considered after a second event in the same ovary or when no anatomical lead point is identified.

options.rationale: Conservative management of confirmed torsion leads to ovarian necrosis; surgery is required regardless of symptom severity. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Torsion Statement)
Imaging delay risks ovarian loss; the diagnosis is established on US with characteristic findings and clinical picture; surgery is required urgently. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Torsion Statement)

Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency; laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation and cystectomy is the standard procedure even when the ovary appears compromised, because ovarian function commonly recovers. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Torsion Statement)

Oophorectomy is reserved for postmenopausal women or clearly necrotic ovary; black or congested appearance after detorsion is not an indication for removal in reproductive-age women. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Torsion Statement)

Laparoscopy is the definitive surgical approach and can include detorsion and cystectomy in the same procedure; routine conversion to laparotomy and oophorectomy is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Torsion Statement)

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception options in Australia include levonorgestrel oral up to 72 hours, ulipristal acetate oral up to 120 hours, and copper intrauterine device up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse or up to 5 days after the earliest expected ovulation. Copper IUD is the most effective with pregnancy rate below 0.1 percent and is preferred when accessible, especially in higher BMI where oral options are less effective. Ulipristal is more effective than levonorgestrel in the 72 to 120 hour window and around the time of ovulation but is contraindicated in breastfeeding for 7 days after dose. STI screening is offered at insertion.
key_points: Copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraceptive (less than 0.1 percent pregnancy)
Window: 5 days post-intercourse or 5 days post-ovulation
Ulipristal up to 120 hours; levonorgestrel up to 72 hours
Oral methods less effective in higher BMI
explanation.pearls: Ulipristal can reduce efficacy of subsequent progestogen contraception; delay start of hormonal contraception for 5 days after ulipristal dose.

options.rationale: Levonorgestrel is licensed for use up to 72 hours and is less effective in higher BMI; copper IUD is more effective and remains effective at this timepoint. (Source: RANZCOG Emergency Contraception)
Double-dose levonorgestrel is sometimes used in BMI above 26 but evidence is limited and it remains less effective than copper IUD at 96 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Emergency Contraception)
Ulipristal is licensed up to 120 hours but is also less effective than copper IUD; copper IUD is preferred when patient is suitable. (Source: RANZCOG Emergency Contraception)

Copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception (pregnancy rate below 0.1 percent) and works up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse or up to 5 days after expected ovulation; suitable in higher BMI. (Source: RANZCOG Emergency Contraception)
Misoprostol is used for medical termination or miscarriage management, not for emergency contraception. (Source: RANZCOG Emergency Contraception)

explanation.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage management follows the four T mnemonic (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin). Atonic PPH refractory to oxytocin bolus is escalated with ergometrine 250 micrograms IM (avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia) and an oxytocin infusion of 40 IU in 1 L crystalloid over 4 hours. Carboprost 250 micrograms IM or intramyometrial is third line and avoided in asthma or pulmonary hypertension. Misoprostol is an alternative. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given as adjunct ideally within 3 hours of birth. Surgical interventions include intrauterine balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation and hysterectomy.
key_points: Ergometrine is second line after oxytocin; avoid in hypertension
Oxytocin infusion 40 IU in 1 L over 4 hours maintains tone
Carboprost 250 micrograms IM is third line; avoid in asthma
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality
explanation.pearls: Intrauterine balloon tamponade is the next step if pharmacological measures fail and acts as both treatment and triage to definitive surgical management.

options.rationale: Carboprost is appropriate later in the algorithm but ergometrine and oxytocin infusion come first when not contraindicated; carboprost is third line in Australian practice. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Management)
Calcium supplementation may be needed during massive transfusion but is not the next uterotonic step; ongoing PPH requires escalating uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Management)
Misoprostol has a slower onset than ergometrine and is generally used when injectable uterotonics are unavailable or contraindicated; not first escalation. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Management)

Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given as adjunctive therapy ideally within 3 hours but does not replace escalating uterotonic; observation alone is dangerous in active atonic PPH. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Management)

Second-line uterotonic after oxytocin bolus failure is ergometrine 250 micrograms IM with simultaneous oxytocin infusion; ergometrine is avoided in hypertension or pre-eclampsia but is appropriate here. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Management)

explanation.summary: About one in five Australian women carries group B streptococcus in the vagina or rectum, and carriage is intermittent. An oral antibiotic course in pregnancy reduces the count briefly but recolonisation from the bowel reservoir is usual well before labour, so antenatal eradication does not lower rates of early onset neonatal disease. The intervention that works is an intravenous beta-lactam given during labour, which achieves bactericidal concentrations in the amniotic fluid and cord blood. The exception is significant bacteriuria with this organism, which is treated when found because it signals heavy colonisation and carries its own maternal risk. In context, screening exists to plan the intrapartum antibiotic, not to trigger antenatal treatment, and women are counselled about that distinction at the time the swab is taken.
key_points: Carriage recurs quickly after oral treatment, so antenatal eradication is not offered.
Intravenous prophylaxis in labour is what reduces early onset neonatal disease.
Significant bacteriuria is the exception and is treated when identified.
Carriage is normal flora, not a sexually transmitted infection.
explanation.pearls: Roughly one in five pregnant women is colonised at any time, and about half of their babies become colonised at birth, yet early onset disease affects well under one percent of those babies.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis
Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Colonisation recurs within weeks of an oral course, so Australian practice defers treatment to the intrapartum period when it protects the newborn. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Oral treatment is indicated when the organism causes disease, such as significant bacteriuria, rather than for asymptomatic vaginal carriage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Vaginal disinfection is used in some settings for skin preparation before surgery, and has not replaced intravenous prophylaxis here. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Partner treatment belongs to sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydia; this organism is normal bowel and vaginal flora. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.rationale: Serial swabbing is reserved for situations where the first result is unreliable or predates the recommended window. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

explanation.summary: The Bishop score quantifies cervical favourability for induction: dilatation, effacement (length), consistency, position and station, each scored 0 to 2 or 0 to 3 to a total of 13. A score below 6 is unfavourable and warrants cervical ripening; 6 or above allows direct amniotomy plus oxytocin. Ripening options are vaginal prostaglandin E2 (dinoprostone) or mechanical (balloon catheter), with similar efficacy and slightly different side-effect profiles. Beyond 41 weeks, induction is recommended to reduce perinatal mortality.
key_points: Bishop score below 6 = unfavourable cervix
Ripening with vaginal PGE2 or balloon catheter is first line
Amniotomy plus oxytocin once Bishop score 6 or above
Induction at 41+ weeks reduces stillbirth risk
explanation.pearls: Balloon catheter is preferred over PGE2 in women with previous caesarean to reduce uterine rupture risk.

options.rationale: An unfavourable cervix (Bishop score below 6) requires cervical ripening before oxytocin and ARM; starting oxytocin first is associated with higher failure and caesarean rates. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)
Amniotomy is not appropriate with a station -2 head and unfavourable cervix; cord prolapse risk and procedural failure are high. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)
Beyond 41 weeks induction is recommended to reduce stillbirth risk; ongoing expectant management to 42 weeks is associated with higher perinatal mortality. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)
There is no obstetric indication for caesarean in a multiparous woman at 41+3 with normal CTG, reassuring growth and no contraindication to vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)

Bishop score 4 is unfavourable; cervical ripening with vaginal prostaglandin E2 or a balloon catheter is first-line, followed by amniotomy and oxytocin when the cervix is favourable. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)

explanation.summary: PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks is managed expectantly with admission, corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart) for fetal lung maturity, latency antibiotics with erythromycin per the ORACLE I trial, and inpatient surveillance for chorioamnionitis (temperature, fetal heart rate, CRP, white cell count). Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection if delivery is anticipated within 24 hours below 30 weeks. Delivery is planned at 34 weeks unless infection, abruption, cord prolapse or fetal compromise mandates earlier delivery.
key_points: Expectant management 24 to 34 weeks with admission and surveillance
Corticosteroids plus erythromycin latency antibiotics standard
Magnesium for neuroprotection below 30 weeks if delivery imminent
Plan delivery at 34 weeks unless complications
explanation.pearls: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided as latency antibiotic in PPROM because of increased necrotising enterocolitis risk; erythromycin remains the agent of choice.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks is managed expectantly with corticosteroids, latency antibiotics (erythromycin per ORACLE I), inpatient observation and delivery at 34 weeks unless infection, abruption or fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Outpatient management of PPROM is associated with higher rates of cord prolapse and chorioamnionitis going undetected; inpatient monitoring is standard in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Without infection, abruption or non-reassuring CTG, immediate delivery at 32 weeks exposes the neonate to prematurity complications without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Active augmentation at 32 weeks without infection or compromise causes iatrogenic prematurity; expectant management with corticosteroid cover prolongs gestation safely. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Without fever, fetal tachycardia, raised CRP or uterine tenderness there is no chorioamnionitis; corticosteroids should not be delayed when PPROM is confirmed between 24 and 34 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate is the standard agent for both eclampsia prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia and treatment of eclamptic seizures. The Australian regimen is 4 g IV loading over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour infusion for 24 hours. Monitoring includes hourly respiratory rate, reflexes and urine output; magnesium toxicity is treated with 1 g calcium gluconate IV. BP target during severe pre-eclampsia is below 160/110, achieved with IV labetalol, hydralazine or oral nifedipine; aim is not normotension but reduction of stroke risk.
key_points: Magnesium 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour for 24 hours
Hourly RR, reflexes and urine output monitoring
Calcium gluconate 1 g IV reverses magnesium toxicity
BP target below 160/110, not normotension
explanation.pearls: Magnesium also provides neonatal neuroprotection when delivery is anticipated below 30 weeks gestation, with a 30 percent reduction in cerebral palsy risk.

options.rationale: The dose is subtherapeutic; standard MAGPIE-derived loading is 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour, which delivers seizure prevention without ongoing escalation. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

Standard Australian regimen for severe pre-eclampsia is magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours, derived from the MAGPIE trial showing approximately halving of eclampsia risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)
Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium for eclampsia prophylaxis based on the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial; magnesium is the standard agent. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)
Benzodiazepines are not first-line eclampsia prophylaxis and cause maternal and neonatal respiratory depression; magnesium has clear superiority. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)
Severe pre-eclampsia with severe features requires immediate magnesium prophylaxis without waiting for eclampsia; reactive management increases morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: PPH management combines pharmacological and mechanical escalation with parallel resuscitation. First line is uterine massage plus oxytocin (IM and IV); second line adds ergometrine (avoid in hypertension) and carboprost (avoid in severe asthma). Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset reduces mortality. Intrauterine balloon tamponade is the next mechanical step before surgical options. Surgical interventions include B-Lynch, uterine artery ligation, and hysterectomy when medical and tamponade therapy fail.
key_points: Stepped escalation: oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, balloon tamponade
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours of PPH onset
Carboprost contraindicated in severe asthma
Surgical options after failure of medical and tamponade therapy
explanation.pearls: Activate massive transfusion protocol when blood loss exceeds 1500 mL with ongoing bleeding or shock index above 1; aim for FFP and platelets at 1:1:1 ratio.

options.rationale: Maximum ergometrine dose in 24 hours is 1 mg (5 doses of 200 mcg) and the patient is already 250 mcg in; a second-line uterotonic should be added in addition. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)

Surgical intervention is reserved for failure of mechanical and pharmacological measures including intrauterine balloon and prostaglandin; uterine atony often responds to escalation without laparotomy. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)

Refractory atonic PPH after first-line oxytocin and ergometrine warrants escalation to carboprost (15-methyl PGF2 alpha) plus intrauterine balloon tamponade and activation of massive transfusion in the setting of ongoing significant blood loss. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given alongside other measures within 3 hours of PPH onset per the WOMAN trial; 4 g is not standard and TXA alone does not address ongoing atony. (Source: WOMAN Trial)
Bimanual compression buys time but stopping pharmacotherapy is unsafe; uterotonic escalation is required for ongoing atonic haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)

explanation.summary: Vaginal birth after caesarean is appropriate for selected women with one previous lower-segment caesarean and no other contraindication, with success rates of approximately 70 percent. Absolute contraindications include previous classical or inverted-T uterine incision, previous uterine rupture, previous myomectomy entering the cavity, and standard contraindications to vaginal birth (placenta praevia, transverse lie). Planned elective caesarean is performed at 36 to 37 weeks for classical incisions to pre-empt spontaneous labour-induced rupture.
key_points: Classical or inverted-T incision = absolute VBAC contraindication
Elective repeat caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks for classical
VBAC after one LSCS has approximately 70 percent success
Continuous CTG and IV access required during TOLAC
explanation.pearls: Uterine rupture rate after one LSCS during trial of labour is approximately 0.5 percent; classical incision rupture rate is up to 10 percent, mostly during spontaneous labour.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Birth After Previous Caesarean

options.rationale: VBAC is contraindicated after a previous classical caesarean incision because of high uterine rupture risk; the lower-segment incision in the second caesarean does not negate the classical scar risk. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC)
Mechanical ripening with a previous classical incision does not eliminate uterine rupture risk; the classical scar precludes trial of labour. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC)
Spontaneous labour does not lower the unacceptable rupture risk of a classical scar; planned elective caesarean is recommended at 36 to 37 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC)

Previous classical caesarean carries 4 to 9 percent uterine rupture risk and is a contraindication to trial of labour; elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks is recommended to pre-empt spontaneous labour. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC)
Baby is already cephalic and ECV is not relevant; the central issue is the classical scar which contraindicates trial of labour irrespective of presentation. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC)

explanation.summary: Antepartum haemorrhage in known placenta praevia mandates admission, large-bore IV access, fluid resuscitation if needed, and group and crossmatch readiness. Vaginal examination is contraindicated. Corticosteroids are given at 22+0 to 34+6 weeks for fetal lung maturity. Anti-D is given to Rh-negative women. Continuous monitoring of mother and fetus continues until bleeding settles. Elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks is standard, brought forward if haemorrhage recurs or becomes massive.
key_points: No vaginal examination in known placenta praevia
Admit, IV access, crossmatch, monitor
Corticosteroids 22+0 to 34+6 weeks for fetal lung maturity
Elective caesarean planned at 36 to 37 weeks
explanation.pearls: Placenta praevia plus prior caesarean increases placenta accreta spectrum risk; tertiary centre delivery with cell-salvage and interventional radiology backup is recommended.

options.rationale: Vaginal examination is contraindicated in known placenta praevia because it can precipitate massive haemorrhage; vaginal birth is not possible with complete praevia. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and accreta)
Placenta praevia with active bleeding requires admission; discharge risks recurrent or massive haemorrhage outside a hospital setting. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and accreta)
ECV is contraindicated in placenta praevia and irrelevant to a cephalic-presenting fetus; placenta praevia mandates caesarean birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and accreta)

With stable maternal and fetal status, immediate caesarean is not required; corticosteroids and observation can prolong gestation safely with appropriate monitoring. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and accreta)

Stable placenta praevia with APH is admitted, IV access secured, crossmatched blood available, corticosteroids given for fetal lung maturity if 22+0 to 34+6 weeks, anti-D if Rh negative, and delivery planned at 36 to 37 weeks unless ongoing haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and accreta)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss of 500 mL or more after vaginal delivery (or 1000 mL after caesarean) in the first 24 hours. The 4Ts framework guides cause: tone (atony, 70 percent), trauma, tissue (retained products), thrombin. Immediate management is parallel: call for help, ABC resuscitation, identify cause, treat. For atony: bimanual fundal massage, additional oxytocin (bolus then infusion), then ergometrine (if no hypertension), then carboprost or misoprostol, then mechanical (balloon, B-Lynch suture), then surgical (interventional radiology, hysterectomy). Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset reduces mortality.
key_points: 4Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin
Atony is most common cause; uterotonic ladder starts with oxytocin
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension/pre-eclampsia
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality
explanation.pearls: Misoprostol 800 micrograms rectally or sublingually is an alternative uterotonic when oxytocin infusion is delayed or refrigeration is unreliable in rural settings.

options.rationale: EUA is reserved for ongoing bleeding despite uterotonics, suspected retained products or trauma; first-line is fundal massage plus additional uterotonic for atony. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary PPH)
Intrauterine balloon tamponade is escalated to when medical management with uterotonics fails to control atonic bleeding, not as the first step. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary PPH)

Uterine atony is the most common cause of primary PPH; immediate bimanual fundal massage plus additional oxytocin (bolus then infusion) is the first-line response while resuscitation and call for help proceed in parallel. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary PPH)
Ergometrine is a second-line uterotonic after additional oxytocin and is contraindicated in hypertension or pre-eclampsia; it is not the immediate next step. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary PPH)
Tranexamic acid is given as adjunct within 3 hours of PPH onset, alongside not instead of mechanical and uterotonic management of atony. (Source: RANZCOG: Primary PPH)

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis is most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and presents with a wedge-shaped tender erythematous area, fever and systemic symptoms. Cornerstone of management is continued effective milk drainage (feeding on the affected side, hand expression or pumping) plus oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics (di(cloxacillin) or flucloxacillin 500 mg every 6 hours for 5 to 7 days) when systemic features are present. Abscess is suspected if a fluctuant area develops or if symptoms fail to improve within 48 to 72 hours; ultrasound and aspiration or surgical drainage are then indicated.
key_points: Continue breastfeeding on the affected side
Antistaphylococcal penicillin 5 to 7 days for systemic features
Ultrasound and drainage if no improvement in 48 to 72 hours
MRSA cover reserved for treatment failure or known risk
explanation.pearls: Inflammatory breast cancer mimics mastitis with peau d'orange skin changes; refer urgently if a non-resolving erythema persists in a woman not lactating or beyond standard treatment course.

options.rationale: Stopping breastfeeding and suppressing lactation worsens mastitis by impairing drainage; continued effective milk removal is central to recovery. (Source: ABM Protocol 36: Mastitis)

Lactational mastitis with systemic features warrants oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics and continued effective milk drainage; review in 48 hours to detect abscess formation requiring drainage. (Source: ABM Protocol 36: Mastitis)
Aspiration is reserved for fluctuant collections suggestive of abscess; in the absence of fluctuance, antibiotic and effective drainage are first-line. (Source: ABM Protocol 36: Mastitis)

MRSA cover is reserved for risk factors (recent hospitalisation, prior MRSA, treatment failure) or known regional prevalence; empirical first-line is antistaphylococcal penicillin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Systemic features (fever, rigors) and persistent over 24 hours mark progression beyond simple engorgement and warrant antibiotics from the outset. (Source: ABM Protocol 36: Mastitis)

explanation.summary: Sensitising events in RhD-negative women with an RhD-positive fetus include trauma, antepartum haemorrhage, external cephalic version, amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling. Anti-D 625 IU IM covers up to 6 mL of fetal red cells; Kleihauer testing quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage and additional anti-D at 125 IU per mL of fetal red cells is given when volume exceeds the routine dose coverage. Anti-D must be given within 72 hours of the sensitising event. Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 weeks does not eliminate the need for additional event-based dosing.
key_points: Sensitising events need event-specific anti-D within 72 hours
Kleihauer quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage volume
Standard 625 IU covers 6 mL fetal red cells; add 125 IU per mL above
Cell-free DNA fetal RhD typing avoids unnecessary anti-D
explanation.pearls: Cell-free DNA fetal RhD genotyping from 11 weeks allows targeted antenatal anti-D only when fetus is RhD positive, avoiding unnecessary blood-product exposure in 40 percent of RhD-negative women carrying RhD-negative fetus.

options.rationale: The Kleihauer indicates fetomaternal haemorrhage exceeding the volume covered by 625 IU; dose must be calculated to cover the actual volume of fetal red cells detected. (Source: NBA Guidelines on Anti-D)

Sensitising events in RhD-negative women carrying RhD-positive fetus require Kleihauer-guided additional anti-D (125 IU per 1 mL fetal RBC) on top of any routine prophylaxis, given within 72 hours and rechecked if large bleed suspected. (Source: NBA Guidelines on Anti-D)

Sensitising events (trauma) require an additional dose regardless of routine antenatal anti-D; Kleihauer volumes above 6 mL fetal red cells require additional anti-D dosing. (Source: NBA Guidelines on Anti-D)

Fixed-dose 1500 IU covers up to 12 mL fetal red cells; with 3.5 mL already documented and ongoing trauma a Kleihauer-guided calculated dose is recommended to prevent underdosing. (Source: NBA Guidelines on Anti-D)

Anti-D prophylaxis after a sensitising event must be given within 72 hours; waiting for antibody development means sensitisation has already occurred and anti-D no longer prevents it. (Source: NBA Guidelines on Anti-D)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency with category 1 caesarean indication when delivery is not imminent vaginally. Immediate management: call for help, declare category 1, manually elevate the presenting part with a vaginal hand to relieve cord compression, position knee-chest or left lateral or Trendelenburg, keep cord in vagina if visible (do not handle excessively to avoid vasospasm), consider bladder filling with 500 to 700 mL via catheter to lift presenting part, tocolysis (terbutaline 250 micrograms SC) if delay is anticipated. Delivery within 30 minutes from diagnosis is the standard.
key_points: Category 1 caesarean: 30-minute decision-to-delivery target
Manual elevation of presenting part throughout transfer
Knee-chest or Trendelenburg positioning
Tocolysis as adjunct when delay anticipated
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for cord prolapse include high presenting part, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy, malpresentation, prematurity and artificial rupture of membranes with unengaged head; controlled ARM at vaginal examination reduces risk.

options.rationale: At 4 cm dilatation and station -2 the head is not deliverable instrumentally; waiting for full dilatation risks irreversible fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord prolapse)

Manual cord replacement is not recommended due to vasospasm risk and high recurrence; immediate category 1 caesarean with manual presenting-part elevation is standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord prolapse)
Oxytocin increases cord compression and worsens fetal compromise; cord prolapse mandates urgent operative delivery rather than augmentation. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord prolapse)

Confirmed cord prolapse with sustained fetal bradycardia is a category 1 caesarean indication; manual cord protection by elevating the presenting part off the cord and maternal positioning are required en route to theatre. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord prolapse)
Tocolysis is adjunctive when delay to theatre is anticipated but does not replace immediate manual cord elevation and category 1 caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord prolapse)

explanation.summary: Endometrial hyperplasia is classified as hyperplasia without atypia or atypical hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, EIN). Tamoxifen increases endometrial cancer risk 2 to 3 fold. Postmenopausal bleeding requires endometrial assessment by transvaginal ultrasound (endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm warrants sampling) and Pipelle biopsy. Atypical hyperplasia has up to 40 percent concurrent endometrial cancer rate at hysterectomy and is treated by total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in postmenopausal women. Hyperplasia without atypia is treated with progestogens (oral or LNG-IUS) with surveillance biopsies.
key_points: Atypia in postmenopausal endometrium: hysterectomy + BSO
Up to 40 percent concurrent endometrial cancer risk at hysterectomy
Without atypia: progestogen, LNG-IUS preferred
Tamoxifen doubles to triples endometrial cancer risk
explanation.pearls: All postmenopausal bleeding warrants assessment regardless of how trivial the volume; endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological malignancy in Australia.

options.rationale: Levonorgestrel-IUS is the conservative option only in patients without atypia or where fertility preservation is required and surgery is contraindicated; in atypical hyperplasia postmenopausal, hysterectomy is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

Atypical endometrial hyperplasia (EIN) in a postmenopausal woman carries up to 40 percent risk of concurrent endometrial cancer; total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the standard of care after MDT review. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

Switching to an aromatase inhibitor may be appropriate after consultation with oncology but does not address the established atypical hyperplasia and concurrent cancer risk; surgery is needed regardless. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

Oral progestogen is conservative therapy for non-atypical hyperplasia in pre-menopausal women or fertility-sparing settings; postmenopausal atypia warrants definitive surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)
Atypical hyperplasia confirmed on biopsy is a surgical indication; repeating Pipelle delays definitive management and risks missing concurrent carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia with severe features includes BP 160/110 or higher, severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, pulmonary oedema, oliguria, platelets under 100, ALT twice normal, creatinine over 90 or fetal growth restriction. Management is parallel: IV antihypertensive (labetalol 20 mg IV repeated to 80 mg, or hydralazine 5 to 10 mg IV) to target BP under 160/110; IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion for at least 24 hours for seizure prophylaxis. Betamethasone is given if under 35 weeks and delivery is anticipated within 7 days. Delivery planning at the earliest gestation balances maternal and fetal risk and is usually 34 to 37 weeks for severe features.
key_points: Severe features mandate IV antihypertensive plus magnesium
Magnesium 4 g load then 1 g/hour for 24 hours minimum
Betamethasone if under 35 weeks and delivery anticipated
Delivery timing balances maternal severity and gestation
explanation.pearls: Magnesium toxicity presents with absent reflexes (over 4 mmol/L), respiratory depression (over 5 mmol/L) and cardiac arrest (over 6 mmol/L); treat with calcium gluconate 1 g IV.

options.rationale: Oral antihypertensive is too slow for severe-range BP with severe features; IV antihypertensive plus magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis is required immediately. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Antihypertensive treatment and magnesium seizure prophylaxis cannot wait for the steroid course; they are given concurrently while corticosteroid is administered. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Severe-range BP with severe features (headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, deranged labs) is a medical emergency requiring inpatient management not outpatient care. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Even when delivery is needed, antihypertensive control and magnesium prophylaxis must be initiated before transfer to theatre to reduce maternal stroke and eclampsia risk. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Pre-eclampsia with severe features requires immediate IV antihypertensive to a target BP under 160/110, magnesium for seizure prophylaxis, betamethasone for lung maturity at 34 weeks if delivery within 7 days is anticipated, and plan for timely delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Endometriosis management follows a stepwise medical-then-surgical approach guided by symptoms, imaging, fertility goals and previous treatments. First-line: NSAIDs plus combined hormonal contraception in continuous regimen, or progestogen (oral, depot or LNG-IUS). Second-line: GnRH analogues with add-back therapy. Surgery (laparoscopic excision or ablation) is for failed medical therapy, large endometriomas (greater than 4 cm), suspected deep infiltrating disease, or fertility concerns. Multidisciplinary care including pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychology improves outcomes.
key_points: Continuous combined hormonal contraception before escalation
GnRH analogue with add-back is second-line medical
Surgery for endometrioma over 4 cm or failed medical therapy
Pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychology as adjuncts
explanation.pearls: GnRH antagonists (elagolix, relugolix) are oral alternatives to depot GnRH agonists and avoid the initial flare phase but still require bone monitoring or add-back.

options.rationale: Cyclical pain on cyclic COCP often improves with continuous regimen to suppress menstruation; this is the next step before escalating to second-line hormonal or surgical management. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
Surgery is reserved for failure of medical therapy, large endometriomas (greater than 4 cm) or fertility concerns; continuous COCP should be trialled first. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

GnRH analogues are typically second-line after continuous hormonal contraception or progestogen failure due to bone-density and vasomotor side effects requiring add-back therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
Adjuncts may help but in moderate to severe endometriosis with imaging-confirmed disease, escalation of hormonal suppression should not be deferred for 6 months. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

LNG-IUS is effective for endometriosis but switching from one hormonal contraception to another without first trialling continuous regimen is not the standard sequence; continuous COCP is simpler and equally efficacious. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage is defined in Australia as 3 or more consecutive losses before 20 weeks (2 or more in some international guidelines). Causes include antiphospholipid syndrome (15 percent, treatable with aspirin plus heparin), parental balanced translocations (3 to 5 percent), uterine anomalies (10 to 15 percent), thyroid disease and unexplained (50 percent). First-line investigations: antiphospholipid antibodies (repeated 12 weeks apart for diagnosis), parental karyotype, thyroid function, pelvic ultrasound. Inherited thrombophilia screening is not routinely recommended because association is weak and treatment unproven.
key_points: Workup after 3 consecutive losses in Australia
Antiphospholipid syndrome is treatable cause (aspirin plus heparin)
Parental karyotype identifies balanced translocations
Inherited thrombophilia screen NOT routinely recommended
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid syndrome requires both clinical criteria (3 or more first-trimester losses, fetal death over 10 weeks, or severe early pre-eclampsia) AND persistent positive antibody on 2 tests at least 12 weeks apart.

options.rationale: Australian guidance after 3 consecutive losses recommends parental karyotype, antiphospholipid antibody screen, thyroid function and pelvic anatomy assessment as first-line workup, all with evidence of treatment options if abnormal. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

Routine inherited thrombophilia testing for recurrent first-trimester miscarriage is not recommended; the association is weak and no treatment is proven to improve outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
Endometrial biopsy for NK cells and chronic endometritis is investigational; not recommended as primary workup in Australian or international guidance. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
Pelvic ultrasound is the first-line anatomical assessment; hysteroscopy and MRI follow only if ultrasound is abnormal or suggests a mullerian anomaly. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

Sperm DNA fragmentation testing has no proven role in routine recurrent miscarriage workup; first-line investigations target maternal antiphospholipid, parental karyotype, thyroid and uterine anatomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: First trimester combined screening at 11+0 to 13+6 weeks combines nuchal translucency, maternal serum PAPP-A and free beta-hCG with maternal age to estimate trisomy 21, 18 and 13 risks. A risk below 1 in 1000 is conventionally classified low-risk and allows continuation of routine antenatal care. The 18 to 22 week morphology ultrasound remains the next scheduled imaging milestone, regardless of combined screen result. NIPT is an alternative or follow-up offered to women who want higher detection rates; diagnostic testing is reserved for high-risk results, known parental abnormalities or after careful counselling for maternal request.
key_points: Combined screen risk under 1 in 1000 is low-risk
Morphology scan at 18 to 22 weeks remains next scheduled imaging
NIPT is optional after low-risk screen, not mandated
Diagnostic invasive testing reserved for high-risk screening
explanation.pearls: An NT above 3.5 mm with normal karyotype still confers a 5 to 10 percent residual risk of congenital cardiac anomaly and warrants a detailed fetal echocardiogram at 20 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: NIPT is offered as an alternative or follow-up to combined screening but is not mandated after a normal low-risk combined screen result; routine NIPT after a reassuring screen is not standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Amniocentesis carries a 1 in 200 procedure-related miscarriage risk and is reserved for high-risk screening, known parental rearrangement or maternal anxiety after counselling; routine use is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: A low-risk combined screen result allows continuation of routine antenatal care; the 18 to 22 week morphology scan remains the next scheduled imaging milestone for structural assessment. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Early fetal echocardiography is reserved for increased nuchal translucency, maternal diabetes, family history or teratogen exposure; isolated low-risk pregnancy does not warrant early cardiac imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Combined screening is performed once at 11+0 to 13+6 weeks; a reassuring result does not require repeat measurement and the window closes at 13+6 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

explanation.summary: Migraine eligibility for combined hormonal contraception depends on aura status and age. Migraine without aura at any age is WHO MEC category 2 (advantages generally outweigh theoretical risks); migraine with aura at any age is category 4 (unacceptable risk) because aura confers an independent ischaemic stroke risk that compounds with combined hormonal contraception. The safest practice is to prescribe combined contraception for migraine without aura under 35 with explicit advice to stop immediately if any aura, focal neurology or worsening headache develops. Aura is defined as gradual development of unilateral fully reversible neurological symptoms over 5 to 60 minutes preceding the headache.
key_points: Migraine without aura under 35: WHO MEC 2 for CHC
Migraine with aura at any age: WHO MEC 4 absolute contraindication
Counsel to stop CHC immediately if aura develops
Aura is fully reversible neurology lasting 5 to 60 minutes
explanation.pearls: An ischaemic stroke odds ratio of approximately 6 for women with migraine with aura on combined hormonal contraception underpins the WHO MEC 4 classification.

sources.label: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC

options.rationale: WHO category 4 applies to migraine with aura at any age; migraine without aura under 35 is only category 2 and not an absolute contraindication. (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC

options.rationale: DMPA is an option but is not the only safe choice; combined methods remain acceptable for migraine without aura under 35 after counselling on warning symptoms. (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC

options.rationale: Copper IUD is acceptable but is not the only option; combined hormonal contraception remains a valid choice for migraine without aura under 35 after appropriate counselling. (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC

options.rationale: Neurology referral is not required to prescribe combined contraception for migraine without aura; the consultation can be completed in primary care with appropriate counselling. (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC

options.rationale: Migraine without aura under age 35 is WHO MEC category 2 for combined hormonal contraception; benefits generally outweigh risks with explicit advice to stop if aura emerges. (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: UK MEC

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined as bleeding that interferes with physical, emotional or quality of life. Initial workup excludes structural causes (ultrasound) and assesses iron status (FBC, ferritin). The levonorgestrel-releasing IUS is first-line for ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding without structural pathology, reducing blood loss by around 90 percent at 12 months. Second-line medical options include tranexamic acid during menses, NSAIDs, combined hormonal contraception and oral progestogens. Surgical options (endometrial ablation, hysterectomy) are reserved for failure of medical management. Iron deficiency anaemia is treated concurrently.
key_points: LNG-IUS first-line for ovulatory HMB without structural pathology
Tranexamic acid 1 g TDS during menses reduces loss 30 to 50 percent
Hysteroscopy reserved for intermenstrual bleeding or treatment failure
Treat iron deficiency concurrently
explanation.pearls: An endometrial thickness above 12 mm on ultrasound in a premenopausal woman with HMB warrants hysteroscopy and biopsy to exclude hyperplasia even with a regular cycle.

options.rationale: Tranexamic acid alone reduces blood loss by 30 to 50 percent but is less effective than the LNG-IUS which is the first-line option for ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Levonorgestrel-releasing IUS is the first-line treatment for ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding with normal uterine cavity; it reduces blood loss by around 90 percent and concurrent iron treats the deficiency. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
Endometrial ablation is reserved for women who have failed or declined medical management including the LNG-IUS, not as first-line definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Hysteroscopy and biopsy are reserved for intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding, suspicious ultrasound or treatment failure; normal pelvic ultrasound in a 38-year-old does not mandate it. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Combined oral contraceptive pill is a reasonable option but the LNG-IUS has superior bleeding reduction and is the recommended first-line therapy for ovulatory menorrhagia. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage is abnormal bleeding from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum. The two leading causes are retained products of conception and endometritis (often co-existing). Workup is FBC, group and screen, CRP, endocervical and high vaginal swabs, and pelvic ultrasound. Retained products typically appear as a heterogeneous echogenic cavity mass with vascularity; an empty cavity points to endometritis or atony. Management of retained products is uterotonics plus antibiotic cover and consideration of suction evacuation; management of endometritis is broad-spectrum antibiotics covering anaerobes (intravenous amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole).
key_points: Secondary PPH: 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum
Ultrasound is first-line imaging to identify retained products
Retained products and endometritis often co-exist
Lochia transition by D14 is alba; fresh red bleeding is abnormal
explanation.pearls: Empirical antibiotic cover for retained products in secondary PPH is intravenous amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole given concurrently with surgical or expectant management decisions.

options.rationale: MRI is not the initial imaging modality for secondary PPH; ultrasound is faster, cheaper and adequate to identify retained products as the first-line investigation. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

Hysteroscopy is reserved for ongoing bleeding after empty ultrasound or for histological confirmation; first-line workup is non-invasive imaging within the same day. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

Endometritis usually presents with fever, foul-smelling discharge and uterine tenderness; afebrile heavy fresh bleeding warrants imaging not empirical antibiotics alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

Secondary PPH with a positive urine pregnancy test and bleeding pattern beyond expected lochial timeline warrants ultrasound to identify retained products which is the most common cause. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)
By day 14 lochia is typically alba (creamy white); a return to fresh red bleeding beyond day 10 is abnormal and warrants investigation, not reassurance. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets, occurring in around 0.5 percent of pregnancies usually with pre-eclampsia. Diagnostic criteria include platelets under 100, AST or ALT above twice the upper limit of normal and evidence of haemolysis (low haptoglobin, raised LDH, raised bilirubin or schistocytes). Mainstay management is delivery; conservative management beyond 34 weeks is contraindicated. Steroids accelerate fetal lung maturity below 34 weeks and may transiently improve maternal platelets. Magnesium sulfate prevents eclampsia and antihypertensives target blood pressure under 160/110.
key_points: HELLP: haemolysis, elevated transaminases, platelets under 100
Delivery within 24 to 48 hours above 34 weeks gestation
Magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis at diagnosis
BP target under 160/110 with IV labetalol or hydralazine
explanation.pearls: Hepatic capsule haematoma rupture occurs in around 1 percent of HELLP and presents with right upper quadrant pain, shoulder tip pain and shock; urgent CT and laparotomy with hepatic packing are life-saving.

sources.label: Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand: Pre-eclampsia

options.rationale: HELLP at 33 weeks warrants magnesium for seizure prophylaxis, antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, antihypertensive control and delivery within 24 to 48 hours after steroid completion. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)

Conservative management beyond 34 weeks gestation in HELLP increases maternal mortality from hepatic rupture, eclampsia and DIC; delivery within 48 hours is indicated after steroids. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)

Right upper quadrant pain with raised transaminases and thrombocytopenia in late pregnancy is HELLP until proven otherwise; surgery without correcting coagulopathy is dangerous. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)

TTP is a differential but pregnancy-related HELLP is more common; presumptive PLEX is reserved for failure to improve postpartum or ADAMTS13 confirmation, not first step. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)

Severe HELLP biochemistry requires the same hour escalation; deferring the management decision until next morning risks maternal seizure, hepatic rupture and fetal compromise overnight. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage is three or more consecutive first-trimester pregnancy losses. Recommended workup includes antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein 1) measured 12 weeks apart, parental karyotype to identify balanced translocations, uterine cavity assessment by 3D ultrasound or saline sonography to detect septum or fibroids, and thyroid function. Empirical interventions including immunoglobulin, prednisolone or LMWH without indication are not supported by current evidence. Aspirin plus LMWH is indicated only for confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome. Despite full workup, around 50 percent of recurrent miscarriage cases remain unexplained.
key_points: Workup after 3 consecutive first-trimester losses
Antiphospholipid antibodies, parental karyotype, uterine cavity, TFTs
Aspirin and LMWH only for confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome
Empirical immunotherapy not supported by evidence
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid antibodies must be confirmed on repeat testing 12 weeks apart to meet diagnostic criteria; a single positive test does not establish the syndrome or justify lifelong therapy.

options.rationale: Aspirin and LMWH are reserved for confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome or other indicated thrombophilia; empirical use without diagnosis carries bleeding risk without proven benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

NK cell testing and immunoglobulin therapy are not supported by evidence and are not recommended in routine recurrent miscarriage workup; they carry cost and unclear benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

Recommended workup after three consecutive first-trimester losses includes antiphospholipid antibodies, parental karyotype, uterine cavity assessment and thyroid function as evidence-based tests prior to next conception. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

HSG assesses tubal patency primarily; uterine cavity is better assessed by 3D ultrasound or saline-infusion sonography, and blood tests should be done in parallel not deferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

Recurrent miscarriage is defined as three or more consecutive losses; this threshold triggers investigation rather than deferring further losses without workup. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Preterm labour under 32 weeks is managed with four parallel actions: tocolysis (nifedipine first-line in Australia, atosiban as second-line), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart), magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection (4 g loading then 1 g/hour infusion for at least 4 hours and up to 24 hours), and in utero transfer to a level 3 NICU. Magnesium reduces cerebral palsy risk by around 30 percent when given under 32 weeks. Antibiotics are added only for confirmed or suspected GBS positive status or preterm pre-labour rupture of membranes.
key_points: Nifedipine first-line tocolysis in Australia
Betamethasone for fetal lung maturity under 34 weeks
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection under 32 weeks
In utero transfer to level 3 NICU under 32 weeks
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection ideally commences at least 4 hours before delivery; if delivery occurs within 4 hours, reduced benefit applies but treatment is still worthwhile to start.

options.rationale: Caesarean is not indicated solely for preterm labour with reassuring CTG; vaginal birth is preferred and tocolysis should be used to enable steroid effect and transfer. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

Indometacin is reserved for under 32 weeks short courses but is not first-line in Australia; magnesium neuroprotection and tertiary transfer are essential under 32 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

Tocolysis is warranted under 34 weeks to allow steroid effect and arrange transfer; allowing precipitous birth locally without level 3 NICU risks worse neonatal outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)
Antenatal corticosteroids must be given as soon as preterm birth is anticipated within 7 days; delaying for 12 hours misses the window for full steroid benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

Preterm labour under 32 weeks warrants tocolysis to delay birth for steroid effect, antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium for neuroprotection and in utero transfer to a level 3 NICU. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

explanation.summary: Australia's renewed National Cervical Screening Program uses primary HPV testing 5-yearly from age 25-74. Result categories: HPV negative (5-year recall), HPV 16/18 positive (always colposcopy regardless of cytology), HPV other oncogenic types positive with reflex cytology (low-grade = 12-month repeat; high-grade = colposcopy). Persistence of HPV other oncogenic at 12-month repeat warrants colposcopy. HPV vaccination does not change screening recommendations. Self-collected vaginal samples are now accepted nationally with equivalent sensitivity to clinician-collected.
key_points: HPV positive non-16/18 plus LSIL = 12-month repeat
HPV 16/18 positive at any time = direct colposcopy
HSIL on cytology = direct colposcopy
Self-collection now accepted nationally
