explanation.pearls: Self-collected HPV vaginal swabs are now offered to all eligible women in Australia regardless of risk factors as of 2022, with equivalent sensitivity for high-grade lesions; this has increased screening participation in under-screened populations including those with prior sexual assault history.

sources.label: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.rationale: Routine 5-year recall is for HPV-negative results; HPV-positive non-16/18 with LSIL needs intermediate-risk follow-up. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.rationale: 6 months is too early for HPV clearance assessment; NCSP specifies 12-month repeat for intermediate-risk results. (Source: NCSP)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.rationale: NCSP intermediate-risk pathway: HPV positive (non-16/18) with reflex cytology showing pLSIL or LSIL is intermediate risk; repeat CST in 12 months to assess HPV persistence. If still HPV-positive at 12 months, refer to colposcopy. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.rationale: Colposcopy is reserved for higher-risk results: HPV 16/18 positive, persistent HPV at repeat 12-month, or high-grade cytology (HSIL). (Source: NCSP)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.rationale: LLETZ is treatment for confirmed CIN2/3 lesions after colposcopy; not appropriate at LSIL stage. (Source: NCSP)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes mellitus is screened in Australian women at 24-28 weeks (earlier if high-risk: prior GDM, BMI 30 or higher, family history, ethnicity, PCOS, prior macrosomia). ADIPS criteria for 75g OGTT: fasting at or above 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour at or above 10.0 mmol/L, 2-hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L; any single value meets diagnosis. Management: structured diet, exercise, blood glucose self-monitoring 4-7 times daily. Insulin or metformin if targets not met (fasting below 5.0, 2-hour below 6.7). Implications: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, increased lifetime maternal T2DM risk (around 50 percent within 10 years). Postpartum OGTT at 6-12 weeks to confirm resolution.
key_points: ADIPS criteria: fasting 5.1, 1-hour 10.0, 2-hour 8.5 (any one = GDM)
MDT pregnancy diabetes clinic referral
Self-monitoring 4x daily target fasting below 5.0, 2-hour below 6.7
Postpartum OGTT at 6-12 weeks (lifetime T2DM risk 50 percent at 10 years)
explanation.pearls: A prior GDM diagnosis carries around a 50 percent risk of developing type 2 diabetes within 10 years, so all women post-GDM should have postpartum 75g OGTT at 6-12 weeks and then 1-2 yearly HbA1c or FBG screening for life.

options.rationale: Results meet GDM diagnostic criteria; cannot be reassured as normal. (Source: ADIPS; RANZCOG)
GDM is diagnosed, not just IFG; requires structured management with self-monitoring. (Source: ADIPS)
Pre-existing T2DM would show HbA1c at or above 6.5 percent and fasting at or above 7 mmol/L; this pattern is gestational diabetes only. (Source: ADIPS)

ADIPS 2014 diagnostic criteria: fasting at or above 5.1, 1-hour at or above 10.0, 2-hour at or above 8.5 - meeting any one criterion at 75g OGTT diagnoses GDM. Here fasting 5.2 and 2-hour 8.7 meet criteria. Management: refer to diabetes-in-pregnancy MDT, dietary review, blood glucose self-monitoring 4x daily. (Source: ADIPS; RANZCOG)
Repeat without intervention misses diagnosis; treatment commenced now reduces macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting causing weight loss of 5 percent or more, dehydration, ketonuria, and electrolyte disturbance, affecting 0.3-1 percent of pregnancies. PUQE score 13 or more is severe. Risk factors: previous HG, family history, multiple pregnancy, molar pregnancy. Admit if dehydrated, ketotic, electrolyte disturbance, or failure of oral antiemetics. Management: IV Hartmann's with K replacement, IV thiamine 100 mg BEFORE glucose (Wernicke prevention), antiemetics (pyridoxine, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, ondansetron - all Category B or B1), DVT prophylaxis, psychological support. Transient hyperthyroidism due to HCG cross-reactivity resolves without treatment.
key_points: Admission criteria: dehydration, ketosis, 5 percent or more weight loss, electrolyte derangement
IV thiamine 100 mg BEFORE glucose (Wernicke prevention)
IV Hartmann's plus K replacement
Multiple antiemetic ladder: pyridoxine, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, ondansetron
explanation.pearls: Wernicke's encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency in hyperemesis gravidarum can be precipitated by IV glucose infusion before thiamine replacement, leading to permanent Korsakoff syndrome in around 80 percent of survivors - always give IV thiamine first.

options.rationale: Oral antiemetics are ineffective in severe HG; saline alone without K replacement risks worsening hypokalaemia. (Source: RANZCOG; AMH)

Severe hyperemesis gravidarum with weight loss 5 percent or more of pre-pregnancy weight, ketonuria, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance requires admission. Management: IV Hartmann's with K replacement, IV thiamine 100 mg before any glucose, IV ondansetron 8 mg 8-hourly (Pregnancy Category B1). (Source: RANZCOG; AMH; KEMH)
Subcutaneous home device is not standard AU first-line; admission is warranted for severe HG. (Source: RANZCOG)
Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis is HCG-mediated, transient, and requires no treatment unless persistent past 20 weeks with symptoms. (Source: AMH; ESA)
Metformin has no role in HG management; ondansetron and supportive care are evidence-based. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Primary PPH (blood loss over 500 mL after vaginal birth or over 1000 mL after caesarean within 24 hours of birth) is most commonly due to uterine atony (4Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin). Stepwise management: bimanual compression, IV access x2, cross-match, blood products if needed. Pharmacological ladder: oxytocin (IV 5 IU plus 40 IU infusion), ergometrine 250 mcg IM (avoid in hypertension or eclampsia), carboprost 250 mcg IM (avoid in asthma), misoprostol PR 800 mcg. TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality. Surgical escalation: balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, hysterectomy as last resort.
key_points: PPH = over 500 mL vaginal or over 1000 mL caesarean
Oxytocin first-line; ergometrine if no HTN; carboprost if no asthma
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality
Surgical escalation: balloon, B-Lynch, ligation, hysterectomy
explanation.pearls: The WOMAN trial showed tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of PPH onset reduces death due to bleeding by approximately 30 percent, with no increase in adverse events; the benefit is lost if administered beyond 3 hours, so prioritise early TXA in any active PPH.

options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-existing hypertension; risk of severe hypertension and stroke. (Source: AMH; RANZCOG PPH)
Misoprostol PR is an adjunct, second or third-line; first-line additional is IV oxytocin escalation. (Source: RANZCOG)
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given alongside (NOT instead of) uterotonics within 3 hours of PPH onset; not the immediate sole next step. (Source: WOMAN trial; RANZCOG)
Carboprost 250 micrograms is IM (not IV) and contraindicated in asthma; not the first-line additional uterotonic. (Source: AMH; RANZCOG)

Australian PPH algorithm (RANZCOG): in primary PPH from uterine atony, additional oxytocin IV (5 IU bolus then 40 IU/500 mL infusion at 125-250 mL/h) is first-line escalation. Ergometrine contraindicated by hypertension. Carboprost IM is second-line. Misoprostol PR is third-line. TXA 1 g IV given concurrently within 3 hours. (Source: RANZCOG; AMH)

explanation.summary: PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women (10-15 percent prevalence). Rotterdam diagnosis: 2 of 3 - oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism (clinical or biochemical), polycystic ovary morphology on USS (20 or more follicles or volume 10 mL or more). Exclude mimics: CAH (17-OHP), prolactinoma, thyroid, Cushing, virilising tumour. Comorbidities: T2DM (3x risk), endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, dyslipidaemia, OSA, NAFLD, mental health. Management: lifestyle (cornerstone), COCP for cycle and androgens, metformin for IR, spironolactone for hirsutism after 6 months COCP. Letrozole first-line for ovulation induction.
key_points: Rotterdam: 2 of 3 criteria plus exclusion of mimics
USS: 20 or more follicles per ovary OR volume 10 mL or more
Annual T2DM screening (OGTT), 4-yearly endometrial USS
Letrozole first-line for ovulation induction
explanation.pearls: Endometrial protection in PCOS-related anovulation is critical: prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure raises endometrial cancer risk around 3-fold; women with cycles over 90 days should receive cyclical progestogen (medroxyprogesterone 10 mg for 10 days every 1-3 months) at minimum even if not using contraception.

options.rationale: Secondary hypogonadism would have low LH and FSH; here LH:FSH ratio is raised, typical of PCOS. (Source: ESA; AMH)
17-OH progesterone is normal, ruling out classical CAH; LOCAH typically has higher levels. (Source: ESA)
Insulin resistance is a feature of PCOS but is not a standalone diagnosis; commencing metformin alone misses other diagnostic and management aspects. (Source: ESA)
Hypothalamic causes typically have low gonadotrophins and low oestrogen; this presentation has hyperandrogenism and PCO morphology. (Source: ESA)

Rotterdam criteria (2003) require 2 of 3: oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovary morphology on USS (20 or more follicles in either ovary or volume 10 mL or more). This patient meets all 3. Management: lifestyle (5-10 percent weight loss restores ovulation in around 50 percent), COCP for cycle and hirsutism, metformin for IR. (Source: International PCOS Network; ESA)

explanation.summary: Intrapartum prophylaxis works by achieving bactericidal amniotic fluid and fetal concentrations during the period the newborn is exposed, which begins with established labour or rupture of the membranes. Induction complicates the timing because ripening can take many hours during which the woman is neither in labour nor ruptured, and giving antibiotics through that whole period adds exposure without benefit. The practical rule is to prescribe the antibiotic on admission but to administer it when contractions establish or the membranes break, and then to continue at the stated interval until birth. Starting too late is the commoner error: a first dose given within an hour of birth is not counted as adequate. In context, induction of labour is now offered to a large proportion of Australian women, so knowing when the clock starts for prophylaxis is an everyday decision on the birth suite.
key_points: Prophylaxis is triggered by established labour or ruptured membranes, not by admission.
Ripening with a balloon alone is not an indication to start the infusion.
Adequate prophylaxis means the first dose at least four hours before birth.
Fever in labour is a separate indication and calls for broad-spectrum cover.
explanation.pearls: Prescribe the antibiotic on admission for induction but set the administration trigger explicitly in the notes, so the dose is not given at balloon insertion or forgotten when labour establishes overnight.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Prophylaxis is timed to the start of true labour or rupture so that adequate concentrations are present during the exposure window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.rationale: Starting with the balloon would be right only if she were already contracting or her membranes had broken. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.rationale: Balloon removal is a procedural landmark, not a physiological one; the trigger is labour or ruptured membranes. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Fever in labour prompts broad-spectrum cover for suspected intrauterine infection, which is a different indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Giving the first dose at full dilatation leaves too little time for transfer across the placenta before birth. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

explanation.summary: VTE is the leading cause of direct maternal mortality in high-income countries. Diagnostic pathway in pregnancy for suspected PE: chest X-ray first to assess for alternative cause, bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound (positive confirms VTE, avoids further radiation), and if negative with persistent suspicion: V/Q scan preferred if CXR clear (lower maternal breast radiation), CTPA preferred if CXR abnormal. D-dimer is not validated in pregnancy. Empiric LMWH if delay to imaging is unavoidable and PE is likely. Treatment: LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily) for duration of pregnancy plus 6 weeks postpartum (minimum 3 months treatment).
key_points: Pregnancy: CXR first, then leg USS, then V/Q (if CXR clear) or CTPA (if CXR abnormal)
D-dimer unreliable in pregnancy
LMWH is treatment of choice (warfarin and DOACs contraindicated)
Duration: pregnancy plus 6 weeks postpartum (min 3 months total)
explanation.pearls: V/Q scanning in pregnancy involves around 0.32 mGy fetal dose (below the 50 mGy threshold for fetal harm) but only around 0.02 mGy maternal breast dose; CTPA delivers 0.06 mGy to fetus but 20-50 mGy to maternal breasts - the breast dose is the deciding factor against CTPA in young women with normal CXR.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and NZ

options.rationale: AU pathway for suspected PE in pregnancy with normal CXR: bilateral compression USS first (positive USS confirms VTE and avoids further radiation); if negative and PE still suspected, V/Q is preferred over CTPA in pregnancy due to lower maternal breast radiation dose. CTPA preferred if CXR abnormal. (Source: RANZCOG; Thrombosis Australia)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and NZ

options.rationale: CTPA is acceptable but V/Q is preferred over CTPA in pregnancy with normal CXR due to lower maternal breast radiation; V/Q has higher fetal radiation but breast cancer risk is the greater concern. (Source: RANZCOG)
MRPA has limited availability and unclear sensitivity in pregnancy; not first-line. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)
Pulmonary embolus can exist without lower limb DVT; further imaging is needed if USS negative. (Source: RANZCOG)
D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy and lacks specificity; cannot be used alone to exclude PE. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: AU first-line for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy refractory to lifestyle measures is pyridoxine plus doxylamine. Second-line options include metoclopramide and prochlorperazine; ondansetron is reserved for failures of these due to uncertain safety signals in the first trimester. Hyperemesis with ketonuria, weight loss over 5 percent, and electrolyte disturbance warrants IV fluid resuscitation, thiamine cover before glucose, and admission if oral hydration cannot be re-established. Corticosteroids are last-line.
key_points: Pyridoxine plus doxylamine is first-line in AU
Ondansetron second or third line due to cleft signal
Thiamine before glucose IV in prolonged vomiting
Steroids last-line under senior obstetric input
explanation.pearls: In refractory hyperemesis with prolonged vomiting beyond 3 weeks, IV thiamine 100 mg before glucose-containing fluids prevents Wernicke encephalopathy that has been reported in pregnancy.

sources.label: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Metoclopramide is second-line; first-line is pyridoxine plus doxylamine before stepping up to dopamine antagonists. (Source: RANZCOG)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: AU practice initiates pyridoxine plus doxylamine as the first-line antiemetic combination in pregnancy for women who have failed lifestyle measures. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are a last-line option after multiple antiemetics have failed and require senior obstetric agreement. (Source: RANZCOG)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Ondansetron is reserved for second-line use after pyridoxine doxylamine and metoclopramide fail in AU due to possible association with orofacial clefts. (Source: RANZCOG)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Phenothiazines are second-line and have a greater extrapyramidal side-effect burden in early pregnancy than the first-line combination. (Source: AMH; RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for GBS-positive women in AU is benzylpenicillin first-line with a 4 hour interval before delivery preferred. Cefazolin is the alternative in mild non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy. Severe allergy with anaphylaxis features requires clindamycin if susceptibility is confirmed or vancomycin if resistance or unknown susceptibility. Inadequate IAP cover prompts neonatal observation per the local pathway.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin first-line for GBS IAP
Cefazolin if mild non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy
Vancomycin if anaphylaxis and clindamycin resistant
At least 4 hours pre-delivery for adequate cover
explanation.pearls: A confirmed past history of anaphylaxis to any beta-lactam is treated as severe penicillin allergy for GBS IAP planning even if the reaction predates allergy clinic testing.

options.rationale: Severe penicillin anaphylaxis with clindamycin resistance leaves vancomycin as the recommended IAP option in AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Guidelines)
Oral macrolides are not appropriate for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis due to inadequate fetal levels and poor evidence base. (Source: RANZCOG)
IM benzathine penicillin is contraindicated in confirmed penicillin anaphylaxis and is not the standard intrapartum regimen. (Source: RANZCOG)
Documented clindamycin resistance on swab means it cannot be relied upon for adequate fetal cover during labour. (Source: RANZCOG)
A clear history of anaphylaxis to a beta-lactam contraindicates cefazolin even though cross-reactivity is low overall. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes between 24 and 34 weeks is managed expectantly to maximise fetal lung maturity if there is no evidence of infection, abruption, or non-reassuring fetal status. Erythromycin for 10 days reduces neonatal infection risk; amoxicillin clavulanate is avoided due to NEC risk. A single course of antenatal corticosteroids accelerates lung maturity. Magnesium neuroprotection is added if delivery is anticipated below 30 weeks gestation.
key_points: Expectant management to 34 weeks if stable
Erythromycin 10 days, avoid clavulanate
Single course antenatal corticosteroids 24 to 34+6
Magnesium neuroprotection if delivery imminent below 30 weeks
explanation.pearls: AFI under 5 cm in PPROM is associated with shorter latency to delivery and higher risk of chorioamnionitis; document daily fetal heart rate, maternal observations, and weekly inflammatory markers to detect occult infection.

options.rationale: Routine immediate delivery at 33 weeks is not supported by current AU practice when both mother and fetus are stable; expectant management to 34 weeks reduces neonatal respiratory morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG)
Amoxicillin clavulanate is avoided in PPROM due to a signal of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis from clavulanate. (Source: RANZCOG)

AU practice for PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks is expectant management with erythromycin antibiotic prophylaxis and a single corticosteroid course aiming for delivery at 34 weeks if stable. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)
Magnesium neuroprotection is added when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours below 30 weeks; antibiotics and steroids remain core elements of PPROM care. (Source: RANZCOG)
Outpatient management of PPROM is not standard in AU due to risk of chorioamnionitis and cord prolapse; admission is recommended. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Under the AU NCSP, the routine cervical screening test is performed every 5 years from age 25 to 74. Detection of oncogenic HPV other than 16/18 with reflex cytology of low-grade or negative triggers a repeat in 12 months; oncogenic HPV 16/18 triggers colposcopy regardless of cytology. High-grade cytology triggers colposcopy. Routine screening from age 25 is performed via self-collection or clinician-collected swab.
key_points: Oncogenic HPV not 16/18 plus LSIL or negative LBC: repeat in 12 months
Oncogenic HPV 16/18: refer to colposcopy
High-grade cytology: refer to colposcopy regardless of HPV type
Self-collection is equivalent to clinician collection from age 25
explanation.pearls: Self-collected samples are now accepted across the AU NCSP and have equivalent sensitivity for HPV detection; offer this option to women who decline a speculum examination.

options.rationale: An oncogenic HPV result on routine screen always requires earlier than 5 year follow-up under the AU NCSP. (Source: NCSP)
Oncogenic HPV not 16/18 with reflex LBC of LSIL or lower is managed by a repeat screen at 12 months under the AU NCSP. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)
Colposcopy is reserved for oncogenic HPV 16/18 detection or high-grade cytology, not for LSIL with non 16/18 HPV at first detection. (Source: NCSP)
LLETZ is performed after biopsy-confirmed high-grade dysplasia and is not indicated for LSIL with non 16/18 HPV. (Source: NCSP)
Mirena does not alter the NCSP follow-up interval; the standard 12 month repeat applies. (Source: NCSP)

explanation.summary: Mirena is AU first-line for heavy menstrual bleeding once structural pathology is excluded and provides effective contraception. Quick-start insertion at any cycle day is acceptable provided pregnancy can be excluded; insertion within the first 7 days of menses provides immediate contraceptive cover, otherwise barrier protection for 7 days. Endometrial sampling is reserved for persistent abnormal bleeding patterns or failed medical management.
key_points: Mirena first-line for heavy menstrual bleeding
Quick-start any cycle day with pregnancy exclusion
Add condom for 7 days if inserted after day 7
Biopsy not required before insertion for typical heavy menses
explanation.pearls: Up to 65 percent of women experience amenorrhoea by 12 months with Mirena, which often resolves the heavy menstrual bleeding without further intervention even when fibroids are present.

options.rationale: Heavy menstrual bleeding is itself an indication to insert sooner rather than later to control ongoing blood loss while iron therapy continues. (Source: RANZCOG)
Mirena is recommended as first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding in AU; tranexamic acid is an alternative if hormonal options are declined. (Source: RANZCOG)

AU Mirena guidance supports quick-start insertion at any time in the cycle once pregnancy is excluded with immediate contraceptive efficacy if inserted within the first 7 days of menses. (Source: FSRH; RANZCOG)
Endometrial sampling is indicated for postmenopausal bleeding, persistent intermenstrual bleeding, or failed initial therapy not for first-line LARC insertion in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG)
Quick-start at any cycle day is acceptable once pregnancy is reasonably excluded; restricting to menses delays effective contraception. (Source: ASHA)

explanation.summary: Trial of labour after a single low-transverse caesarean has a 60-80 percent success rate in AU populations and an absolute uterine rupture risk of around 0.5 percent. Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is recommended throughout established labour as fetal heart rate abnormality is the earliest sign of scar rupture. Induction with prostaglandins increases rupture risk; mechanical methods and cautious oxytocin are preferred. Elective repeat caesarean has lower rupture risk but higher placenta accreta spectrum risk in subsequent pregnancies.
key_points: VBAC success 60-80 percent after single low-transverse LSCS
Absolute uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5 percent
Continuous EFM in established VBAC labour
Prostaglandin induction increases rupture risk
explanation.pearls: Inter-pregnancy interval below 12 months is associated with up to a 3-fold higher rupture risk during VBAC; this should be incorporated into individualised counselling.

options.rationale: Prostaglandin induction is associated with a 2 to 3 fold higher rupture risk and is generally avoided in favour of mechanical or oxytocin-only methods. (Source: RANZCOG)

RANZCOG quotes a 60-80 percent VBAC success rate after one prior LSCS in women without contraindications; 70-75 percent is the central estimate for AU populations. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Caesarean)
Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is recommended during established labour after caesarean to detect early signs of uterine rupture. (Source: RANZCOG)
The absolute risk of uterine rupture during VBAC after a single low-transverse LSCS is approximately 0.5 percent, not 5 percent. (Source: RANZCOG)
Maternal mortality is comparable between successful VBAC and elective repeat caesarean and lowest with successful VBAC overall. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Refractory primary PPH after failure of oxytocin and ergometrine requires escalation to a prostaglandin uterotonic with carboprost the AU first choice. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given early ideally within 3 hours of birth with a second dose at 30 minutes if bleeding continues. Activation of massive transfusion protocol with goal-directed correction of fibrinogen and platelets accompanies pharmacological measures. Definitive surgical control with intrauterine balloon, B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, or hysterectomy follows if bleeding persists.
key_points: Carboprost 250 micrograms IM every 15 minutes up to 8 doses
Total ergometrine maximum 1 mg in 24 hours
Tranexamic acid first dose within 3 hours of birth
Fibrinogen under 2 g/L predicts ongoing PPH severity
explanation.pearls: Carboprost causes bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma; in asthmatic women with refractory PPH, intrauterine misoprostol 800 micrograms is the next prostaglandin option.

options.rationale: Maximum ergometrine total is 1 mg; further doses risk severe hypertension and coronary spasm. (Source: AMH; RANZCOG)
Recombinant factor VIIa is reserved for life-threatening haemorrhage refractory to all conventional measures including surgical intervention. (Source: RANZCOG)
A second 1 g dose of tranexamic acid is given at 30 minutes if bleeding continues but does not replace the next uterotonic step. (Source: RANZCOG)
Misoprostol is a lower-evidence option in AU practice and reserved for settings where carboprost is unavailable. (Source: RANZCOG)
Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2alpha) is the appropriate next uterotonic step after oxytocin and ergometrine fail; up to 8 doses at 15 minute intervals are permitted. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

explanation.summary: Gestational hypertension is defined as new-onset BP at or above 140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. AU SOMANZ guidance recommends induction of labour at 37 weeks because expectant management beyond term increases progression to pre-eclampsia and severe maternal events. Antihypertensive therapy is targeted at BP under 135/85; labetalol, methyldopa, and nifedipine are first-line options in pregnancy. Antenatal surveillance with weekly bloods and urine until delivery is standard.
key_points: Gestational hypertension confirmed at term: induction at 37 weeks
First-line antihypertensives: labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine
BP target under 135/85 in pregnancy
Vaginal birth preferred unless other obstetric indication
explanation.pearls: Up to 40 percent of women with gestational hypertension at term will develop pre-eclampsia within 5 weeks if expectantly managed beyond 37 weeks, justifying timed induction at this gestation.

options.rationale: Expectant management beyond 37 weeks in confirmed gestational hypertension increases maternal complications without clear neonatal benefit. (Source: SOMANZ)
Inpatient observation is reserved for severe BP or features of pre-eclampsia; delivery should not be delayed for proteinuria surveillance at term. (Source: SOMANZ)
Vaginal birth via induction is preferred unless there is a separate obstetric indication for caesarean section. (Source: SOMANZ)
Delaying delivery to 41 weeks in confirmed gestational hypertension is not consistent with AU evidence-based practice. (Source: SOMANZ)

AU practice recommends induction of labour at 37 weeks once gestational hypertension is confirmed at term as it reduces maternal morbidity without significant neonatal harm. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Monochorionic diamniotic twins share a single placenta and are at risk of twin to twin transfusion syndrome, selective fetal growth restriction, and twin anaemia polycythaemia sequence. Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for biometry, deepest vertical pocket, and umbilical artery Doppler enables early detection. Delivery is planned at 36 to 36+6 weeks for uncomplicated MCDA twins to balance prematurity risk against late stillbirth risk.
key_points: MCDA fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks
DCDA four weekly ultrasound from 20 weeks
Delivery 36 to 36+6 for uncomplicated MCDA
Delivery 37 to 37+6 for uncomplicated DCDA
explanation.pearls: Discordance of amniotic fluid deepest vertical pocket over 8 cm in one sac with under 2 cm in the other before 26 weeks defines twin to twin transfusion syndrome and triggers urgent fetal medicine referral.

options.rationale: Four weekly surveillance from 20 weeks is the dichorionic schedule and is inadequate for monochorionic twins. (Source: RANZCOG)
Weekly ultrasound is not the routine schedule unless TTTS or sFGR is identified; fortnightly from 16 weeks is standard. (Source: RANZCOG)
Eight weekly imaging is inadequate to detect transfusion syndrome and 39 week delivery is past the recommended 36 to 36+6 timing for MCDA twins. (Source: RANZCOG)
AU and international guidance recommends fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to detect twin to twin transfusion and selective growth restriction in MCDA twins. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
Monochorionic pregnancies require ultrasound not CTG for transfusion surveillance which cannot be detected by trace monitoring. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but life-threatening third trimester disorder of fatty acid oxidation in the fetus with maternal microvesicular steatosis. Synthetic liver failure produces hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, coagulopathy out of proportion to thrombocytopenia, and lactic acidosis. The Swansea criteria require 6 or more clinical or biochemical features to make the diagnosis. Definitive management is urgent delivery and supportive care including glucose replacement, blood products for coagulopathy, and intensive care monitoring; recovery is usually slow but complete with timely delivery.
key_points: AFLP: hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, coagulopathy out of proportion to platelets
HELLP: low platelets, raised LDH, microangiopathic haemolysis predominate
Swansea criteria: at least 6 of 14 features for AFLP diagnosis
Urgent delivery is the definitive treatment for AFLP
explanation.pearls: AFLP is associated with fetal long chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency; offer postnatal genetic screening of mother and infant to inform future pregnancies and neonatal feeding.

options.rationale: Transaminases over 300 occur in both conditions; the discriminator is the pattern of synthetic failure and metabolic disturbance not the absolute liver enzyme level. (Source: RANZCOG)
Severe hypertension with proteinuria favours pre-eclampsia or HELLP; AFLP is typically associated with mild or absent hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG)
Hepatic synthetic failure with hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, INR rise disproportionate to platelet drop, and lactic acidosis distinguishes AFLP from HELLP. (Source: RANZCOG; Swansea Criteria)
Right upper quadrant pain occurs in both conditions and is not discriminating. (Source: RANZCOG)
Thrombocytopenia is the defining feature of HELLP not AFLP; in AFLP the platelet count is often relatively preserved early. (Source: RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: Induction of labour between 41+0 and 41+3 weeks reduces perinatal mortality, meconium aspiration, and the need for emergency caesarean compared with expectant management. The method is chosen on Bishop score: amniotomy plus oxytocin for favourable cervix and prostaglandin or balloon for unfavourable cervix. Postdates alone is not an indication for caesarean. Counselling addresses the small absolute mortality reduction and the practical implications of a planned admission.
key_points: 41+0 to 41+3 weeks is the routine induction window
Bishop score guides method choice
Favourable cervix: amniotomy plus oxytocin
Unfavourable cervix: PG or balloon then amniotomy
explanation.pearls: Routine induction at 41 weeks reduces perinatal mortality from about 3 to 0.4 per 1000 with no increase in caesarean rates, which is the basis for the RANZCOG default 41+0 to 41+3 window.

options.rationale: Stillbirth and meconium aspiration risk rise after 41 weeks and become significant beyond 42 weeks; expectant management to 43 weeks is not recommended. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)

Induction at 41+0 to 41+3 weeks reduces perinatal mortality and meconium aspiration with no increase in caesarean rate, and amniotomy plus oxytocin suits a favourable cervix. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)
Postdates alone is not an indication for caesarean when the cervix is favourable and the fetus is well. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)
Mechanical ripening is reserved for unfavourable cervix; with Bishop score 8 the cervix is already favourable. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)
A stretch and sweep alone delays definitive induction; perinatal risk continues to rise during that interval. (Source: RANZCOG: Induction of labour)

explanation.summary: Painful latch and cracked nipples in early breastfeeding most often reflect positioning and attachment problems rather than infection or tongue tie. First-line management is structured lactation consultant assessment with observed feed and correction of attachment. Antibiotics are reserved for confirmed infection. Frenotomy is considered only after lactation review with failure of optimised positioning. Weight loss up to 7 to 10 percent in the first week is within normal limits.
key_points: Painful latch usually due to attachment, not infection
Lactation consultant review with feed observation is first-line
Antibiotics only if signs of infection
Frenotomy only after lactation optimisation
explanation.pearls: Audible clicking during feeds typically indicates poor seal from shallow attachment; correcting the latch frequently resolves both nipple pain and click without any device or surgical intervention.

options.rationale: There is no fever, erythema, induration, or purulent discharge; antibiotics are not first-line for painful latch alone. (Source: ABA; Therapeutic Guidelines)
Frenotomy is considered only after thorough lactation assessment with failure of optimised positioning, not as the first step. (Source: ABA: Breastfeeding)
Painful latch with shallow attachment is most often a positioning and attachment problem that benefits from structured lactation consultant review. (Source: ABA; RANZCOG)
Cessation is premature; mother and baby benefit from troubleshooting before stopping breastfeeding. (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines)
Nipple shields are a short-term adjunct, not a substitute for fixing positioning; long-term use can reduce milk transfer. (Source: ABA)

explanation.summary: External cephalic version at 37 weeks is recommended for uncomplicated singleton breech because it reduces the rate of caesarean birth. Contraindications include placenta praevia, antepartum haemorrhage, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy, uterine scar where ECV is locally contraindicated, fetal compromise, and oligohydramnios. The procedure is performed in a unit with CTG monitoring, theatre access, and tocolysis with terbutaline. Anti-D is given to Rhesus negative women.
key_points: Offer ECV from 37 weeks for uncomplicated breech
Tocolysis with terbutaline improves success
Done with CTG monitoring and theatre access
Anti-D given if Rhesus negative
explanation.pearls: Successful ECV rates are around 50 percent overall but higher in multiparous women with relaxed abdomen, posterior placenta, and ample liquor; success approaches 70 percent in those subgroups.

options.rationale: ECV should be offered to all eligible women with breech at term as it reduces caesarean rates compared with no ECV. (Source: RANZCOG: ECV)
ECV at 37 weeks with terbutaline tocolysis and CTG monitoring is the recommended approach for uncomplicated term breech. (Source: RANZCOG: ECV)
Vaginal breech birth is an option but should not be offered instead of ECV; the choice is sequential. (Source: RANZCOG: ECV)
Complementary techniques have low-quality evidence and delay definitive ECV; they are not the standard first option. (Source: RANZCOG: ECV)
Waiting until 39 weeks misses the optimal window for ECV and increases the chance of breech caesarean by default. (Source: RANZCOG: ECV)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia carries a high perinatal mortality if undiagnosed because membrane rupture tears unprotected fetal vessels crossing the cervix. The Apt or alkali denaturation test can confirm fetal origin of blood in stable cases. When CTG shows a sinusoidal pattern with fresh bleeding the diagnosis is fetal exsanguination and category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes is mandatory. Antenatal diagnosis with planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks before spontaneous labour is the prevention strategy.
key_points: Sinusoidal CTG plus PV bleeding equals fetal exsanguination
Category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes
Steroids and magnesium are not relevant in active fetal compromise
Antenatal diagnosis enables planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks
explanation.pearls: Fetal blood volume at term is only about 80 mL/kg so even 100 mL of fresh PV bleeding from vasa praevia can exsanguinate a term infant in minutes; the sinusoidal CTG is a late and ominous sign.

options.rationale: Sinusoidal CTG with fresh PV bleeding in known vasa praevia indicates fetal exsanguination and mandates immediate category 1 caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)
The bleeding is fetal not maternal; maternal transfusion does not address fetal exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)
Magnesium delays delivery; in a category 1 fetal emergency the priority is delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Magnesium for neuroprotection)
Steroid course takes 24 to 48 hours and cannot be awaited when fetal exsanguination is underway. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)
Vaginal birth in confirmed vasa praevia with bleeding has a high fetal mortality and is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury that extends into rectal mucosa is a fourth degree tear and must be repaired in theatre with adequate lighting, regional or general anaesthesia, appropriate instruments, and an experienced operator. The internal anal sphincter is repaired end to end and the external sphincter by end to end or overlap technique. Postoperative care includes laxatives, single dose intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis, and pelvic floor physiotherapy referral.
key_points: Theatre repair for third and fourth degree tears
Repair at earliest safe opportunity
IAS end to end; EAS end to end or overlap
Postop laxatives, antibiotics, and physiotherapy
explanation.pearls: Single dose intravenous cephalosporin and metronidazole at OASIS repair reduces wound infection from about 24 to 8 percent at six weeks, which is why prophylaxis is part of the RANZCOG bundle.

options.rationale: Third or fourth degree tears require repair in theatre with adequate lighting, anaesthesia, and surgical instruments to optimise outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS)
Birth suite repair of fourth degree tears is associated with poorer visualisation and higher long-term continence morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS)
Delayed repair increases infection and dehiscence risk; repair should be undertaken at the earliest safe opportunity. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS)
Packing is not the management of a fresh fourth degree tear; obstetric repair in theatre is the standard. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS)
Sphincter repair must be done at the same time as mucosal repair to maximise functional recovery. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS)

explanation.summary: The 2023 International PCOS Evidence-Based Guideline recommends letrozole as first-line ovulation induction in anovulatory PCOS, with higher live birth rates than clomifene in most subgroups and particularly in women with elevated BMI. Metformin is an adjunct in women with insulin resistance or impaired glucose tolerance. Gonadotrophins, IVF, and ovarian drilling are reserved for first-line failure. Pre-conception counselling includes weight optimisation, folate, and rubella status.
key_points: Letrozole first-line for anovulatory PCOS
Higher live birth rate than clomifene in obesity
Metformin is adjunctive, not monotherapy
Gonadotrophins and drilling are second-line
explanation.pearls: Letrozole achieves live birth rates around 27 percent versus 19 percent for clomifene in obese anovulatory PCOS within six cycles, which underpins the 2023 PCOS guideline switch.

options.rationale: Letrozole is first-line ovulation induction in PCOS with higher live birth rates than clomifene, especially in women with obesity. (Source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline; RANZCOG)
Metformin is an adjunct that may improve ovulation but is inferior to letrozole for live birth in anovulatory PCOS. (Source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline)
Clomifene is second-line because letrozole achieves higher live birth rates in anovulatory PCOS, particularly with obesity. (Source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline)
Gonadotrophins are reserved for letrozole and clomifene failure due to higher cost, monitoring burden, and OHSS risk. (Source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline)
Surgical drilling is reserved for letrozole or clomifene failure due to surgical and adhesion risks. (Source: 2023 International PCOS Guideline)

explanation.summary: Recurrent urinary tract infection in postmenopausal women is frequently driven by genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which alters vaginal flora and local mucosal defences. Vaginal oestrogen pessary or cream is first-line and reduces recurrence with minimal systemic absorption. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is reserved for vaginal oestrogen failure due to resistance concerns. Cranberry has inconsistent evidence. Cystoscopy is indicated for haematuria or persistent symptoms despite treatment.
key_points: Vaginal oestrogen is first-line for recurrent UTI in postmenopausal women
Reduces recurrence with minimal systemic absorption
Antibiotic prophylaxis reserved for vaginal oestrogen failure
Cranberry has inconsistent evidence
explanation.pearls: Vaginal oestriol pessary reduces postmenopausal recurrent UTI rates by approximately 50 percent within six months and is safe in most women with prior breast cancer if symptoms are severe after specialist discussion.

options.rationale: Antibiotic prophylaxis does not address atrophy and increases resistance; non-antibiotic options come first. (Source: RACGP: Recurrent UTI)
Cranberry has inconsistent evidence and does not treat the underlying genitourinary atrophy contributing to recurrence. (Source: Cochrane; RACGP)
Systemic HRT is not indicated for isolated genitourinary symptoms and carries broader hormonal risks. (Source: AMS; RANZCOG)
Vaginal oestrogen treats atrophy and reduces recurrent UTI rates in postmenopausal women with safety profile preferable to antibiotics. (Source: AMS; RANZCOG)
Cystoscopy has already been performed and is normal; further endoscopic workup is not indicated. (Source: RACGP: Recurrent UTI)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but life-threatening obstetric emergency presenting in late labour or shortly after birth with sudden hypoxia, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Management is supportive: airway and breathing support, massive transfusion protocol activation, expedited delivery, and ICU level care. There is no specific antidote. Survival has improved markedly with early MTP activation and aggressive resuscitation. Differential diagnosis includes anaphylaxis, pulmonary embolism, and septic shock, but the coagulopathy with peripartum onset is characteristic.
key_points: AFE: sudden hypoxia, hypotension, and DIC peripartum
Activate MTP early
Expedite delivery if not yet born
ICU level supportive care; no specific antidote
explanation.pearls: Amniotic fluid embolism mortality has fallen from over 80 percent historically to around 20 to 30 percent with rapid MTP activation; the diagnostic triad of hypoxia, hypotension, and consumption coagulopathy in labour is the operational definition.

options.rationale: There is no rash, wheeze, or trigger; anaphylaxis treatment alone misses the haematological collapse of AFE. (Source: ASCIA; RANZCOG)
AFE causes cardiogenic shock and DIC; massive transfusion plus expedited delivery and supportive care is the standard approach. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse)
Anticoagulation is contraindicated in a patient already coagulopathic with active haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse)
Standard third stage management does not address the acute coagulopathic shock and delays definitive resuscitation. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse)
Single drug therapy alone misses the volume, blood product, and surgical needs of AFE; it is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse)

explanation.summary: Puerperal mastitis is initially managed with effective breast emptying, analgesia, and oral flucloxacillin or cefalexin (or clindamycin if penicillin allergic). Failure to improve within 24 to 48 hours, a persistent tender lump, or fluctuance suggests abscess and warrants ultrasound. Modern management uses ultrasound-guided needle aspiration and may need repeat aspiration over several days, avoiding surgical incision in most cases. Breastfeeding from the affected breast continues whenever the baby will accept it; if not, hand expression or pumping prevents milk stasis.
key_points: First-line antibiotic is flucloxacillin or cefalexin
Failure to improve at 24 to 48 hours raises suspicion of abscess
Ultrasound confirms collection; needle aspiration is first line
Breastfeeding should continue from the affected breast
Incision and drainage is for failed aspiration or necrosis
explanation.pearls: MRSA cover (clindamycin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is added when there is no improvement on first-line therapy or when local MRSA prevalence is high, especially in the Northern Territory.

options.rationale: Antibiotic switching alone does not drain an abscess and delays definitive management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Anaerobic cover is not indicated in standard puerperal mastitis or abscess and adds no benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Continued emptying of the breast is essential to recovery; suppression of lactation worsens the situation and is not indicated. (Source: ABM Clinical Protocol 36: Mastitis)

A fluctuant mass that has not improved on 24 hours of appropriate antibiotic requires ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of any confirmed collection, with breastfeeding continued. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Breastfeeding)

Incision and drainage is reserved for collections that fail repeated needle aspiration or large skin necrosis; needle aspiration is the contemporary first step. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Breastfeeding)

explanation.summary: Australia uses a hybrid screening approach for early-onset group B streptococcal disease prevention. Universal antenatal swabbing at 35 to 37 weeks is widely adopted; risk-based prophylaxis is the alternative pathway. Indications for intrapartum prophylaxis include positive antenatal swab, GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy, previous infant with invasive GBS disease, or any of (preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes over 18 hours, intrapartum fever 38 degrees or higher) when GBS status is unknown. Benzylpenicillin is first line, cefazolin if non-severe penicillin allergy, clindamycin (after susceptibility) for severe allergy, and vancomycin for resistant or severely allergic patients.
key_points: Australian screening occurs at 35 to 37 weeks gestation
Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g 4-hourly is first line
Cefazolin replaces it for non-severe penicillin allergy
Clindamycin (with susceptibility) replaces it for severe allergy
Adequate prophylaxis requires at least 4 hours before delivery
explanation.pearls: Vancomycin is the back-up for severe penicillin allergy when clindamycin susceptibility is not confirmed or the isolate is resistant.

options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend benzylpenicillin 3 g IV loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth for GBS-positive women in labour without penicillin allergy. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)
Cefazolin is reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy; benzylpenicillin remains first line when no allergy exists. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)
Clindamycin is for severe penicillin allergy with confirmed clindamycin susceptibility of the isolate. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)
Oral antibiotics do not reach adequate intrapartum concentrations and are not used for GBS intrapartum prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)
Antenatal screening at 35 to 37 weeks is sufficient; repeat swabbing in labour delays effective prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage describes vaginal bleeding before 20 weeks with a closed cervix and a viable intrauterine pregnancy. The 2019 PRISM trial demonstrated a benefit of vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily in women with bleeding and at least one previous miscarriage, continued until 16 weeks of gestation. The number needed to treat is greatest in women with three or more previous miscarriages. Women without previous miscarriage do not benefit. Anti-D 250 IU IM is given to Rh-negative women with significant first-trimester bleeding after 12 weeks; before 12 weeks the threshold depends on local policy.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage = bleeding plus closed cervix plus viable pregnancy
Vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg BD until 16 weeks helps subgroup with prior miscarriage
Greatest NNT benefit in women with 3 or more previous miscarriages
No benefit demonstrated in women with no previous miscarriage
Consider anti-D in Rh-negative women per local thresholds
explanation.pearls: Vaginal route is preferred because of higher endometrial bioavailability of micronised progesterone compared with oral administration, where first-pass metabolism is substantial.

options.rationale: Intramuscular medroxyprogesterone is not used in threatened miscarriage and carries unnecessary risk. (Source: PRISM trial; RCOG green-top 25)
Oral progestogens have not been shown to improve outcomes in this setting and are not recommended. (Source: PRISM trial; RCOG green-top 25)

Vaginal progesterone modestly improves live birth rates in women with vaginal bleeding plus a history of previous miscarriage, so reassurance alone misses an evidence-based intervention. (Source: PRISM trial; RCOG green-top 25)

Vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily until 16 weeks improves live birth rates in women with vaginal bleeding and one or more previous miscarriages, based on the PRISM trial and adopted in RANZCOG and RCOG guidance. (Source: PRISM trial; RCOG green-top 25)
Admission is unnecessary for stable threatened miscarriage with a viable scan and beta hCG is not the relevant follow-up once viability is confirmed. (Source: PRISM trial; RCOG green-top 25)

explanation.summary: Vaginal birth after caesarean is a reasonable option for most women after one previous low transverse caesarean for non-recurring indication. Success rates are approximately 70 to 75 percent in pooled cohorts. Uterine rupture risk is approximately 0.5 percent overall in spontaneous labour, rising with induction (especially with prostaglandins), augmentation with oxytocin, short inter-delivery interval (under 18 months), and macrosomia. Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is recommended because fetal heart rate decelerations are the earliest sign of dehiscence. Decisions should be supported with written information and documented preference.
key_points: VBAC success around 70 to 75 percent after non-recurring indication
Uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5 percent in spontaneous labour
Prostaglandin induction substantially increases rupture risk
Continuous CTG in labour after caesarean is recommended
Epidural does not contraindicate VBAC and does not mask rupture
explanation.pearls: Mechanical induction using a Foley catheter has a more favourable safety profile in women planning VBAC than prostaglandins when induction is indicated.

options.rationale: A single previous LSCS for non-recurring indication is not a contraindication; VBAC is a reasonable choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

Australian audit and international meta-analyses report VBAC success rates around 70 to 75 percent after non-recurring indication, with uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5 percent. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)
Prostaglandin induction substantially increases rupture risk and is generally avoided in scarred uteri. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)
Continuous CTG monitoring is recommended in labour after caesarean for early detection of fetal heart rate abnormalities heralding scar dehiscence. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)
Epidural analgesia is not contraindicated; pain breakthrough or fetal heart abnormalities remain reliable rupture signals. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) risk rises sharply with each prior caesarean delivery especially in the presence of placenta praevia (approximately 40 percent risk after three prior caesareans with anterior praevia). Ultrasound features include loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, abnormal uteroplacental interface, and bridging vessels into bladder. MRI is reserved for posterior placentas or assessment of parametrial extension. Definitive management is planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 weeks at a tertiary centre after corticosteroid course, with multidisciplinary team, cell salvage, blood bank, and interventional radiology on standby. Conservative uterus-preserving approaches are reserved for selected cases at expert centres.
key_points: Three prior caesareans plus anterior praevia carry approximately 40 percent PAS risk
Ultrasound features: lost clear zone, lacunae, bridging vessels
Plan caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 weeks after corticosteroids
Multidisciplinary tertiary centre with cell salvage and IR
Vaginal birth and elective embolisation are not standard
explanation.pearls: If antenatal imaging is equivocal but suspicion is high, formal MRI with PAS protocol can refine surgical planning especially when posterior placenta limits ultrasound assessment.

options.rationale: Placenta praevia with accreta spectrum is an absolute contraindication to vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)
Planned caesarean hysterectomy is scheduled before spontaneous labour, not after, to avoid catastrophic bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

Suspected placenta accreta spectrum should be managed at a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team and planned caesarean hysterectomy typically at 34 to 36 weeks after corticosteroids, with cell salvage and interventional radiology available. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)
Prophylactic embolisation before delivery is not standard; interventional radiology is used intra or post-operatively in selected cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

Delivery at a non-tertiary site lacking interventional radiology, blood bank, and gynaecological oncology back-up substantially increases maternal mortality. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) is defined by lesions extending more than 5 mm under the peritoneum. The most predictive symptoms are cyclical bowel or bladder pain. The International Deep Endometriosis Analysis (IDEA) group has standardised transvaginal ultrasound assessment for the pouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, vagina, rectum and bladder. Specialist TVUS in experienced hands is the preferred first imaging and can identify rectovaginal nodules. Pelvic MRI is reserved for ultrasound non-diagnostic or surgical planning. Treatment combines hormonal suppression with multidisciplinary surgical planning (gynaecology and colorectal) in advanced disease.
key_points: Cyclical dyschezia and rectal bleeding suggest deep bowel endometriosis
Standard transabdominal ultrasound often misses DIE
Specialised TVUS with IDEA protocol is first-line imaging
MRI is reserved for surgical planning when TVUS inconclusive
Combine hormonal therapy with multidisciplinary surgical planning
explanation.pearls: The sliding sign test on transvaginal ultrasound assesses pouch of Douglas obliteration; absent sliding has high specificity for rectovaginal endometriosis.

options.rationale: Cyclical rectal bleeding strictly with menses points to bowel endometriosis rather than malignancy; colonoscopy adds little here and is not first line. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
Empirical GnRH agonist without mapping deep disease misses surgical planning opportunities and is not first line at this stage. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
Mirena is an effective hormonal option but it does not establish the extent of deep disease in a patient with rectovaginal nodule and bowel symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
CA-125 lacks specificity and a further drug trial without imaging delays a clearer diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

Specialised transvaginal ultrasound by an experienced operator using the deep infiltrating endometriosis bowel protocol is the recommended first imaging in suspected DIE, with MRI reserved for surgical planning when ultrasound is inconclusive. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most reliably treatable cause of recurrent miscarriage. Sapporo criteria require persistent positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti-beta-2 glycoprotein-1 on at least two occasions 12 weeks apart plus clinical criteria (3 or more consecutive early losses, one or more late losses at 10 weeks or beyond, or severe placental insufficiency). Treatment of obstetric APS is low-dose aspirin commencing preconception plus prophylactic LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg daily) from positive pregnancy test until 6 weeks postpartum. Karyotype testing of products is recommended after recurrent loss; balanced translocations in one parent require genetic counselling.
key_points: Persistent antibody positivity over 12 weeks plus clinical criteria define APS
Aspirin from preconception plus LMWH from positive pregnancy test
Continue LMWH until 6 weeks postpartum
Warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy
Karyotype products and parents to exclude balanced translocations
explanation.pearls: Women with previous arterial thrombosis on a background of APS require therapeutic-dose LMWH rather than prophylactic doses during pregnancy.

options.rationale: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome with three or more consecutive early miscarriages is treated with low-dose aspirin from preconception plus prophylactic LMWH from positive pregnancy test until 6 weeks postpartum. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
Warfarin is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy; LMWH is the chosen anticoagulant. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
Steroid monotherapy does not improve outcomes in obstetric APS and is not recommended. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
IVIG is not first-line in obstetric APS and trial evidence does not support routine use. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
Hydroxychloroquine is adjunctive in some APS protocols but does not replace aspirin and LMWH as the established regimen. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding management starts with exclusion of structural and systemic causes (FBC, ferritin, TSH, pelvic ultrasound), then a hierarchy of medical treatments (levonorgestrel intrauterine system, tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, combined hormonal therapy) before surgical options. Endometrial sampling is indicated in women aged 45 or older, or younger with risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia (obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome, tamoxifen, family history of Lynch syndrome, unopposed oestrogen), or with persistent symptoms despite treatment. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy gives the highest sensitivity for focal lesions compared with blind Pipelle sampling.
key_points: Sample endometrium in women aged 45 plus with persistent bleeding
Sample younger women with hyperplasia risk factors
Hysteroscopy with biopsy outperforms blind sampling for focal lesions
Exclude pathology before ablation or hysterectomy
Treat iron deficiency in parallel
explanation.pearls: Endometrial thickness cut-offs from postmenopausal women do not apply in premenopausal heavy menstrual bleeding; cyclical changes mean any value can be normal at different cycle phases.

options.rationale: Medical options without endometrial sampling miss a potential endometrial pathology in a high-risk woman with failed first-line treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
Endometrial ablation is contraindicated until endometrial pathology has been excluded by sampling in a woman at high risk of hyperplasia. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Definitive surgery without histological clarity risks operating with unrecognised malignancy and may alter the surgical approach (subtotal vs total, oncological clearance). (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Persistent heavy menstrual bleeding despite a levonorgestrel IUS in a woman with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and aged over 45 meets thresholds for endometrial sampling to exclude hyperplasia or carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
Pelvic ultrasound was recently done with the device in situ; repeating without sampling is less informative than hysteroscopy with biopsy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Gestational hypertension is defined as new hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. Australian SOMANZ-endorsed first-line oral antihypertensives are labetalol, methyldopa and slow-release nifedipine. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and atenolol are contraindicated. Target BP is around 135/85 mmHg based on the CHIPS trial; close monitoring for progression to pre-eclampsia is essential with repeat bloods and urine PCR weekly.
key_points: SOMANZ first-line oral agents in pregnancy: labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine SR
Avoid ACEi, ARB, atenolol and thiazide-like diuretics
Target BP around 135/85 mmHg per CHIPS
Weekly bloods (FBC, LFT, UEC, urate), urine PCR and growth scans
explanation.pearls: Choose labetalol 100 mg twice daily titrating to 200 mg three times daily and aim BP around 135/85 mmHg per CHIPS rather than tighter or looser targets - delays of further escalation often track to BP exceeding 160/110 mmHg requiring acute therapy.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement: Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2020

options.rationale: Atenolol is associated with reduced fetal growth in pregnancy and is not recommended as first-line; labetalol, methyldopa or nifedipine are preferred. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)

Labetalol is a SOMANZ first-line antihypertensive in pregnancy alongside methyldopa and nifedipine; target BP is around 135/85 mmHg under the CHIPS trial-informed approach now adopted in Australian practice. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)
ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal renal injury and oligohydramnios; absolute contraindication after the first trimester. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)
Oral hydralazine has unpredictable absorption and is not a SOMANZ first-line oral agent; IV hydralazine is reserved for acute severe hypertension. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)

Thiazide-like diuretics are not first-line in pregnancy because of intravascular volume depletion in patients already at risk of placental hypoperfusion. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia (BP at least 160/110 with end-organ dysfunction such as transaminitis, thrombocytopenia, severe headache or right upper quadrant pain) is an indication for magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis. The standard SOMANZ regimen is 4 g IV loading over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/h IV infusion continued for at least 24 hours after delivery or the last seizure. Toxicity is monitored by reflexes (loss of patellar reflex at 4-7 mmol/L), respiratory rate (depression at 7-12 mmol/L) and urine output (over 30 mL/h). Calcium gluconate 1 g IV reverses toxicity.
key_points: Loading: 4 g IV over 20 minutes
Maintenance: 1 g/h IV infusion
Continue at least 24 hours postpartum or post-seizure
Calcium gluconate 1 g IV reverses toxicity
explanation.pearls: Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest clinical marker of magnesium toxicity (plasma level 4-7 mmol/L); stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g IV slowly rather than rechecking levels and waiting.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement: Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2020

options.rationale: Loading dose of 1 g is sub-therapeutic; standard SOMANZ regimen is 4 g IV over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/h IV maintenance. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)
The IM Pritchard regimen is an alternative in low-resource settings without IV pump capacity; in an Australian birth suite, the IV regimen is standard. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)
Loading at 8 g exceeds safety threshold and risks respiratory and cardiac depression; standard load is 4 g IV over 20 minutes. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)
A single bolus does not maintain therapeutic plasma levels for seizure prophylaxis; sustained infusion is required for at least 24 hours postpartum. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)

Standard Australian SOMANZ regimen is 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/h IV infusion continued for at least 24 hours postpartum or post-seizure, with regular reflex, respiratory and urine output monitoring to detect early toxicity. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2014)

explanation.summary: Clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed by maternal fever plus features including maternal tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling amniotic fluid or leucocytosis. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend ampicillin 2 g IV every 6 hours plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily as empiric therapy, with metronidazole 500 mg IV every 12 hours added if caesarean delivery is required to cover anaerobes. Delivery is part of treatment; antibiotics should not delay delivery decisions. Postpartum antibiotic course continues until clinical improvement and afebrile for 24 hours.
key_points: Empiric: ampicillin + gentamicin IV; add metronidazole at caesarean
Do not wait for cultures
Delivery is part of treatment
Continue antibiotics until afebrile for 24 hours postpartum
explanation.pearls: When chorioamnionitis is suspected, give ampicillin 2 g IV plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV within the first hour and book the caesarean theatre if clinical deterioration follows; adding metronidazole at the start of caesarean prevents post-caesarean endometritis.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement: Maternal Group B Streptococcus 2019

options.rationale: Ampicillin alone covers GBS but lacks coverage for the Gram-negative and anaerobic flora typical of chorioamnionitis; combination therapy is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)
Cefazolin alone does not adequately cover anaerobes and Enterococcus implicated in chorioamnionitis; combination regimen is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend ampicillin plus gentamicin for chorioamnionitis with metronidazole added if caesarean is required for anaerobic coverage of operative wound and endometritis risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

Vancomycin and ceftriaxone are not the recommended Australian empiric combination for chorioamnionitis and provide unnecessary MRSA coverage with reduced enterococcal cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

Withholding empiric antibiotics in clinical chorioamnionitis with maternal sepsis features and fetal tachycardia increases neonatal sepsis and maternal endometritis risk; therapy must begin immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic 2019)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse with a pulsating cord and sustained fetal deceleration is a category 1 obstetric emergency. The first responder elevates the presenting part with the examining hand and positions the woman in knee-chest or exaggerated Sims to relieve compression. Bladder filling via a Foley catheter with 500-700 mL of saline can substitute for manual elevation if transfer is prolonged. Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 mcg SC) reduces contractions. Definitive management is category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes unless vaginal delivery is imminent and faster.
key_points: Elevate presenting part off cord with examining hand
Knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position
Bladder filling 500-700 mL if transfer delayed
Category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes
explanation.pearls: Fill the bladder with 500-700 mL of saline through a Foley catheter when transfer to theatre will be more than 10 minutes - this maintains presenting-part elevation without an exhausted clinician's hand and buys time.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 50 Umbilical Cord Prolapse 2014

options.rationale: Manual cord reduction is not recommended outside of selected expert-led trials and is associated with cord vasospasm and fetal demise; the immediate priority is to relieve compression and expedite delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement 2020)

Left lateral alone is insufficient for established cord prolapse with a sustained deceleration; immediate elevation of the presenting part and theatre transfer are required. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement 2020)

Oxytocin will worsen cord compression by increasing uterine contractions; tocolysis with terbutaline is often added while the patient is transferred to theatre. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement 2020)

RANZCOG recommends immediate elevation of the presenting part to relieve cord compression, knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position, bladder filling 500-700 mL if transfer is prolonged, and category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes for non-imminent vaginal delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement 2020)

Fetal blood sampling is contraindicated when there is acute cord compression and an immediate delivery indication; the diagnosis is clinical and management is immediate. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement 2020)

explanation.summary: Retained placenta is defined as failure of placental delivery within 30 minutes of birth despite active management of the third stage. With ongoing bleeding, transfer to theatre for manual removal under regional or general anaesthesia is the standard Australian practice with single-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis. Bladder emptying, IV access, group and crossmatch, and uterotonics post-removal are part of the bundle. Examination of the uterine cavity after removal excludes retained products and accreta spectrum.
key_points: Retained placenta >30 min with bleeding: transfer to theatre
Manual removal under regional or general anaesthesia
Single-dose prophylactic IV antibiotic (e.g. ampicillin + metronidazole)
Inspect uterine cavity after removal for retained tissue and accreta
explanation.pearls: If bleeding is brisk at 30 minutes with the placenta retained, transfer to theatre rather than persisting with cord traction - umbilical vein oxytocin and additional uterotonics do not address the mechanical issue of failed placental separation.

options.rationale: Placenta not delivered after 30 minutes of active management with ongoing bleeding is a retained placenta indication for transfer to theatre, manual removal under regional or general anaesthesia, and single-dose IV antibiotic prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement 2017)
Umbilical vein oxytocin has limited evidence and delays definitive management when ongoing bleeding is occurring; not the recommended Australian practice. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement 2017)
Vigorous fundal pressure risks uterine inversion and cord avulsion; manual removal under anaesthesia is the safer next step. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement 2017)
Further delay with ongoing bleeding risks evolving haemorrhage; intervention is indicated now. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement 2017)
Carboprost is for uterine atony with PPH, not for retained placenta with a contracted uterus; the indication here is mechanical separation under anaesthesia. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement 2017)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is a clinical diagnosis when the head delivers but routine traction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder. The RANZCOG-endorsed HELPERR mnemonic is: Help (call), Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts hyperflexion), Pressure (suprapubic, directed away from impacted shoulder), Enter manoeuvres (Rubin, Wood's screw), Remove posterior arm, Roll the patient onto all fours. McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves the majority of cases. Fundal pressure is contraindicated. Cleidotomy and symphysiotomy are last-resort manoeuvres.
key_points: HELPERR: Help, Episiotomy assessment, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure, Enter, Remove arm, Roll
McRoberts + suprapubic pressure resolves around 50-60%
Fundal pressure is contraindicated
Document time intervals between manoeuvres
explanation.pearls: When the head delivers and turtles, call for help and hyperflex maternal hips (McRoberts) within 30 seconds rather than escalating traction or attempting internal rotation first - downward traction force should never exceed routine because brachial plexus injury rises sharply with axial force.

options.rationale: Symphysiotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre with high maternal morbidity reserved for cases where all other measures fail; it is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Statement 2020)

Deliberate cleidotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre with significant fetal morbidity and is reserved for failure of all other steps; not the first manoeuvre. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Statement 2020)
Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction and increases uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury risk. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Statement 2020)
Internal rotation manoeuvres come after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure in the HELPERR sequence; they are step 4-5, not step 1. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Statement 2020)

RANZCOG HELPERR sequence opens with Help (call for additional team members), Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic) before internal manoeuvres; McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves around 50-60% of cases. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Statement 2020)

explanation.summary: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological cancer in Australian women. After tissue diagnosis (typically by pipelle biopsy in clinic), staging requires pelvic MRI to assess depth of myometrial invasion and cervical stromal involvement, and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to assess for metastatic disease. PET-CT is reserved for high-risk histology (serous, clear cell, carcinosarcoma) or recurrence. Definitive treatment is surgical staging (total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, with or without sentinel lymph node biopsy) followed by adjuvant therapy based on FIGO stage and risk group.
key_points: Pipelle biopsy first; MRI pelvis + CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging
MRI assesses myometrial invasion depth and cervical involvement
PET-CT for high-risk histology or recurrence
Definitive treatment is surgical staging
explanation.pearls: When endometrial pipelle confirms cancer, request pelvic MRI to assess myometrial invasion depth and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis simultaneously rather than waiting on MDM - this typically saves 7-14 days to definitive surgical planning.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022
RANZCOG College Statement: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding 2020

options.rationale: PET-CT is not first-line staging for endometrial cancer; it is reserved for selected high-risk histology or recurrence assessment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022

options.rationale: Pelvic MRI is the modality of choice for assessing depth of myometrial invasion and cervical stromal involvement, both of which inform surgical planning; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis assesses metastatic disease. (Source: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022

options.rationale: Abdominal ultrasound is inadequate for staging because it cannot assess depth of myometrial invasion, lymph nodes or distant disease. (Source: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022
