options.rationale: Histology is already established by pipelle biopsy; hysteroscopy is not required for staging once tissue diagnosis is made and may delay definitive surgical staging. (Source: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022

options.rationale: Plain CXR underdetects metastases; CT chest is preferred and combined with MRI pelvis for local staging. (Source: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia eviQ Endometrial Cancer 2022

explanation.summary: Intrapartum antibiotic chemoprophylaxis for GBS-colonised women reduces early-onset neonatal GBS disease. First-line is intravenous benzylpenicillin (3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery) given as soon as labour is established or membranes rupture, irrespective of membrane status. Cefazolin is used for low-risk penicillin allergy. Clindamycin (with confirmed susceptibility) or vancomycin is reserved for severe penicillin allergy. Adequate prophylaxis requires at least 4 hours before delivery for optimal benefit.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g every 4 hours is first-line
Cefazolin for low-risk penicillin allergy
Clindamycin with susceptibility or vancomycin for severe allergy
Optimal benefit requires at least 4 hours before delivery
explanation.pearls: When a GBS-positive woman is in labour with a non-allergic history, give benzylpenicillin 3 g IV stat then 1.8 g every 4 hours; aim for at least one dose 4 hours before delivery to maximise neonatal protection rather than withholding until membrane rupture.

options.rationale: Ampicillin is an acceptable alternative but the RANZCOG and Therapeutic Guidelines recommendation in Australia is benzylpenicillin as the first-line agent in penicillin-tolerant women. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus 2022)
Oral amoxicillin has not been shown to achieve adequate amniotic fluid concentrations for GBS prevention; intravenous administration is required. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus 2022)

Clindamycin is reserved for women with documented severe penicillin hypersensitivity and confirmed clindamycin susceptibility; it is not used routinely. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus 2022)

Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery is first-line intrapartum chemoprophylaxis in penicillin-tolerant women with GBS colonisation. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus 2022)

Intrapartum chemoprophylaxis is given as soon as labour is established regardless of membrane status to allow adequate amniotic fluid concentrations before delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus 2022)

explanation.summary: PCOS in adults is diagnosed by Rotterdam criteria, with the 2023 international evidence-based guideline retaining two-of-three features (oligo-ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology) after exclusion of mimickers such as thyroid disorders, hyperprolactinaemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome and androgen-secreting tumours. Polycystic ovarian morphology threshold is 20 or more follicles per ovary on high-frequency transducers or AMH above the laboratory threshold. Initial management addresses cycle regulation, fertility planning and cardiometabolic risk.
key_points: Rotterdam two-of-three: oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism, morphology
Exclude thyroid, prolactin, CAH, Cushing's, androgen tumours
Morphology threshold is 20+ follicles per ovary on high-frequency transducer
AMH may substitute for ultrasound morphology in adults
explanation.pearls: When cycle length consistently exceeds 35 days plus hirsutism and elevated free androgen index occur with normal mimicker bloods, diagnose PCOS without further confirmatory testing rather than requiring all three Rotterdam features.

sources.label: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023

options.rationale: Cycle history of variable cycles to 90 days establishes oligo-ovulation; progestogen challenge is not required for the diagnosis. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023

options.rationale: Rotterdam criteria require any two of the three features, not all three, after exclusion of mimics; metabolic features are not part of the diagnostic criteria. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023

options.rationale: The 2023 international guideline lowered the threshold for polycystic ovarian morphology to 20 or more follicles per ovary on high-frequency transducers, but the criterion is met by the combination of clinical, biochemical and morphological features in adults. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023

options.rationale: AMH can substitute for morphology in adults under the 2023 guideline but ultrasound morphology is still valid; the diagnosis here rests on oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism and morphology. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023

options.rationale: Rotterdam criteria require two of three: oligo-ovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology after exclusion of mimics; this patient meets all three. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS 2023

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is diagnosed by persistent vomiting plus over 5% pre-pregnancy weight loss, ketonuria and dehydration. Management requires admission for crystalloid rehydration and parenteral antiemetic. Thiamine 100 mg must precede any dextrose-containing infusion in patients with protracted vomiting to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. First-line parenteral antiemetics include metoclopramide and prochlorperazine; ondansetron is added or used early when other agents fail. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: HG diagnosis: persistent vomiting, >5% weight loss, ketonuria, dehydration
Admit for IV rehydration and parenteral antiemetics when severe
Thiamine 100 mg before dextrose to prevent Wernicke
Corticosteroids reserved for refractory cases
explanation.pearls: When a pregnant patient with hyperemesis requires intravenous fluids, give intravenous thiamine 100 mg before any dextrose-containing fluid and start metoclopramide 10 mg every 8 hours rather than escalating oral therapy.

sources.label: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023
Therapeutic Guidelines Gastrointestinal: Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy 2024

options.rationale: Severe hyperemesis with ketonuria, weight loss and orthostasis requires admission for parenteral rehydration and antiemetic escalation; thiamine before dextrose prevents Wernicke encephalopathy in protracted vomiting. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023

options.rationale: Severe hyperemesis with ketonuria and over 5% weight loss requires admission rather than further oral therapy at home; oral wafers will not be tolerated in active vomiting. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023

options.rationale: Dextrose administration before thiamine in protracted vomiting risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must precede any dextrose-containing fluid. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after failure of multiple antiemetics, and the timing within the first trimester is more cautious due to a small cleft palate signal. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023

options.rationale: Her bedside ultrasound has already confirmed a viable singleton intrauterine pregnancy; resuscitation and antiemetic escalation should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2023

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is appropriate for haemodynamically stable women with confirmed unruptured ectopic pregnancy, beta-hCG below 5000 IU/L, no fetal heart activity, an adnexal mass under 35 mm, no significant free fluid, normal renal and liver function and reliable follow-up. Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre is given with day-4 and day-7 beta-hCG measurement; a fall of 15% or more between days 4 and 7 indicates response, otherwise a second dose or surgery is required. Patients require pregnancy-prevention counselling for at least three months post-treatment due to methotrexate teratogenicity.
key_points: Eligibility: stable, bHCG <5000, no FH, mass <35 mm, no significant free fluid, normal renal and liver function
Single dose 50 mg per square metre intramuscularly
Day 4 to day 7 fall of >=15% indicates response
Pregnancy prevention for at least 3 months post-treatment
explanation.pearls: Offer methotrexate for unruptured ectopic with beta-hCG <5000 IU/L, no fetal heart and mass <35 mm; check day-4 and day-7 beta-hCG and give a second dose if the day 4 to day 7 fall is under 15%.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: Expectant management requires plateauing or falling beta-hCG, no symptoms and an adnexal mass under 30 mm; her beta-hCG is rising and she has symptoms, so expectant management is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: She meets eligibility for single-dose methotrexate: haemodynamic stability, beta-hCG below 5000 IU/L, no fetal heart activity, no significant free fluid, normal renal and liver function, and reliable follow-up. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: Medical management is appropriate first-line for eligible women and avoids loss of the tube; surgery is reserved for those who do not meet methotrexate criteria, who fail medical therapy or who have ruptured. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: Salpingostomy is generally inferior to salpingectomy when the contralateral tube is healthy; methotrexate instillation is not routine intraoperative practice. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: Mifepristone and misoprostol are used for intrauterine pregnancy termination, not ectopic pregnancy; they do not resolve tubal trophoblast. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy 2023

explanation.summary: Major placenta praevia (placenta covering the internal os) is a contraindication to vaginal birth. Planned caesarean delivery is recommended at 36 to 37 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids in stable women. After an antepartum bleed, inpatient management until delivery is generally recommended. Prior caesarean section combined with placenta praevia substantially raises the risk of placenta accreta spectrum and warrants additional imaging (specialised ultrasound or MRI), multidisciplinary planning and delivery in a centre with interventional radiology and blood bank capacity.
key_points: Major praevia: planned caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks
Antenatal corticosteroids before preterm caesarean
Prior caesarean + praevia = placenta accreta spectrum risk; image specifically
Inpatient observation after antepartum haemorrhage until delivery
explanation.pearls: When a woman with major placenta praevia and prior caesareans has an antepartum bleed at 35 weeks, plan caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks after steroids and arrange targeted placenta accreta spectrum imaging rather than aiming for term or attempting vaginal trial.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023

options.rationale: With cessation of bleeding, stable observations and reactive cardiotocography, expectant inpatient management with planned delivery at 36 to 37 weeks reduces neonatal morbidity compared with immediate preterm delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023

options.rationale: Major placenta praevia where the placenta covers the os is an absolute contraindication to vaginal delivery regardless of bleeding pattern; the placental edge does not retract sufficiently with continued growth to allow safe vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023

options.rationale: Major placenta praevia with prior caesareans warrants planned caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids, with active assessment for placenta accreta spectrum given the major risk factors. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023

options.rationale: Induction of labour is contraindicated for major placenta praevia; planned caesarean is the only appropriate mode of delivery in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023

options.rationale: Inpatient observation after an antepartum haemorrhage with placenta praevia is recommended until delivery; outpatient management is reserved for highly selected stable women with rapid hospital access. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum 2023

explanation.summary: PPROM at 31 weeks is managed with admission, antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly 24 hours apart for two doses), latency antibiotics (erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 10 days; amoxicillin with clavulanic acid avoided due to neonatal necrotising enterocolitis risk) and avoidance of digital vaginal examination to reduce ascending infection. Expectant management is continued until 34 weeks unless chorioamnionitis, fetal distress or other complications develop. Magnesium sulfate fetal neuroprotection is given when preterm birth is imminent.
key_points: Erythromycin is the latency antibiotic; amoxicillin with clavulanic acid contraindicated
Avoid digital examination
Antenatal corticosteroids 24 hours apart
Expectant management to 34 weeks unless complications develop
explanation.pearls: For PPROM under 34 weeks without chorioamnionitis or fetal distress, give betamethasone plus erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 10 days and avoid amoxicillin with clavulanic acid and digital examinations, planning delivery at 34 weeks if no complications arise.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023

options.rationale: PPROM requires inpatient management for monitoring of chorioamnionitis and fetal status; outpatient management and amoxicillin alone are inappropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023

options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is contraindicated in PPROM because of a documented association with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis; erythromycin is the recommended latency antibiotic. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023

options.rationale: Expectant management at 31 weeks until 34 weeks is recommended when there is no chorioamnionitis, fetal distress or other indication for delivery; immediate induction increases neonatal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023

options.rationale: PPROM management at 31 weeks includes admission, antenatal corticosteroids, latency antibiotics with erythromycin (no amoxicillin with clavulanic acid due to necrotising enterocolitis risk) and avoidance of digital examinations to reduce ascending infection. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023

options.rationale: Digital examination is avoided in PPROM as it accelerates ascending infection; magnesium sulfate neuroprotection is indicated only when preterm birth is imminent within 24 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes 2023

explanation.summary: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome complicates around 10 to 15% of monochorionic twin pregnancies. Diagnosis requires monochorionicity plus oligohydramnios (deepest vertical pool below 2 cm) in the donor twin and polyhydramnios (deepest vertical pool above 8 cm before 20 weeks, 10 cm after) in the recipient. Quintero staging incorporates bladder visibility, Doppler abnormalities, fetal hydrops and demise. Fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses is the standard of care for Quintero stage II or higher TTTS diagnosed before 26 weeks, with substantially superior twin survival compared with amnioreduction.
key_points: TTTS: oligo (DVP <2 cm) + poly (DVP >8 cm before 20 weeks) in MC twins
Quintero II = absent donor bladder
Fetoscopic laser ablation is the standard of care before 26 weeks
Laser is superior to serial amnioreduction for twin survival and neurodevelopment
explanation.pearls: When a monochorionic twin pregnancy shows DVP <2 cm in one twin and DVP >8 cm in the other before 20 weeks, refer to a fetal medicine centre for fetoscopic laser ablation within 24 to 48 hours rather than continuing fortnightly surveillance or attempting amnioreduction first.

sources.label: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: Delivery at 19 weeks is non-viable and is not an appropriate management option; in-utero laser treatment is the standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: TTTS at Quintero stage II with absent donor bladder cannot wait two weeks; delay risks progression to Quintero stage III to V and significant loss in fetal salvage rates. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: Amnioreduction has worse long-term twin survival and neurodevelopmental outcomes than laser ablation and should only be considered when laser is unavailable or contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for late or severe TTTS where one twin is severely compromised and laser is not feasible; it is not first-line for Quintero stage II TTTS at 19 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023

options.rationale: Quintero stage I or higher twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome diagnosed before 26 weeks is best treated with fetoscopic laser ablation, which has superior twin survival outcomes compared with serial amnioreduction; referral is time-critical. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023)
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy 2023

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is the presence of unprotected fetal vessels running through the membranes near the cervical os, classically associated with a succenturiate or bilobed placenta or with a velamentous cord insertion. Rupture of membranes shears these vessels and causes rapid fetal exsanguination, presenting as painless fresh PV bleeding with a sinusoidal CTG within minutes. The intervention is immediate category 1 caesarean section; any delay for examination, tocolysis, or imaging risks fetal death. Antenatally diagnosed vasa praevia is delivered electively at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids.
key_points: Painless PV bleed plus sinusoidal CTG after SROM with a known succenturiate lobe is vasa praevia
Fetal blood volume is small so exsanguination occurs within minutes
Treatment is category 1 caesarean - not vaginal delivery or tocolysis
Antenatal diagnosis allows elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after steroids
explanation.pearls: Sinusoidal CTG plus fresh PV bleed plus succenturiate lobe equals vasa praevia equals category 1 caesarean. Vaginal examination only worsens the bleed.

options.rationale: Augmentation in suspected vasa praevia accelerates exsanguination of fetal blood through ruptured vessels; fetal mortality without immediate delivery exceeds 50 percent. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa Praevia)

A sinusoidal CTG with fresh PV bleeding after membrane rupture in a woman with known succenturiate lobe is vasa praevia until proven otherwise; fetal blood loss is rapid and immediate category 1 caesarean is the only intervention that prevents fetal death. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa Praevia)

Digital examination risks further laceration of the vasa praevia vessels and adds no useful information when a category 1 caesarean is already indicated by the sinusoidal CTG. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa Praevia)

Tocolysis and antenatal corticosteroids assume time to delay delivery; in active vasa praevia haemorrhage fetal demise occurs within minutes and steroid course timing is irrelevant. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa Praevia)

Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection is appropriate before preterm delivery under 30 weeks gestation; at 36 weeks it is not indicated and does not address the imminent fetal exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG: Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection)

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare but life-threatening late-pregnancy disorder distinguished from HELLP by hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy and a coagulopathy that often exceeds the platelet drop. The Swansea criteria provide a clinical framework with six or more of vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia, encephalopathy, raised bilirubin, hypoglycaemia, raised urate, leucocytosis, ascites or bright liver on ultrasound, raised transaminases, raised ammonia, raised creatinine, coagulopathy, and microvesicular steatosis on biopsy. Management is rapid correction of hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy and electrolytes followed by prompt delivery, which is the only definitive treatment.
key_points: Hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, and coagulopathy distinguish AFLP from HELLP
Swansea criteria provide a structured diagnostic framework
Delivery is the only definitive treatment - do not delay for steroids
Stabilise with dextrose, FFP and cryoprecipitate before transferring to theatre
explanation.pearls: Profound hypoglycaemia and disproportionate coagulopathy in late pregnancy is AFLP, not HELLP. Steroid cover does not justify delaying delivery in this setting.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy
Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists Green-top Guideline 43: AFLP

options.rationale: Hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, coagulopathy and lactic acidosis are not features of HELLP and point to acute fatty liver of pregnancy; expectant management is unsafe given progressive liver failure. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is identified by Swansea criteria including encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia and coagulopathy; treatment is rapid maternal stabilisation with dextrose and blood products followed by delivery, which is the only intervention that halts the disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine has been used as an adjunct in some hepatic failure scenarios but is not the primary intervention in acute fatty liver of pregnancy, where delivery is curative. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Plasma exchange is reserved for refractory cases after delivery or for TTP; in acute fatty liver of pregnancy delivery itself reverses the underlying mitochondrial dysfunction. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Maternal coagulopathy and hepatic failure preclude delaying delivery for steroid cover; the neonatal team must manage prematurity after the immediate maternal threat is addressed. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency in which the fetal cord descends through the cervix with the presenting part still high, causing rapid fetal compromise through compression and vasospasm. Immediate manoeuvres are aimed at relieving compression: manual elevation of the presenting part by the examining hand, knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position, and where transfer is prolonged, bladder filling with 500 mL warm saline via a Foley catheter. Definitive management is category 1 caesarean section unless vaginal delivery is imminent. Avoid handling the cord and avoid exposing it to atmospheric temperature.
key_points: Manual elevation plus knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position relieves cord compression
Bladder filling is an adjunct when transfer to theatre is delayed
Category 1 caesarean is the definitive intervention
Do not handle or pull on the cord; avoid cooling and traction
explanation.pearls: Manual elevation by the examining hand remains the most effective immediate manoeuvre and stays in place until the abdomen is open. Knee-chest gravity-assists this.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 50: Umbilical Cord Prolapse

options.rationale: Pulling on the cord and exposing it to atmospheric temperature provoke vasospasm and worsen fetal compromise; warm saline soaks are no longer recommended. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

Augmentation traps the cord further against the presenting part and worsens fetal compromise; the goal is to relieve cord compression and deliver by caesarean unless vaginal delivery is imminent. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

Manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord plus knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position relieves compression while the patient is transferred for category 1 caesarean section; tocolysis with terbutaline may be added if delivery is delayed. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)
The cervix is only 4 cm dilated and the head is high; vacuum delivery is unsafe and inappropriate at this station and would delay definitive caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

Bladder filling is a useful adjunct when transfer is prolonged, but manual elevation in the knee-chest position is the immediate first-line manoeuvre alongside an emergency category 1 call. (Source: RANZCOG: Cord Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis affects 5 to 10 percent of women within 12 months of birth, typically in those with positive anti-TPO antibodies. The classical course is a thyrotoxic phase from 6 weeks to 6 months due to release of preformed hormone, followed by a hypothyroid phase from 3 to 12 months, with most women returning to euthyroid status. Low radioiodine uptake distinguishes it from Graves disease. Management of the thyrotoxic phase is symptomatic with propranolol; thionamides and radioactive iodine are not indicated. The hypothyroid phase warrants levothyroxine if symptomatic, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding poorly. Long-term annual TSH monitoring is recommended as 20 percent develop permanent hypothyroidism.
key_points: Postpartum thyroiditis is destructive thyroiditis with low radioiodine uptake
Anti-TPO positive women are at highest risk
Thyrotoxic phase is managed with beta blockade only
Annual TSH surveillance is required because permanent hypothyroidism develops in about 20 percent
explanation.pearls: Low radioiodine uptake plus positive anti-TPO in the first year after birth equals postpartum thyroiditis. Reach for propranolol, not carbimazole.

options.rationale: Postpartum thyroiditis is not driven by new hormone synthesis; thionamides have no role because the thyrotoxicosis is from preformed hormone release and remits spontaneously. (Source: ESA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guidance)

Ablative therapy is reserved for primary hyperthyroidism with high uptake; in postpartum thyroiditis radioactive iodine is contraindicated and ineffective because uptake is already suppressed. (Source: ESA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guidance)

Levothyroxine is not indicated during the thyrotoxic phase and may exacerbate symptoms; treatment in the hypothyroid phase is reserved for symptomatic women or those planning pregnancy. (Source: ESA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guidance)

Postpartum thyroiditis is identified by transient thyrotoxicosis with low radioiodine uptake and positive anti-TPO; symptomatic beta-blockade and serial thyroid function tests are first-line, with an expected hypothyroid phase before recovery in most women. (Source: ESA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guidance)

Surgery is not indicated for postpartum thyroiditis; the natural history is self-limiting and recurrence in future pregnancies is best managed by surveillance, not pre-emptive resection. (Source: ESA Postpartum Thyroiditis Guidance)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise and warrants urgent investigation. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line test, with an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less providing reassurance in women not on hormone therapy. Persistent bleeding or thickness above 4 mm requires hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy. Obesity, type 2 diabetes, nulliparity, late menopause, and unopposed oestrogen exposure are major risk factors. CA-125, CT, and MRI have no role in primary workup; MRI is used after tissue diagnosis for staging. About 10 percent of women presenting with postmenopausal bleeding have endometrial cancer.
key_points: Any postmenopausal bleed warrants TVUS as first-line investigation
Endometrial thickness above 4 mm needs hysteroscopy and biopsy
Obesity and T2DM increase endometrial cancer risk
MRI is for staging only, after tissue diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Even one episode of postmenopausal bleeding mandates a TVUS within 2 weeks; an endometrial thickness above 4 mm always escalates to hysteroscopy and biopsy.

options.rationale: Any postmenopausal bleed is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise; reassurance without investigation misses up to 10 percent of women with malignancy. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer)

Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line investigation in postmenopausal bleeding; an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less in a woman not on hormone therapy is reassuring, while thickness above 4 mm or persistent bleeding requires hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer)

CA-125 is non-specific in early endometrial cancer and CT does not visualise the endometrium reliably; transvaginal ultrasound is the appropriate first investigation. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer)
Cervical screening targets cervical cancer; postmenopausal bleeding requires endometrial assessment, which is not addressed by an HPV test. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer)

MRI is reserved for staging once a tissue diagnosis of endometrial cancer is established; primary diagnostic workup uses transvaginal ultrasound and tissue sampling. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer)

explanation.summary: Mirror syndrome describes maternal pre-eclampsia like illness occurring in association with fetal hydrops, named because maternal oedema mirrors fetal hydrops. It carries significant maternal risk including pulmonary oedema, severe hypertension, and progression to eclampsia, and resolves only with delivery or with reversal of the underlying fetal disease. While time permits, maternal hypertension is controlled, antenatal corticosteroids are given for lung maturity, and magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection in deliveries below 30 weeks gestation. Delivery is the only definitive maternal treatment and should generally be planned within 24 to 48 hours.
key_points: Mirror syndrome is pre-eclampsia like illness associated with fetal hydrops
Maternal oedema, hypertension, proteinuria and HELLP-like changes occur together
Delivery is the only definitive treatment for the maternal disease
Where time allows, give corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate before delivering
explanation.pearls: Maternal oedema with fetal hydrops is mirror syndrome until proven otherwise; delivery is the maternal cure, not diuresis or expectant management.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Mirror Syndrome

options.rationale: Mirror syndrome resolves only with delivery or resolution of the fetal hydrops; conservative management to 34 weeks risks maternal pulmonary oedema and severe pre-eclampsia complications. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection are still given where time permits because they substantially improve neonatal outcomes; complete omission is not standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Mirror syndrome is a pre-eclampsia like state driven by fetal hydrops and resolves only with delivery; while time allows, hypertension is controlled, corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate are given for fetal benefit, and delivery is planned within 24 to 48 hours. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Intrauterine transfusion is part of fetal therapy in selected hydrops aetiologies but does not reliably reverse maternal mirror syndrome quickly enough to defer delivery in this presentation. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Diuresis treats a symptom and does not address the underlying maternal disease; aggressive diuresis can worsen intravascular depletion in pre-eclampsia spectrum disorders. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Concealed placental abruption with fetal bradycardia and coagulopathy is an immediate threat to both mother and baby. A fibrinogen below 2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage is a strong predictor of progression to massive haemorrhage and must be corrected early with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, not fresh frozen plasma alone. Initial resuscitation uses the massive transfusion protocol with packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate in a balanced ratio, with O negative blood while cross-match completes. Tranexamic acid is an adjunct. Delivery is by category 1 caesarean section. Postpartum surveillance for DIC and renal failure is essential.
key_points: Concealed abruption with fetal bradycardia is a category 1 caesarean indication
Fibrinogen below 2 g/L is a strong predictor of major haemorrhage
Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is required - FFP alone is insufficient
Tranexamic acid is an adjunct, not a substitute for blood products
explanation.pearls: Maintain fibrinogen above 2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage; cryoprecipitate provides 30 to 50 mg/kg of fibrinogen and is faster than FFP.

options.rationale: Fetal bradycardia and maternal haemodynamic instability mandate immediate delivery by caesarean; vaginal delivery is not appropriate when the fetus is decompensating and the mother is shocked. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

Concealed placental abruption with coagulopathy and fetal bradycardia is a category 1 emergency requiring activation of the massive transfusion protocol, early cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate to maintain fibrinogen above 2 g/L, and immediate caesarean delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

Waiting for cross-matched blood while the fetus and mother decompensate is unsafe; O negative blood and the massive transfusion pack are used while cross-match completes. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines)

FFP alone does not replace fibrinogen rapidly; in obstetric haemorrhage with fibrinogen below 2 g/L cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is essential, alongside packed cells and platelets. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Guidelines)
Tranexamic acid is an adjunct to massive transfusion in major obstetric haemorrhage but is not a substitute for blood product resuscitation and delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion in pregnancy is a surgical emergency that presents with sudden severe iliac fossa pain, vomiting, and an enlarged ovary with reduced or absent doppler flow on ultrasound. Doppler flow can occasionally remain present due to dual ovarian blood supply, so clinical suspicion drives the diagnosis. Standard of care is urgent laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation; even ovaries that appear dusky or necrotic can recover function. Oophorectomy is reserved for clearly necrotic or malignant masses. Surgery is safe in the second trimester and is preferred to expectant management because of the risk of ovarian loss.
key_points: Sudden severe iliac fossa pain plus enlarged ovary plus absent doppler equals torsion
Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation is first-line
Even dusky ovaries often recover; routine oophorectomy is not warranted
Surgery is safe in the second trimester and is preferred to observation
explanation.pearls: Doppler flow being present does not exclude torsion - dual ovarian supply from uterine and ovarian arteries means flow can persist; clinical features and ovarian size drive the call to theatre.

options.rationale: Observation in suspected ovarian torsion risks irreversible ovarian necrosis within hours; the diagnosis mandates urgent surgical intervention. (Source: RANZCOG: Adnexal Mass in Pregnancy)

Sudden severe pelvic pain with an enlarged ovary and absent doppler flow is ovarian torsion; urgent laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation is the standard of care, even when the ovary appears dusky, as recovery of function is common. (Source: RANZCOG: Adnexal Mass in Pregnancy)

Routine oophorectomy is not standard; current evidence supports detorsion and conservation even in apparently necrotic ovaries because viable tissue often recovers, and thromboembolic risk does not warrant pre-emptive removal. (Source: RANZCOG: Adnexal Mass in Pregnancy)
Aspiration does not address torsion or restore blood flow and risks spillage of malignant cells if the mass is neoplastic; surgical detorsion is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Adnexal Mass in Pregnancy)
Tocolysis does not treat ovarian torsion and observation delays definitive surgery; surgical intervention is safe at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG: Adnexal Mass in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Vulval lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis that presents with pruritus, soreness, white wrinkled plaques, architectural loss, and the figure-of-eight perineal-perianal pattern. It carries a 4 to 5 percent lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma and warrants annual clinical review. First-line treatment is a potent topical corticosteroid, classically clobetasol propionate 0.05 percent ointment, applied nightly for 4 weeks, alternate nights for 4 weeks, and then twice weekly indefinitely as maintenance. Emollients and avoidance of irritants support the regimen. Surgery is reserved for adhesions or biopsy-confirmed neoplasia. Symptoms refractory to potent steroid warrant repeat biopsy to exclude differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia.
key_points: Lichen sclerosus is treated with potent topical steroid as first-line, not mild steroid or antifungal
Annual review captures the 4 to 5 percent lifetime risk of vulval SCC
Maintenance therapy twice weekly is required to prevent flares and scarring
Repeat biopsy if refractory to potent steroid to exclude dVIN
explanation.pearls: Clobetasol 0.05 percent ointment nightly for 4 weeks, alternate nights for 4 weeks, then twice weekly maintenance is the AU standard; annual review is non-negotiable.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen Sclerosus

options.rationale: Mild topical steroids are insufficient to control vulval lichen sclerosus; under-treatment increases scarring and the lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Disorders)
Topical oestrogen treats vulvovaginal atrophy, not lichen sclerosus; while it may be a comfort measure, it does not treat the underlying lichenoid inflammation. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Disorders)

Australian guidance treats vulval lichen sclerosus with potent topical steroid such as clobetasol propionate 0.05 percent, initially nightly for 4 weeks, alternate nights for 4 weeks, then twice weekly maintenance, with annual review for the 4 to 5 percent lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Disorders)
Lichen sclerosus is not infective and antifungal therapy is ineffective; biopsy has already confirmed the diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Disorders)
Vulvectomy is not indicated for uncomplicated lichen sclerosus; surgery is reserved for biopsy-confirmed dysplasia or carcinoma, or for symptomatic adhesions. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval Disorders)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy with ferritin below 30 micrograms/L is treated with oral iron first line. Failure of response, intolerance, or presentation in late pregnancy with insufficient time to correct stores triggers intravenous iron. Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg as a single infusion is the most common Australian regimen and can be given from the second trimester onward. Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or imminent delivery with anticipated haemorrhage.
key_points: Oral iron first line if tolerated and time to correct
IV iron from second trimester if oral failure or intolerance
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg single infusion is the AU standard
Transfusion only for haemodynamic compromise or imminent haemorrhage risk
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG and NBA: IV ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg single infusion from 2nd trimester onwards when oral iron fails or is poorly tolerated, with ferritin under 30 micrograms/L.

sources.label: NBA Patient Blood Management Module 5: Obstetrics

options.rationale: Increasing oral iron dose worsens gastrointestinal side effects, reduces adherence further, and rarely closes a haemoglobin gap before delivery; intravenous iron is recommended when oral therapy has failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

After demonstrated oral iron failure or intolerance in the second or third trimester, intravenous iron is the recommended treatment to restore stores before delivery; ferric carboxymaltose can be given in one outpatient infusion. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise or planned delivery with risk of significant haemorrhage; routine antenatal transfusion at 92 g/L is not indicated. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Module 5: Obstetrics)
source_refs: NBA Patient Blood Management Module 5: Obstetrics

options.rationale: Bone marrow biopsy is invasive and not indicated when ferritin under 30 micrograms/L with microcytic indices already establishes iron deficiency; haemoglobinopathy screen would be a less invasive next step if relevant. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

Dietary iron alone cannot correct established iron deficiency anaemia with ferritin 12 in the third trimester; abandoning supplementation guarantees worsening anaemia before birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: ADIPS diagnoses gestational diabetes when at least one 75 gram OGTT value meets: fasting at least 5.1 mmol/L, 1 hour at least 10.0 mmol/L, or 2 hour at least 8.5 mmol/L. Diagnosis triggers diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic referral, dietary review, glucose monitoring, and consideration of metformin or insulin if targets not met within 1 to 2 weeks. Overt diabetes is a separate diagnosis with higher thresholds.
key_points: ADIPS fasting cut-off 5.1 mmol/L
ADIPS 1-hour cut-off 10.0 mmol/L
ADIPS 2-hour cut-off 8.5 mmol/L
Any single value meeting threshold confirms GDM
explanation.pearls: Australian ADIPS 75g OGTT thresholds for GDM: fasting at least 5.1, 1 hour at least 10.0, 2 hour at least 8.5 mmol/L. Any one value reached makes the diagnosis.

options.rationale: ADIPS uses fasting at least 5.1, 1 hour at least 10.0, and 2 hour at least 8.5 mmol/L; the 1 hour 9.8 here is below the 1 hour cut-off but the 2 hour value warrants attention if any threshold met. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines 2014)

The fasting value is 5.3 which exceeds the ADIPS fasting cut-off of 5.1, but the 2 hour value of 7.6 is below the 2 hour cut-off of 8.5; only the fasting criterion is met. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines 2014)

ADIPS diagnoses GDM if any single value is reached: fasting at least 5.1, 1 hour at least 10.0, or 2 hour at least 8.5 mmol/L; this patient meets the fasting cut-off so diagnosis is confirmed. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines 2014)

Pregnancy uses GDM diagnostic criteria that differ from non-pregnant IGT thresholds; meeting any ADIPS value confirms GDM and there is no diagnostic repeat in pregnancy. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines 2014)

Overt diabetes thresholds are fasting at least 7.0 or HbA1c at least 6.5 percent or random at least 11.1 mmol/L; this patient meets GDM but not overt diabetes criteria. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines 2014)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis is monitored clinically rather than biochemically. Toxicity appears in a reliable sequence as the level rises: loss of the patellar reflex first, then respiratory depression, then cardiac conduction failure, so hourly patellar reflexes and respiratory rate detect the problem while it is still reversible. Magnesium is cleared entirely by the kidney, which makes hourly urine output the third essential observation, and the infusion is reduced or stopped if output falls below about 100 mL over four hours. Serum magnesium levels are reserved for women with renal impairment, persistent oliguria or clinical signs of toxicity, where the clinical picture is unreliable. If toxicity is suspected the infusion stops and intravenous calcium gluconate is given. In context, pre-eclampsia is a multisystem placental disease whose definitive treatment is birth, and magnesium buys the time needed to give corticosteroids, control blood pressure and deliver the woman safely.
key_points: Hourly patellar reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output while the infusion runs.
Reflexes disappear before respiratory depression develops.
Magnesium is renally cleared, so oliguria means reduce or stop the infusion.
Serum levels are for renal impairment, oliguria or suspected toxicity.
explanation.pearls: Document the reflexes each hour by name rather than as a tick: an absent patellar reflex is the single observation that should stop the infusion before anyone reaches for a level.

sources.label: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.rationale: Magnesium toxicity is detected clinically and in a predictable order: reflexes are lost before respiratory depression, and renal clearance is tracked by urine output, so hourly bedside observation replaces routine serum levels in a woman with normal renal function. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.rationale: Serum levels are indicated when renal impairment, oliguria or clinical signs of toxicity make the clinical assessment unreliable. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.rationale: Continuous fetal monitoring is warranted for fetal compromise or once labour is established, but four-hourly maternal observation is far too infrequent on this infusion. (Source: RANZCOG)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.rationale: Hourly assays would be used in a research protocol; they lag behind the clinical signs and expose the woman to repeated venepuncture for no benefit. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.rationale: Serial platelet counts track disease progression and guide regional anaesthesia, but they say nothing about magnesium safety. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

explanation.summary: Active management of the third stage of labour involves intramuscular oxytocin 10 units within 1 minute of birth, delayed cord clamping at 1 to 3 minutes when possible, and controlled cord traction with uterine guarding once the uterus contracts. This reduces postpartum haemorrhage rates compared with physiological management. Ergometrine combinations are added in higher-risk women without hypertension; carboprost and misoprostol are second-line agents.
key_points: Active management reduces PPH risk 2 to 3 fold
IM oxytocin 10 units within 1 minute is first line
Delayed cord clamping unless baby resuscitation required
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG active third stage = IM oxytocin 10 units within 1 minute + delayed cord clamping + controlled cord traction; combination oxytocin-ergometrine reserved for higher-risk women without hypertension.

sources.label: WHO Recommendations for the Prevention and Treatment of PPH

options.rationale: Physiological third stage is associated with around 2 to 3 times the postpartum haemorrhage risk of active management; active management is recommended for all women without contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

Ergometrine monotherapy is not first line because hypertension is a contraindication and the side effect profile is inferior to oxytocin; combined oxytocin-ergometrine is reserved for higher-risk women without hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

Active third stage management with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units, delayed cord clamping, and controlled cord traction reduces PPH risk and is recommended for all women without contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Carboprost is reserved for atonic PPH after oxytocin and ergometrine fail; its side effect burden makes it unsuitable for routine prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

Misoprostol is reserved for settings where injectable uterotonics are unavailable; oxytocin is more effective and is the agent of choice in an Australian birth suite. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Chorionicity must be established as early as possible in twin pregnancy because it dictates surveillance frequency and risk of complications such as twin-to-twin transfusion. The first trimester between 11 and 13+6 weeks is the optimal window, using the lambda sign for dichorionic and T sign for monochorionic. Accuracy falls beyond 14 weeks and chorionicity cannot be reliably inferred from conception mode because single embryos can divide.
key_points: Best window 11 to 13+6 weeks for lambda vs T sign
Accuracy falls beyond 14 weeks
Single embryo transfer can still produce monochorionic twins
Counting placental masses alone is unreliable
explanation.pearls: Twin chorionicity is best determined at 11 to 13+6 weeks using lambda (dichorionic) vs T sign (monochorionic) at the inter-twin membrane insertion; do not infer from IVF embryo transfer history.

sources.label: NICE NG137: Twin and triplet pregnancy

options.rationale: Accurate chorionicity determination is best between 11 and 13+6 weeks when the lambda sign indicates dichorionic and the T sign indicates monochorionic; after 14 weeks accuracy falls. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

Zygosity and chorionicity are not interchangeable; CVS carries a procedural loss risk and is not the routine approach to chorionicity determination, which is ultrasonographic. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

Chorionicity becomes unreliable to determine by sign after 14 weeks; deferring to 20 weeks risks misclassification with implications for surveillance and outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

A single embryo transfer that subsequently divides produces monochorionic twins; chorionicity must be confirmed by ultrasound rather than assumed from the conception history. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

Two placental masses can occur in dichorionic and occasionally fused monochorionic twins; the lambda and T signs at the inter-twin membrane insertion are the accurate markers. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome with progressive biochemistry (falling platelets, rising transaminases) at 31 to 34 weeks gestation mandates delivery without waiting to complete antenatal corticosteroids. Mode of delivery balances cervical status, gestation, and maternal stability; emergent caesarean is common at very preterm gestations or when induction is unlikely to succeed quickly. Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis, blood pressure is controlled, and corrective transfusion is reserved for active bleeding or operative thresholds.
key_points: Progressive HELLP biochemistry mandates delivery
Do not wait for full steroid course if deteriorating
Caesarean common at very preterm gestation
Platelet target for caesarean around 50 x10^9/L; do not transfuse prophylactically
explanation.pearls: HELLP delivery threshold: progressive worsening (falling platelets, rising AST/ALT) means deliver now; finishing the corticosteroid course is desirable but does not override deterioration.

options.rationale: HELLP with falling platelets and rising transaminases is progressive; delaying past 24 to 48 hours to complete steroids is acceptable only when biochemistry is stable, not deteriorating. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Expectant management to 34 weeks in HELLP with progressive maternal deterioration risks abruption, eclampsia, hepatic rupture, and DIC; high-dose steroids do not modify maternal HELLP progression. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Worsening biochemistry with falling platelets, rising transaminases, and persistent symptoms in HELLP mandates delivery without delay; partial corticosteroid benefit is accepted and category 2 caesarean is appropriate given the cervix and prematurity. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Induction with progressing biochemistry and prematurity is unlikely to achieve timely birth before maternal complications; expedited caesarean is preferred. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Prophylactic platelets do not stop the HELLP progression and routine transfusion threshold for delivery is around 50 for caesarean; this does not address the underlying need for delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Term PROM is managed with offer of induction rather than open-ended expectant management because immediate induction reduces chorioamnionitis without increasing caesarean rate (TERMPROM trial). Oxytocin is the typical induction agent in PROM. Intrapartum antibiotics (benzylpenicillin or clindamycin if allergic) are added if labour has not commenced by 18 to 24 hours, or sooner if GBS positive. Expectant management requires defined monitoring intervals.
key_points: Offer induction at term PROM (TERMPROM trial)
Oxytocin is first-line induction in PROM
Antibiotics if not labouring by 18 to 24 hours
Reduced chorioamnionitis without increased caesarean
explanation.pearls: Term PROM: offer induction with oxytocin and add intrapartum antibiotics if labour not established by 18 to 24 hours; TERMPROM trial supports immediate over expectant management.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Open-ended expectant management without a defined plan increases chorioamnionitis risk; RANZCOG suggests offering induction by 24 hours for term PROM. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Caesarean is not indicated for term PROM with reassuring fetal status, cephalic presentation, and no contraindication to induction. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Discharge with no observation plan misses early infection and exceeds the safe expectant window in term PROM; review at minimum every 12 hours is required if expectant. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: RANZCOG advises offering induction at term PROM rather than open-ended expectant management because immediate induction reduces chorioamnionitis without increasing caesarean rate; intrapartum antibiotics are added if not in labour by 18 to 24 hours. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Vaginal prostaglandin in unfavourable cervix is one option, but high-dose misoprostol regimens are not the RANZCOG default and oxytocin induction is appropriate first line for PROM. (Source: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

explanation.summary: Endometriosis with failure of first-line hormonal and NSAID therapy and clinically significant disease (deep infiltrating disease, endometrioma over 3 cm with persistent symptoms) is escalated to laparoscopic excisional surgery in centres with appropriate expertise. Cystectomy is preferred over ablation for endometriomas because of lower recurrence. GnRH agonist trials are options when surgery is declined or deferred but do not replace it for advanced disease. Future fertility is discussed pre-operatively.
key_points: Surgery indicated when medical therapy fails or DIE/endometrioma over 3 cm
Laparoscopic excision and cystectomy preferred
Cystectomy reduces endometrioma recurrence vs ablation
Fertility counselling before surgery essential
explanation.pearls: Endometriosis pathway: COCP/NSAID first, GnRH agonist if surgery deferred, surgery (laparoscopic excision + cystectomy) for DIE or endometrioma over 3 cm with persistent symptoms.

options.rationale: DMPA can suppress symptoms but causes bone density loss and a delay to return of fertility of up to 9 months; it is not the preferred next-line for women planning future pregnancy with deep disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Guideline)
Tamoxifen is not used for endometriosis; in fact it has been associated with endometrial pathology and is the wrong drug class for this indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Guideline)

Fertility-focused IVF is appropriate when conception is the immediate goal; she wishes to preserve fertility but is not currently trying to conceive, so symptom management remains primary. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Guideline)

After medical therapy failure with deep infiltrating endometriosis and an endometrioma over 3 cm causing persistent symptoms, laparoscopic excision is recommended; cystectomy is preferred over ablation for endometrioma recurrence reduction. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Guideline)

GnRH agonists with add-back can suppress symptoms temporarily, but with deep disease and an endometrioma over 3 cm not improving on combined oral contraceptive, surgery is the recommended next step. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy in Australia is made on transvaginal ultrasound visualising an extrauterine sac or adnexal mass together with a serum beta-hCG above the transvaginal discriminatory zone of 1500 IU/L and an empty uterus. Once diagnosed, choice between expectant, medical (methotrexate), and surgical (laparoscopic salpingectomy preferred, salpingostomy if contralateral tube damaged) management depends on hCG level, size, presence of fetal heart, symptoms, and patient preference. Anti-D prophylaxis is given to RhD-negative women.
key_points: Discriminatory zone TVUS: 1500 IU/L (TAUS 2000).
Empty uterus + adnexal mass + hCG > 1500 = ectopic.
Methotrexate criteria: stable, hCG <5000, <35mm, no FH, compliant.
Anti-D 250 IU IM if RhD negative.
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate dose is 50 mg/m^2 IM with day-4 and day-7 hCG; if hCG falls under 15 percent between day 4 and 7, repeat dose; suboptimal fall requires surgery.

sources.label: AFP: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.rationale: Ambulatory expectant management is reserved for women with low and falling hCG, no visualised ectopic, and minimal symptoms; this woman has a visualised mass, prior ectopic and ongoing pain. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

Diagnosis is already secure on transvaginal imaging plus hCG; deferring intervention by weeks risks rupture, and elective scheduling is not appropriate for confirmed ectopic. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

The discriminatory zone is exceeded (>1500 IU/L by TVUS) with no intrauterine pregnancy and a visualised extrauterine mass in a high-risk woman; delay risks tubal rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

Methotrexate eligibility requires confirmation of haemodynamic stability, hCG criteria, size, no fetal heart, no rupture, ability to comply with follow-up, and exclusion of contraindications; it is not a default first move. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

A beta-hCG above the transvaginal discriminatory zone of 1500 IU/L with an empty uterus and visualised adnexal mass meets criteria for ectopic pregnancy; admission for staged decision on medical (methotrexate) versus surgical (laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingostomy) management is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed by Amsel criteria (3 of 4: pH above 4.5, positive whiff with KOH, clue cells on saline microscopy, thin homogenous grey discharge) or Nugent score on Gram stain. First-line treatment in Australia is oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days. Topical metronidazole gel or clindamycin cream are equivalent alternatives in non-pregnant women. Routine partner treatment is not recommended. Recurrence is common; in recurrent BV, suppressive metronidazole vaginal gel twice weekly for 4 to 6 months is used.
key_points: Amsel: pH>4.5, whiff+, clue cells, thin grey discharge.
First-line: oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 7 days.
Avoid 2 g single dose (higher recurrence).
No routine partner treatment for BV.
explanation.pearls: Counsel disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol during metronidazole and for 24 hours after; pregnant women with symptomatic BV are treated similarly because BV increases preterm birth risk.

options.rationale: Routine partner treatment is not recommended in BV because it does not reduce recurrence; the 2 g single dose also has higher recurrence than the 7-day regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Vaginitis)
She is asymptomatic for STI, recently screened, and has Amsel-positive BV; empiric STI cover is not indicated and does not treat BV. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Vaginitis)

Confirmed BV in a symptomatic woman warrants treatment to reduce symptoms and to lower risk of post-procedural infection if any uterine instrumentation is needed; watchful waiting is inappropriate when diagnostic criteria are met. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Vaginitis)

Amsel criteria (pH above 4.5, clue cells, positive whiff test, thin homogenous discharge) confirm BV; first-line in Australia is oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 7 days. Single 2 g dose has higher recurrence and is second line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Vaginitis)

Fluconazole treats candidiasis, which presents with itch, white curdy discharge, normal pH below 4.5, and pseudohyphae on microscopy; her findings (pH 5.2, whiff positive, clue cells) confirm bacterial vaginosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Vaginitis)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse with a fully dilated cervix is delivered immediately by the fastest route. For a cephalic singleton at full dilatation, instrumental vaginal delivery is the fastest. For a transverse second twin at full dilatation with an experienced operator, internal podalic version and breech extraction is the standard. If the cervix is not fully dilated, knee-chest position, manual elevation of the presenting part, bladder filling with warm saline and tocolysis with terbutaline are used to buy time for transfer to theatre for category-1 caesarean. Cord replacement is not recommended.
key_points: Full dilatation + experienced operator = fastest vaginal route.
Transverse second twin: internal version + breech extraction.
Not fully dilated: knee-chest, elevate part, fill bladder, transfer.
Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 mcg SC) for transfer.
explanation.pearls: Bladder filling with 500 mL warm saline elevates the presenting part better than manual elevation during prolonged transfer; document time from prolapse to delivery as it predicts neonatal outcome.

options.rationale: Knee-chest plus transfer is the standard manoeuvre for cord prolapse with the cervix not fully dilated; with full dilatation and an operator able to deliver the second twin, vaginal delivery is faster and avoids the time cost of theatre transfer. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance)

With a fully dilated cervix, an experienced operator, functioning epidural, and immediate threat to the fetus, internal podalic version and breech extraction is faster than transfer to theatre for caesarean and is the recommended management for cord prolapse with the second twin under these conditions. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance)

The fetus is in prolonged bradycardia from cord compression and the second twin is transverse: pushing will not deliver a transverse fetus, and delay risks fetal demise. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance)

Cord replacement is not recommended (high risk of further compression and vasospasm), and waiting 15 minutes risks hypoxic injury; immediate delivery is required. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance)

Tocolysis and bladder filling are adjuncts during transfer to theatre when the cervix is not fully dilated; with full dilatation and a deliverable second twin, immediate operative vaginal delivery or internal version is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance)

explanation.summary: Severe OHSS results from VEGF-mediated capillary leak after hCG-triggered ovarian stimulation; risk peaks 7 to 10 days post-trigger and worsens markedly if pregnancy supervenes (endogenous hCG). Management is admission, careful crystalloid resuscitation, LMWH thromboprophylaxis (VTE risk is markedly elevated), paracentesis for tense ascites, freeze-all of embryos, and serial monitoring of haematocrit, electrolytes, and renal function. Diuretics and cabergoline have specific limited roles. Critical-care escalation is needed if ARDS or thromboembolism develops.
key_points: Severe OHSS: haemoconcentration, oliguria, ascites, effusions.
Risk peaks day 7-10 post-trigger; worsens with pregnancy.
Crystalloid + LMWH + paracentesis if tense.
Freeze all embryos in severe cases.
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for OHSS include young age, low BMI, PCOS, high antral follicle count, oocyte retrieval >20, and rising serum oestradiol above 11000 pmol/L on trigger day; GnRH agonist trigger with freeze-all virtually eliminates severe OHSS in high-risk women.

options.rationale: Diuretics in OHSS worsen intravascular depletion (the problem is third-spacing with low effective circulating volume) and risk acute kidney injury and venous thromboembolism; not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement)

Ovarian aspiration is contraindicated because of haemorrhage and torsion risk; OHSS treatment targets the fluid third-space (ascitic drainage) and supportive care, not the ovaries themselves. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement)

Severe OHSS management combines volume resuscitation with crystalloid +/- albumin, thromboprophylaxis (LMWH for at least the haemoconcentration period), respiratory support with therapeutic paracentesis if tense ascites, and admission with strict monitoring; deferred embryo transfer is already in place to prevent worsening from endogenous hCG. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement)

Pregnancy generates endogenous hCG which prolongs and worsens OHSS for weeks; fresh transfer should be cancelled with embryos cryopreserved for frozen transfer once recovered. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement)

She meets severe OHSS criteria (haemoconcentration, oliguria, ascites with effusions, hyponatraemia, raised creatinine); discharge is unsafe and severe OHSS requires inpatient care. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS Statement)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency in pregnancy is treated with oral elemental iron 60 to 100 mg daily or alternate days (better tolerated, equally effective) as first line. IV iron is indicated for intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia, failure of oral therapy, gestation late in pregnancy where rapid replenishment is needed, or non-adherence. Australian options are ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg (single dose) or iron polymaltose (slower infusion); both have a low rate of hypersensitivity. RBC transfusion is reserved for severe symptomatic anaemia near delivery.
key_points: First line: oral elemental iron 60-100 mg alternate days.
IV iron when intolerant, malabsorption, failed oral, late gestation.
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg single dose preferred in AU.
Transfusion only for severe symptomatic anaemia near delivery.
explanation.pearls: Counsel that IV ferric carboxymaltose can cause transient hypophosphataemia (rarely symptomatic) and pseudoanaphylactic Fishbane reactions in 1 to 2 percent; pause infusion if symptoms occur and restart slower.

options.rationale: Documented oral iron intolerance, failure to reach therapeutic response, and second-trimester timing make a single dose of IV ferric carboxymaltose (or iron polymaltose) the recommended option in Australia, with monitoring for hypersensitivity. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

Tolerance issues prevent adherence already; increasing frequency worsens GI side effects, and Australian guidelines now favour alternate-day or single-dose oral iron with switch to IV iron if not tolerated. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

Hb is only mildly reduced and she is asymptomatic; transfusion is reserved for severe symptomatic anaemia or proximity to delivery, not stable iron deficiency early in the third trimester. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

Erythropoietin is reserved for renal anaemia or specific scenarios (chronic disease, Jehovah's witness) and is not indicated for routine pregnancy iron deficiency where IV iron is effective. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

Persistent intolerance limits adherence; while alternate-day oral iron is reasonable first-line, this woman has already failed an oral trial and her gestation makes IV iron preferable now. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis is most often staphylococcal and results from milk stasis and nipple trauma. Management combines continued breastfeeding (start on the affected side; the milk is safe for baby and drainage is therapeutic), warm compresses, analgesia and oral antibiotics if systemic features, persistent symptoms beyond 24 hours, or nipple breakdown. Australian first-line is dicloxacillin or flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5 to 7 days; cefalexin for mild penicillin allergy; clindamycin for severe allergy. Lack of improvement after 48 hours prompts ultrasound to exclude abscess.
key_points: Continue breastfeeding from affected side - drainage is therapeutic.
First-line: oral flucloxacillin/dicloxacillin 500 mg QID 5-7 days.
Cefalexin if mild penicillin allergy.
Ultrasound if not improving by 48 h - abscess exclusion.
explanation.pearls: Persistent erythema or a palpable lump after antibiotics in a postpartum woman over 30 years old should be biopsied to exclude inflammatory breast cancer, which can mimic refractory mastitis.

options.rationale: IV vancomycin is reserved for severe infection, sepsis, treatment failure or proven MRSA; first presentation of community lactational mastitis is treated with oral anti-staphylococcal therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)

She has systemic illness with fever and tender erythema persisting beyond 24 hours; Therapeutic Guidelines recommend empiric antibiotics for women with fever, tachycardia, and not improving with feeding alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)

Australian first-line treatment for lactational mastitis with systemic features is continued breastfeeding (start on the affected side), warm compresses, analgesia, and oral dicloxacillin or flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5 to 7 days; cefalexin if mild penicillin allergy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)

No fluctuance or abscess on clinical examination; ultrasound is indicated if no improvement after 48 hours of antibiotics or a discrete mass is felt, not for first presentation of straightforward mastitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)

Continuing breastfeeding from the affected side is recommended to maintain drainage; cessation worsens stasis and risks abscess formation, and flucloxacillin is compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Mastitis)

explanation.summary: Postpartum endometritis is a polymicrobial pelvic infection (Gram-positives including enterococci, Gram-negatives, and anaerobes) with risk factors of prolonged ROM, caesarean section, prolonged labour, and intrapartum manipulation. Standard Australian therapy is intravenous ampicillin (covers enterococci) plus gentamicin (Gram-negatives) plus metronidazole (anaerobes) until afebrile for 24 to 48 hours, then oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (or doxycycline plus metronidazole for penicillin-allergic) to complete a typical 5 to 10 day course. Check for retained products with ultrasound if no improvement at 48 hours.
key_points: Polymicrobial: needs Gram+/Gram-/anaerobe cover.
IV amp + gent + metronidazole until afebrile 24-48 h.
Step down to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate.
USS for retained products if no improvement at 48 h.
explanation.pearls: Failure to defervesce by 48 to 72 hours despite appropriate antibiotics should prompt USS for retained products, abscess or septic pelvic thrombophlebitis (rare but life-threatening; suspect if persistent fever with normal imaging).

options.rationale: Cefazolin has poor anaerobic and enterococcal cover and doxycycline is not first-line for endometritis; the polymicrobial pelvic infection needs gentamicin plus metronidazole cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

Postpartum endometritis with fever, tachycardia and rising inflammatory markers requires inpatient intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics until afebrile, not oral outpatient therapy which has higher failure rates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

Carbapenem monotherapy is excessive for first presentation in an otherwise stable woman and risks selecting resistance; ampicillin/gentamicin/metronidazole is the targeted Australian first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

Australian Therapeutic Guidelines for postpartum endometritis use IV ampicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin plus metronidazole to cover the polymicrobial pelvic flora until afebrile for 24 to 48 hours, then step down to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

Clindamycin alone gives inadequate gram-negative cover; standard Australian therapy adds gentamicin (and ampicillin for enterococci) for full polymicrobial coverage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

explanation.summary: Primary genital HSV acquired within 6 weeks of delivery carries 30 to 50 percent vertical transmission risk at vaginal birth because maternal IgG has not seroconverted in time to protect the neonate. Management is suppressive valaciclovir (500 mg BD or aciclovir 400 mg TDS) from diagnosis to delivery, plus elective caesarean before labour or ROM. For recurrent HSV at term, suppression from 36 weeks reduces shedding and a vaginal birth is acceptable unless lesions are present at labour. Neonatal HSV (skin/eye/mouth, CNS, or disseminated) is treated with IV aciclovir.
key_points: Primary HSV <6w from delivery: 30-50 percent transmission risk.
Treat with valaciclovir 500 mg BD + elective caesarean.
Recurrent HSV at term: suppress from 36w, vaginal birth ok if no lesions.
Neonatal HSV: IV aciclovir; high morbidity if missed.
explanation.pearls: Always test for HIV alongside HSV because of shared transmission risk; counsel that future pregnancies usually need suppression from 36 weeks even if vaginal birth is then possible.

options.rationale: Without antiviral suppression and a delivery plan, the woman is at high risk of vaginal birth on lesions with substantial neonatal HSV transmission; active management is required. (Source: RANZCOG Genital Herpes in Pregnancy)

Primary genital HSV acquired in the third trimester carries 30 to 50 percent vertical transmission risk at vaginal birth (no protective maternal IgG by delivery); caesarean section is recommended to reduce neonatal HSV. (Source: RANZCOG Genital Herpes in Pregnancy)
