First-episode genital HSV within 6 weeks of expected delivery is managed with suppressive valaciclovir 500 mg BD from diagnosis and elective caesarean before labour or ROM because maternal IgG has not yet seroconverted to protect the neonate. (Source: RANZCOG Genital Herpes in Pregnancy)

Suppressive antiviral from diagnosis reduces shedding at delivery; deferring therapy until labour misses the prevention window for primary HSV and does not change the indication for caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Genital Herpes in Pregnancy)

Avoiding invasive monitoring helps in recurrent HSV but is insufficient alone in a primary third-trimester episode; caesarean is required because of the high transmission risk. (Source: RANZCOG Genital Herpes in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks reduced rates of sensitisation in RhD-negative women to under 0.3 percent. Event-driven anti-D is additionally indicated for sensitising episodes such as bleeding, amniocentesis, external cephalic version or trauma after 12 weeks. Postnatal dose is given within 72 hours when cord blood confirms a RhD-positive baby. Indirect Coombs should be checked at booking and at 28 weeks before prophylaxis to detect pre-existing immune anti-D.
key_points: Two routine antenatal doses at 28 and 34 weeks for RhD-negative women.
Postnatal dose within 72 hours if baby is RhD-positive.
Event-driven dose for sensitising episodes after 12 weeks.
Always recheck indirect Coombs before each routine dose.
Aim is to prevent maternal anti-D formation, not treat existing immunisation.
explanation.pearls: Add a Kleihauer-Betke test if a sensitising event is large (placental abruption, abdominal trauma) - if fetal cells exceed 6 mL, give additional 125 IU anti-D per 1 mL of fetal blood beyond standard dose.

sources.label: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin
National Blood Authority Australia Anti-D Guidelines

options.rationale: Australian RANZCOG guidance is for routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks for RhD-negative women without immune anti-D, plus a postnatal dose within 72 hours if the baby is RhD-positive. (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Postnatal-only protocols were superseded because they failed to prevent third-trimester sensitisation; antenatal prophylaxis is now standard in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Withholding routine antenatal prophylaxis would miss silent feto-maternal haemorrhage in the third trimester and risks sensitisation before delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Monthly dosing exceeds the evidence base, increases donor exposure and is not recommended in Australia; the program is two routine doses plus event-driven doses. (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: A single 28-week dose is not the Australian schedule; the recommended program includes a second routine dose at 34 weeks because anti-D level wanes before delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is a marker of increased baseline ischaemic stroke risk; adding combined hormonal contraception multiplies that risk and is classified UKMEC 4 (unacceptable). Migraine without aura at any age is UKMEC 2 for initiation. Acceptable methods in aura include all progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, LNG-IUS, DMPA - DMPA UKMEC 2) and copper IUD (UKMEC 1). Triptan use itself does not change contraception eligibility. Always document the migraine subtype before prescribing.
key_points: Migraine with aura - combined methods UKMEC 4 at any age.
Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, LNG-IUS) are UKMEC 1 or 2.
Copper IUD UKMEC 1 - non-hormonal alternative.
Aura defined as fully reversible visual, sensory or speech symptoms developing over 5 to 20 minutes.
New aura developing on combined contraception is an absolute indication to stop it immediately.
explanation.pearls: If a woman without aura develops aura while taking a combined pill, stop it the same day and switch to a progestogen-only method - the relative stroke risk rises eight-fold in this scenario.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare UKMEC

options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 4 (unacceptable health risk) in migraine with aura because of arterial ischaemic stroke risk; cannot be prescribed. (Source: FSRH UKMEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare UKMEC

options.rationale: Cyclical use of a combined pill still exposes the patient to oestrogen and is UKMEC 4 in migraine with aura; the contraindication does not depend on duration of use. (Source: FSRH UKMEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare UKMEC

options.rationale: Migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal methods due to ischaemic stroke risk; progestogen-only LARC (LNG-IUS) is category 1 and aligns with her preference for non-daily dosing. (Source: FSRH UKMEC; eTG)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare UKMEC

options.rationale: The ring contains ethinylestradiol and is also UKMEC 4 with migraine with aura; route of delivery does not change the oestrogen-driven stroke risk. (Source: FSRH UKMEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare UKMEC

options.rationale: Transdermal combined contraceptive patches are also UKMEC 4 in migraine with aura; oestrogen-containing methods are contraindicated regardless of route. (Source: FSRH UKMEC)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare UKMEC

explanation.summary: Three established options exist for emergency contraception in Australia: copper IUD (up to 120 hours, most effective, ongoing contraception), oral ulipristal acetate (up to 120 hours), and oral levonorgestrel (up to 72 hours). Pregnancy testing should be negative at presentation. Counsel that ulipristal interferes with progestogen-based contraception for 5 days, so hormonal contraception should be delayed accordingly. Repeat pregnancy test in 3 weeks if next period is delayed or lighter than expected.
key_points: Copper IUD up to 120 hours - most effective.
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg up to 120 hours - oral first-line.
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg up to 72 hours only.
Ulipristal delays restart of progestogen contraception by 5 days.
Repeat pregnancy test in 3 weeks if delayed menses.
explanation.pearls: If BMI is over 26, double the levonorgestrel dose to 3 mg or use ulipristal or copper IUD instead - standard 1.5 mg levonorgestrel is markedly less effective at higher BMI.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare Emergency Contraception

options.rationale: Yuzpe regimen has high nausea/vomiting rates and inferior efficacy and is reserved for situations where dedicated emergency contraception is unavailable. (Source: FSRH Emergency Contraception)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare Emergency Contraception

options.rationale: LNG-IUS is not currently endorsed as emergency contraception in Australian guidance; the copper IUD remains the only IUD method licensed and recommended for this indication. (Source: FSRH Emergency Contraception)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare Emergency Contraception

options.rationale: Copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception (failure under 0.1 percent) and may be inserted up to 120 hours after unprotected sex or 5 days after expected ovulation, with the added benefit of ongoing contraception. (Source: FSRH Emergency Contraception)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare Emergency Contraception

options.rationale: Ulipristal is effective up to 120 hours after intercourse but is less effective than copper IUD overall and does not provide ongoing contraception; a reasonable alternative if she declines IUD. (Source: FSRH Emergency Contraception)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare Emergency Contraception

options.rationale: Levonorgestrel is licensed only up to 72 hours and is less effective than ulipristal or copper IUD; at 78 hours it is outside the licensed window. (Source: FSRH Emergency Contraception)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare Emergency Contraception

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage is defined as three or more consecutive losses in Australian guidance (some bodies now use two). Identifiable causes include antiphospholipid syndrome (5 to 15 percent), parental chromosomal rearrangement (3 to 5 percent), uterine anomalies (10 to 15 percent on imaging), uncontrolled thyroid disease and diabetes. About 50 percent remain unexplained. Treatment is cause-directed - aspirin plus LMWH for confirmed APS doubles live-birth rates. Routine inherited thrombophilia screening, immune therapies and progesterone for unexplained loss are not supported.
key_points: Define as 3 (or 2 per some guidelines) consecutive pregnancy losses.
First-line tests: APS screen, karyotype both partners, pelvic USS, TFT.
APS treatment: low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH from positive pregnancy test.
Inherited thrombophilia screen not routinely indicated.
Around 50 percent remain unexplained with good prognosis on supportive care.
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid antibodies must be positive on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart to confirm APS - a single result is not sufficient before committing to long-term aspirin plus LMWH.

options.rationale: Australian and RCOG guidance recommend offering antiphospholipid screen (lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, anti-beta2 GPI), parental karyotyping, pelvic imaging for uterine anatomy and thyroid function after three consecutive losses. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage)
Luteal phase defect testing is not validated and luteal phase support has unclear benefit in unselected recurrent miscarriage. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage)
Endometrial biopsy and TORCH panel are not routine first-line investigations; chronic endometritis is emerging research but not standard. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage)

Inherited thrombophilia screening is not recommended for recurrent first-trimester loss outside research settings; only antiphospholipid syndrome screening is supported. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage)
Waiting until a fourth loss delays diagnosis; uterine cavity assessment is part of the initial workup at three consecutive losses. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Subfertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (6 months if the woman is 35 or older). Australian initial workup includes mid-luteal progesterone for ovulation, TSH, prolactin, FBE, pelvic USS for anatomy and AFC, plus semen analysis for the partner. Tubal patency testing (HyCoSy or HSG) is added if these are normal. Time to referral to a fertility specialist is shorter (6 months) if the woman is 35 or older, has known anovulation, tubal disease, endometriosis or significant male factor.
key_points: Define subfertility: 12 months (or 6 months if woman 35+).
First-line female: mid-luteal progesterone, TSH, prolactin, pelvic USS.
First-line male: semen analysis (WHO 2021 criteria).
AMH guides IVF planning, not natural fertility prognosis.
Early specialist referral if known tubal, endometriosis or male factor.
explanation.pearls: Mid-luteal progesterone greater than 30 nmol/L confirms ovulation; persistently low results despite regular cycles suggest luteal-phase deficiency or anovulatory bleeds, prompting cycle tracking with serial USS.

options.rationale: Australian primary care guidance recommends mid-luteal progesterone (about 7 days before next expected period) to confirm ovulation as the first-line test in regular cycles, alongside semen analysis for the male partner. (Source: RACGP Fertility)
Postcoital testing has poor reproducibility and is no longer recommended in mainstream subfertility workup. (Source: RACGP Fertility)
AMH is useful for predicting IVF response and timing decisions but does not predict natural fertility and is not first-line in a woman under 35 with regular cycles. (Source: RACGP Fertility)
Laparoscopy is reserved for suspected endometriosis or after non-invasive tests; it is not an initial investigation in unexplained subfertility. (Source: RACGP Fertility)
Tubal patency testing is second-line, indicated when basic ovulation and semen tests are normal or when pelvic infection or endometriosis is suspected. (Source: RACGP Fertility)

explanation.summary: PCOS is diagnosed by Rotterdam criteria (any 2 of oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism clinical or biochemical, polycystic morphology) after excluding mimics. Management is goal-directed: COCP for cycle regulation, hirsutism and contraception; metformin if metabolic features dominate or in addition; anti-androgens (spironolactone, cyproterone) for hirsutism on top of reliable contraception. Lifestyle change is foundational - even 5 percent weight loss improves cycle regularity and metabolic profile. Annual screening for impaired glucose tolerance and mental health.
key_points: Rotterdam: any 2 of oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic morphology.
COCP first-line if not pregnancy-seeking.
Metformin if metabolic features predominate or alongside COCP.
Spironolactone for hirsutism only with reliable contraception.
Lifestyle first - 5 percent weight loss restores cycles in many.
explanation.pearls: Endometrial cancer risk in PCOS rises sharply if menses occur fewer than every 3 months; either COCP or cyclical progestogen for endometrial protection is mandatory long-term.

options.rationale: International evidence-based PCOS guideline first-line for cycle regulation, hyperandrogenism and contraception is a combined oral contraceptive, in combination with lifestyle modification. (Source: International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline)

Metformin is recommended as an adjunct or first-line if metabolic features predominate, but COCP outperforms metformin for hirsutism and menstrual regulation. (Source: International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline)
Anti-androgens require effective contraception because of risk of feminisation of a male fetus; should follow or accompany COCP, not precede it. (Source: International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline)
Clomifene is an ovulation induction agent for women seeking conception, not for cycle regulation in a woman avoiding pregnancy. (Source: International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline)

Cyclical progestogen protects the endometrium but does not address hirsutism, contraception or cardiovascular risk; less complete than COCP for this patient. (Source: International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline)

explanation.summary: The renewed Australian National Cervical Screening Program from December 2017 uses HPV-based primary testing for women 25 to 74 years every 5 years if oncogenic HPV is not detected. HPV 16/18 detection prompts direct colposcopy. HPV non-16/18 detection prompts reflex cytology - high-grade cytology to colposcopy, low-grade or normal cytology to 12-month repeat HPV. Self-collection is offered universally as an option since July 2022. Exit testing at 70 to 74 ends screening if HPV-negative.
key_points: Routine screen: HPV-based, age 25 to 74, every 5 years.
HPV 16/18 detected: refer for colposcopy.
HPV non-16/18: reflex cytology; high-grade triages to colposcopy.
Self-collection now universally available.
Vaccinated women still need screening - vaccine does not cover all oncogenic types.
explanation.pearls: Self-collected vaginal swabs have equivalent sensitivity to clinician-collected samples for HPV detection - offer them to women who decline speculum examination including survivors of trauma.

options.rationale: Screening starts at age 25 regardless of pregnancy status; deferring to age 30 misses preventable high-grade abnormalities. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

The National Cervical Screening Program uses HPV-based primary screening from age 25 to 74 every 5 years if oncogenic HPV is not detected, with reflex liquid-based cytology when HPV positive. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

Australia replaced 2-yearly Pap cytology with 5-yearly HPV primary testing in 2017 because HPV testing has superior sensitivity for high-grade lesions. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

Three-yearly screening is recommended for women who are HPV positive non-16/18 with low-grade cytology under the surveillance pathway, not as primary interval. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

Colposcopy is not a screening test; it is indicated only for HPV 16/18 detection, persistent HPV other-types with abnormal cytology, or symptoms. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Endometrial hyperplasia is divided into hyperplasia without atypia (1 to 3 percent progression) and atypical hyperplasia (28 percent progression and high rate of co-existent endometrioid adenocarcinoma). Postmenopausal women with atypia are offered total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Premenopausal women wishing fertility receive LNG-IUS with 3 to 6 monthly biopsies until two consecutive negative samples. Risk factors include unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, PCOS, Lynch syndrome, obesity and chronic anovulation.
key_points: Atypia: 25 to 40 percent concurrent carcinoma risk; hysterectomy + BSO if postmenopausal.
No atypia: progestogen treatment (oral or LNG-IUS) and surveillance.
LNG-IUS preferred fertility-sparing option for atypia.
Endometrial ablation contraindicated in atypia.
Manage obesity and oestrogen exposure to prevent recurrence.
explanation.pearls: Lynch syndrome screening (Amsterdam criteria or immunohistochemistry on the hysterectomy specimen for MMR proteins) is indicated for all atypical hyperplasia cases under age 50.

options.rationale: Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia carries a 25 to 40 percent risk of concurrent endometrial carcinoma and 28 percent progression risk; total hysterectomy with BSO is first-line in postmenopausal women. (Source: RANZCOG Endometrial Hyperplasia)

Oral high-dose progestogens are an alternative when surgery is contraindicated; LNG-IUS gives more consistent endometrial exposure when medical therapy is required. (Source: RANZCOG Endometrial Hyperplasia)
Delayed treatment of confirmed atypical hyperplasia risks progression to invasive carcinoma; biopsy already confirms the lesion. (Source: RANZCOG Endometrial Hyperplasia)

LNG-IUS is reserved for atypical hyperplasia in fertility-sparing or unfit-for-surgery women with 6-monthly endometrial biopsies; not first-line in postmenopausal women fit for surgery. (Source: RANZCOG Endometrial Hyperplasia)

Endometrial ablation is contraindicated in atypical hyperplasia because residual endometrial tissue can harbour or develop carcinoma that is then occult on subsequent imaging. (Source: RANZCOG Endometrial Hyperplasia)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding from small intramural or subserosal fibroids with a normal cavity responds well to LNG-IUS (Mirena). Submucosal fibroids (FIGO type 0, 1, 2) distort the cavity and may displace the device - hysteroscopic myomectomy is preferred. Tranexamic acid and NSAIDs are useful adjuncts on bleeding days. GnRH agonists with add-back are reserved for pre-operative shrinkage or perimenopausal bridging. UAE, focused ultrasound, myomectomy and hysterectomy are procedural options matched to fertility wishes and symptom severity.
key_points: Intramural fibroid + normal cavity: LNG-IUS first.
Submucosal fibroid: hysteroscopic myomectomy.
Tranexamic acid and NSAIDs on bleeding days as adjuncts.
GnRH agonist - short-term pre-op or perimenopausal bridging.
Hysterectomy is definitive if family complete and other measures fail.
explanation.pearls: A submucosal fibroid greater than 50 percent intramural (FIGO type 2) often expels an LNG-IUS within 3 months - check cavity contour with saline-infusion sonohysterography before insertion if uncertain.

options.rationale: UAE is a uterus-conserving procedural option after failed or unsuitable medical therapy; medical management with LNG-IUS is offered first when appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)
Combined oral contraceptive reduces bleeding modestly compared with LNG-IUS and exposes the patient to oestrogen; second-line in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)
Hysterectomy is definitive but the patient explicitly wishes to avoid major surgery; medical therapy should be tried first when feasible. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

RANZCOG and RACGP first-line medical therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding from intramural fibroids with normal cavity is LNG-IUS, with reduction in bleeding of around 80 percent at 6 months. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)
GnRH agonists are used short-term pre-operatively to shrink fibroids or in selected cases; not first-line long-term medical therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by intractable nausea/vomiting with weight loss greater than 5 percent, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, typically peaking 8 to 12 weeks. PUQE-24 stratifies severity. First-line outpatient is pyridoxine plus doxylamine; second-line metoclopramide, ondansetron or prochlorperazine. Admission criteria include failure of oral antiemetics, ketonuria 2+ or more, weight loss greater than 5 percent and inability to tolerate oral fluids. Always give thiamine 100 mg IV before glucose-containing fluids to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
key_points: PUQE-24 score guides outpatient versus inpatient.
Thiamine before dextrose to prevent Wernicke.
First-line oral: pyridoxine + doxylamine.
Second-line: metoclopramide, ondansetron, prochlorperazine.
Refractory: corticosteroids or admission to nutritional support.
explanation.pearls: Suspect molar pregnancy when nausea is severe and beta-hCG is markedly elevated (over 200000 IU/L) without a viable singleton on ultrasound - send a TVUS even when nausea seems to explain the picture.

sources.label: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Discharge is inappropriate with significant ketonuria, postural drop and failed first-line oral therapy; she needs IV rehydration and parenteral antiemetic. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: PUQE 13 or more with dehydration and ketonuria warrants admission; thiamine before glucose-containing fluids prevents Wernicke encephalopathy; ondansetron is second-line antiemetic when pyridoxine and doxylamine fail in Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Giving dextrose before thiamine in a malnourished pregnant woman risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must come first. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after failure of conventional antiemetics; not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate with frequent vomiting and dehydration; IV antiemetics and IV fluids are required initially. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy typically presents in the third trimester with itch (often palms/soles) and raised bile acids without a rash. Stillbirth risk rises sharply once total bile acids reach 100 micromol/L or more. Pruritus is managed symptomatically with ursodeoxycholic acid (improves itch and biochemistry but not stillbirth at high levels). Delivery timing is bile-acid driven: under 40 micromol/L delivery by 39 weeks; 40 to 99 deliver by 38 to 39 weeks; 100 or more deliver by 35 to 36 weeks. Symptoms resolve within days of birth; recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancy is 60 to 90 percent.
key_points: Bile acids 100+ - deliver at 35 to 36 weeks.
Bile acids 40 to 99 - deliver by 38 to 39 weeks.
Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch but not stillbirth at high bile-acid levels.
CTG and Doppler do not predict stillbirth in cholestasis.
Recurrence risk 60 to 90 percent in subsequent pregnancies.
explanation.pearls: Postnatal recovery of bile acids and ALT should occur within 4 to 6 weeks; persistent abnormalities warrant hepatology referral for chronic cholestatic liver disease and oestrogen-containing contraception should be deferred until biochemistry normalises.

options.rationale: Cholestasis itself is not an indication for caesarean, and 39 weeks is too late given the bile-acid threshold; vaginal birth at 36 weeks is appropriate. (Source: RCOG Obstetric Cholestasis Green-top)

CTG and Doppler do not reliably predict stillbirth in cholestasis; reassuring surveillance does not justify expectant management when bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L. (Source: RCOG Obstetric Cholestasis Green-top)
Outpatient temporising at this bile-acid level delays delivery beyond the 35 to 36 week stillbirth-risk inflection point. (Source: RCOG Obstetric Cholestasis Green-top)

Total bile acids 100 micromol/L or more substantially elevate the risk of stillbirth from around 35 weeks; RANZCOG and RCOG support induction at 36 weeks to minimise that risk. (Source: RCOG Obstetric Cholestasis Green-top)

Ursodeoxycholic acid improves maternal pruritus but no major trial has shown reduced stillbirth at high bile-acid levels; deferring delivery for medical optimisation is not supported. (Source: RCOG Obstetric Cholestasis Green-top)

explanation.summary: Significant varicella exposure in pregnancy (household, indoors more than 5 minutes face to face, or hospital ward contact) requires confirmation of maternal immunity. If IgG-negative, give VZIG within 96 hours (up to 10 days is licensed in some sources) to attenuate maternal disease and reduce fetal infection. If chickenpox subsequently develops, oral aciclovir within 24 hours of rash onset is offered if more than 20 weeks. IV aciclovir for any pneumonitis, neurological involvement or severe disease. Maternal exposure within 7 days of delivery requires neonatal VZIG.
key_points: Confirm immunity with VZV IgG urgently after exposure.
Non-immune - VZIG within 96 hours of exposure.
If rash develops over 20 weeks - oral aciclovir within 24 hours.
Severe maternal disease or pneumonitis - IV aciclovir.
Vaccinate postnatally before discharge if non-immune.
explanation.pearls: Fetal varicella syndrome (skin scarring along dermatomes, limb hypoplasia, chorioretinitis) occurs only with maternal infection before 20 weeks; later infection risks neonatal disease if maternal rash develops 7 days before to 7 days after delivery.

options.rationale: Oral aciclovir prophylaxis is reserved for situations where VZIG is unavailable or after 96 hours; VZIG within 96 hours remains the preferred first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Varicella in Pregnancy)

Maternal chickenpox in pregnancy carries 1 to 2 percent fetal varicella syndrome before 28 weeks and severe maternal morbidity from varicella pneumonitis; reassurance alone is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Varicella in Pregnancy)
Live varicella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy; it cannot be used for post-exposure prophylaxis in pregnant women. (Source: RANZCOG Varicella in Pregnancy)
IV aciclovir is reserved for established varicella complicated by pneumonitis or severe disease, not asymptomatic post-exposure prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Varicella in Pregnancy)

Australian guidance is to confirm non-immunity by urgent VZV IgG and administer VZIG within 96 hours of exposure if negative, to reduce maternal severity and fetal infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG Varicella in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Postnatal hypertension follows pre-eclampsia in around 30 percent of cases and can peak at days 3 to 6. Target BP under 140/90 (or under 135/85 if comorbid). Breastfeeding-compatible agents include enalapril and captopril (preferred), labetalol, nifedipine MR, and metoprolol. Avoid methyldopa (postnatal depression risk), atenolol (concentrates in milk), ARBs in newborn period and diuretics during established breastfeeding. Review BP weekly until controlled and at 6 weeks postnatal; refer to cardiovascular health review by 6 months given doubled lifetime CV risk.
key_points: Target BP under 140/90 postnatal.
First-line breastfeeding: enalapril or captopril.
Second-line: labetalol, nifedipine MR, metoprolol.
Avoid: methyldopa postnatal, atenolol in breastfeeding, ARBs.
Lifetime CV risk doubled - refer for 6-month review.
explanation.pearls: Pre-eclampsia predicts a doubling of lifetime cardiovascular and stroke risk - schedule a 6-month structured cardiovascular review with lipids, glucose and BMI rather than treating it as a one-off pregnancy event.

options.rationale: Methyldopa is a pregnancy agent with sedative and depressive effects; it is generally avoided postnatally because better-tolerated options are available. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Atenolol is concentrated in breast milk and is generally avoided in breastfeeding mothers due to risk of neonatal bradycardia and hypoglycaemia. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)
BP 152/98 with bradycardia at 6 days postpartum needs intervention now; delaying review for a week risks severe hypertension and cardiovascular events. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Enalapril is the postnatal antihypertensive of choice when labetalol is poorly tolerated or BP remains elevated; it is compatible with breastfeeding and has good cardiovascular evidence. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Nifedipine add-on is reasonable, but the woman is bradycardic on labetalol; switching to enalapril removes the symptomatic side effect rather than compounding it. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: The modified WHO classification of maternal cardiovascular risk classes pulmonary arterial hypertension, severe systemic ventricular dysfunction (EF under 30 percent or NYHA III/IV), severe mitral or aortic stenosis, severe coarctation, Marfan with aortic root over 45 mm and bicuspid valve with aortic root over 50 mm as class IV - pregnancy contraindicated. Counselling should be non-judgemental but explicit and accompanied by effective contraception, ideally LNG-IUS. If pregnancy occurs, urgent referral to a tertiary cardio-obstetric service for early termination discussion or coordinated specialised care.
key_points: Modified WHO IV cardiac disease - pregnancy contraindicated.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension carries up to 30 percent maternal mortality.
Effective contraception, ideally LNG-IUS, is essential.
Macitentan and ambrisentan are major teratogens.
Refer accidental pregnancy urgently to tertiary cardio-obstetric service.
explanation.pearls: Insertion of an LNG-IUS in a patient with significant pulmonary hypertension should be performed in a monitored setting because vasovagal response to insertion can precipitate pulmonary hypertensive crisis - have IV access and anaesthetic backup available.

sources.label: ESC Cardiovascular Disease during Pregnancy Guidelines

options.rationale: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is WHO class IV (pregnancy contraindicated; maternal mortality up to 30 percent); LARC (LNG-IUS) is the preferred contraceptive in modified WHO 4 cardiac disease. (Source: RANZCOG Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy)

Surrogacy may be discussed but only after frank discussion of contraindication; first step is to offer effective contraception and refer to a high-risk team. (Source: RANZCOG Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy)

Caesarean does not alter the maternal mortality from peripartum cardiac decompensation and pulmonary hypertensive crisis; mode of delivery does not change the underlying contraindication. (Source: RANZCOG Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy)

Endothelin receptor antagonists are teratogenic but ceasing all pulmonary vasodilators destabilises maternal physiology; pregnancy itself remains contraindicated regardless of medication adjustment. (Source: RANZCOG Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy)
Macitentan is an endothelin receptor antagonist with severe teratogenicity (limb and craniofacial defects); cannot continue without contraception. (Source: RANZCOG Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: OASIS occurs in around 2 to 3 percent of vaginal births. Sultan classification: 3a less than 50 percent EAS thickness; 3b more than 50 percent EAS thickness; 3c full thickness EAS with IAS involvement; 4 includes rectal mucosa. Repair in theatre with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (typically amoxicillin-clavulanate or cefazolin plus metronidazole) by an experienced operator. Postoperative analgesia, laxatives for 10 to 14 days, dedicated physiotherapy and follow-up at 6 to 12 weeks. Future delivery: counselling about elective caesarean if symptomatic, vaginal birth otherwise reasonable.
key_points: Sultan 3c: more than 50 percent EAS + IAS involvement.
Theatre repair with regional or general anaesthesia.
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics at repair and oral course postnatal.
Postoperative laxatives 10 to 14 days, no NSAIDs after 4th degree.
Follow-up at 6 to 12 weeks with symptom review and physiotherapy.
explanation.pearls: Endoanal ultrasound at 12 weeks postnatal is the gold-standard assessment of repair integrity and predicts the success of subsequent vaginal delivery; offer it to all OASIS patients planning further pregnancies.

sources.label: RCOG Third- and Fourth-degree Perineal Tears Green-top

options.rationale: Delaying repair beyond 12 hours increases infection risk and impairs healing; repair should occur as soon as conditions allow. (Source: RANZCOG Perineal Trauma)
Sphincter ends must be identified and reapproximated; closing skin only without sphincter repair leaves anal incontinence risk extremely high. (Source: RANZCOG Perineal Trauma)

Third-degree tears require repair in theatre with adequate lighting, regional or general anaesthesia and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics; primary repair on labour bed risks poor outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG Perineal Trauma)
Bedside repair of OASIS is associated with poorer functional outcomes; theatre conditions with surgical assistance are required. (Source: RANZCOG Perineal Trauma)

Defunctioning stoma is not used routinely for OASIS; primary repair in theatre with antibiotics is standard, with stoma reserved for fourth-degree tears with rectal involvement and breakdown. (Source: RANZCOG Perineal Trauma)

explanation.summary: TTTS complicates around 15 percent of MCDA pregnancies and is diagnosed by DVP under 2 cm in donor and DVP over 8 cm in recipient before 20 weeks (or over 10 cm at 20 to 26 weeks). Quintero staging from I (oligo + poly, both bladders seen) through V (death of one twin) guides counselling. Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses is first-line for stages II to IV between 16 and 26 weeks, with dual survival around 65 percent. Without treatment, perinatal mortality is up to 90 percent. MCDA twins should be scanned every 2 weeks from 16 weeks.
key_points: MCDA twins: 2-weekly USS from 16 weeks.
TTTS: DVP under 2 cm donor + over 8 cm recipient.
Quintero stages I to V.
Fetoscopic laser is first-line for stages II to IV.
Dual survival around 65 percent post-laser.
explanation.pearls: Twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence (TAPS) is the chronic counterpart of TTTS without amniotic fluid discordance - diagnose with middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity discordance (donor MCA PSV over 1.5 MoM, recipient under 0.8 MoM).

options.rationale: Quintero I TTTS without treatment progresses in 30 percent of cases with poor outcomes; expectant management is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
Maternal indometacin causes premature ductal closure and is not part of standard TTTS management. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

Quintero stage I TTTS in MCDA twins at 19 weeks (DVP under 2 cm donor and over 8 cm recipient) is treated with fetoscopic laser photocoagulation, the only therapy shown to improve dual survival. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
Amnioreduction provides only symptomatic relief and is inferior to laser for dual survival; reserved for late-presenting or post-laser cases. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
Selective reduction is reserved for very severe disease with one moribund twin or significant anomaly; not appropriate for Quintero stage I. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is suspected when there is painless mid-trimester loss/preterm birth, especially recurrent. Indication-based cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks is offered after three or more mid-trimester losses. Ultrasound-indicated cerclage at 16 to 24 weeks is offered when prior mid-trimester loss/preterm birth and cervical length less than 25 mm. Rescue cerclage may be offered for cervical dilatation before 26 weeks without infection or membrane rupture. Vaginal progesterone is added if cervical length is less than 25 mm in absence of prior preterm birth history.
key_points: History-indicated cerclage: 3+ mid-trimester losses, place 12-14 weeks.
USS-indicated cerclage: prior PTB + CL under 25 mm at 16-24 weeks.
Rescue cerclage: dilated cervix without infection or PROM under 26 weeks.
Vaginal progesterone: CL under 25 mm without prior PTB.
Exclude infection before any cerclage placement.
explanation.pearls: Bulging membranes can be reduced with steep Trendelenburg and bladder filling before McDonald suture placement - a 16-gauge urinary catheter draining and clamping with 500 mL saline often lifts membranes high enough to allow safe suture passage.

options.rationale: Progesterone alone is appropriate for short cervix without prior preterm birth, but rescue cerclage adds benefit in this high-risk history; progesterone alone is insufficient here. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)
Delaying intervention risks rapid further dilatation and membrane rupture; this patient meets criteria for rescue cerclage now. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)
Pessary use in singleton cervical insufficiency has not consistently reduced preterm birth in trials; cerclage is the evidence-based intervention here. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)
Bed rest has not been shown to prolong pregnancy and increases thromboembolic risk; not an effective stand-alone intervention. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

Two prior mid-trimester losses with short cervix on TVUS support rescue cerclage; with no current infection or membrane rupture, McDonald cerclage offers prolongation of pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Atonic PPH accounts for around 70 percent of major obstetric haemorrhage. Stepwise medical management: oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV then 40 IU infusion, ergometrine 250 to 500 mcg IM or slow IV (avoid if HTN, pre-eclampsia or cardiovascular disease), carboprost 250 mcg IM every 15 minutes up to 8 doses (avoid in asthma), misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual or rectal, and IV tranexamic acid 1 g (repeatable once at 30 minutes). Mechanical measures include bimanual compression, intrauterine balloon tamponade, B-lynch suture and uterine artery ligation; hysterectomy is the last resort.
key_points: Oxytocin first-line; ergometrine second except in HTN.
Carboprost third-line; avoid in asthma.
Misoprostol useful alternative.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV, repeatable at 30 minutes.
Escalate to balloon, B-lynch, ligation, hysterectomy if persistent.
explanation.pearls: Recombinant factor VIIa is reserved for major obstetric haemorrhage with normalised acidosis, calcium and platelets - giving it earlier into a coagulopathic patient does not work and risks thromboembolism.

sources.label: WOMAN Trial Tranexamic Acid in PPH

options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is appropriate after maximal pharmacological therapy has failed, not before completing the uterotonic ladder; carboprost should be tried first. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)
Repeat ergometrine adds little after one failed dose and risks severe hypertension; the next pharmacological step is carboprost. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)
Misoprostol is acceptable when carboprost is contraindicated or unavailable, but carboprost is preferred next-line in this asthma-free patient. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)
Carboprost is the next-line uterotonic after oxytocin and ergometrine have failed in atonic PPH; absence of asthma history makes it appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)
A second dose of tranexamic acid is reasonable if bleeding continues 30 minutes after the first, but does not address ongoing uterine atony; carboprost is needed. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

explanation.summary: Complete hydatidiform mole presents with markedly elevated beta-hCG, snowstorm ultrasound, theca lutein cysts and may cause biochemical hyperthyroidism from beta-hCG cross-reactivity at the TSH receptor. Suction curettage under anaesthesia is the definitive Australian management with histological confirmation. Serial weekly beta-hCG until three consecutive undetectable values then monthly for 6 months detects gestational trophoblastic neoplasia early. Effective contraception is required throughout surveillance to avoid confounding hCG interpretation. Anti-D is given to RhD-negative women at evacuation.
key_points: Complete mole - snowstorm uterus, very high hCG, no fetal parts.
Suction curettage is the definitive treatment.
Serial hCG surveillance detects neoplasia early.
Effective contraception for 6 months protects monitoring.
Theca lutein cysts regress spontaneously.
explanation.pearls: Notify the patient that any subsequent pregnancy needs an early ultrasound at 7-8 weeks and a 6-week postnatal hCG because of the 1-2 percent risk of recurrence.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 38 Gestational Trophoblastic Disease

options.rationale: Medical evacuation with prostaglandins risks haemorrhage and embolisation of trophoblastic tissue and is contraindicated for molar pregnancy management. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)
Imaging and biochemistry are already diagnostic of complete molar pregnancy and delay risks ongoing haemorrhage, hyperthyroidism and pre-eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

Hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy is overtreatment that destroys fertility; theca lutein cysts regress spontaneously and oophorectomy is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

Suction curettage with histology and structured serial beta-hCG surveillance is the standard Australian management; persistent trophoblastic disease is detected by plateauing or rising hCG. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)
Methotrexate is for confirmed gestational trophoblastic neoplasia after evacuation with rising or plateau hCG, not for primary mole management. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease)

explanation.summary: Chorionicity is the single most important determinant of risk and surveillance in twin pregnancy. The T-sign with a thin two-layer membrane indicates monochorionic-diamniotic placentation; the lambda or twin-peak sign indicates dichorionic. Monochorionic twins need fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome surveillance and selective fetal growth restriction. Dichorionic twins need 4-weekly ultrasound from 24 weeks. First trimester is the optimal window for chorionicity assessment because signs become less reliable later in pregnancy.
key_points: T-sign equals monochorionic, lambda-sign equals dichorionic.
Determine chorionicity in the first trimester.
Monochorionic twins need fortnightly surveillance from 16 weeks.
Dichorionic twins need 4-weekly surveillance from 24 weeks.
Refer monochorionic twins early to maternal-fetal medicine.
explanation.pearls: If chorionicity is unclear or assessment is delayed past 14 weeks, treat as monochorionic for the more intensive surveillance schedule rather than risk under-monitoring.

sources.label: ISUOG Practice Guidelines Role of Ultrasound in Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Crown-rump length concordance reassures about size but does not determine chorionicity. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
Yolk sac number helps assess amnionicity in early pregnancy but is no longer reliable after 10 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
Two separate placentas confirm dichorionic but a single placental mass does not exclude dichorionic; first trimester signs are most accurate. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
Discordant fetal sex confirms dichorionic but concordant sex does not exclude dichorionic; ultrasound signs remain primary. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)
The T-sign with a thin two-layer intertwin membrane reliably identifies monochorionic-diamniotic placentation when assessed before 14 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: The manoeuvres that relieve shoulder dystocia also make maternal injury more likely, and the two complications to look for immediately are postpartum haemorrhage, which follows in roughly one in nine of these births, and obstetric anal sphincter injury, which follows in roughly one in twenty five. Both are found by deliberate examination and observation rather than by waiting for them to announce themselves: a systematic inspection of the perineum with a rectal examination to assess the sphincter, and close attention to blood loss and uterine tone through the third stage and the hour afterwards. Documentation of the manoeuvres used, the head to body interval, which shoulder was anterior and who was present is completed at the same time, and the baby is examined for arm movement and clavicular injury. In context, a structured debrief with the parents afterwards is part of the standard, since these births are frightening to witness.
key_points: Postpartum haemorrhage complicates about eleven percent of shoulder dystocia births.
Obstetric anal sphincter injury complicates about four percent.
Examine the perineum and sphincter deliberately rather than waiting for symptoms.
Document manoeuvres, head to body interval, anterior shoulder and personnel.
explanation.pearls: Examine the newborn for arm movement and clavicular crepitus before the parents leave the birth room, and record the findings, because brachial plexus injury noticed later is hard to date.

options.rationale: Shoulder dystocia raises the risk of both obstetric anal sphincter injury and postpartum haemorrhage, so both are actively sought. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder dystocia)
Theatre is needed when a sphincter injury is found or bleeding cannot be controlled in the birth room. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Shoulder dystocia)
Imaging is reserved for a woman with severe pubic pain and difficulty weight bearing afterwards. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Shoulder dystocia)
Tranexamic acid and cross matching belong to the management of an established postpartum haemorrhage. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Shoulder dystocia)
Delaying repair is appropriate only when a woman is too unstable, and a bladder scan is a separate issue. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed when blood pressure is at least 160/110 or hypertension is accompanied by end-organ involvement such as cerebral, hepatic or renal dysfunction. Magnesium sulfate is the first-line eclampsia prophylaxis (Magpie trial), reducing seizures by about 58 percent compared with placebo. Loading dose is 4 g IV over 20 minutes followed by 1 g per hour for 24 hours postpartum. Monitor for toxicity: loss of patellar reflexes (level 3.5-5 mmol/L), respiratory depression (above 5), cardiac arrest (above 10). Calcium gluconate 1 g is the antidote.
key_points: Magnesium sulfate is the first-line eclampsia prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia.
Loading 4 g IV over 20 min, then 1 g/h for 24 hours postpartum.
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output, magnesium level.
Calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote to magnesium toxicity.
Delivery is the only definitive treatment - plan within 24-48 hours.
explanation.pearls: Reduce magnesium infusion rate to 0.5 g per hour if creatinine clearance falls below 30 mL/min because magnesium is renally cleared and toxicity risk rises quickly.

options.rationale: Hydralazine targets blood pressure but does not prevent eclamptic seizures, which is the priority neurological intervention here. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Nifedipine controls blood pressure but does not provide eclampsia seizure prophylaxis and routine ward monitoring is inadequate. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Antenatal steroids are routinely indicated before 35 weeks and the priority here is preventing eclampsia, not lung maturation. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Diuretics are not indicated and may worsen volume status; pre-eclampsia is a vasoconstrictive intravascular volume-deplete state. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Magnesium sulfate is the proven eclampsia prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia with cerebral irritability features and is more effective than antiepileptic alternatives. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid index above 24 cm or single deepest pocket above 8 cm) has identifiable causes in about 30 percent of cases: gestational diabetes, fetal anomalies (oesophageal atresia, duodenal atresia, neuromuscular disorders affecting swallowing), congenital infection (CMV, parvovirus, syphilis), red cell alloimmunisation and twin-twin transfusion. Workup includes repeat OGTT, detailed anatomy ultrasound, antibody screen, serology and consideration of fetal karyotype if structural anomaly is present. Severe symptomatic polyhydramnios may need amnioreduction; otherwise expectant management with growth surveillance and delivery planning.
key_points: AFI above 24 cm or SDP above 8 cm defines polyhydramnios.
Workup includes OGTT, detailed anatomy, serology, antibody screen.
Causes: diabetes, anomalies, infection, alloimmunisation, twins.
Amnioreduction for severe maternal symptoms only.
Active third stage management - risk of postpartum haemorrhage.
explanation.pearls: Watch for occult fetal anomaly even with normal anatomy scan - oesophageal atresia (absent or small stomach bubble) and duodenal atresia (double bubble) are easily missed on routine views.

options.rationale: Polyhydramnios warrants targeted workup at the time of diagnosis rather than 4-week delay because gestational diabetes can develop after 28 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Polyhydramnios)
Polyhydramnios requires repeat OGTT for late-onset gestational diabetes and detailed re-evaluation of fetal anatomy for swallowing or obstructive abnormalities. (Source: RANZCOG Polyhydramnios)
Amnioreduction is reserved for severe maternal symptoms or preterm labour risk and is not first-line workup. (Source: RANZCOG Polyhydramnios)
Indometacin is rarely used past 32 weeks because of ductus arteriosus risk and is not first-line management. (Source: RANZCOG Polyhydramnios)
Iatrogenic preterm delivery for polyhydramnios alone is inappropriate without other indications and ignores prematurity-related morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG Polyhydramnios)

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk is increased about 20-fold versus baseline non-pregnant women. Australian guidelines stratify based on risk factors: pre-existing (prior VTE, thrombophilia, age above 35, BMI above 30), obstetric (emergency caesarean, prolonged labour, multiple pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, infection), and behavioural (immobility, dehydration). Two or more risk factors post-caesarean warrant 10 days enoxaparin 40 mg daily, while prior VTE, thrombophilia, or multiple major risk factors require 6 weeks. Mechanical methods (stockings, early mobilisation) are universal. DOACs and warfarin are unsafe in breastfeeding, so LMWH is preferred.
key_points: Risk stratify every postpartum woman.
Caesarean plus 2+ risk factors equals 10 days LMWH.
Prior VTE or thrombophilia equals 6 weeks LMWH.
Mechanical prophylaxis is universal.
LMWH is breastfeeding-safe; DOACs and warfarin are not.
explanation.pearls: Wait at least 4 hours after epidural removal before next prophylactic LMWH dose, and 24 hours before any therapeutic dose, to minimise spinal haematoma risk per ANZCA neuraxial recommendations.

sources.label: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum
ANZCA Anticoagulation and Neuraxial Anaesthesia Guidance

options.rationale: Pharmacological prophylaxis is generally started 6-12 hours postoperatively after caesarean once haemostasis is secured and bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: Caesarean delivery with additional risk factors (BMI above 30, age above 35, emergency procedure) warrants 10 days of LMWH plus mechanical methods. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: Six weeks of prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk patients (prior VTE, thrombophilia, more risk factors); this case warrants 10 days. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated in breastfeeding due to limited safety data and active excretion in breast milk. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum

options.rationale: Caesarean delivery with two or more additional risk factors meets the threshold for LMWH; withholding prophylaxis underestimates VTE risk. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum)
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy and Postpartum

explanation.summary: Perimenopausal women still require contraception alongside symptom management. Transdermal estradiol avoids first-pass hepatic effect and has lower VTE and stroke risk than oral oestrogen, making it preferred in women over 45 or with cardiovascular risk factors. A LNG-IUD provides both contraception and endometrial protection from systemic oestrogen and is the preferred progestogen in perimenopause. Sequential or cyclical progestogen suits women still having periods to give predictable bleeds; continuous combined is for women past 12 months amenorrhoea. Stop hormonal contraception at 55 or 12 months amenorrhoea above 50.
key_points: Transdermal oestrogen has lower VTE and stroke risk than oral.
LNG-IUD covers endometrial protection and contraception.
Sequential progestogen for perimenopause, continuous when postmenopausal.
Continue contraception until 55 or 12 months amenorrhoea after 50.
Avoid HRT in active breast cancer, VTE, undiagnosed PV bleeding.
explanation.pearls: Use estradiol gel or patch and add micronised progesterone 200 mg orally at night for 12 days monthly if LNG-IUD declined - this combination has the most favourable breast cancer and VTE risk profile among oral options.

sources.label: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy
NICE NG23 Menopause Diagnosis and Management

options.rationale: Continuous combined regimens are designed for postmenopausal women; in perimenopause they cause unscheduled bleeding because of ongoing endogenous cycles. (Source: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy

options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with intact uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma regardless of endogenous activity. (Source: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy

options.rationale: Transdermal oestrogen with a LNG-IUD gives effective symptom control, endometrial protection and contraception, the preferred perimenopausal combination. (Source: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy

options.rationale: Standard combined oral contraceptive doses are higher than menopausal hormone therapy and carry greater cardiovascular and VTE risk especially above 50. (Source: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy

options.rationale: Oral equine oestrogen has higher VTE risk than transdermal estradiol and condoms are less reliable contraception in perimenopause. (Source: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AMS Information Sheet Menopausal Hormone Therapy

explanation.summary: Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) classically follows uterine instrumentation, especially repeated evacuation of retained products of conception, and presents as secondary amenorrhoea or hypomenorrhoea with infertility. The hormonal axis is intact: FSH, LH, oestradiol, prolactin, TSH and AMH are normal. Diagnosis is by saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy. Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis is the treatment, with adjuncts (oestrogen, balloon, intrauterine devices) to prevent re-adhesion and improved pregnancy outcomes after treatment. Future evacuations should be done under ultrasound guidance to minimise recurrence.
key_points: Asherman = intrauterine adhesions after instrumentation in pregnancy.
Normal hormonal axis with secondary amenorrhoea after D and C.
Diagnose with saline sonohysterography or hysteroscopy.
Treat with hysteroscopic adhesiolysis and adhesion prevention.
Future evacuations under ultrasound guidance.
explanation.pearls: When recurrent miscarriage prompts repeat evacuation, suction curettage under ultrasound guidance halves the risk of new adhesion formation compared with blind sharp curettage; counsel and plan for image-guided procedures.

sources.label: AAGL Practice Guidelines on Intrauterine Adhesions

options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is unnecessary when prolactin is normal and the clinical setting points to a structural endometrial cause. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)
Day 21 progesterone is unreliable in amenorrhoea (no day 21 reference) and does not address the most likely intrauterine adhesion diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)
Hormonal therapy without investigating intrauterine pathology delays diagnosis; structural adhesions will not respond to hormone therapy alone. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)
Direct visualisation by saline sonohysterography or hysteroscopy is the standard investigation for suspected Asherman syndrome after instrumentation. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)
Laparoscopy evaluates pelvic structures but not the uterine cavity which is the site of suspected pathology here. (Source: RANZCOG Asherman Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Vulval lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis causing porcelain-white atrophic plaques, architectural distortion (loss of labia minora, clitoral phimosis, introital narrowing), itch and dyspareunia. Diagnosis is clinical with biopsy to confirm and exclude differential VIN or squamous cell carcinoma. First-line treatment is ultra-potent topical steroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05 percent ointment) nightly for 4 weeks, then alternate nights for 4 weeks, then twice weekly maintenance. Lifelong follow-up because of about 5 percent risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma. Daily emollient, avoid soap, treat any concurrent candidiasis or dermatitis.
key_points: Porcelain-white plaques with architectural distortion - think lichen sclerosus.
Biopsy confirms diagnosis and excludes VIN or SCC.
Clobetasol 0.05 percent ointment is first-line.
Lifelong monitoring - 5 percent risk of vulval SCC.
Use emollient, avoid soap, treat candida or dermatitis.
explanation.pearls: Resistant lichen sclerosus or steroid-tachyphylaxis can be managed with topical tacrolimus 0.1 percent off-label, but use under specialist supervision because the long-term risk of SCC with calcineurin inhibitors on vulval skin is not fully established.

sources.label: British Association of Dermatologists Lichen Sclerosus Guideline

options.rationale: Architectural change and porcelain-white plaques are not consistent with chronic candidiasis; lichen sclerosus is the likely diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Lichen Sclerosus)

Biopsy confirms diagnosis and excludes differential vulval intraepithelial neoplasia; ultra-potent topical steroid is the first-line treatment for lichen sclerosus. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Lichen Sclerosus)
Surgery is reserved for biopsy-confirmed neoplastic change or severe scarring causing functional problems unresponsive to medical therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Lichen Sclerosus)
Vaginal oestrogen may help atrophy but does not treat lichen sclerosus, which requires steroid therapy after biopsy. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Lichen Sclerosus)
Oral antifungal is not indicated when there is no microbiological evidence of candidiasis and morphology suggests lichen sclerosus. (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Lichen Sclerosus)

explanation.summary: Bishop score combines cervical dilation, effacement, consistency, position and station to determine induction approach. Score below 6 indicates unripe cervix and need for cervical ripening (prostaglandin E2 gel or pessary, or mechanical balloon catheter) before amniotomy and oxytocin, while Bishop at least 7 (favourable) allows direct ARM with oxytocin. Continuous CTG monitoring is needed with prostaglandins due to risk of hyperstimulation. Induction at 41+0 to 41+3 reduces perinatal mortality versus expectant management. Always counsel on indication, alternatives, success rates and risk of failed induction.
key_points: Bishop score guides induction method.
Below 6 - ripen with prostaglandin or balloon first.
At least 7 - direct ARM plus oxytocin.
Continuous CTG with prostaglandin induction.
Induce at 41+0 to 41+3 weeks to reduce stillbirth.
explanation.pearls: Mechanical methods (Cook double balloon or single Foley) are preferred over prostaglandins for ripening in women with prior caesarean, asthma or fetal heart rate concerns; balloon does not cause tachysystole and avoids the hyperstimulation risk of prostaglandins.

options.rationale: Oxytocin is inefficient on an unripe cervix (Bishop 4) and significantly increases caesarean rate; pre-ripening is required first. (Source: RANZCOG Induction of Labour)
Amniotomy alone with unfavourable cervix often fails; cervical ripening before ARM improves successful vaginal delivery rates. (Source: RANZCOG Induction of Labour)
Beyond 41+0 weeks, induction is recommended; further expectant management increases stillbirth and perinatal morbidity risk. (Source: RANZCOG Induction of Labour)
Misoprostol requires CTG monitoring during ripening due to risk of uterine tachysystole and fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG Induction of Labour)
Bishop score under 6 requires cervical ripening with prostaglandin or balloon first, followed by ARM and oxytocin once the cervix is favourable. (Source: RANZCOG Induction of Labour)

explanation.summary: Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) are first-line in postpartum women because of high effectiveness and minimal user dependency. The LNG-IUD provides 5 to 8 years of contraception, reduces menstrual bleeding and is compatible with breastfeeding. Insertion at the 6-week postnatal check is standard; immediate postpartum insertion (within 10 minutes of placental delivery) is gaining favour but has higher expulsion rates. Combined hormonal contraception is delayed until at least 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women because of VTE risk and potential lactation reduction. Etonogestrel implant is an equally good LARC choice if intrauterine device is declined.
key_points: LARC preferred in postpartum and most other settings.
Combined hormonal contraception delayed in breastfeeding until 6 weeks.
LAM unreliable once solids start or menses returns.
DMPA acceptable but delayed return to fertility.
POP needs strict daily timing within a 3-hour window.
explanation.pearls: Etonogestrel subdermal implant offers 3 years of contraception with no insertion-related expulsion risk and is the preferred LARC if a patient declines an intrauterine procedure or wants the option to remove without a clinic visit.

options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is not recommended before 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women and may reduce milk supply. (Source: Australian Contraception Handbook)
LAM efficacy falls rapidly once solids start, feeds drop below every 4 hours, or menses returns; the patient needs reliable longer-term contraception. (Source: Australian Contraception Handbook)
LNG-IUD is long-acting, reversible, safe in breastfeeding and avoids daily compliance issues; insertion at the 6-week check is standard. (Source: Australian Contraception Handbook)
DMPA is acceptable but delayed return to fertility for up to 12 months is a disadvantage when conception is planned in 18 months. (Source: Australian Contraception Handbook)
POP requires strict daily compliance with a 3-hour window which the patient has stated she cannot reliably maintain. (Source: Australian Contraception Handbook)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is diagnosed when nausea and vomiting in pregnancy cause weight loss above 5%, dehydration or ketosis. First-line outpatient therapy is pyridoxine with doxylamine; metoclopramide and ondansetron are added if no response. Admission criteria include inability to tolerate oral fluids, ketonuria, electrolyte derangement and weight loss above 5%. Inpatient therapy is IV rehydration with Hartmann, parenteral antiemetics and thiamine before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Refractory cases benefit from corticosteroids. Screen for thyroid dysfunction (transient gestational thyrotoxicosis is common from high beta-hCG) but treat only if persistent and clinically significant.
key_points: Diagnose HG with 5% weight loss, dehydration or ketosis.
Thiamine 100 mg IV before any dextrose.
Hartmann preferred over saline for IV rehydration.
Pyridoxine with doxylamine remains first-line oral therapy.
Beta-hCG mediated transient hyperthyroidism rarely needs treatment.
explanation.pearls: Ondansetron in the first trimester has been associated with a small absolute increase in cleft palate (around 3 extra per 10000 births); informed consent is standard but it remains widely used given the morbidity of untreated hyperemesis.

sources.label: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Severe dehydration with ketonuria and orthostatic hypotension requires admission and IV rehydration, not outpatient management. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after failure of standard antiemetics; oral therapy is not feasible in this patient. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Glucose without thiamine cover risks Wernicke encephalopathy; Hartmann is the preferred crystalloid and electrolyte correction must not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Admission for IV rehydration with thiamine prophylaxis and structured antiemetic regimen is standard for severe hyperemesis with dehydration and ketosis. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Termination is not first-line management; most hyperemesis settles with adequate medical therapy by 16 to 20 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss over 500 mL after vaginal birth or 1000 mL after caesarean within 24 hours. The 4 Ts identify cause: tone (atony, most common), trauma, tissue (retained), thrombin (coagulopathy). Stepwise medical management for atony: oxytocin 5 to 10 IU IV plus infusion, ergometrine 250 micrograms IM, carboprost 250 micrograms IM, misoprostol 800 micrograms PR. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth reduces death from bleeding (WOMAN trial) and should be given early. Mechanical escalation includes uterine balloon tamponade then surgical interventions (B-Lynch, internal iliac ligation, hysterectomy).
key_points: Oxytocin infusion plus ergometrine is the standard second step.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality.
Avoid ergometrine in pre-eclampsia or hypertension.
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma.
Activate MTP early when bleeding exceeds 1500 mL.
explanation.pearls: Quantitative blood loss assessment using calibrated drapes and weighed swabs detects PPH earlier than visual estimation, which routinely underestimates loss by 30 to 50%.

sources.label: WHO Recommendations on Prevention and Treatment of PPH

options.rationale: Misoprostol is second-line and not as effective as injectable uterotonics; ergometrine is preferred next if not contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Theatre is the next step only after medical management and mechanical tamponade have failed; immediate hysterectomy is not the second step. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Carboprost is third-line after oxytocin and ergometrine fail; skipping ergometrine is not standard. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Mechanical tamponade with the Bakri balloon is a later step after medical therapy fails; pharmacological escalation comes first. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Ergometrine plus tranexamic acid is second-line after oxytocin failure for atonic PPH and reduces death from bleeding when given within 3 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses HPV testing with reflex cytology, with 5-yearly screening from age 25 to 74. Result categories are: HPV negative (5-year recall), intermediate risk (HPV not 16/18 with normal, possible LSIL or LSIL cytology - repeat at 12 months), and higher risk (HPV 16/18 or HSIL+ cytology - colposcopy referral). Self-collection has been available to all eligible women since 2022. Symptomatic patients with bleeding or visible lesion require a co-test regardless of routine schedule. Recently vaccinated cohorts still need screening.
key_points: 5-yearly HPV-based screening from age 25 to 74.
HPV 16/18 or HSIL cytology triggers colposcopy.
Intermediate risk gets a 12-month repeat CST.
Self-collection now available for all eligible women.
Vaccination does not replace screening.
explanation.pearls: A persistent intermediate-risk result at 12 months (still HPV positive not 16/18) escalates to colposcopy referral regardless of cytology grade; persistence is the key trigger.

sources.label: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia

options.rationale: Colposcopy is reserved for HPV 16/18, HSIL, glandular abnormalities or persistent intermediate-risk results, not LSIL on the first detection. (Source: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia)
source_refs: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia

options.rationale: Intermediate-risk result (HPV not 16/18 with LSIL) is managed by repeat CST at 12 months; most HPV infections clear spontaneously within this interval. (Source: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia)
source_refs: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia

options.rationale: 5-year recall applies only to HPV-negative results; HPV-positive intermediate risk requires 12-month repeat. (Source: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia)
source_refs: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia

options.rationale: HPV vaccination does not treat established infection; vaccination would have been beneficial pre-exposure but is not therapeutic. (Source: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia)
source_refs: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia

options.rationale: LEEP is treatment for biopsy-confirmed HSIL, not a diagnostic step in LSIL with intermediate-risk HPV. (Source: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia)
source_refs: NCSP Guidelines for Cervical Screening in Australia

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes between 24 and 34 weeks is managed expectantly with admission, antenatal corticosteroids and latency antibiotics, aiming to reach 34 weeks unless chorioamnionitis, abruption or non-reassuring fetal status supervene. Erythromycin (10 days) is the recommended latency antibiotic from the ORACLE I trial; amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is contraindicated because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. Surveillance includes daily fetal monitoring and inflammatory markers and prompt delivery for clinical chorioamnionitis. Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection is reserved for imminent delivery below 30 to 32 weeks.
key_points: Expectant management to 34 weeks if uncomplicated.
Erythromycin 250 mg QID for 10 days as latency antibiotic.
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid contraindicated (raises neonatal NEC).
Magnesium neuroprotection only when delivery imminent.
Deliver early if infection, abruption or fetal compromise.
explanation.pearls: Digital examination dramatically shortens latency and increases infection risk; rely on sterile speculum and ultrasound to assess cervical change in PPROM unless labour is established.

sources.label: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM
Queensland Clinical Guidelines Preterm Labour and Birth

options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid increases neonatal necrotising enterocolitis risk and is contraindicated in PPROM; inpatient care is the standard model. (Source: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 31 weeks adds prematurity risk; expectant management to 34 weeks reduces neonatal morbidity in uncomplicated PPROM. (Source: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

options.rationale: Magnesium neuroprotection is given when preterm delivery is imminent within 24 hours, not for stable expectant management without labour. (Source: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

options.rationale: Expectant management with antenatal corticosteroids and prophylactic erythromycin until 34 weeks is standard for uncomplicated PPROM after 24 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

options.rationale: Tocolysis is not recommended in PPROM without contractions; prophylactic latency antibiotics are standard. (Source: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM)
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes and PPROM

explanation.summary: Obstetric cholestasis is diagnosed by maternal pruritus (often palms and soles, worse at night) with raised bile acids and normal anatomy on imaging. Stillbirth risk rises sharply with bile acids above 100 micromol/L and is materially elevated above 40. Management is symptomatic UDCA with weekly biochemistry and planned early delivery: at 35 to 36 weeks if bile acids above 100, at 36 to 37 weeks for 40 to 99, at 38 to 39 weeks for under 40. Symptoms and biochemistry resolve within weeks of delivery. Recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies is 60 to 70%. Exclude viral hepatitis and biliary disease.
key_points: Bile acids over 100 carry the highest stillbirth risk.
UDCA improves itch and liver biochemistry.
Delivery timing depends on peak bile acid level.
CTG and ultrasound do not reliably predict OC stillbirth.
Recurrence is common in subsequent pregnancies.
explanation.pearls: Bile acid samples in obstetric cholestasis are most accurate when taken non-fasting since postprandial elevation peaks 2 to 4 hours after a meal and gives the highest detected value.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy

options.rationale: UDCA improves maternal pruritus and biochemistry; bile acids in this range warrant delivery at 37 to 38 weeks because of perinatal mortality risk. (Source: RANZCOG Obstetric Cholestasis)
Bile acids above 40 micromol/L confer increased stillbirth risk and warrant active management with earlier delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Obstetric Cholestasis)
Vitamin K and immediate delivery are not first-line at bile acids 60; UDCA and planned delivery at 37 to 38 weeks is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Obstetric Cholestasis)
Sedating antihistamines may help itch at night but do not address stillbirth risk; UDCA and earlier delivery are required. (Source: RANZCOG Obstetric Cholestasis)
N-acetylcysteine has no role in obstetric cholestasis; CTG does not reliably predict the sudden stillbirth seen in this condition. (Source: RANZCOG Obstetric Cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency with a narrow window for ovarian salvage. Classic features are sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting; pain may wax and wane as the ovary detorts and retorts. Ultrasound shows an enlarged ovary, often with a cyst over 5 cm acting as the lead point, and reduced or absent Doppler flow; flow can be preserved in early or partial torsion so Doppler does not exclude the diagnosis. Management is urgent laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation, including for ovaries that appear dusky at theatre because most will regain function. Cystectomy or oophoropexy may be considered at the same operation.
key_points: Severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting suggests torsion.
Ultrasound with Doppler is first-line, but normal flow does not exclude.
Laparoscopic detorsion is the standard intervention.
Preserve dusky ovaries; most regain function.
Consider oophoropexy if predisposing anatomy.
explanation.pearls: Right-sided torsion is more common than left because the sigmoid colon fixes the left adnexa, and a cyst above 5 cm is the most common predisposing lesion in adolescents.

options.rationale: Delayed surgery for suspected torsion risks ovarian necrosis; the ovary cannot be salvaged once infarcted. (Source: RANZCOG Adnexal Torsion)
Ultrasound is the imaging of choice in suspected torsion; CT delays definitive treatment and adds radiation in an adolescent. (Source: RANZCOG Adnexal Torsion)
