Termination decisions require diagnostic confirmation; combined screening provides a risk estimate, not a diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG Prenatal Screening)

explanation.summary: Maternal GBS colonisation is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis in Australia. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis with intravenous benzylpenicillin reduces vertical transmission and early-onset disease by around 80%. The Australian universal screening approach uses a vaginal-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks; risk-based approaches without screening are still used in some centres. The time of the first antibiotic dose feeds directly into the neonatal observation pathway after delivery.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin 3 g intravenous loading then 1.8 g 4-hourly is first line for women without penicillin allergy
Cefazolin is used for low-risk penicillin allergy and clindamycin or vancomycin for high-risk allergy
Adequate prophylaxis means at least one dose 4 hours or more before delivery
Prelabour caesarean section with intact membranes does not require intrapartum prophylaxis
Intrapartum fever above 38 °C triggers broader spectrum antibiotics for chorioamnionitis cover
explanation.pearls: A neonatal early-onset sepsis risk calculator is used at term to integrate maternal antibiotic timing, GBS status and clinical findings into observation versus active treatment decisions.

options.rationale: Universal intrapartum prophylaxis for GBS carriers is recommended in Australia regardless of intrapartum temperature; antibiotics are not contingent on developing chorioamnionitis. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

Intrapartum benzylpenicillin 3 g loading and 1.8 g 4-hourly is the Australian first-line regimen for a GBS-colonised labouring woman without penicillin allergy; documenting the dose time is essential for the newborn risk pathway. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

Vancomycin is reserved for women with high-risk penicillin allergy or proven clindamycin resistance; it is not first-line for a woman with no penicillin allergy. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)
Oral antibiotics do not achieve reliable intra-amniotic concentrations for prophylaxis; intravenous administration is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

GBS colonisation alone is not an indication for caesarean section; prelabour caesarean section with intact membranes is the only delivery mode that does not require intrapartum prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding affects around one in four women in Australia and is a major cause of iron deficiency anaemia. The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device is first-line medical therapy because it reduces blood loss by about 90% and preserves fertility. Tranexamic acid and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories are useful when an intrauterine device is declined or unsuitable. Surgical options are reserved for completed families or failed medical therapy.
key_points: Levonorgestrel intrauterine device reduces menstrual blood loss by around 90%
Combined oral contraceptive pill, tranexamic acid and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories are second-line non-invasive options
Endometrial ablation and hysterectomy are reserved for completed families or failed medical therapy
Iron deficiency anaemia from blood loss requires concurrent iron replacement
Ultrasound is performed to exclude fibroids, polyps and endometrial thickening before treatment
explanation.pearls: Counsel women that irregular bleeding is common in the first three to six months after a levonorgestrel intrauterine device insertion, peaking at four months before settling into oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea.

options.rationale: Endometrial ablation is reserved for women who have completed childbearing and have failed medical therapy; it is not appropriate when fertility preservation is desired. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Hysteroscopy is indicated for abnormal ultrasound findings, persistent intermenstrual bleeding or failed medical therapy, not as first-line management of regular heavy menstrual bleeding with a normal ultrasound. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Cyclical oral progestogens are less effective than the levonorgestrel intrauterine device and are reserved for women who decline an intrauterine device or have contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)
Hysterectomy is a definitive option but is reserved for completed families and failed medical therapy; it does not preserve fertility. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device reduces menstrual blood loss by around 90% and is first-line medical therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding in Australia; it preserves fertility and treats coexisting iron deficiency anaemia. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Routine preconception supplementation in Australia comprises folic acid 400 micrograms daily and iodine 150 micrograms daily. Folic acid must start at least one month before conception and continue through the first trimester to span the neural tube closure window. Iodine continues throughout pregnancy and lactation because of the increased thyroid demand and reduced placental iodine reserves. High-dose folic acid 5 mg is reserved for higher-risk women, including those with previous neural tube defects, diabetes, antiepileptic use or body mass index over 30.
key_points: Folic acid 400 micrograms daily preconception through first trimester is the routine dose
Iodine 150 micrograms daily is recommended preconception through pregnancy and lactation
High-dose folic acid 5 mg is reserved for previous neural tube defect, diabetes, antiepileptics or BMI over 30
Vitamin A above 10,000 international units daily is teratogenic and should be avoided
Rubella, varicella and pertussis serology should be checked and updated preconception
explanation.pearls: Women on valproate or carbamazepine require 5 mg folic acid preconception and ongoing antiepileptic review by a neurologist because of the high risk of neural tube and other major malformations.

options.rationale: Folic acid 400 micrograms daily for at least one month before conception through the first trimester reduces neural tube defects, and iodine 150 micrograms daily is recommended throughout preconception, pregnancy and lactation in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy Counselling)

Folic acid given only after a positive pregnancy test misses the critical neural tube closure window at 21 to 28 days post-conception; supplementation must precede conception. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy Counselling)

High-dose folic acid 5 mg is reserved for higher-risk women: previous neural tube defect, diabetes, antiepileptic use, body mass index over 30, or family history; not for low-risk women. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy Counselling)

High-dose vitamin A is teratogenic in early pregnancy and routine omega-3 or antioxidant supplementation has no fertility or anomaly-prevention benefit at this dose. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy Counselling)

Routine elemental iron and calcium are not universally recommended preconception in women without deficiency; folic acid must precede conception to be effective. (Source: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy Counselling)

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes is diagnosed by a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed between 24 and 28 weeks gestation, using the ADIPS thresholds of fasting 5.1, 1-hour 10.0 and 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L. A single value above threshold establishes the diagnosis. First-line management is lifestyle modification with home capillary glucose monitoring before adding insulin or metformin. Untreated gestational diabetes increases macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, preterm birth and operative delivery rates.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1-hour 10.0, 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L; one value above threshold is diagnostic
Lifestyle modification is first line for at least 1 to 2 weeks before adding pharmacotherapy
Insulin remains first-line pharmacotherapy in Australia though metformin is increasingly accepted
Targets are fasting under 5.0 mmol/L and 1-hour postprandial under 7.4 mmol/L
Postpartum 75 g oral glucose tolerance test is repeated at 6 to 12 weeks to detect persisting diabetes
explanation.pearls: Women diagnosed with gestational diabetes have a 50% lifetime risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes and should have annual fasting glucose or 2-yearly oral glucose tolerance testing postpartum.

options.rationale: Her 1-hour value of 9.6 mmol/L is above the ADIPS threshold of 8.5 mmol/L and meets criteria for gestational diabetes; describing the test as normal is incorrect. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Consensus)

A single value at or above the ADIPS thresholds (fasting 5.1, 1-hour 10.0, 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L) confirms gestational diabetes; multidisciplinary care with self-monitoring and lifestyle measures is standard first-line management. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Consensus)

Australian criteria do not require repeat testing when any one value is above threshold; deferring action loses critical time for glycaemic optimisation. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Consensus)

First-line management of gestational diabetes is lifestyle modification with home glucose monitoring; pharmacotherapy is added if targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks of intervention. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Consensus)

HbA1c is not used to make a gestational diabetes diagnosis after 20 weeks in Australian practice; the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test remains the standard. (Source: ADIPS Gestational Diabetes Consensus)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption is a clinical diagnosis suggested by painful vaginal bleeding, tense tender uterus and fetal compromise. Concealed haemorrhage means external blood loss underestimates total loss; maternal observations and fetal status are more reliable. Resuscitation, massive transfusion activation and category 1 caesarean section are the time-critical steps. Disseminated intravascular coagulation complicates around 10% of significant abruptions and is anticipated with empirical fibrinogen and platelet replacement.
key_points: Concealed haemorrhage means external blood loss underestimates true blood loss
Tetanic uterus and fetal bradycardia indicate major abruption requiring urgent delivery
Tocolysis is contraindicated when maternal or fetal compromise is present
Massive transfusion activation should be early, not after coagulopathy is confirmed
Disseminated intravascular coagulation complicates around 10% of significant abruptions
explanation.pearls: Fibrinogen below 2 g/L is the earliest and most sensitive coagulation marker for abruption-related disseminated intravascular coagulation and should trigger cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate replacement.

options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is appropriate when delivery is anticipated under 30 weeks; at 34 weeks it is no longer indicated, and resuscitation and delivery must not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

Maternal shock with a non-reassuring cardiotocograph at this gestation mandates urgent delivery rather than expectant monitoring; ongoing concealed haemorrhage will worsen. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

Tocolysis is contraindicated in placental abruption with maternal or fetal compromise; prolonging pregnancy risks progressive concealed haemorrhage, coagulopathy and intrauterine death. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

The picture of haemodynamic compromise, tetanic uterus and fetal bradycardia indicates major placental abruption; immediate resuscitation with category 1 caesarean section is required to deliver the fetus and address ongoing concealed haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)
Placental abruption is a clinical diagnosis; advanced imaging delays delivery and does not change management in the setting of shock and fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is an unpredictable obstetric emergency where downward traction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder after the head. The HELPERR mnemonic structures the response: call for Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs in McRoberts, suprapubic Pressure, Enter manoeuvres, Remove posterior arm and Roll the patient. McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves around 40 to 60% of cases. Fundal pressure is contraindicated and downward axial traction must remain gentle to avoid brachial plexus injury.
key_points: McRoberts and suprapubic pressure are the first-line manoeuvres in HELPERR
Fundal pressure is contraindicated and risks uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury
Time the head delivery and call for senior help immediately
Internal manoeuvres such as Rubin or Woods screw follow if McRoberts fails
Document time intervals, manoeuvres performed and personnel present
explanation.pearls: Brachial plexus injuries occur in 4 to 16% of shoulder dystocia cases but most resolve fully by 12 months; counsel parents about the favourable prognosis to reduce psychological harm.

options.rationale: McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure is the first-line intervention in the HELPERR sequence and resolves around 40 to 60% of shoulder dystocia cases without further escalation. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)

Fundal pressure worsens shoulder impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury; downward traction beyond gentle routine traction risks brachial plexus injury. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)
Symphysiotomy is a last-resort intervention reserved for failed internal manoeuvres and Zavanelli; it is not the first-line approach. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)

The Zavanelli manoeuvre is reserved for failed internal rotational manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery; it is not the first step in shoulder dystocia management. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)
Uterotonics and tocolytics have no role in the first-line manoeuvres for shoulder dystocia; the problem is mechanical impaction, not uterine activity. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. The transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness cutoff is 4 mm in Australian practice; women above this threshold require hysteroscopic visualisation with directed endometrial sampling. Risk factors include obesity, type 2 diabetes, unopposed oestrogen exposure, tamoxifen use and Lynch syndrome. Endometrioid adenocarcinoma carries a favourable prognosis when caught at FIGO stage 1, with overall 5-year survival around 90%.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise
Endometrial thickness above 4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound mandates histological sampling
Obesity, diabetes, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen and Lynch syndrome raise risk
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is preferred over blind pipelle when ultrasound is abnormal
Recurrent bleeding after a normal pipelle still requires hysteroscopic re-evaluation
explanation.pearls: Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) accounts for around 2 to 5% of endometrial cancers and should be considered when diagnosis occurs under age 50 or with a family history of colorectal cancer.

options.rationale: Postmenopausal bleeding requires histological sampling because endometrial cancer can occur with thicknesses above 4 mm and watchful waiting risks delayed diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal Bleeding)
Empirical progestogen therapy does not address the diagnostic question and can mask underlying endometrial malignancy; sampling is required first. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Any postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness above 4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound requires hysteroscopic visualisation and directed sampling; obesity and diabetes raise the pretest probability further. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal Bleeding)
Magnetic resonance imaging is used for staging once endometrial cancer is histologically confirmed, not as a primary diagnostic test. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal Bleeding)
An endometrial thickness above 4 mm in a woman with postmenopausal bleeding mandates sampling regardless of the patient demographics; reassurance is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage above 1000 mL or with haemodynamic compromise requires a stepwise pharmacological and surgical response. The Australian ladder is uterine massage and oxytocin, then ergometrine, tranexamic acid and an oxytocin infusion, then carboprost or misoprostol, and finally tamponade and surgical haemostasis. Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of delivery reduces death from postpartum haemorrhage by around 30%. Ergometrine is avoided only with pre-eclampsia or pre-existing hypertension.
key_points: Uterine atony is the cause of around 70% of primary postpartum haemorrhage cases
Ergometrine 250 micrograms is the second-line uterotonic unless hypertension is present
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours reduces postpartum haemorrhage mortality by around 30%
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma because of bronchospasm risk
Bakri balloon tamponade controls bleeding before laparotomy and uterine compression sutures
explanation.pearls: Fibrinogen falls early in postpartum haemorrhage; a level below 2 g/L predicts severe haemorrhage and warrants early cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate replacement.

options.rationale: Misoprostol is slower onset than parenteral uterotonics and is reserved for settings with no other agents available; intravenous oxytocin and ergometrine are first-line. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

Surgical and tamponade interventions follow when pharmacological uterotonics fail; the next step after oxytocin is ergometrine and tranexamic acid before escalation. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Body mass index is not a contraindication to ergometrine; her blood pressure is low rather than high, so ergometrine is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)
Carboprost is a third-line uterotonic used after ergometrine has failed or is contraindicated; jumping to it skips a step in the Australian algorithm. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

After initial oxytocin fails, the Australian PPH ladder is ergometrine with tranexamic acid 1 g (given within 3 hours of birth) plus an oxytocin infusion; prepare for theatre if bleeding continues. (Source: RANZCOG: Postpartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Nausea and vomiting affect up to 80% of pregnancies and a smaller proportion progress to hyperemesis gravidarum. SOMANZ recommends a stepped approach: lifestyle measures, then pyridoxine plus doxylamine, then metoclopramide or promethazine, with ondansetron reserved for resistant cases. Indications for admission include ketonuria, weight loss above 5%, electrolyte disturbance or inability to tolerate any oral intake. Persistent severe symptoms warrant thyroid function, urinalysis and consideration of molar pregnancy.
key_points: First-line is pyridoxine 25 mg three times daily plus doxylamine 12.5 mg nocte
Ondansetron is later line because of first-trimester cleft palate signal and constipation
Admission triggered by ketonuria, weight loss over 5% or electrolyte disturbance
Thiamine 100 mg cover for any prolonged vomiting before glucose-containing fluids
Persistent severe symptoms prompt workup for molar pregnancy and thyroid dysfunction
explanation.pearls: Thiamine 100 mg intravenous or oral is given before any dextrose-containing fluid in prolonged hyperemesis to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

options.rationale: Pyridoxine plus doxylamine is the first-line combination for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy in Australian and international guidelines because it has the best safety evidence and is effective for mild to moderate symptoms. (Source: SOMANZ Hyperemesis Guideline)

Ondansetron is reserved for failure of first-line measures because of cleft palate signal in some first-trimester studies and constipation risk; pyridoxine and doxylamine are preferred initially. (Source: SOMANZ Hyperemesis Guideline)

Admission with intravenous therapy is reserved for hyperemesis gravidarum with ketonuria, weight loss over 5%, dehydration or electrolyte disturbance, not for mild outpatient nausea. (Source: SOMANZ Hyperemesis Guideline)

Symptoms troubling enough to cause weight loss warrant pharmacological treatment to prevent progression to hyperemesis; lifestyle advice alone is insufficient at this point. (Source: SOMANZ Hyperemesis Guideline)
Promethazine is a second-line agent and routine thyroid testing is unnecessary in mild symptoms with a TSH already documented as normal. (Source: SOMANZ Hyperemesis Guideline)

explanation.summary: Early-onset group B Streptococcus disease is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis. Australian practice has shifted to universal culture-based screening with a combined vaginal-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks gestation, because culture results remain predictive of intrapartum colonisation for roughly five weeks. Women who screen positive, who have GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy, or who have a previous baby with invasive GBS disease are offered intrapartum benzylpenicillin. The risk-based approach is retained for unbooked women or those with unknown status at the onset of labour with risk factors.
key_points: Swab at 35 to 37 weeks gestation, combined vaginal and rectal
Universal screening rather than risk-based is the current Australian standard
Intrapartum benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours is first line
GBS bacteriuria in current pregnancy is an automatic prophylaxis indication
Risk-based approach applies if status unknown at labour onset
explanation.pearls: GBS bacteriuria at any threshold during the current pregnancy warrants intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis and treatment of the urinary tract infection at the time of detection.

options.rationale: Australian RANZCOG guidance recommends universal vaginal-rectal swab screening at 35 to 37 weeks because culture remains valid for around 5 weeks and predicts colonisation status at delivery. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)
Rectal sampling is essential for sensitivity and 28 weeks is too early; recolonisation between sampling and birth limits the predictive value of earlier swabs. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)
Urine culture detects only heavy colonisation and misses most carriers; it does not replace vaginal-rectal swabbing in the universal screening pathway. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

Australia uses universal culture-based screening rather than a risk-based approach; previous well-baby status does not waive current pregnancy screening because colonisation varies. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)
Sampling at 40 weeks is too close to delivery for culture turnaround; 35 to 37 weeks balances result validity with time to inform intrapartum decisions. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance prioritises long-acting reversible contraception postpartum because of high typical-use effectiveness and adherence-free protection. Levonorgestrel and copper intrauterine devices and the etonogestrel implant are all breastfeeding-compatible and can be inserted at or after 6 weeks postpartum (some are inserted immediately after delivery). Combined hormonal methods are avoided until 6 weeks postpartum because of venous thromboembolism risk and possible impact on milk supply. Progestogen-only methods and depot are acceptable alternatives if a LARC is declined.
key_points: Long-acting reversible contraception is first line postpartum
Combined hormonal contraception avoided in first 6 weeks postpartum
Levonorgestrel IUD and etonogestrel implant are breastfeeding compatible
Lactational amenorrhoea requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months
Depot is effective but second line because of bone density and weight concerns
explanation.pearls: Lactational amenorrhoea provides over 98% protection only while all three conditions hold: exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months.

options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum because of venous thromboembolism risk and may reduce milk supply in some breastfeeding women. (Source: Family Planning Australia Postpartum Contraception)

Depot is effective and breastfeeding-compatible but is not preferred first line because of bone density and weight implications; long-acting reversible contraception is generally preferred when available. (Source: Family Planning Australia Postpartum Contraception)

Long-acting reversible contraception with the levonorgestrel IUD is first-line postpartum because it is highly effective, breastfeeding-compatible and avoids combined hormone risks; insertion at 6 weeks postpartum is safe. (Source: Family Planning Australia Postpartum Contraception)

Lactational amenorrhoea requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months; reliance on it alone has higher failure than long-acting reversible contraception and many women want greater certainty. (Source: Family Planning Australia Postpartum Contraception)

Progestogen-only pills are breastfeeding-compatible but daily adherence makes them less effective than long-acting reversible contraception, which is preferred when available. (Source: Family Planning Australia Postpartum Contraception)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance supports empirical medical therapy for suspected endometriosis with typical history and normal pelvic ultrasound rather than proceeding directly to laparoscopy. Continuous combined hormonal contraception is first line, with progestogen-only options (norethisterone or levonorgestrel IUD) as alternatives. Laparoscopy with excision is reserved for failure of medical therapy after 3 to 6 months, fertility concerns or suspected deep infiltrating disease. CA-125 has no role in routine endometriosis diagnosis or monitoring.
key_points: Continuous COCP is first-line empirical therapy in suspected endometriosis
Laparoscopy reserved for medical failure, fertility planning or deep disease suspicion
CA-125 is non-specific and not used routinely
Levonorgestrel IUD is an effective progestogen-only alternative
GnRH agonists are specialist-initiated with add-back therapy
explanation.pearls: Continuous COCP without a withdrawal bleed (skipping the inactive pills) is the preferred empirical regimen for suspected endometriosis because cyclical menses drive pain.

options.rationale: Laparoscopy is reserved for failure of medical therapy, fertility concerns or suspicion of deep infiltrating disease; an empirical hormonal trial is recommended first. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Statement)
NSAIDs help dysmenorrhoea but do not suppress endometriotic lesions; hormonal suppression is the appropriate next step in suspected endometriosis. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Statement)
CA-125 is non-specific and elevated in many gynaecological conditions; it is not used to diagnose or monitor endometriosis in routine practice. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Statement)

Continuous combined hormonal contraception is first-line empiric therapy for suspected endometriosis without contraindication; persistence beyond a 3 to 6 month trial warrants specialist referral. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Statement)
GnRH analogues are reserved for specialist use after failure of first-line hormonal therapy because of cost, bone density effects and the need for add-back. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Statement)

explanation.summary: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis prevents rhesus D alloimmunisation by neutralising fetal red cells crossing the placenta. The Australian schedule administers 625 IU intramuscular anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks for non-immunised rhesus D negative women, plus postpartum prophylaxis if the baby is rhesus D positive, and an additional dose after any sensitising event such as antepartum bleeding, external cephalic version, abdominal trauma or invasive procedure. Implementation has reduced sensitisation rates below 1% per at-risk pregnancy.
key_points: Routine antenatal anti-D given at 28 and 34 weeks, 625 IU each dose
Postpartum anti-D within 72 hours if baby is rhesus D positive
Additional doses for sensitising events (bleeding, ECV, trauma, CVS, amniocentesis)
Antibody screen at 28 weeks before prophylaxis to detect prior sensitisation
Kleihauer test after large fetomaternal haemorrhage to guide additional dosing
explanation.pearls: An additional 625 IU dose covers up to 6 mL fetomaternal haemorrhage; a Kleihauer test above this threshold prompts dose escalation calculated per millilitre.

options.rationale: Routine antenatal prophylaxis is given to all rhesus D negative women with a negative antibody screen regardless of previous pregnancy or prior anti-D, because antibodies wane and silent sensitisation can occur. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

Fetal RHD testing is not yet routinely funded in Australia for this purpose; current standard is universal antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks for non-immunised women. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

Australian routine antenatal prophylaxis uses 625 IU anti-D at 28 weeks and 34 weeks with a postpartum dose if the baby is rhesus D positive; this regimen near eliminates new sensitisations. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)
Australia uses the two-dose 625 IU regimen at 28 and 34 weeks; a single 1500 IU dose is an alternative used elsewhere but is not the current Australian schedule. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)
Anti-D timing matters because most silent transplacental haemorrhages occur in the third trimester; deferring to 36 weeks leaves a window of unprotected sensitisation. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed by BP at or above 160/110 with proteinuria or with any organ involvement. Immediate priorities are rapid BP control (intravenous labetalol or hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine), magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, antenatal corticosteroid course completion if under 35 weeks, and transfer to a tertiary obstetric unit. Delivery is the only definitive treatment but timing balances maternal stability against fetal maturity; expectant management may continue at 32 weeks once stable.
key_points: Target BP under 160/110 within an hour using intravenous labetalol, hydralazine or oral nifedipine
Magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g per hour for seizure prophylaxis once severe
Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if under 35 weeks
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated because of precipitous drops
Transfer to a tertiary unit with NICU support before delivery if maternal and fetal stable
explanation.pearls: Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity, occurring at a serum level of 5 to 6 mmol/L before respiratory depression at 7.5 mmol/L.

options.rationale: Oral antihypertensive is slow to act in severe hypertension with end-organ symptoms; intravenous antihypertensive is required for rapid control alongside magnesium and transfer. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Magnesium is given prophylactically once severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed, before any seizure; immediate delivery at a regional centre without neonatal capability for 32 weeks is unsafe when transfer is possible. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Sublingual nifedipine causes precipitous drops in blood pressure with fetal compromise; oral immediate-release nifedipine is acceptable but never sublingual, and magnesium is indicated. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Severe pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks needs rapid intravenous BP control, magnesium for seizure prophylaxis, completion of corticosteroid course for fetal lung maturity and transfer to a tertiary unit with neonatal intensive care. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Diuretics are not indicated unless pulmonary oedema is present and methyldopa is too slow for severe acute hypertension; intravenous labetalol or hydralazine is required. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency. Immediate management aims to relieve cord compression while organising delivery: manual elevation of the presenting part through the vagina, knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, tocolysis if uterine activity is contributing, and bladder filling only if transfer to theatre is delayed. Delivery is by category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes of decision unless the cervix is fully dilated and instrumental delivery is rapidly achievable. Neonatal resuscitation team must attend.
key_points: Manual elevation of the presenting part is the first physical action
Knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position relieves cord compression
Category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes of decision if cervix not fully dilated
Bladder filling is an adjunct only when delivery is delayed
Tocolysis with terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneous reduces contractions during transfer
explanation.pearls: Subcutaneous terbutaline 250 micrograms is the recommended tocolytic during transfer for cord prolapse, providing 15 to 30 minutes of uterine relaxation.

options.rationale: Oxytocin worsens cord compression by increasing contractions; the cervix is not fully dilated so vaginal delivery is not possible and emergency caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)
Cord prolapse with abnormal fetal heart trace is a category 1 caesarean decision because of immediate fetal compromise; 60 minutes is too slow. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

Elevating the presenting part and adopting knee-chest position relieves cord compression while preparing for immediate category 1 caesarean delivery within 30 minutes of decision. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

Bladder filling is a useful adjunct only when there is transport delay; even then, definitive management is immediate category 1 caesarean rather than elective deferral. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)
Cord prolapse with bradycardia is an immediate fetal emergency; waiting 10 minutes loses critical time and risks hypoxic-ischaemic injury. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

explanation.summary: Suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy requires a modified diagnostic pathway because D-dimer is unreliable. Bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound is performed first; a positive proximal DVT obviates the need for further chest imaging. If ultrasound is negative, ventilation-perfusion scan is preferred over CTPA when the chest x-ray is normal because of lower maternal breast radiation, while CTPA is preferred when chest x-ray is abnormal. Therapeutic dose low-molecular-weight heparin is started while awaiting imaging.
key_points: D-dimer is not reliable in pregnancy
Bilateral leg ultrasound first; positive proximal DVT means no chest imaging needed
V/Q preferred over CTPA when CXR normal (lower breast radiation)
CTPA preferred if CXR abnormal because V/Q less interpretable
Therapeutic LMWH commenced while awaiting confirmation
explanation.pearls: Enoxaparin in pregnancy is dosed by booking weight, typically 1 mg/kg twice daily for treatment, with anti-Xa monitoring not routinely required.

options.rationale: D-dimer is physiologically elevated throughout pregnancy and cannot be used to rule out venous thromboembolism in pregnant women. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

Imaging confirmation is required because anticoagulating without diagnosis exposes mother and fetus to bleeding risk during a 6 month course; therapeutic enoxaparin is commenced while awaiting imaging. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

Australian guidance recommends bilateral leg ultrasound first because a positive proximal DVT confirms the indication for anticoagulation and avoids fetal radiation exposure from CTPA or V/Q. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

CTPA delivers higher breast radiation than V/Q and is not preferred first line unless chest x-ray is abnormal; in pregnancy with normal chest x-ray, V/Q is favoured if leg ultrasound is negative. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)
Cardiac MRI does not reliably image the pulmonary vasculature to diagnose or exclude pulmonary embolism and is not part of the diagnostic pathway. (Source: RANZCOG VTE in Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is the leading cause of obstetric hysterectomy and major haemorrhage. Risk rises sharply with each previous caesarean particularly in the setting of placenta praevia. Australian guidance mandates prospective tertiary multidisciplinary care including obstetrics, anaesthetics, urology, interventional radiology, neonatal intensive care, haematology and blood bank. Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after corticosteroids balances prematurity against the risk of unscheduled bleeding. Options include caesarean hysterectomy or leaving the placenta in situ followed by methotrexate or delayed hysterectomy.
key_points: Prior caesarean plus placenta praevia is the strongest risk factor
Planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks after corticosteroids in a tertiary unit
Multidisciplinary planning: obstetrics, urology, anaesthetics, blood bank, NICU
Vaginal birth and trial of labour are absolutely contraindicated
Options include hysterectomy or leaving placenta in situ
explanation.pearls: The risk of placenta accreta with placenta praevia rises from around 3% with no previous caesarean to over 60% with three or more previous caesareans.

options.rationale: Trial of labour is absolutely contraindicated with placenta praevia and accreta spectrum because of catastrophic haemorrhage risk; planned operative delivery is mandatory. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Statement)

Australian guidance recommends planned multidisciplinary caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with corticosteroids, blood products on standby, urology support, and consideration of caesarean hysterectomy versus leaving the placenta in situ based on intra-operative findings. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Statement)

Deferring to 39 weeks risks emergency presentation with massive haemorrhage; tertiary planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks with full team and blood products is required. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Statement)

ECV and vaginal birth are contraindicated with placenta praevia and accreta spectrum because of catastrophic haemorrhage risk; planned caesarean is the only safe route. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Statement)

Care must be at a tertiary unit with prospective MDT involvement; reactive specialist involvement after injury misses the point of planned coordinated care. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Statement)

explanation.summary: Australian SOMANZ guidance defines gestational hypertension as new-onset BP 140/90 mmHg or higher after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ involvement. Treatment with oral labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa starts once BP is sustained above 140/90, aiming for 110 to 140 systolic and 80 to 85 diastolic. Severe hypertension (160/110) requires admission and parenteral therapy. Aspirin for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis is commenced before 16 weeks in at-risk pregnancies, not at presentation of established hypertension.
key_points: Gestational hypertension is sustained BP 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks without proteinuria
Treat sustained BP 140/90 or higher with labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa
Severe hypertension 160/110 or higher requires admission and IV therapy
Atenolol is avoided due to fetal growth restriction risk
Aspirin pre-eclampsia prophylaxis is started before 16 weeks for at-risk pregnancies, not at later presentation
explanation.pearls: BP target in pregnancy under antihypertensive treatment is 110 to 140 systolic and 80 to 85 diastolic per SOMANZ; tighter targets do not improve fetal outcomes and risk placental hypoperfusion.

options.rationale: Aspirin pre-eclampsia prophylaxis is started before 16 weeks gestation; at 33 weeks it provides no benefit and does not treat established hypertension. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

IV hydralazine and magnesium sulfate are reserved for severe hypertension at 160/110 or higher or for established pre-eclampsia with severe features; this woman has neither. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
Sustained BP over 140/90 in pregnancy mandates treatment to reduce the risk of progression to severe hypertension, stroke and placental abruption. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Atenolol is associated with fetal growth restriction in pregnancy and is not recommended in Australian guidelines; labetalol, oral nifedipine or methyldopa are preferred. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Persistent BP over 140/90 mmHg without proteinuria after 20 weeks meets gestational hypertension criteria; SOMANZ recommends antihypertensive treatment when sustained BP exceeds 140/90, with labetalol as first-line in Australia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and mortality when given before preterm birth. Australian guidance is two doses of IM betamethasone 11.4 mg, 24 hours apart, ideally completed in the 24 hours to 7 days before birth, and offered up to 34+6 weeks. Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is given up to 32+0 weeks when birth is anticipated within 24 hours. Tertiary in-utero transfer is preferred over ex-utero transfer for births under 32 weeks.
key_points: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, 2 doses 24 hours apart, is the Australian standard antenatal corticosteroid
Benefit extends from 24 hours to 7 days before birth
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is offered up to 32+0 weeks when imminent preterm birth is expected
In-utero transfer to a tertiary centre is preferred for anticipated birth under 32 weeks
Tocolysis with nifedipine can delay birth 48 hours to allow corticosteroid effect but does not improve neonatal outcomes alone
explanation.pearls: A single repeat (rescue) course of betamethasone may be considered if the initial course was over 7 days ago and birth is again imminent before 32 weeks, but more than one repeat course is associated with reduced birth weight and head circumference.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Preterm labour and birth

options.rationale: Threatened preterm birth at 30+2 weeks warrants two doses of betamethasone 24 hours apart to mature fetal lungs, magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before 30 weeks would be missed but is still given under 32 weeks at imminent birth, and tertiary transfer ensures neonatal capability. (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids Statement)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Preterm labour and birth

options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is recommended in Australia up to 32+0 weeks when birth is anticipated within 24 hours; withholding it misses the neurodevelopmental benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids Statement)

The Australian standard for antenatal corticosteroids is betamethasone IM in two doses 24 hours apart; dexamethasone is an alternative with a different dosing schedule and IV use is non-standard. Immediate caesarean is not indicated without a fetal or maternal compromise trigger. (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids Statement)

Corticosteroids must be given as soon as preterm birth is anticipated within 7 days; the first dose still confers benefit even if birth occurs before the second dose. (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids Statement)

Vaginal progesterone is preventative and started earlier in pregnancy; corticosteroids are recommended up to 34+6 weeks for threatened preterm birth in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids Statement)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage is defined in Australia as 3 or more consecutive pregnancy losses before 20 weeks. Investigation identifies a treatable cause in around half of couples. Standard first-line workup includes parental karyotyping, antiphospholipid antibody screen, pelvic ultrasound, and thyroid function. Antiphospholipid syndrome is treated in subsequent pregnancies with aspirin plus low-molecular-weight heparin. Inherited thrombophilia screening is not routinely indicated for first-trimester losses.
key_points: Recurrent miscarriage in Australia is 3 or more consecutive losses before 20 weeks
Investigation finds a treatable cause in about 50% of couples
Parental karyotype, antiphospholipid antibodies and pelvic ultrasound are first-line
Antiphospholipid syndrome warrants aspirin plus LMWH in subsequent pregnancies
Inherited thrombophilia panels are not routinely indicated for early pregnancy losses
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid antibody testing must be repeated 12 weeks apart with persistent positivity required for syndrome diagnosis; a single positive test is not sufficient and treatment based on one result is overtreatment.

options.rationale: Recurrent miscarriage (3 or more consecutive losses in Australia) increases the chance of finding a treatable cause to around 50%; reassurance alone misses antiphospholipid syndrome which is treatable. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Statement)

Three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages meet RANZCOG criteria for recurrent miscarriage workup including parental karyotype, antiphospholipid antibodies and uterine assessment. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Statement)

Inherited thrombophilia screening is not routinely recommended for first-trimester recurrent miscarriage; the evidence base does not support empirical aspirin without a positive antiphospholipid result. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Statement)

Preimplantation genetic testing is not first-line for recurrent miscarriage; investigation precedes assisted reproduction decisions and there is no evidence of subfertility. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Statement)

Hysteroscopy is reserved for abnormal pelvic ultrasound or suspected uterine cavity pathology; endometritis screening is not routine first-line testing. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Statement)

explanation.summary: Preconception care in type 1 diabetes aims for HbA1c under 6.5%, folate 5 mg daily from at least 3 months pre-pregnancy, effective contraception until targets are reached, retinal review and renal assessment. ACE inhibitors, statins and ARBs are stopped before conception. CGM access during pregnancy improves outcomes and is funded for type 1 diabetes in Australia. Folic acid 5 mg compensates for higher neural tube defect risk.
key_points: Target HbA1c under 6.5% before conception in type 1 diabetes
Folic acid 5 mg daily from preconception through first trimester
Stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs and statins before conception
Document retinal and renal status before pregnancy
Continuous glucose monitoring is funded for type 1 diabetes in pregnancy in Australia
explanation.pearls: Insulin requirements typically fall in the first trimester (risk of hypoglycaemia), then rise from 18 weeks to peak around 36 weeks at 1.5 to 2 times pre-pregnancy doses; women should be counselled to anticipate these shifts before pregnancy.

options.rationale: ADIPS preconception care for type 1 diabetes targets HbA1c under 6.5% to reduce congenital anomaly risk, high-dose folate from preconception, and effective contraception until glycaemic targets are reached. (Source: ADIPS Diabetes in Pregnancy Guideline)

Conception with HbA1c over 8% carries a 4 to 10 fold increased risk of major congenital malformation; optimisation is needed first. Glargine has acceptable pregnancy safety data and a switch is not required. (Source: ADIPS Diabetes in Pregnancy Guideline)

Metformin is not the standard adjunct in type 1 diabetes preconception and folic acid dose should be 5 mg (not 500 micrograms) due to higher neural tube defect baseline risk. (Source: ADIPS Diabetes in Pregnancy Guideline)

Photocoagulation is for proliferative or severe non-proliferative disease, not background retinopathy; pregnancy planning continues alongside ophthalmology surveillance. (Source: ADIPS Diabetes in Pregnancy Guideline)

Microalbuminuria with preserved eGFR in established type 1 diabetes is expected and does not require biopsy; nephrology referral is reserved for declining GFR or heavy proteinuria. (Source: ADIPS Diabetes in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome complicates around 10% of monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies via unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses. Quintero staging uses bladder, Doppler and hydrops findings; Stage I is amniotic fluid discordance with both bladders visible. Australian management funnels through a fetal therapy centre, where fetoscopic laser ablation between 16 and 26 weeks is the definitive first-line treatment for Stage II and beyond and most Stage I cases. Surveillance in MCDA twins is fortnightly from 16 weeks.
key_points: TTTS occurs in around 10% of monochorionic diamniotic twins
Quintero Stage I is DVP under 2 cm in one sac and over 8 cm in the other with both bladders visible
Fortnightly ultrasound surveillance from 16 weeks is standard for MCDA twins
Fetoscopic laser ablation is the first-line treatment in Australia for Stage II and above and most Stage I
Amnioreduction is second-line when laser is unavailable
explanation.pearls: Recipient twin features include polyhydramnios, large bladder and cardiac hypertrophy from volume overload; donor twin features include oligohydramnios, small or absent bladder (stuck twin) and growth restriction, and the mortality rate without treatment exceeds 80% at Stage III.

options.rationale: Delivery at 19 weeks is below viability and would be lethal; medical therapy is fetoscopic laser. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Statement)

DVP discordance crossing the 2 and 8 cm thresholds defines TTTS and is not normal variation; delay risks rapid progression to Stage II with disappearing bladder. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Statement)

Amnioreduction is now second-line in TTTS and is reserved for circumstances where fetoscopic laser is unavailable or contraindicated; laser is the definitive Australian first-line treatment for Stage II and above and most Stage I cases. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Statement)

DVP under 2 cm in one sac plus over 8 cm in the other meets Quintero stage I twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome; in monochorionic twins this mandates referral to a fetal therapy centre because Stage II to IV may develop quickly. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Statement)

The DVP discordance and absence of severe Doppler abnormalities fits TTTS more than isolated selective growth restriction; both can coexist but the immediate referral pathway is the same. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Painless antepartum bleeding with a placenta within 2 cm of the internal os should be managed as placenta praevia until proven otherwise. Australian management is inpatient observation, antenatal corticosteroids before 34+6 weeks, Rh status check with Anti-D for Rh-negative women, avoidance of digital examination, and tertiary transfer for neonatal capability. Planned caesarean is at 36 to 37+6 weeks for major praevia. Prior caesarean section plus anterior low-lying placenta should also trigger evaluation for placenta accreta spectrum.
key_points: Painless APH with placenta within 2 cm of os is praevia until proven otherwise
No digital examination until praevia is excluded
Antenatal corticosteroids if before 34+6 weeks
Tertiary transfer for neonatal intensive care capability
Prior caesarean plus anterior low-lying placenta requires placenta accreta spectrum evaluation
explanation.pearls: A Kleihauer-Betke test should be sent in any Rh-negative woman with significant antepartum bleeding to size the feto-maternal haemorrhage and dose Anti-D 625 IU per 6 mL of fetal red cell volume in excess of standard dose.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement

options.rationale: There is no contraction or hypertension to treat; magnesium for tocolysis is not standard and methyldopa is not indicated. The maternal tachycardia reflects anxiety and mild blood loss, not hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement

options.rationale: Digital examination in low-lying placenta can precipitate catastrophic haemorrhage and is contraindicated until placental position is confirmed not to be praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement

options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean is reserved for maternal or fetal compromise; this woman is stable with reassuring CTG and the priority is corticosteroids and stabilisation. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement

options.rationale: Active bleeding with low-lying placenta requires inpatient observation due to the high risk of recurrent and unpredictable major haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement

options.rationale: Bleeding with low-lying placenta within 2 cm of os requires inpatient observation, corticosteroids before 34+6 weeks, Anti-D for Rh-negative or to confirm need, no digital exam (haemorrhage risk), and tertiary transfer for neonatal capability. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Statement

explanation.summary: Australian guidance treats iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy with oral iron as first-line, switching to intravenous iron if there is intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia or insufficient time to delivery. Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg as a single infusion is the preferred IV product, given from the second trimester. Replenishing iron before birth reduces postpartum transfusion and improves maternal symptoms. Postpartum iron deficiency is also common and warrants screening at 6 weeks.
key_points: Treat IDA in pregnancy with oral iron first-line
Switch to IV iron for intolerance, malabsorption, severe anaemia or short time to delivery
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg single infusion is standard in Australia from second trimester
Transfusion is reserved for severe anaemia or compromise, generally Hb under 70 g/L
Postpartum iron deficiency screening at 6 weeks identifies persistent depletion
explanation.pearls: Alternate-day oral iron lowers hepcidin response and yields slightly higher fractional absorption than daily dosing; however, in pregnancy the absolute dose required to correct deficiency by term is rarely achievable by oral route alone once Hb is under 100 g/L past 30 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement
Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Iron Guidance

options.rationale: Higher-dose oral iron worsens gastrointestinal side effects and rarely reaches target Hb in this timeframe; she has documented intolerance and only 7 weeks to birth. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement

options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia at 32 weeks with prior intolerance and short interval to birth (under 8 weeks) is an indication for IV iron in Australia; ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg is the standard single-dose option and replenishes stores rapidly before delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement
Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Iron Guidance

options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for severe anaemia (typically Hb under 70 g/L) or symptomatic compromise; ferric carboxymaltose is preferred and avoids transfusion risks while replenishing stores. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Iron Guidance)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood Iron Guidance

options.rationale: Alternate-day oral dosing improves absorption efficiency but the absolute uptake is still small and insufficient before delivery with this Hb and timeframe. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement

options.rationale: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are not standard for pregnancy iron deficiency anaemia in the absence of chronic kidney disease; IV iron alone is the recommended escalation. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency Anaemia in Pregnancy Statement

explanation.summary: Second-trimester medical termination in Australia uses mifepristone 200 mg orally followed 24 to 48 hours later by misoprostol 400 micrograms vaginally or buccally every 3 hours until birth. Surgical dilatation and evacuation is an alternative in centres with appropriate expertise and cervical preparation. After 22 weeks in some jurisdictions feticide with intracardiac potassium chloride is considered. Care includes bereavement support, lactation suppression with cabergoline, contraception planning and Rh status review with Anti-D for Rh-negative women.
key_points: Mifepristone priming followed by misoprostol is the Australian second-trimester medical regimen
Surgical D&E requires cervical preparation and trained operators
Feticide with intracardiac potassium chloride is considered from 22 weeks in some jurisdictions
Bereavement support and lactation suppression with cabergoline are routine
Anti-D is given to Rh-negative women undergoing termination at any gestation
explanation.pearls: Cabergoline 1 mg as a single dose given within 24 hours of birth suppresses lactation after second-trimester loss; bromocriptine is no longer used in Australia because of stroke and cardiac risk in this setting.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Termination of Pregnancy Clinical Practice Guideline
NSW Health Termination of Pregnancy Policy Directive

options.rationale: Mifepristone priming significantly shortens induction-to-delivery time at this gestation; misoprostol alone is less effective and CTG monitoring after a lethal diagnosis adds no value. (Source: RANZCOG Termination of Pregnancy Statement)

Surgical D&E at 21 weeks requires cervical preparation with mifepristone or osmotic dilators and access to a surgeon trained in second-trimester procedures; outpatient sedation without preparation is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Termination of Pregnancy Statement)

Australian second-trimester medical termination uses mifepristone priming followed by misoprostol; combined regimens shorten induction time and reduce blood loss. Bereavement care and lactation suppression counselling are core components. (Source: RANZCOG Termination of Pregnancy Statement)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Termination of Pregnancy Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Oxytocin alone is rarely effective for cervical priming at 21 weeks; the standard regimen is mifepristone plus misoprostol, with oxytocin reserved for retained placenta. CTG monitoring is not appropriate after lethal diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG Termination of Pregnancy Statement)

After 16 weeks, terminations in NSW for serious fetal conditions are accessed in tertiary services with two-doctor approval per the Abortion Law Reform Act 2019; gestational age is not a clinical bar at 21 weeks when the woman has chosen termination. (Source: NSW Health Termination of Pregnancy Policy Directive)
source_refs: NSW Health Termination of Pregnancy Policy Directive

explanation.summary: PPROM at 34 to 36+6 weeks is managed by admission, latency antibiotics with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral erythromycin and observation for signs of chorioamnionitis. The PPROMT trial supports planned expectant management to 37 weeks unless there is infection, abruption or non-reassuring fetal status. Antenatal corticosteroids are not given after 34+6 weeks. Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection is used in threatened preterm birth under 30-32 weeks, not at 34 weeks.
key_points: PPROM 34-36 weeks: admit, latency antibiotics, observe for chorioamnionitis
Antibiotics: benzylpenicillin plus erythromycin
Planned delivery by 37 weeks if no infection or compromise
Antenatal steroids beyond 34+6 weeks are generally not indicated
Magnesium neuroprotection is for preterm birth under 30-32 weeks
explanation.pearls: PPROMT (Lancet 2016) showed planned expectant management at 34-36 weeks reduced neonatal respiratory distress without increasing chorioamnionitis or sepsis compared with immediate birth; intrapartum group B strep cover is added if swab is positive or unknown.

options.rationale: Inpatient surveillance and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics are standard after PPROM under 37 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)
Cephalic presentation with reassuring trace and no labour or chorioamnionitis is not an indication for immediate caesarean at 34 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)
At 34 weeks magnesium sulfate neuroprotection is not indicated (used under 30-32 weeks) and tocolysis is not used in PPROM after 34 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal Corticosteroids)

PPROM at 34 weeks is managed by admission, latency antibiotics (benzylpenicillin plus erythromycin), observation for chorioamnionitis and planned delivery by 37 weeks if conservative management continues. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)

Routine immediate induction at 34 weeks does not improve outcomes versus expectant management to 37 weeks in uncomplicated PPROM; trial evidence (PPROMT) favours expectant management. (Source: RANZCOG: PPROM)

explanation.summary: The Australian ADIPS diagnostic 75 g 2 hour OGTT thresholds for gestational diabetes are fasting 5.1 mmol/L, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L and 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L. Any single abnormal value confirms the diagnosis. First-line management is referral to a diabetes in pregnancy clinic, home capillary glucose monitoring four times daily, individualised lifestyle and dietary advice. Metformin or insulin is added if targets are not met after a 1 to 2 week trial. HbA1c is not used to diagnose GDM in pregnancy.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L
Any one abnormal OGTT value confirms GDM
First-line: diabetes in pregnancy clinic, SMBG, lifestyle
Add metformin or insulin if targets not met after 1-2 weeks
Postpartum 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks to reclassify
explanation.pearls: Women with GDM have a 50% lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes; arrange a 75 g 2 hour OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum and an annual fasting glucose or HbA1c thereafter, plus encourage breastfeeding and weight optimisation.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Treatment of GDM

options.rationale: ADIPS 75 g OGTT diagnostic thresholds (fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L) are met (1 hour 11.2) confirming GDM; first-line management is the diabetes in pregnancy clinic with self-monitoring and lifestyle intervention. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Treatment of GDM

options.rationale: Only one OGTT value needs to exceed the ADIPS threshold to confirm GDM; the 1 hour value of 11.2 meets the criterion. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)
OGTT values, not HbA1c, define GDM in pregnancy and the 1 hour value here is diagnostic; reassurance misses the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)

Pharmacotherapy follows a trial of dietary and lifestyle intervention with home glucose monitoring; immediate metformin without monitoring is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Treatment of GDM)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and Treatment of GDM

options.rationale: Australia uses the 75 g 2-hour OGTT with ADIPS thresholds; the 100 g 3-hour Carpenter-Coustan test is not the diagnostic standard here. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines GDM)

explanation.summary: Postpartum endometritis is a polymicrobial infection of the endometrial cavity that follows caesarean section more often than vaginal birth. Australian guidance recommends intravenous ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole as empirical first-line cover. Treatment is continued intravenously until 24 hours after clinical resolution and then stepped down to oral therapy. Retained products of conception or pelvic abscess require imaging and source control.
key_points: Empirical IV regimen: ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole
Treat IV until 24 hours afebrile and clinically well, then oral step-down
Most common after caesarean section, polymicrobial
Imaging if no response by 48-72 hours or features of retained products
Source control with evacuation or drainage when indicated
explanation.pearls: Failure to respond within 48-72 hours warrants pelvic ultrasound or CT for retained products, septic pelvic vein thrombophlebitis or abscess; ovarian vein thrombosis often presents with right-sided pain and fever unresponsive to antibiotics alone.

options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin monotherapy does not cover anaerobes or gram-negative organisms commonly seen in postpartum endometritis and the patient warrants intravenous therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Australian guidance for postpartum endometritis is intravenous ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole, continued for 24 hours after clinical resolution before stepping down to oral cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Endometritis is typically polymicrobial; flucloxacillin alone misses anaerobes and gram-negatives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Ceftriaxone monotherapy lacks adequate anaerobic cover for endometritis; combination therapy or piperacillin-tazobactam is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Vancomycin is not first-line for endometritis without proven MRSA; drainage is reserved for retained products or abscess on imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Letrozole has replaced clomifene as first-line ovulation induction in anovulatory PCOS infertility based on the 2018 international evidence-based guideline endorsed by RANZCOG. Letrozole is dosed 2.5 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 2, with stepwise escalation by 2.5 mg per cycle to a maximum of 7.5 mg. Lifestyle optimisation should occur in parallel. Metformin is reserved as adjunct; gonadotrophins and ovarian drilling are later-line.
key_points: Letrozole 2.5 mg days 2-6 is first-line ovulation induction in PCOS
Stepwise dose escalation to 7.5 mg if anovulation persists
Clomifene is now second-line after letrozole
Metformin is adjunctive, not primary ovulation induction
Gonadotrophins and ovarian drilling are third-line
explanation.pearls: Letrozole has lower multiple-pregnancy rates than clomifene and a similar safety profile in women with PCOS; cycle tracking with mid-luteal progesterone (over 30 nmol/L) confirms ovulation and a positive response to therapy.

options.rationale: Letrozole has displaced clomifene as first-line ovulation induction in PCOS because of higher ovulation and live birth rates per the PCOS international guideline. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS)

Metformin monotherapy has limited efficacy for pregnancy in PCOS infertility; it may augment letrozole or clomifene in selected women but is not first-line for ovulation induction. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS)

Letrozole is first-line ovulation induction in PCOS, dosed 2.5 mg days 2 to 6 with cycle tracking and stepwise dose escalation to a maximum of 7.5 mg if anovulation persists. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS)
Gonadotrophin injection is third-line after letrozole or clomifene failure due to higher cost and ovarian hyperstimulation risk. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS)
Ovarian drilling is a second-line surgical option after pharmacological induction has failed and is not preferred initial therapy. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological features warrants rapid blood pressure control with intravenous labetalol or hydralazine (or oral nifedipine) plus intravenous magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis. Australian SOMANZ dosing for magnesium is 4 g over 20 minutes loading then 1 g per hour maintenance, with hourly monitoring of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. The target blood pressure is 140 to 150 over 90 to 100 mmHg; faster reductions risk fetal compromise.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia: rapid BP control plus magnesium sulfate prophylaxis
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 min loading then 1 g/hr maintenance
Target BP 140-150/90-100 mmHg, not normotension
Monitor reflexes, RR, urine output hourly; calcium gluconate antidote
Definitive treatment is delivery once stable
explanation.pearls: Magnesium toxicity progresses from loss of patellar reflexes to respiratory depression and cardiac arrest; the antidote is intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes, given alongside cessation of the magnesium infusion.

options.rationale: Methyldopa has slow onset and is used for chronic, not acute, control; severe hypertension with end-organ features needs intravenous or rapid-acting therapy. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose is 4 g (not 6 g) over 15-20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour maintenance per SOMANZ. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Magnesium loading is 4 g and maintenance is 1 g per hour; the dosing in this option is incorrect. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Australian SOMANZ guidance for severe pre-eclampsia: rapid blood pressure lowering with labetalol or hydralazine, magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes loading then 1 g per hour maintenance with reflex and respiratory rate monitoring. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Glyceryl trinitrate is reserved for pulmonary oedema; benzodiazepines are not standard seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia (magnesium is superior). (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is recognised by the turtle sign and failure of routine axial traction. The HELPERR sequence begins with calling for help, evaluating for episiotomy, legs in McRoberts, suprapubic pressure, enter internal manoeuvres (Rubin and Woods screw), remove the posterior arm and roll. Fundal pressure is contraindicated. Zavanelli replacement and symphysiotomy are last-resort manoeuvres. Most resolve with McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure alone.
key_points: Diagnosis: turtle sign and failed axial traction
HELPERR: Help, Evaluate episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter manoeuvres, Remove posterior arm, Roll
Fundal pressure is contraindicated
Most resolve with McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure
Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are last resort
explanation.pearls: Document time intervals between manoeuvres, the order applied and which shoulder was anterior; brachial plexus injury risk is highest with prolonged head-to-body delivery interval and inappropriately applied lateral traction.

options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia and increases the risk of brachial plexus injury and uterine rupture. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)
Forceps rotation is not part of the shoulder dystocia sequence and risks fetal injury; manoeuvres focus on widening the pelvic outlet and rotating the shoulder. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)
Symphysiotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre with significant maternal morbidity and is not the next step after a failed initial axial traction. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)
Zavanelli is the absolute last resort after the full HELPERR sequence has failed; the next manoeuvre is McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)

The HELPERR sequence starts with calling for help, McRoberts and suprapubic pressure; this combination resolves the majority of shoulder dystocias before internal manoeuvres are needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage management follows the four T causes (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) with simultaneous resuscitation and uterotonic escalation. Uterine atony is treated with an oxytocin infusion, ergometrine, misoprostol and carboprost in sequence. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension; carboprost is contraindicated in asthma. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given within 3 hours of onset as per WOMAN trial evidence. Balloon tamponade or surgical haemostasis follows if pharmacological measures fail.
key_points: Uterotonic ladder: oxytocin, ergometrine, misoprostol, carboprost
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset
Balloon tamponade if pharmacological measures fail
explanation.pearls: Use a rule of '1 g, 1 g, 1 g' aide-memoire in PPH: 1 g tranexamic acid IV, 1 g fibrinogen concentrate if hypofibrinogenaemia, and a target packed-cell to FFP ratio of 1:1 in major obstetric haemorrhage activation.

options.rationale: With ergometrine contraindicated in chronic hypertension, the next steps are an oxytocin infusion plus misoprostol plus TXA within 3 hours of PPH onset with continued mechanical measures. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)
Carboprost should be avoided in asthmatic patients and is generally a third-line uterotonic; misoprostol or oxytocin infusion plus TXA come first in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV should be given within 3 hours of PPH onset; omitting TXA misses a major guideline-recommended step. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)
Vasopressors are not first-line in early PPH where the priority is uterine tone, volume resuscitation and pharmacological haemostasis. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)
Ergometrine is contraindicated in chronic hypertension because it can precipitate hypertensive crisis. (Source: RANZCOG: PPH)

explanation.summary: Under the Australian National Cervical Screening Program, primary HPV testing is performed 5-yearly from age 25. HPV 16 or 18 detected is high risk and triggers immediate colposcopy referral. HPV other (non-16/18) detected with negative or low-grade reflex cytology is intermediate risk and triggers a repeat HPV test in 12 months. Persistent HPV at 12 months prompts colposcopy referral. Self-collection is an alternative primary screening option, not a confirmatory test.
key_points: Primary HPV testing 5-yearly from age 25
HPV 16/18 detected: refer for colposcopy
HPV other with negative or low-grade cytology: repeat HPV in 12 months
Persistent HPV at 12 months: refer for colposcopy
Self-collected swab is alternative primary screening, not confirmatory
explanation.pearls: Co-test with cytology is reserved for symptomatic women, follow-up of treated high-grade lesions, immunosuppressed women, and DES-exposed women; routine screening is HPV alone with reflex cytology only when HPV is detected.

sources.label: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines
Cancer Council Australia: Cervical Cancer Screening

options.rationale: Colposcopy is indicated for HPV 16/18 detection or for any HPV with possible high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or worse on reflex cytology, not for HPV other with negative cytology. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.rationale: Under the NCSP intermediate-risk pathway, HPV other detected with negative reflex cytology is followed by a repeat HPV test in 12 months; persistence at that point triggers colposcopy referral. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines
Cancer Council Australia: Cervical Cancer Screening

options.rationale: HPV detected (any type) returns the patient to a 12-month follow-up, not 5-yearly screening. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.rationale: Self-collection is offered as an alternative primary screening option, not a confirmatory test after a positive practitioner-collected specimen. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

options.rationale: Topical imiquimod is not part of standard cervical screening management; clearance of HPV is monitored by repeat testing alone. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines

explanation.summary: Monochorionic-diamniotic twins share a placenta with vascular anastomoses, putting them at risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. The Quintero staging system uses deepest vertical pocket discordance (under 2 cm in one sac, over 8 cm in the other before 20 weeks or over 10 cm after) as the diagnostic criterion. Stage I has fluid discordance alone, stage II adds absent bladder visualisation in the donor, stages III to V add Doppler abnormality, hydrops and demise. Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of anastomoses is the standard treatment for stages II and above before 26 weeks. RANZCOG recommends fortnightly DVP, growth and MCA-PSV scans from 16 weeks for all MCDA pregnancies.
key_points: MCDA twins: fortnightly DVP, growth and Doppler from 16 weeks
TTTS diagnosis: DVP under 2 cm one sac plus over 8 cm other before 20 weeks
Stage I = fluid discordance only; stage II = donor bladder not seen
Fetoscopic laser is treatment of choice for stage II or higher before 26 weeks
MCA-PSV over 1.5 MoM in either twin suggests TAPS and warrants referral
explanation.pearls: T-sign at the placental insertion (rather than lambda) confirms monochorionicity in the first trimester; this single scan finding redirects the entire antenatal surveillance pathway for the rest of the pregnancy.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy
ISUOG Practice Guidelines: role of ultrasound in twin pregnancy

options.rationale: The combination of DVP under 2 cm in one sac and over 8 cm in the other meets diagnostic criteria for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, which mandates urgent specialist review rather than routine follow-up. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Amnioreduction is a temporising measure and is inferior to fetoscopic laser photocoagulation for Stage II TTTS before 26 weeks; referral for laser is the recommended definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids and delivery are not indicated for a stable 18-week pregnancy without fetal compromise, prelabour rupture of membranes or imminent preterm birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Quintero stage I TTTS with progressing discordance, or stage II once oligohydramnios is present (DVP under 2 cm) with polyhydramnios (DVP over 8 cm before 20 weeks), is referred to a fetoscopic laser centre; fortnightly DVP, growth and MCA-PSV monitoring continues.
