(Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Monochorionic twins share the same karyotype and parvovirus is not a typical cause of isolated discordant fluid volumes; the picture is intrinsic to placental vascular anastomoses. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is a clinical diagnosis based on a history of recurrent painless mid-trimester losses without infection, bleeding or contractions. RANZCOG recommends history-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks gestation in women with three or more prior second-trimester losses or preterm births before 28 weeks. Surveillance with transvaginal cervical length and ultrasound-indicated cerclage at length under 25 mm is reserved for those with one or two prior events. Cerclage is removed at 36 to 37 weeks or earlier in preterm labour. Outcomes are best when the procedure is performed before any cervical shortening develops.
key_points: History-indicated cerclage: 3+ prior 2nd-trimester losses or PTB before 28 weeks
Place at 12-14 weeks under regional anaesthesia
Ultrasound-indicated cerclage: cervical length under 25 mm before 24 weeks with 1-2 prior PTB
Remove cerclage at 36-37 weeks or in established preterm labour
Bed rest has no benefit and increases VTE risk
explanation.pearls: Classical cervical insufficiency presents with painless cervical dilatation in the late second trimester followed by membrane rupture and rapid expulsion; this is distinct from infection-driven preterm labour and requires a structural rather than tocolytic response.

options.rationale: Progesterone with surveillance is appropriate for a single prior preterm birth or short cervix, but three prior mid-trimester losses meet criteria for history-indicated rather than ultrasound-indicated cerclage. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage)

Three or more prior second-trimester losses with the classical painless dilatation pattern is the prototypical indication for history-indicated cerclage placed at 12 to 14 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage)

Transabdominal cerclage is reserved for failed transvaginal cerclage or for women with prior trachelectomy or extensive cervical loss, not as first-line treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage)

Bed rest is not effective in cervical insufficiency and has documented harms including venous thromboembolism, deconditioning and psychological distress. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage)

Doing nothing despite a clear history of cervical insufficiency abandons an intervention that reduces the risk of preterm delivery by around 50% in appropriately selected women. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical insufficiency and cerclage)

explanation.summary: Operative vaginal birth choice considers station, position, caput, moulding, pelvic capacity and operator skill. Outlet vacuum is suitable when the head is on the perineum or OA at low station with no significant caput or moulding. Vacuum has lower maternal genital trauma but more cephalhaematoma and retinal haemorrhage; forceps has higher perineal trauma but lower failure. The three-pull, two-detachment, 20-minute rule is widely used; failure mandates escalation. Trial of instrumental in theatre is reserved for midcavity or rotational deliveries with potential for caesarean section.
key_points: Outlet vacuum criteria: OA vertex, +2 or lower, no caput or moulding, bladder empty
Vacuum stop rule: 3 pulls, 2 pop-offs, 20 minutes - do not exceed
Forceps preferred over vacuum if maternal effort poor or fetus preterm under 34 weeks
Trial of instrumental in theatre for midcavity or rotational
Document indication, position, station, instrument, pulls and complications
explanation.pearls: If the head is not visible at the introitus between contractions and the sagittal suture is not in the AP diameter, treat as midcavity and move to theatre - underestimating station outside theatre is a recurring root cause of bad outcomes in coronial reviews.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 26: Assisted vaginal birth

options.rationale: Late decelerations with a rising scalp lactate over 4 mmol/L meets criteria for expedited delivery; continued pushing is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

An OA vertex at +2 with full engagement, no caput and no moulding meets criteria for outlet instrumental birth; category 1 caesarean is more morbid and slower in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Rotational forceps are not indicated for an already OA position and require theatre and trial-of-instrumental settings under regional anaesthesia, not labour-ward perineal infiltration. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)
More than two pop-offs is a failed vacuum and represents an indication to stop and reassess, not to continue to three detachments. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

OA vertex at +2 with no caput or moulding, working epidural and full bladder empty meets criteria for outlet vacuum in the labour room with the recognised three-pull, two-detachment stop rule. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

explanation.summary: Around 3% of singleton pregnancies present breech at term. RANZCOG recommends offering external cephalic version from 37+0 weeks in uncomplicated cases. Success rates are 40 to 60% and higher in multiparous women, posterior placenta, normal amniotic fluid and complete or footling breech. Contraindications include placenta praevia, abnormal CTG, ruptured membranes, recent antepartum haemorrhage, multiple pregnancy and prior classical caesarean. Tocolysis with terbutaline or salbutamol improves success; anti-D is given to Rh-negative women. If ECV fails or is declined, planned caesarean section reduces perinatal mortality compared with planned vaginal breech (Term Breech Trial).
key_points: Offer ECV from 37+0 weeks in uncomplicated breech
Success 40-60%; higher in multips, normal AFI, posterior placenta
Tocolysis (salbutamol or terbutaline) improves success
Anti-D 625 IU if Rh negative; CTG before and after
Planned caesarean reduces perinatal mortality vs vaginal breech (Term Breech Trial)
explanation.pearls: An anterior placenta is not a contraindication to ECV but reduces success by about 15%; offering ECV remains worthwhile because the only alternatives are caesarean section or planned vaginal breech, each with their own counselling burden.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term
Cochrane review: External cephalic version for breech presentation at term

options.rationale: Recommending caesarean without first offering ECV omits an evidence-based intervention that achieves cephalic version in around 50% of attempts and reduces caesarean rates. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term

options.rationale: Postural and complementary measures do not have robust evidence of effect on persistent breech presentation at term in RANZCOG-aligned guidance. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term

options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends offering ECV from 37+0 weeks in uncomplicated breech with appropriate facilities; success around 40 to 60% and reduces caesarean for breech significantly. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term

options.rationale: Planned vaginal breech requires senior obstetric and neonatal expertise and is offered after counselling, not as a first step that bypasses ECV. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term

options.rationale: Induction of labour with a breech presentation is not standard practice and prostaglandin induction with breech presentation is not recommended in Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of breech presentation at term

explanation.summary: VBAC after one prior LSCS has a 60-80% success rate, with the strongest predictor being prior vaginal delivery. RANZCOG endorses VBAC in units with on-site theatre, anaesthesia, blood bank and neonatal resuscitation. Continuous CTG in labour, IV access and group and hold are standard. Uterine rupture risk in spontaneous labour is 0.2-0.7%; this rises to 1-1.5% with oxytocin augmentation and 2-2.5% with prostaglandin induction. Contraindications include prior classical or T-incision, prior uterine rupture, three or more prior caesareans and placenta praevia or accreta.
key_points: VBAC success after 1 LSCS: 60-80%, higher with prior vaginal birth
Rupture risk spontaneous labour: 0.2-0.7%; oxytocin 1-1.5%; PGE2 2-2.5%
Continuous CTG, IV access, group and hold are standard
Contraindications: classical/T-incision, prior rupture, 3+ prior LSCS, placenta praevia
Mechanical (Foley) preferred over prostaglandin for induction
explanation.pearls: Bandl's ring, sudden fetal heart deceleration with loss of station, scar tenderness and haematuria are textbook rupture signs but the most reliable in modern practice is a sudden non-reassuring CTG with maternal haemodynamic change - act on the CTG, not on waiting for classical signs.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: One prior LSCS with no contraindications and a prior vaginal birth confers a 70-75% VBAC success rate; uterine rupture risk in spontaneous labour is approximately 0.5%. Continuous CTG, IV access and group and hold are standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: One prior LSCS is not a contraindication to VBAC and her prior vaginal birth is a strong predictor of success. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Prostaglandin induction in VBAC is associated with a substantially increased uterine rupture risk (around 2-2.5%) and is generally avoided in Australian practice; mechanical induction is preferred if induction is needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: VBAC requires immediate access to emergency caesarean and on-site neonatal resuscitation; home VBAC is not endorsed by RANZCOG given the consequences of uterine rupture. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Mode-of-birth decisions are made earlier so that planning and consent are documented; cervical examination at 38 weeks does not reliably predict VBAC success. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by intractable vomiting, weight loss over 5% of pre-pregnancy weight, ketosis and electrolyte disturbance. Initial management is admission for IV crystalloid (typically saline with added potassium chloride), parenteral antiemetics (metoclopramide, ondansetron, prochlorperazine) and thiamine 100 mg IV daily before any glucose-containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Pyridoxine plus doxylamine remains first-line outpatient therapy. Ultrasound is arranged to exclude molar pregnancy or multiple gestation if not already done. Refractory cases need corticosteroids or admission for nutritional support.
key_points: HG diagnosis: vomiting + over 5% weight loss + ketosis + electrolyte disturbance
Thiamine 100 mg IV BEFORE any glucose-containing fluid to prevent Wernicke
Replace K aggressively if under 3.5; saline + KCl
Pyridoxine + doxylamine first-line outpatient; ondansetron/metoclopramide if needed
Refractory: corticosteroids, TPN, ultrasound to exclude molar
explanation.pearls: Confusion, ataxia or ophthalmoplegia in a vomiting pregnant woman is Wernicke encephalopathy until proven otherwise; give 500 mg thiamine IV TDS for 3 days, then 250 mg daily, before any dextrose - the cost of missing this is permanent Korsakoff amnesia.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: Giving dextrose before thiamine in a thiamine-replete-unknown patient with prolonged vomiting risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; ketosis and electrolyte derangement also mandate IV rehydration first. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: Hypokalaemia at 3.2 mmol/L requires correction and any patient with prolonged vomiting needs thiamine before any glucose-containing fluid. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: PUQE-equivalent severe HG with weight loss over 5%, ketonuria, hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia warrants admission; thiamine 100 mg IV is given before glucose, and saline-with-potassium replaces losses. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: TPN is reserved for refractory cases unable to maintain weight despite enteral feeding; first-line is rehydration, electrolyte and thiamine replacement with antiemetics. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

options.rationale: Imaging for molar or multiple pregnancy is appropriate but does not delay rehydration, thiamine and antiemetic therapy in a haemodynamically unwell patient. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum

explanation.summary: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome is defined by recurrent pregnancy loss (3 or more under 10 weeks, or 1 or more after 10 weeks of morphologically normal fetus, or 1 or more preterm birth before 34 weeks due to severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency) plus persistent positive antiphospholipid antibodies on two samples 12 weeks apart. Lupus anticoagulant alone is sufficient. Treatment in pregnancy is low-dose aspirin from positive pregnancy test plus prophylactic LMWH until 6 weeks postpartum. Live birth rates improve from around 10% untreated to 70 to 80% with aspirin plus LMWH.
key_points: Obstetric APS: 3+ losses under 10 weeks, OR 1+ loss after 10 weeks, OR 1+ severe early-PET preterm birth
PLUS persistent aPL on 2 samples 12 weeks apart (LA, ACL, or B2GP1)
Treatment: aspirin 100 mg daily + enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily through pregnancy
Continue LMWH 6 weeks postpartum
Warfarin contraindicated 6-12 weeks (embryopathy)
explanation.pearls: Triple-positive APS (LA + ACL + B2GP1) carries the highest thrombotic and pregnancy risk; this patient has only single-positive LA but persistent positivity twice still meets criteria - do not require all three to make the diagnosis.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management
ESHRE Guideline: Recurrent pregnancy loss 2022 update

options.rationale: Warfarin is teratogenic between 6 and 12 weeks gestation (warfarin embryopathy) and is contraindicated in early pregnancy in obstetric APS. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management

options.rationale: Three or more first-trimester losses plus persistent LA on two occasions 12 weeks apart meets Sydney/Sapporo classification for obstetric APS; treatment is low-dose aspirin from positive pregnancy test plus prophylactic LMWH. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management

options.rationale: NK-cell immunotherapy and IVIG are not supported by evidence for recurrent miscarriage and are not recommended in current Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management

options.rationale: Persistent LA alone on two samples 12 weeks apart with three first-trimester losses meets obstetric APS criteria; treatment is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management

options.rationale: High-dose prednisolone is associated with gestational diabetes, hypertension and preterm birth without improving live-birth rate in APS and is not recommended. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage investigation and management

explanation.summary: Heterotopic pregnancy is rare in spontaneous conceptions (1 in 30,000) but rises to around 1 in 100 after IVF, particularly with multiple embryo transfer. Diagnosis hinges on visualising an intrauterine pregnancy AND a separate adnexal mass; serial beta-hCG is unhelpful because trends are confounded by the viable IUP. Management of a symptomatic tubal heterotopic in a stable patient is laparoscopic salpingectomy with minimal uterine manipulation. Methotrexate is contraindicated when the IUP is desired. Reported live-birth rate of the IUP after surgical management is 60 to 70%.
key_points: Heterotopic risk: 1 in 30,000 spontaneous, 1 in 100 after IVF
Serial beta-hCG cannot diagnose - rely on ultrasound visualisation
Methotrexate contraindicated if IUP is desired
Laparoscopic salpingectomy is first-line for symptomatic tubal heterotopic
KCl injection is option for cornual, cervical, scar heterotopic
explanation.pearls: After IVF embryo transfer, persistent unilateral pain or unexplained free fluid in the presence of a normal-appearing IUP should trigger careful adnexal sweep on TVS - the intrauterine sac is reassuring on autopilot but does not rule out a co-located ectopic.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.rationale: Methotrexate would terminate the viable intrauterine pregnancy and is contraindicated in heterotopic pregnancy where the intrauterine pregnancy is viable and desired. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.rationale: Symptomatic right iliac fossa pain with free fluid and an adnexal ring complex in an IVF pregnancy is heterotopic until proven otherwise; deferring intervention 48 hours risks rupture. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.rationale: KCl instillation is a second-line technique for non-tubal heterotopic pregnancies (cornual, cervical, caesarean scar) and is not the first-line approach for symptomatic tubal heterotopic with peritoneal fluid. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.rationale: Symptomatic tubal heterotopic pregnancy with free peritoneal fluid in a haemodynamically stable woman is managed by laparoscopic salpingectomy under GA with minimal uterine manipulation; methotrexate cannot be used due to the coexisting viable IUP. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

options.rationale: Sacrificing a viable, desired intrauterine pregnancy is not justified; published IVF heterotopic series report ongoing IUP rates over 60% after laparoscopic salpingectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis and management of ectopic pregnancy

explanation.summary: The NCSP replaced Pap smears with primary HPV testing every 5 years from 2017 for women aged 25 to 74. The reflex pathway depends on whether HPV 16 or 18 (higher risk types) are detected. Any HPV 16 or 18 positive is referred to colposcopy regardless of cytology. Other oncogenic types ("oncogenic non-16/18" - types 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 68) are triaged by reflex cytology: normal or LSIL goes to repeat HPV at 12 months, HSIL or higher goes to colposcopy. Self-collection is now offered as the primary screening method to all eligible women.
key_points: NCSP: primary HPV every 5 years, ages 25-74
HPV 16/18 positive: refer to colposcopy regardless of cytology
Oncogenic non-16/18 + normal/LSIL: repeat HPV at 12 months
Oncogenic non-16/18 + HSIL or higher: colposcopy
Self-collection now equivalent to clinician-collected screening
explanation.pearls: Co-test (HPV + cytology) is reserved for surveillance of treated high-grade lesions; for primary screening in 2024 the HPV result drives the pathway and the cytology is reflex - reading the LSIL but ignoring the HPV 16 reverses the decision logic.

sources.label: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024
Cancer Council Australia: Cervical cancer prevention and screening

options.rationale: HPV 16 or 18 detection on the primary screen is referred directly to colposcopy regardless of cytology because of the higher progression risk associated with type 16. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024

options.rationale: HPV 16/18 positive on primary CST is referred to colposcopy without further repeat HPV testing; self-collection is a primary screening option, not a triage tool. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024

options.rationale: Treating without histological diagnosis is not appropriate; colposcopy with directed biopsy is required to confirm or exclude high-grade dysplasia before any ablative or excisional therapy. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024

options.rationale: HPV vaccination is not used to manage existing HPV infection or to alter screening intervals in already-infected patients. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024

options.rationale: Under the 2024 NCSP, HPV 16 or 18 on the primary screen is referred directly to colposcopy; the cytology grade does not alter the referral pathway because of type 16's elevated progression risk. (Source: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024)
source_refs: NCSP National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines 2024

explanation.summary: Endometriosis is managed in a stepped approach. First-line medical therapy is COCP (cyclic or continuous) or progestogen (norethisterone, dienogest) for pain. LNG-IUS and GnRH agonist with add-back are second-line. Surgical management with excision (preferred over ablation) is indicated when medical therapy fails, when deep infiltrating disease is suspected on imaging or examination, when there is symptomatic endometrioma over 3 cm, or when fertility is desired. Surgery for deep disease involving bowel, ureter or rectovaginal septum should occur in tertiary units with multidisciplinary expertise. CA-125 lacks specificity but is often elevated in DIE.
key_points: First-line medical: continuous COCP or progestogen
Second-line medical: LNG-IUS or GnRH agonist with add-back
Surgical excision: failed medical therapy, DIE, endometrioma over 3 cm, infertility
Excision preferred over ablation for recurrence rates
DIE surgery requires tertiary unit with bowel/ureter expertise
explanation.pearls: Endometrioma surgery in women planning pregnancy must weigh recurrence and adhesion benefits against AMH and ovarian reserve loss from cystectomy; in women with deep infiltrating disease who want fertility, multidisciplinary discussion before any operation is essential.

options.rationale: Failed adequate hormonal therapy plus deep infiltrating endometriosis features on examination and imaging is the standard threshold for diagnostic laparoscopy with planned excision at a tertiary unit. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis clinical care standard)

GnRH agonist is a reasonable medical second-line for some women but does not address mechanical deep infiltrating disease causing fixed pelvic anatomy; surgical excision is recommended where DIE is suspected. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis clinical care standard)

LNG-IUS can help with pain in selected patients but is unlikely to control symptoms driven by deep infiltrating disease with rectovaginal nodule, and delays definitive diagnosis and management. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis clinical care standard)

Definitive surgery with BSO in a 27-year-old nulligravid woman is not appropriate before fertility-sparing excisional options are tried; conservation of ovarian function is a priority. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis clinical care standard)

Multidisciplinary care including physio and pain services is valuable but does not replace excisional surgery for symptomatic deep infiltrating disease after failed medical therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis clinical care standard)

explanation.summary: Vulval lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with bimodal age distribution (prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women). Classical findings are figure-of-eight pale atrophic plaques sparing the vagina, with architectural change (clitoral hood fusion, labial resorption, posterior fourchette fissuring). Diagnosis is clinical for typical cases; biopsy is reserved for atypical features, treatment failure, focal mass or ulceration. First-line treatment is ultrapotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol 0.05% ointment) nightly induction, then taper to twice-weekly maintenance, with annual surveillance for differentiated VIN and vulval SCC (lifetime risk around 4 to 5%).
key_points: Bimodal age: prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women
Typical: figure-of-eight white plaques, architectural change, vagina spared
First-line: clobetasol 0.05% ointment OD induction, then twice-weekly maintenance
Biopsy if atypical features, treatment failure, focal mass or ulceration
Lifetime SCC risk 4-5%: annual surveillance lifelong
explanation.pearls: Painful fissures at the posterior fourchette in a postmenopausal woman with dyspareunia is a classical presentation of LS; lubricant alone is a routine misstep that misses the diagnosis and lets architectural change progress to permanent introital narrowing.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus
BAD Clinical Guideline: Vulval lichen sclerosus

options.rationale: The architectural change with loss of labia minora and clitoral hood fusion is characteristic of lichen sclerosus rather than atrophic vulvovaginitis, and topical oestrogen is not the first-line treatment. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus

options.rationale: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid induction-then-taper-then-maintenance is standard for classic LS; biopsy is reserved for atypical lesions, treatment failure, ulceration or focal masses. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus

options.rationale: Typical LS without ulceration, induration, focal mass or persistence despite therapy does not require urgent oncology referral or biopsy; ongoing surveillance is enough. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus

options.rationale: Mild-potency corticosteroids are insufficient for LS; under-treatment risks ongoing inflammation, scarring and progression. Ultrapotent steroids are recommended for induction. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus

options.rationale: Recurrent candidiasis does not produce architectural change; the clinical picture is LS, not candidiasis, and antifungals will not help. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Lichen sclerosus

explanation.summary: Stress urinary incontinence in women is initially managed conservatively with supervised pelvic floor muscle training (8 to 12 weeks of at least three sets of eight to twelve contractions daily under physiotherapist guidance), lifestyle modification (weight loss if BMI over 25, reduction in caffeine and bladder irritants, smoking cessation), and bladder training. Urodynamics are reserved for failed conservative therapy, mixed picture or planning surgery. Mid-urethral sling is the standard surgical option after failure of conservative measures; recent Australian regulatory restrictions on mesh have shifted toward autologous fascial sling and Burch colposuspension in some women.
key_points: First-line SUI: supervised PFMT 8-12 weeks + lifestyle (weight, caffeine, smoking)
Antimuscarinics treat urgency, not SUI - check diary for symptom phenotype
Topical oestrogen for postmenopausal urogenital atrophy contribution
Urodynamics: failed conservative therapy or planning surgery
Surgery: mid-urethral sling, autologous fascial sling, Burch colposuspension
explanation.pearls: Bladder diary with paired symptom triggers is the most cost-effective single test - it distinguishes pure stress from urgency-predominant or mixed, separates polydipsia-driven volume from low-volume incontinence, and dictates whether pelvic floor training or antimuscarinics are appropriate.

sources.label: Continence Foundation of Australia: Clinical guidelines

options.rationale: Urodynamics are reserved for failed conservative therapy or for mixed/atypical pictures, not first-line for clinically obvious pure SUI. (Source: RACGP: Urinary incontinence in women)
Surgical mid-urethral sling is reserved for failed adequate conservative therapy in Australian practice; supervised pelvic floor training is first-line. (Source: RACGP: Urinary incontinence in women)
Antimuscarinics treat urgency or urge incontinence, not stress incontinence; this patient has no urgency component. (Source: RACGP: Urinary incontinence in women)

Supervised pelvic floor training (8-12 weeks) plus lifestyle modification (weight loss, caffeine reduction) is the recommended first-line for SUI in Australia; surgical and pharmacological options are second-line. (Source: RACGP: Urinary incontinence in women)

Topical oestrogen is helpful for postmenopausal urogenital atrophy contributing to incontinence but is not first-line in a still-menstruating premenopausal woman with classical SUI. (Source: RACGP: Urinary incontinence in women)

explanation.summary: Absolute contraindications to systemic menopausal hormone therapy include current or prior breast cancer, current or prior oestrogen-dependent cancer (e.g. some endometrial cancers), undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, active VTE or known thrombophilia with prior thrombosis, active liver disease, untreated severe hypertension and known cardiovascular disease. Non-hormonal options for VMS include SSRIs (paroxetine, escitalopram), SNRIs (venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine), gabapentin, pregabalin, oxybutynin and CBT. Tibolone is contraindicated in breast cancer survivors. Vaginal oestrogen for urogenital atrophy in breast cancer survivors is generally avoided during active aromatase inhibitor therapy; it can be considered after MDT discussion otherwise.
key_points: Absolute MHT contraindications: prior breast/oestrogen-dependent cancer, active VTE, severe liver disease
Non-hormonal VMS: SSRI/SNRI (venlafaxine, escitalopram), gabapentin, oxybutynin
Paroxetine + tamoxifen: avoid (CYP2D6 interaction reduces tamoxifen efficacy)
Tibolone contraindicated in breast cancer survivors (LIBERATE)
Vaginal oestrogen for urogenital atrophy: avoid with aromatase inhibitors
explanation.pearls: Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit CYP2D6 and reduce conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite endoxifen; in a tamoxifen-taking patient, switch to venlafaxine or escitalopram instead of paroxetine for VMS or depression.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement
Cancer Australia: Menopausal hormone therapy after breast cancer

options.rationale: Prior hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer is a contraindication to systemic menopausal hormone therapy regardless of time since treatment. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement

options.rationale: Tibolone is associated with increased breast cancer recurrence (LIBERATE trial) and is contraindicated in breast cancer survivors. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement

options.rationale: Venlafaxine is an effective non-hormonal option for VMS in women in whom MHT is contraindicated; SSRIs/SNRIs and gabapentin are recommended in breast cancer survivors. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement

options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen treats urogenital atrophy, not systemic vasomotor symptoms, and is best avoided in breast cancer survivors during active aromatase inhibitor therapy; not the answer for VMS. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement

options.rationale: Phytoestrogen efficacy is at best equivalent to placebo for VMS and they have not been shown safe long-term in oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer survivors. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: MHT position statement

explanation.summary: Australian intrapartum GBS prophylaxis follows a screening approach with universal vaginal-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks. Positive carriers receive IAP in labour from labour onset or rupture of membranes. First-line is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery. Penicillin allergy with low anaphylaxis risk: cefazolin 2 g loading then 1 g every 8 hours. High-risk penicillin allergy: clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours if susceptible, otherwise vancomycin. Risk-factor-based prophylaxis (no swab, preterm, ROM over 18 h, fever, previous GBS infant) is also used when swab unavailable.
key_points: Universal vaginal-rectal swab at 35-37 weeks
Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV loading then 1.8 g q4h until birth (first-line)
Cefazolin 2 g then 1 g q8h for mild penicillin allergy
Clindamycin or vancomycin for severe penicillin allergy
IAP started at least 4 hours before delivery for full benefit
explanation.pearls: Previous infant with invasive GBS disease is itself an automatic indication for IAP in this pregnancy without screening - that risk persists despite negative current swab.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Azithromycin is not an accepted intrapartum prophylactic agent for GBS; macrolides do not reliably eradicate maternal colonisation or prevent vertical transmission. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: IAP must begin at least 4 hours before delivery to ensure adequate placental and fetal levels; waiting until 8 cm or after rupture risks insufficient coverage. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: RANZCOG and KEMH protocols give benzylpenicillin 3 g IV loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours from labour onset or rupture of membranes until birth in penicillin non-allergic women colonised with GBS. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for severe penicillin allergy with cefazolin contraindicated and clindamycin-resistant GBS; it is not first-line in a non-allergic woman. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Previous unaffected baby is not protective against GBS transmission in subsequent pregnancies if maternal colonisation is now positive; IAP is still indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Australian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society (ADIPS) 2017 criteria diagnose gestational diabetes mellitus on a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks (or earlier if high risk) with any one of: fasting plasma glucose at or above 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour at or above 10.0 mmol/L, or 2-hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L. Overt diabetes in pregnancy is fasting at or above 7.0, random at or above 11.1 or HbA1c at or above 6.5 percent. Initial GDM management is medical nutrition therapy, blood glucose self-monitoring (fasting and 1- or 2-hour postprandials), exercise advice and multidisciplinary review. Metformin or insulin is added if glycaemic targets are not met after one to two weeks.
key_points: 75g OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1-hr 10.0, 2-hr 8.5 mmol/L
Any single value above threshold = GDM
Overt DM in pregnancy: FPG 7.0+, random 11.1+, HbA1c 6.5%+
First-line: diet, exercise, SMBG, dietitian
Targets: fasting under 5.0, 1-hr under 7.4, 2-hr under 6.7 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Early OGTT (under 20 weeks) in high-risk women with previous GDM, BMI over 35, prior macrosomic baby or family history catches preexisting type 2 diabetes that would otherwise be misdiagnosed as GDM.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy requires fasting glucose at or above 7.0, random or 2-hour at or above 11.1, or HbA1c at or above 6.5 percent; her values do not meet these thresholds and she is not overtly diabetic. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2017: Diagnosis of GDM)

ADIPS Australian thresholds are lower than the WHO cut-offs quoted, and fasting of 5.3 already exceeds 5.1 mmol/L; the WHO 2013 criteria align closely with ADIPS rather than disagreeing. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2017: Diagnosis of GDM)

ADIPS 2017 thresholds for GDM by 75 g OGTT: fasting at or above 5.1, 1-hour at or above 10.0, 2-hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L; her fasting 5.3 alone qualifies. Initial management is SMBG, dietitian and multidisciplinary clinic. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2017: Diagnosis of GDM)

IGT as a pre-pregnancy concept does not apply during pregnancy; ADIPS uses GDM diagnosis with the lower thresholds and starts management on a single confirmed test. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2017: Diagnosis of GDM)
Pre-test carbohydrate priming is not required; a single OGTT with any value above threshold establishes the diagnosis under ADIPS without repeat. (Source: ADIPS Consensus 2017: Diagnosis of GDM)

explanation.summary: Postpartum endometritis is most common after caesarean section, prolonged rupture of membranes, multiple vaginal examinations and chorioamnionitis. Clinical features include fever above 38, uterine tenderness, foul lochia and leucocytosis after the first 24 hours postpartum. Therapeutic Guidelines empirical regimen is intravenous ampicillin or amoxicillin 2 g 6-hourly, gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily and metronidazole 500 mg 12-hourly, continued until 24 to 48 hours afebrile. Step down to oral amoxicillin clavulanate to complete 7 days total in clinical responders. Re-evaluate for retained products of conception, abscess or septic pelvic thrombophlebitis if no response by 48 hours.
key_points: Postpartum endometritis is polymicrobial: aerobic and anaerobic flora
IV ampi/amoxi + gentamicin + metronidazole first-line
Step down to oral amox-clav at 24-48 hr afebrile
Total duration 7 days
If no response by 48 h, consider retained products, abscess, SPVT
explanation.pearls: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis classically presents as persistent fever despite adequate antibiotics; treat with therapeutic anticoagulation as the cardinal diagnostic and therapeutic step.

options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic recommends triple IV cover (ampicillin or amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole) for postpartum endometritis to cover Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic flora until 24 to 48 hours afebrile, then step down to oral amoxicillin clavulanate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

Postpartum endometritis with fever, leucocytosis and uterine tenderness requires inpatient IV antibiotics until afebrile; oral monotherapy delays response and increases complications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

PID regimens do not adequately cover the polymicrobial pathogens of post-CS endometritis (including anaerobes); the clinical context is endometritis not classic PID. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

Piperacillin tazobactam is reserved for severe sepsis or treatment failure; first-line for uncomplicated endometritis is the narrower triple-agent regimen which is effective and cheaper. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

Withholding antibiotics in suspected endometritis with fever and leucocytosis risks progression to bacteraemia or sepsis; empirical therapy is started immediately after cultures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endometritis)

explanation.summary: Australian National Blood Authority guidance for routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis in RhD-negative non-immunised women is 625 IU of anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly at 28 weeks AND at 34 weeks. A further 625 IU is given within 72 hours of birth if the baby is RhD-positive (cord blood test). Event-driven doses are added for any sensitising event: miscarriage or termination at 12+ weeks (250 IU before 12 weeks, 625 IU at or after), ectopic pregnancy, antepartum haemorrhage, abdominal trauma, external cephalic version, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling. Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage and guides additional dosing.
key_points: 625 IU IM at 28 weeks AND 34 weeks (routine antenatal)
625 IU IM within 72 h of birth if baby Rh-positive
Event-driven doses for sensitising events
Kleihauer-Betke for FMH quantification
Confirm by indirect antiglobulin test for ongoing antibody screening
explanation.pearls: If anti-D is missed within 72 hours, give up to 9 to 10 days post-event - residual benefit persists even beyond the 72-hour window.

sources.label: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics

options.rationale: Cell-free fetal DNA-directed prophylaxis is in use in some jurisdictions but not yet standard NBA-recommended Australian practice; default is universal Rh-D negative non-immunised prophylaxis. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics

options.rationale: Two-dose schedule (28 and 34 weeks) is the routine Australian recommendation; single late dose is not standard practice here. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics

options.rationale: 1250 IU is the dose used in some single-dose international regimens but Australian practice uses 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics

options.rationale: Antenatal prophylaxis significantly reduces alloimmunisation; postnatal-only dosing is outdated practice and not endorsed by NBA. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics

options.rationale: Australian National Blood Authority guidance for RhD-negative women without anti-D antibodies is routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks (625 IU IM each) plus postnatal dose if baby is Rh-positive, plus event-driven doses. (Source: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics)
source_refs: NBA: Guidelines for the prophylactic use of Rh D immunoglobulin in obstetrics

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by systolic BP at or above 160 or diastolic at or above 110 mmHg, persistent neurological symptoms, severe right upper quadrant or epigastric pain with raised transaminases, pulmonary oedema, oliguria, thrombocytopenia under 100, or fetal compromise. Management at any gestation includes intravenous magnesium sulfate (4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours postnatally) for seizure prophylaxis, rapid BP control with labetalol, hydralazine or oral nifedipine targeting under 160/110, antenatal corticosteroids if under 34+6 weeks for lung maturity, and planned delivery after maternal stabilisation (typically within 24 to 48 hours at 32 weeks).
key_points: Severe BP threshold 160/110 with end-organ features
Mg sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hr for seizure prophylaxis and ongoing 24 h postnatal
BP control: IV labetalol, hydralazine or oral nifedipine to under 160/110
Betamethasone if under 34+6 weeks
Delivery after stabilisation, typically within 24-48 h
explanation.pearls: Magnesium toxicity is monitored by hourly checks of patellar reflex, respiratory rate (over 12) and urine output (over 30 mL/h); IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% is the antidote.

options.rationale: Aspirin and calcium are primary prevention strategies started early in pregnancy; once severe pre-eclampsia has developed at 32 weeks these are not appropriate as a substitute for acute stabilisation and planned delivery. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)

Severe-range blood pressure with neurological symptoms and end-organ involvement excludes outpatient management; methyldopa is not used acutely for severe pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)

Severe pre-eclampsia is not an absolute indication for category 1 caesarean unless there is fetal compromise or eclampsia not controlled by magnesium; planned delivery (vaginal or CS) after stabilisation is appropriate. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)

Furosemide is not used unless pulmonary oedema is established; magnesium is indicated for severe pre-eclampsia regardless of clonus to prevent seizures; steroids should be given for fetal lung maturity at this gestation. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)

Severe pre-eclampsia (BP at or above 160/110 plus end-organ involvement) at 32 weeks requires magnesium for seizure prophylaxis, urgent BP control, antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, and planned delivery after stabilisation typically within 24 to 48 hours. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy 2023)

explanation.summary: Placenta praevia is the abnormal implantation of the placenta over or near the internal cervical os and is a leading cause of painless antepartum haemorrhage. Major praevia (covering os) is delivered by elective caesarean at 36+0 to 37+6 weeks if stable. Symptomatic bleeding mandates admission, two large-bore IV cannulas, FBC, group and hold (or crossmatch if significant), Kleihauer if Rh-negative, anti-D, antenatal corticosteroids if under 34+6 weeks, and strict avoidance of vaginal examination. Previous caesarean increases risk of placenta accreta spectrum, which should be assessed by MRI or detailed ultrasound at 32 to 34 weeks before delivery planning.
key_points: Painless bright PV bleed = praevia until proven otherwise
Never perform digital VE in known praevia
Admit, large-bore IV, crossmatch, betamethasone if under 34+6
Plan elective CS 36+0 to 37+6 weeks
Prior CS plus anterior praevia = accreta spectrum risk (MRI/US workup)
explanation.pearls: Vasa praevia is a separate entity with painless PV bleed at membrane rupture - small volume but rapid fetal exsanguination; high index of suspicion if velamentous cord insertion noted antenatally.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia
RCOG: Placenta praevia, placenta accreta and vasa praevia (Green-top 27a)

options.rationale: Discharge after a 200 mL bleed in known praevia is unsafe due to risk of further haemorrhage; inpatient observation is mandated until delivery in most cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia

options.rationale: Digital examination is contraindicated in known praevia because it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage; vaginal birth is not planned in complete praevia. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia

options.rationale: A symptomatic praevia at 34 weeks with a 200 mL bleed mandates inpatient admission, IV access, crossmatched blood available, antenatal corticosteroids if not previously given, strict avoidance of vaginal examination, and consultant-level planning for elective caesarean (typically at 36 to 37 weeks if stable). (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia

options.rationale: Category 1 delivery is reserved for ongoing maternal haemodynamic compromise, fetal compromise or massive haemorrhage; the woman is stable so stabilisation and planned delivery is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia

options.rationale: Indometacin tocolysis is not used at 34 weeks for praevia bleeding and ongoing outpatient management after a significant bleed is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia, accreta and vasa praevia

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency in which the cord descends below the presenting part after membrane rupture, leading to compression and fetal hypoxia. Immediate management has three pillars: relieve cord compression, monitor fetus, and expedite delivery. Compression relief by knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg with manual elevation of the presenting part by the examining hand kept in the vagina, plus filling the bladder with 500 mL saline via Foley if transfer is required. Tocolysis with subcutaneous terbutaline 250 mcg buys time. Definitive treatment is category 1 caesarean section unless full dilatation with imminent vaginal birth allows safer assisted vaginal delivery.
key_points: Knee-chest position or steep Trendelenburg
Manual elevation of presenting part in vagina until delivery
Tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg SC
Category 1 CS (decision-to-delivery 30 min)
Bladder filling 500 mL for transfer if delay anticipated
explanation.pearls: Avoid handling or warming the prolapsed cord beyond gentle replacement - vasospasm worsens fetal hypoxia and aggressive manipulation increases the risk of cord rupture.

options.rationale: At 4 cm dilatation vaginal birth is not imminent and pushing is not effective; rotational forceps in this scenario is unsafe. CS is the appropriate route. (Source: RANZCOG: Umbilical cord prolapse)

Immediate cord decompression by knee-chest/Trendelenburg with manual elevation, plus activation of category 1 CS (within 30 minutes) and bridging tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg SC, is the RANZCOG standard for cord prolapse with fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Umbilical cord prolapse)
Attempting to replace the cord risks further trauma and does not address the underlying compression; definitive delivery is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Umbilical cord prolapse)
Augmentation will worsen cord compression by increasing the strength of contractions against the cord; tocolysis (the opposite) is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Umbilical cord prolapse)

Bladder filling is a recognised adjunct for transfer over longer distances but immediate operative delivery on-site is preferred when theatre is available; transfer delays definitive care. (Source: RANZCOG: Umbilical cord prolapse)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is the inability to deliver the anterior shoulder with routine axial traction after delivery of the head. It is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate, systematic management following the HELPERR mnemonic. Step 1: call for HELP. Step 2: consider Episiotomy (to assist internal manoeuvres if needed). Step 3: Legs in McRoberts (hyperflexion at hips onto maternal abdomen). Step 4: Pressure suprapubically (Rubin I, directed posteriorly and laterally). Step 5: Enter pelvis for internal rotational manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods corkscrew, reverse Woods). Step 6: Remove posterior arm. Step 7: Roll patient to all-fours (Gaskin manoeuvre). Documentation of time elapsed at each step is mandatory.
key_points: Call for help and start the clock
McRoberts + suprapubic pressure: first-line, resolves over 50 percent
Avoid fundal pressure (impacts the shoulder)
Internal manoeuvres: Rubin II, Woods, reverse Woods, posterior arm delivery
Last resort: Zavanelli or symphysiotomy
explanation.pearls: Brachial plexus injury is associated with both excessive lateral traction on the head and prolonged shoulder dystocia; calm, controlled progression through HELPERR minimises injury risk.

options.rationale: Episiotomy alone does not relieve bony obstruction at the pubic symphysis; it may help access for internal manoeuvres but is not the first step. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)

RANZCOG and RCOG HELPERR algorithm starts with McRoberts and suprapubic pressure as first-line manoeuvres because they resolve over 50 percent of shoulder dystocias with low complication rates. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)
Fundal pressure worsens shoulder dystocia by impacting the anterior shoulder further against the symphysis and is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)
Zavanelli is reserved for failure of all first and second-line manoeuvres; it has high morbidity and is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)
Cord cutting at this stage offers no benefit while the head is delivered; the priority is mechanical disimpaction of the shoulder. (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) after molar pregnancy is diagnosed by FIGO criteria: (1) plateau in serum hCG over 4 measurements during at least 3 weeks, (2) rise in hCG by 10 percent or more over 3 measurements during at least 2 weeks, (3) histological evidence of choriocarcinoma, or (4) persistence of hCG above 6 months. Staging uses FIGO anatomic stage and modified WHO prognostic score (age, antecedent pregnancy, interval, hCG, tumour size, sites and number of metastases, prior chemo). Score under 7 = low-risk treated with single-agent methotrexate or actinomycin-D. Score 7+ or stage IV = high-risk treated with EMA-CO. Australian women are referred to specialist tertiary GTD centres for staging and treatment, with monitoring by serial hCG to undetectable.
key_points: FIGO post-molar GTN diagnosis: plateau (4 over 3 weeks) or rise (10%+ over 2 weeks)
Stage by CXR, pelvic US, then CT/MRI if indicated
WHO prognostic score: under 7 = low-risk (single agent MTX)
7+ or distant mets = high-risk (EMA-CO)
Strict contraception during and 12 months after chemotherapy
explanation.pearls: Phantom hCG from heterophile antibodies (rarely with hook effect at very high titres) is a key DDx in apparent plateau without imaging findings; urine hCG and serial dilution rule it out before committing to chemotherapy.

options.rationale: FIGO criteria for GTN after molar pregnancy include a plateau of hCG over 4 measurements across at least 3 weeks (days 1, 7, 14, 21), so this woman has GTN; tertiary referral, staging and stratified chemotherapy (single-agent MTX for low-risk, EMA-CO for high-risk) is the standard pathway. (Source: FIGO 2018: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia)

FIGO criteria for diagnosis of post-molar GTN are already met (plateau of 4 measurements over 3 weeks); waiting another 4 weeks delays curative chemotherapy. (Source: FIGO 2018: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia)

Repeat curettage is reserved for selected cases of persistent intracavitary trophoblastic tissue; the plateau in hCG with an intramyometrial mass requires chemotherapy rather than repeat surgery alone. (Source: FIGO 2018: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia)

Fertility-sparing chemotherapy cures over 95 percent of low-risk post-molar GTN; hysterectomy is reserved for women who have completed family or for chemoresistant disease. (Source: FIGO 2018: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia)

EMA-CO is reserved for high-risk GTN (FIGO score 7 or above), CNS or hepatic metastases or methotrexate failure; low-risk patients receive single-agent MTX or actinomycin-D after staging. (Source: FIGO 2018: Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia)

explanation.summary: Rotterdam criteria require two of three: oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after exclusion of mimics (thyroid, prolactin, CAH). When all three are met as here, the diagnosis is secure. Initial management for a woman not trying to conceive centres on COCP for cycle regulation and androgen control, metformin for metabolic features, and lifestyle intervention. Letrozole is for women seeking pregnancy; cyproterone monotherapy is second-line for refractory hirsutism. AMH and OGTT add little to a clinically clear case.
key_points: Rotterdam: 2 of 3 - oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, PCO morphology; exclude thyroid, prolactin, CAH
First-line for non-conceiving woman: combined oral contraceptive plus lifestyle; metformin for metabolic features
Letrozole is first-line for ovulation induction when fertility is the goal, not for general PCOS treatment
Cyproterone or spironolactone is added if 6 months of COCP plus lifestyle does not control hirsutism
explanation.pearls: When Rotterdam criteria are met and CAH/thyroid/prolactin are normal, the diagnosis is made: do not delay treatment waiting for AMH or repeat ultrasound, and pick management based on whether the woman is currently trying to conceive.

options.rationale: Letrozole ovulation induction is reserved for women trying to conceive; she is not planning pregnancy and current management priorities are menstrual cycle control, hyperandrogenism and metabolic risk. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS 2023)

Cushing's, phaeochromocytoma and dyslipidaemia are not routine exclusions for PCOS diagnosis; she has already had appropriate exclusion of thyroid, prolactin, CAH and pregnancy-related causes. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS 2023)

She meets all three Rotterdam criteria, secondary causes have been excluded, and the international evidence-based guideline supports COCP for menstrual regulation and hyperandrogenism with metformin as adjunct for metabolic features. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS 2023)

Cyproterone monotherapy is not first-line: COCP plus anti-androgen is reserved for inadequate response after 6 months of COCP, and contraception is mandatory due to teratogenicity of anti-androgens in pregnancy. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS 2023)

Repeat imaging adds no value when the Rotterdam criteria are clearly met; AMH is supportive but is not required to confirm a clinically secure diagnosis. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS 2023)

explanation.summary: Australian National Blood Authority guidance separates anti-D prophylaxis indications by gestation. Before 12 weeks, anti-D is required for sensitising events that disrupt the choriodecidual interface (miscarriage, termination, ectopic, chorionic villus sampling) but is NOT required for threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy. From 13 weeks, all sensitising events trigger 625 IU anti-D, and routine 625 IU doses are given at 28 and 34 weeks regardless. Quantitative fetomaternal haemorrhage testing applies from 20 weeks. Invasive fetal genotyping is not routinely used.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage with viable IUP under 12 weeks: anti-D NOT recommended
Miscarriage, termination, ectopic, CVS under 12 weeks: 250 IU anti-D within 72 hours
Sensitising event 13 weeks or beyond: 625 IU anti-D within 72 hours
Routine antenatal: 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks for Rh D negative women without preformed anti-D
explanation.pearls: First-trimester anti-D decisions hinge on event type, not bleed volume: a viable pregnancy with threatened miscarriage does not need anti-D, but a miscarriage, ectopic or termination under 12 weeks needs 250 IU.

sources.label: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Invasive fetal Rh typing is not indicated for antenatal anti-D decisions; non-invasive prenatal Rh-D genotyping from maternal plasma is increasingly available but not part of the standard sensitising-event response. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: The 625 IU dose is for sensitising events at or after 13 weeks and for routine 28- and 34-week antenatal prophylaxis; it is not recommended in a viable first-trimester pregnancy with threatened miscarriage. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Quantitative fetomaternal haemorrhage testing is not used to guide first-trimester anti-D decisions; anti-D in this gestation is determined by clinical event type, not by quantified bleed volume. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Australian guidance does not recommend routine anti-D prophylaxis for threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy under 12 weeks; sensitising events at this gestation do not produce significant fetomaternal haemorrhage. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Anti-D is not required for threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy before 12 weeks; routine Kleihauer testing in the first trimester is also not recommended in Australian guidance. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Active genital chlamydia is a temporary contraindication to IUD insertion because instrumentation through an infected cervix can precipitate pelvic inflammatory disease. The correct sequence is treat (doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days), partner notification and contact tracing, then insertion once treatment is complete. Australian guidance prefers doxycycline over single-dose azithromycin for genital chlamydia. Routine test of cure is not recommended for uncomplicated cases, but a test of reinfection at 3 months is standard. Copper IUD as emergency contraception requires the same infection-free status.
key_points: Active chlamydia/gonorrhoea/PID is MEC category 4 for IUD insertion (temporary)
First-line chlamydia: oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Partner notification and contact tracing for partners in the past 6 months
Test of reinfection at 3 months for chlamydia; no routine test of cure
explanation.pearls: Always swab before insertion: an asymptomatic positive NAAT changes management - treat, trace, then reschedule the IUD, never insert through an active infection regardless of how stable her partnership appears.

sources.label: Family Planning NSW: IUD insertion clinical guidance

options.rationale: Inserting an IUD through a chlamydia-infected cervix substantially increases the risk of ascending pelvic infection; defer insertion until treatment is complete, and Australian first-line for genital chlamydia is doxycycline not azithromycin. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Untreated active chlamydia at insertion markedly raises PID risk; routine test-of-cure is not recommended for uncomplicated chlamydia in Australia but a test-of-reinfection at 3 months is. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Doxycycline is preferred over azithromycin for genital chlamydia in Australia due to higher cure rates, and partner notification through contact tracing rather than empirical co-prescription is the recommended approach. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Active genital chlamydia is a contraindication to insertion of any IUD (copper or hormonal); switching device type does not address the underlying infection-related ascending risk. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

Active chlamydia infection is a temporary contraindication to IUD insertion under MEC category 4 for current cervicitis or PID; treat first, perform contact tracing, then schedule insertion once treatment is complete. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Cyclic mastalgia is common, bilateral and luteal-phase predominant. After excluding red flags (dominant mass, skin tethering, bloody nipple discharge, axillary nodes, age above BreastScreen threshold), first-line management is education, well-fitted supportive bra, simple analgesia and a symptom diary over 3 months. Imaging adds little in cyclic, bilateral, mass-free disease. Pharmacological options (tamoxifen, danazol) are reserved for severe refractory cases due to their adverse effect profile. Evidence for dietary interventions and vitamin E is weak.
key_points: Cyclic mastalgia: bilateral, luteal-phase, resolves with menses, often nodular
Red flags: dominant mass, skin tethering, blood-stained nipple discharge, axillary lymphadenopathy
First-line: supportive bra including sports bra at night during symptomatic week, simple analgesia, symptom diary
Tamoxifen 10 mg daily is reserved for severe refractory disease after lifestyle measures fail
explanation.pearls: A well-fitted supportive bra (even at night during the symptomatic week) achieves clinically meaningful relief in around 70% of women with cyclic mastalgia and should be the first prescription you write.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Breast cancer red flags

options.rationale: Cyclic bilateral mastalgia without a dominant mass or other red flags has a very low malignancy yield from imaging; routine imaging is not the first step and urgent surgical referral is not indicated. (Source: RACGP: Mastalgia clinical guidance)

Combined oral contraceptive pills can either improve or worsen mastalgia and are not recommended as first-line therapy for cyclic breast pain in a woman with regular cycles and no contraceptive need. (Source: RACGP: Mastalgia clinical guidance)

Evidence for caffeine restriction, low-fat diet and vitamin E in mastalgia is weak and inconsistent; these may be discussed but are not the recommended first-line intervention package. (Source: RACGP: Mastalgia clinical guidance)

Cyclic mastalgia without a dominant mass or red flags has reassurance, supportive bra fitting, analgesia and a 3-month diary as first-line management; imaging and pharmacotherapy are reserved for refractory cases. (Source: RACGP: Mastalgia clinical guidance)

Tamoxifen and danazol are reserved for severe refractory cyclic mastalgia after lifestyle measures have failed; they carry significant adverse effects and are not first-line in primary care for an unscreened initial presentation. (Source: RACGP: Mastalgia clinical guidance)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is the presence of unprotected fetal vessels in the membranes overlying or near the internal cervical os, typically associated with velamentous cord insertion (type 1) or vessels between placental lobes (type 2), and is most common after IVF and with low-lying or bilobed placentas. Undiagnosed vasa praevia carries fetal mortality above 50% at membrane rupture; prenatally diagnosed and managed with planned elective caesarean before labour, perinatal outcomes are excellent. The Australian package includes a follow-up scan, antenatal corticosteroids, hospitalisation around 30 to 32 weeks and elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks.
key_points: Risk factors: velamentous cord insertion, IVF pregnancy, bilobed/succenturiate placenta, low-lying placenta
Type 1: velamentous insertion with vessels across os; Type 2: vessels between placental lobes
Plan elective caesarean between 34+0 and 36+0 weeks, antenatal corticosteroids beforehand
Consider admission from 30 to 32 weeks given risk of unheralded membrane rupture
explanation.pearls: Prenatally diagnosed vasa praevia delivered by elective caesarean before labour has near-zero perinatal mortality; the only way to lose that benefit is to await spontaneous labour and risk vessel rupture at membrane rupture.

options.rationale: While placenta praevia frequently migrates, vasa praevia rarely resolves; vaginal delivery risks fatal fetal exsanguination from vessel rupture at membrane rupture. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia statement)

Cerclage is not used in vasa praevia management and bed rest has no proven benefit; the established intervention is elective caesarean before onset of labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia statement)

Diagnosed vasa praevia is managed with a follow-up scan in the third trimester, antenatal steroids in the late preterm period, planned elective caesarean section at 34 to 36 weeks before labour, and consideration of hospitalisation from around 30 to 32 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia statement)

Delivery at 39 weeks risks spontaneous labour and membrane rupture leading to fetal exsanguination; planned caesarean between 34 and 36 weeks balances the risks of prematurity against the risk of catastrophic vessel rupture. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia statement)

Prenatally diagnosed vasa praevia with planned caesarean section has excellent perinatal outcomes; termination is not an appropriate counselling offer based on this diagnosis alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia statement)

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis is an autoimmune destructive thyroiditis affecting 5 to 10% of postpartum women, usually within the first year. Three patterns: transient thyrotoxic only, transient hypothyroid only, or biphasic (thyrotoxic followed by hypothyroid). Symptomatic hypothyroidism with TSH above 10 mIU/L is treated with levothyroxine; treatment is typically transient with attempted withdrawal at around 12 months, although 20 to 30% develop permanent hypothyroidism. Beta-blockers are used in the thyrotoxic phase. Radioactive iodine uptake studies are contraindicated in breastfeeding women.
key_points: Postpartum thyroiditis: autoimmune destructive thyroiditis, 5 to 10% of postpartum women
Pattern: thyrotoxic only, hypothyroid only, or biphasic (thyrotoxic then hypothyroid)
Treat symptomatic hypothyroid phase with levothyroxine; attempt withdrawal at 12 months
20 to 30% develop permanent hypothyroidism so lifelong follow-up is required
explanation.pearls: Anti-TPO antibodies positive in early pregnancy predict postpartum thyroiditis: screen women with anti-TPO at 6 weeks, 3 and 6 months postpartum, and warn them that 'low mood and fatigue at 4 to 6 months' may be thyroid before it is depression.

options.rationale: Her biochemistry shows hypothyroid (not thyrotoxic) phase disease, so a beta-blocker is not indicated and uptake imaging is not the next step in the hypothyroid phase of postpartum thyroiditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Postpartum thyroiditis)

Symptomatic postpartum thyroiditis in the hypothyroid phase with TSH above 10 mIU/L and low free T4 is treated with levothyroxine; treatment is usually transient with attempted withdrawal at around 12 months, and lifelong hypothyroidism develops in roughly 20 to 30% of women. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Postpartum thyroiditis)

Her EPDS is below the screening cut-off and her clinical and biochemical picture clearly identifies postpartum thyroiditis as the explanation for her symptoms; antidepressant therapy is not the indicated next step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Postpartum thyroiditis)

Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in breastfeeding and is not the diagnostic axis here; her hypothyroid biochemistry, anti-TPO positivity and timing are characteristic of postpartum thyroiditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Postpartum thyroiditis)

With a TSH above 10 mIU/L, a low free T4, anti-TPO positivity and clear hypothyroid symptoms, expectant management would prolong morbidity; treatment is indicated and improves symptoms within weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Postpartum thyroiditis)

explanation.summary: For non-rotational low or outlet instrumental delivery with the fetus in occiput-anterior, vacuum is generally preferred over forceps because of lower maternal genital trauma and OASIS rates, although forceps have lower failure rates. Pre-requisites include full dilatation, ruptured membranes, known position, empty bladder, head no more than one-fifth palpable, station at or below the ischial spines, effective analgesia, suitable operator and theatre access for caesarean if unsuccessful. Kielland or other rotational forceps are reserved for malposition; abort the vacuum after three pulls without descent or three cup detachments.
key_points: Vacuum preferred for outlet or low non-rotational delivery in OA position
Pre-requisites: full dilatation, ruptured membranes, OA known position, empty bladder, head one-fifth or less palpable, station spines or below
Vacuum abort: three pulls without descent or three cup detachments
Rotational forceps (Kielland) only for malposition (OT or OP); requires experienced operator
explanation.pearls: If the head is at +2 station OA with reassuring trace and a tired primigravid, vacuum is the right tool; if there is malposition (OT or OP) or you need rapid delivery for non-reassuring trace with the head deeply engaged, forceps usually beats vacuum.

options.rationale: She has already had adequate contractions through 90 minutes of active pushing in a primigravid woman; further augmentation rather than expediting birth would be inappropriate at this point. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Kielland forceps are reserved for malposition (occiput-transverse or occiput-posterior) requiring rotation; the fetus is OA so rotational forceps are not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Outlet forceps would be reasonable when the head is on the perineum and visible without separating the labia; at +2 station vacuum is generally preferred for a non-rotational instrumental delivery in this OA position. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Vacuum is preferred for a non-rotational outlet/low cavity delivery at OA position with a reassuring CTG, an empty bladder and minimal moulding/caput; the abort rule (three pulls or three detachments) is standard practice. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

She meets criteria for instrumental delivery (fully dilated, OA, low station, reassuring CTG, empty bladder, suitable operator); jumping to caesarean is not the most appropriate next step. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare third-trimester microvesicular steatosis with mortality if untreated. The Swansea criteria (need 6 of 14) include vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria/polydipsia, encephalopathy, raised bilirubin (above 14 micromol/L), hypoglycaemia (under 4 mmol/L), raised urate (above 0.34 mmol/L), leukocytosis (above 11 x10^9/L), ascites or bright liver, raised transaminases (above 42 U/L), raised ammonia, renal impairment, coagulopathy, and microvesicular steatosis on biopsy. Discrimination from HELLP turns on coagulopathy without thrombocytopenia, hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy and hyperammonaemia. Treatment is maternal stabilisation, correction of coagulopathy, dextrose and prompt delivery.
key_points: Swansea criteria for AFLP: need 6 of 14; absence of microvesicular steatosis on biopsy does not exclude AFLP
HELLP vs AFLP: HELLP has thrombocytopenia and haemolysis; AFLP has hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy without thrombocytopenia, encephalopathy
Definitive therapy: maternal stabilisation then prompt delivery, usually within 24 hours
Recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies up to 20 to 25%; LCHAD deficiency screening for the neonate
explanation.pearls: Hypoglycaemia in a jaundiced third-trimester woman is AFLP until proven otherwise; the combination of low BGL, coagulopathy without thrombocytopenia, and raised ammonia is the discriminator from HELLP and forces immediate delivery planning.

sources.label: BSG/RCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Intrahepatic cholestasis presents with pruritus and raised bile acids without coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia or encephalopathy; delaying delivery to 37 weeks would risk maternal liver failure and fetal demise in AFLP. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

Liver biopsy is rarely indicated in pregnancy due to coagulopathy and time pressure; the diagnosis is established clinically and biochemically using Swansea criteria and definitive treatment is delivery, not awaiting histology. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

She fulfils at least 6 of the 14 Swansea criteria for acute fatty liver of pregnancy (vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria/polydipsia, encephalopathy, raised bilirubin, hypoglycaemia, raised urate, raised transaminases, raised ammonia, coagulopathy, bright liver, leukocytosis); definitive treatment is prompt delivery after maternal stabilisation. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

HELLP requires thrombocytopenia (under 100 x10^9/L) which is absent here; the biochemistry pattern with hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy without thrombocytopenia, hyperammonaemia and bright liver fits acute fatty liver of pregnancy, and conservative management is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)

Liver transplantation is exceptional in AFLP and only considered for women who fail to improve after delivery; the immediate intervention is prompt delivery with intensive supportive care. (Source: RANZCOG: Liver disease in pregnancy)
