explanation.summary: ADIPS 2014 diagnostic thresholds on the 75 g OGTT are fasting at or above 5.1, 1-hour at or above 10.0, or 2-hour at or above 8.5 mmol/L; one abnormal value is sufficient for diagnosis of GDM. Initial management is dietary and exercise advice with home blood glucose monitoring and predefined targets. Pharmacotherapy is added if targets are not consistently met after about 1-2 weeks of lifestyle measures. Overt diabetes in pregnancy is a separate, more stringent diagnostic category.
key_points: ADIPS GDM thresholds: fasting >=5.1, 1-hour >=10.0, 2-hour >=8.5; one abnormal value diagnostic
Targets: fasting <5.0, 1-hour <7.4 or 2-hour <6.7 mmol/L
Diet first; metformin or insulin added if targets not met
explanation.pearls: Overt diabetes in pregnancy (fasting >=7.0 or HbA1c >=6.5%) is distinct from GDM and warrants urgent referral plus fetal echocardiography due to higher congenital malformation risk.

options.rationale: ADIPS diagnostic thresholds for GDM on the 75 g OGTT are fasting at or above 5.1, 1-hour at or above 10.0, or 2-hour at or above 8.5; only one abnormal value is required and this woman meets two. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

Overt diabetes in pregnancy requires fasting glucose at or above 7.0, random over 11.1 or HbA1c at or above 6.5 percent; her values meet GDM thresholds only, not overt diabetes. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)
ADIPS criteria diagnose GDM on a single abnormal value above the threshold; this woman has two abnormal values and clearly meets criteria. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)
There is no role for repeating the OGTT when the diagnostic threshold is met; delay risks worsening glycaemic control and fetal macrosomia. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

Initial GDM management in Australia is diet and exercise with self-monitored blood glucose; pharmacotherapy is added if glycaemic targets are not met after a trial of lifestyle measures. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for GDM)

explanation.summary: Single-dose IM methotrexate is appropriate for haemodynamically stable women with unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy, bHCG below ~5000 IU/L (varying by protocol), no fetal cardiac activity, adnexal mass below ~3.5 cm, no free fluid (or only minimal), normal LFTs and RFTs, no contraindications and capacity for follow-up. Dose is 50 mg/m squared with bHCG measured on day 4 and day 7; a >=15% fall between day 4 and day 7 predicts success. Failure or rising bHCG prompts a second dose or surgery.
key_points: Methotrexate criteria: stable, bHCG <5000 (centres vary), no FH, mass <3.5 cm, no significant free fluid, normal LFT/RFT, reliable
Surgical management preferred if ruptured, unstable, or methotrexate failure
Counsel re: photosensitivity, avoid folate, avoid alcohol and conception for 3 months
explanation.pearls: Two-dose regimen used when initial bHCG is 3500-5000 or marginal; single-dose preferred at lower bHCG due to less toxicity but with slightly higher need for second-dose rescue.

options.rationale: She meets criteria for single-dose methotrexate (stable, bHCG below 5000, no FH, mass below 3.5 cm, no free fluid, normal LFTs and RFTs, reliable for follow-up). (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Ectopic Pregnancy)

Expectant management is generally reserved for bHCG below ~1000 with falling trend; at 2840 with visible adnexal mass methotrexate or surgery is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Ectopic Pregnancy)

Salpingectomy is appropriate when methotrexate criteria are not met or when the contralateral tube is healthy; this patient meets methotrexate criteria and prefers fertility-sparing therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Ectopic Pregnancy)

Salpingostomy is more morbid than methotrexate when methotrexate criteria are met, carries trophoblast-persistence risk, and is reserved for surgical cases where the tube is to be preserved. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Ectopic Pregnancy)
The two-dose regimen is reserved for higher bHCG (around 3500-5000) or larger masses; her values fit single-dose protocol which has lower toxicity. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: The HELPERR mnemonic for shoulder dystocia is: Call for Help, consider Episiotomy (only if needed for internal access), Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal rotation manoeuvres including Woods and Rubin), Remove (posterior arm), and Roll (all fours/Gaskin). McRoberts hyperflexion with suprapubic pressure resolves around 90% of shoulder dystocia cases by reorientating the pelvis. Fundal pressure should not be applied. Time is recorded carefully due to risk of hypoxic injury.
key_points: First manoeuvre: McRoberts + suprapubic pressure (resolves most cases)
Never apply fundal pressure (worsens impaction, risk of uterine rupture)
Internal manoeuvres (Woods, Rubin, posterior arm) follow if external fail
explanation.pearls: Time-to-delivery beyond 5 minutes increases hypoxic injury risk substantially; team-based simulation training improves outcomes.

options.rationale: Shoulder dystocia is a bony pelvic problem, not a soft-tissue problem; episiotomy does not relieve the dystocia and is performed only if it would facilitate internal manoeuvres. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder Dystocia)

McRoberts with suprapubic pressure is the first-line manoeuvre in HELPERR and resolves the majority of shoulder dystocia cases by rotating the pelvis to release the anterior shoulder. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder Dystocia)
Woods screw is an internal manoeuvre attempted only after external manoeuvres (McRoberts and suprapubic pressure) have failed in the HELPERR sequence. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder Dystocia)
Delivery of the posterior arm is an effective later manoeuvre in HELPERR after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure but is not the first-line step. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder Dystocia)
Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre when all other options have failed; it is not a first-line response to shoulder dystocia. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Shoulder Dystocia)

explanation.summary: Indications for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in Australia include GBS bacteriuria in current pregnancy, positive GBS screening swab at 35-37 weeks, previous baby with invasive GBS disease, preterm labour less than 37 weeks with unknown GBS status, prolonged ROM at least 18 hours, and maternal intrapartum fever. First-line is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth. Cefazolin is for mild penicillin allergy; clindamycin (if sensitive) or vancomycin for anaphylactic allergy.
key_points: Preterm labour with unknown GBS status = treat empirically
First-line: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g 4-hourly
Goal: at least 4 hours of antibiotic before birth
explanation.pearls: Erythromycin for PPROM (ORACLE study) is to prolong latency, not for GBS prophylaxis; both interventions may be needed concurrently when preterm rupture progresses to labour.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Maternal GBS prophylaxis

options.rationale: At less than 37 weeks gestation with unknown GBS status, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis should be commenced empirically without waiting for swab results, as labour onset before 37 weeks is itself an indication. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Group B Streptococcus)

Preterm labour with unknown maternal GBS status is an indication for empirical intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis throughout labour to reduce neonatal early-onset GBS disease. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Group B Streptococcus)
Erythromycin is the antibiotic of choice for PPROM not in labour to prolong latency; it is not adequate intrapartum GBS prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Group B Streptococcus)

Cefazolin is reserved for mild non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy; penicillin is the first-line agent because of its narrow spectrum and excellent neonatal outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Group B Streptococcus)

Oral antibiotics do not achieve adequate intrapartum concentrations; intravenous benzylpenicillin is required at least 4 hours before birth for optimal neonatal protection. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Group B Streptococcus)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is diagnosed by intractable nausea and vomiting in pregnancy with weight loss (typically >5%), dehydration and electrolyte disturbance. Admission criteria include inability to tolerate oral fluids, ketonuria, weight loss, electrolyte derangement, or failed outpatient management. Inpatient care includes IV rehydration with crystalloid, electrolyte correction (especially potassium), IV thiamine 100 mg before any dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and parenteral antiemetic (ondansetron, metoclopramide, or promethazine).
key_points: Admission triggers: weight loss >5%, ketonuria, hypokalaemia, orthostatic hypotension
Always thiamine before glucose-containing fluids (Wernicke prevention)
Steroids and TPN are last-line for refractory cases
explanation.pearls: Ondansetron has reassuring safety data in pregnancy; the historical first-trimester cleft palate signal has not been confirmed in larger Australian and international studies.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 69: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Severe hyperemesis with hypokalaemia, ketonuria and orthostatic hypotension requires admission for IV rehydration, parenteral antiemetic, IV thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and electrolyte correction. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Hyperemesis Gravidarum)

Orthostatic hypotension, hypokalaemia 3.2 and 6 percent weight loss are objective markers of severe hyperemesis warranting admission rather than community oral therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Hyperemesis Gravidarum)

Corticosteroids are reserved for severe refractory hyperemesis after first- and second-line antiemetics plus IV rehydration have failed in the inpatient setting. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Hyperemesis Gravidarum)
Haloperidol is a later-line antiemetic and is not used in isolation without rehydration; the patient is clearly dehydrated and needs IV fluids. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Hyperemesis Gravidarum)

TPN is reserved for prolonged severe cases with significant nutritional deficit unresponsive to enteral support; it is not first-line at this stage and has significant complication rates. (Source: RANZCOG Statement: Hyperemesis Gravidarum)

explanation.summary: Urogenital atrophy after breast cancer is common and often refractory to non-hormonal therapy. Low-dose vaginal oestrogen (estradiol pessary 10 mcg twice weekly or oestriol cream) has minimal systemic absorption and observational data support safety in women with prior ER-positive disease, particularly after non-hormonal therapy has failed. The decision should be shared with the breast oncology team and the woman counselled regarding the small uncertain risk. Systemic HRT and ospemifene are not used after breast cancer.
key_points: Refractory urogenital atrophy post-BC: low-dose vaginal oestrogen with oncology input
Systemic HRT contraindicated after ER+ breast cancer
Non-hormonal first; escalate to vaginal oestrogen if inadequate
explanation.pearls: Women on aromatase inhibitors may have greater systemic absorption concerns from vaginal oestrogen than those off oncological therapy; oncology team input is essential.

sources.label: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors

options.rationale: Systemic combined HRT is contraindicated in women with prior ER-positive breast cancer due to recurrence risk; even if vasomotor symptoms were predominant other agents would be preferred. (Source: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors)
source_refs: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors

options.rationale: She has trialled non-hormonal therapy adequately without benefit; continuing the same approach indefinitely is inadequate when refractory urogenital atrophy is causing recurrent UTIs and dyspareunia. (Source: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors)
source_refs: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors

options.rationale: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen has minimal systemic absorption and is considered an option for severe refractory urogenital atrophy after early breast cancer, after shared decision-making with the oncology team. (Source: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors)
source_refs: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors

options.rationale: Ospemifene is contraindicated in women with active breast cancer and not recommended after breast cancer in Australian guidance due to insufficient safety data. (Source: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors)
source_refs: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors

options.rationale: Intravaginal prasterone has limited safety data in breast cancer survivors and is not first-line; vaginal oestrogen at low dose has more established data with shared oncology decision-making. (Source: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors)
source_refs: AMS Position Statement: HRT in Breast Cancer Survivors

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program (NCSP) tests primarily for HPV with reflex LBC if HPV is detected. HPV 16 or 18 positive results carry a higher risk of CIN3 or invasive cancer and warrant direct colposcopy referral regardless of LBC result. HPV-other-positive with negative LBC repeats in 12 months. HPV-other-positive with possible or definite HSIL on LBC requires colposcopy. HPV negative results return to 5-yearly routine screening.
key_points: HPV 16/18 positive: colposcopy referral regardless of LBC
HPV-other + negative LBC: repeat in 12 months
HPV negative: 5-yearly routine screening interval
explanation.pearls: Self-collection of vaginal HPV swab is now offered to all eligible women in Australia and has equivalent sensitivity for high-risk HPV detection; reflex LBC still requires clinician-collected cervical sample if HPV positive.

options.rationale: Repeat in 12 months is the pathway for HPV-other-than-16/18 positive with negative LBC, not for HPV 16/18 positive which mandates colposcopy regardless of LBC. (Source: NCSP Clinical Management Guidelines)
Five-yearly screening applies only to HPV-negative results; an HPV 16 positive test requires direct colposcopy referral. (Source: NCSP Clinical Management Guidelines)
Imiquimod has no established role in cervical HPV management; topical immunomodulators are used for external anogenital warts not endocervical HPV. (Source: NCSP Clinical Management Guidelines)

Under the Australian NCSP, HPV 16 or 18 positive on CST mandates direct referral to colposcopy regardless of reflex LBC result, because of the higher associated risk of CIN3 or invasive cancer. (Source: NCSP Clinical Management Guidelines)

Endometrial sampling is irrelevant to cervical HPV; it is indicated for abnormal uterine bleeding or post-menopausal bleeding, neither of which is present here. (Source: NCSP Clinical Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage is defined as vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy with a closed cervix and a viable intrauterine pregnancy. Management is expectant with reassurance, safety netting and repeat ultrasound in 7-10 days, since most pregnancies continue beyond the bleeding episode. Anti-D immunoglobulin is offered only if rhesus negative and beyond 12 weeks gestation or for any intervention. Routine progesterone is not effective in women without prior miscarriages; the PRISM trial demonstrated modest benefit only in women with two or more prior losses.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage: bleeding with closed cervix and viable IUP - expectant management
Anti-D not routinely needed before 12 weeks unless intervention performed
Progesterone supplementation only if recurrent prior miscarriage (PRISM)
explanation.pearls: Subchorionic haematoma identified on ultrasound is associated with mildly increased miscarriage risk but does not change expectant management; activity restriction has no evidence base.

options.rationale: Methotrexate is for tubal ectopic pregnancy; an intrauterine live pregnancy with threatened miscarriage is managed expectantly. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)
Surgical evacuation is for incomplete or missed miscarriage; a viable live intrauterine pregnancy must not be terminated for threatened miscarriage. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)

Inpatient observation is not warranted for a stable threatened miscarriage with light spotting and confirmed live intrauterine pregnancy; outpatient management is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)

Routine progesterone supplementation and bed rest are not effective for threatened miscarriage with no history of recurrent loss; PRISM trial showed benefit only with prior miscarriages. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)

Threatened miscarriage with a confirmed live intrauterine pregnancy is managed expectantly with safety netting and a follow-up scan in 7-10 days; most progress beyond the bleeding episode. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)

explanation.summary: Single-dose methotrexate is appropriate for selected stable women with tubal ectopic pregnancy: beta-hCG below 5000 (some centres below 3500), adnexal mass under 35 mm, no fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid suggesting rupture, normal full blood examination, liver and renal function, and reliable follow-up. Dosing is methotrexate 50 mg per square metre intramuscularly with beta-hCG on days 4 and 7; a fall of at least 15% between those days indicates response. The woman avoids folic acid, NSAIDs, alcohol and conception for 3 months. Surgical salpingectomy is preferred when criteria are not met.
key_points: MTX single-dose criteria: hCG under 5000, mass under 35 mm, no cardiac activity, stable
Monitor hCG on day 4 and day 7; aim for 15% fall between these days
Avoid folate, NSAIDs, alcohol and conception for 3 months
explanation.pearls: If hCG fall between days 4 and 7 is less than 15%, give a second dose of methotrexate; persistent rise or new symptoms triggers surgical management.

options.rationale: She meets criteria for single-dose methotrexate (stable, hCG below 5000, mass under 35 mm, no cardiac activity, normal bloods, reliable follow-up); 15% fall day 4 to day 7 indicates success. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)
Stable women meeting criteria for medical management can be offered methotrexate; surgery is not mandatory for every tubal ectopic. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)
Expectant management is for falling hCG below 1000 with no symptoms; this woman has rising hCG with symptoms and a visible mass needing active management. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)
Misoprostol and mifepristone are for intrauterine miscarriage; methotrexate is the medical option for tubal ectopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)
Salpingostomy with intraoperative methotrexate is not standard practice; salpingectomy is preferred when surgery is needed and patient meets medical criteria. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: The 2023 International PCOS Guideline (led by Monash University and endorsed in Australia) recommends letrozole as the first-line pharmacological agent for ovulation induction in polycystic ovarian syndrome with anovulatory subfertility, given superior live birth rates and lower multiple pregnancy risk compared with clomifene. Dosing starts at 2.5 mg from day 2 to 6 with escalation if no ovulation, to a maximum of 7.5 mg daily, for 5 to 6 ovulatory cycles. Metformin is an adjunct, particularly in higher BMI or insulin-resistant patients, and clomifene is now considered second-line.
key_points: Letrozole 2.5 mg days 2-6 is first-line in PCOS (2023 guideline)
Higher live birth and lower multiple pregnancy vs clomifene
Metformin is adjunct; IVF is third-line after failed ovulation induction
explanation.pearls: Letrozole is off-label for ovulation induction in some jurisdictions but is supported by the international PCOS guideline and Monash IVF Australian practice; teratogenicity concerns have been refuted in well-conducted trials.

options.rationale: Gonadotropins are second or third line after letrozole and clomifene due to higher cost, multiple pregnancy risk and ovarian hyperstimulation; not first-line in PCOS. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023 (Monash))

Letrozole is the first-line ovulation induction agent in PCOS per the 2023 International PCOS Guideline, with higher live birth rates than clomifene and lower multiple pregnancy risk. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023 (Monash))
Metformin alone has lower live birth rates than letrozole or clomifene; it is an adjunct, not first-line monotherapy for ovulation induction. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023 (Monash))

IVF is third-line in PCOS after ovulation induction failure; it is not first-line for an otherwise straightforward anovulatory presentation at age 28. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023 (Monash))
Clomifene is now second-line behind letrozole due to lower live birth rates and higher multiple pregnancy rates in PCOS. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023 (Monash))

explanation.summary: From 4 weeks postpartum, the levonorgestrel intrauterine device can be inserted safely in breastfeeding women and is category 1 by the WHO and Family Planning Australia. It provides 5 years of highly effective long-acting reversible contraception with minimal maintenance and the added benefit of reducing menstrual loss over time. Combined oral contraceptives are restricted in breastfeeding women under 6 weeks postpartum because of venous thromboembolism risk and theoretical lactation suppression. Etonogestrel implant and progestogen-only pill are safe alternatives if IUD is declined or contraindicated.
key_points: LNG-IUD from 4 weeks postpartum is category 1 in breastfeeding women
COCP is restricted under 6 weeks postpartum and avoided if breastfeeding under 6 weeks
Etonogestrel implant and POP are safe alternatives at any postnatal time
explanation.pearls: Immediate post-placental IUD insertion (within 10 minutes of delivery) is increasingly offered in Australian tertiary centres; expulsion rates are higher than interval insertion but acceptability and continuation are improved.

options.rationale: LAM efficacy declines with mixed feeding and time and is not appropriate when the woman explicitly wants long-acting reversible contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Postpartum Contraception)

COCP is restricted under 6 weeks postpartum and is category 4 in breastfeeding women under 6 weeks postpartum due to VTE and lactation suppression. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Postpartum Contraception)

Levonorgestrel IUD can be safely inserted from 4 weeks postpartum, is category 1 in breastfeeding women, and provides 5 years of highly effective long-acting reversible contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Postpartum Contraception)

Permanent sterilisation is not the most appropriate option when reversible long-acting reversible contraception meets her stated 5-year horizon and avoids surgical risks. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Postpartum Contraception)

POP is safe in breastfeeding but does not meet her stated preference for long-acting reversible contraception; LARC is more effective and lower-maintenance. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Postpartum Contraception)

explanation.summary: Planned vaginal birth after a single previous low transverse caesarean is appropriate for selected women without absolute contraindications. RANZCOG counselling quotes a success rate of 72-75% and a uterine rupture rate of approximately 0.5%. VBAC should be conducted in a facility with continuous intrapartum CTG monitoring, IV access, and immediate access to theatre and blood. Spontaneous labour is preferred over induction; if induction is required, mechanical methods or low-dose oxytocin are used rather than prostaglandins, which carry a fivefold higher rupture risk. Elective repeat caesarean is timed at 39 plus 0 weeks.
key_points: VBAC success quoted as 72-75% in suitable candidates
Uterine rupture risk approximately 0.5%; continuous CTG and immediate theatre access required
Avoid prostaglandins for induction in VBAC; if induced, use mechanical methods or oxytocin
explanation.pearls: Two previous caesareans, classical scar, prior uterine rupture, induction at unfavourable cervix, and short inter-pregnancy interval each substantially raise rupture risk and may shift recommendation toward elective repeat caesarean.

sources.label: NSW Health: Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.rationale: Mandatory repeat caesarean is not consistent with shared decision-making; VBAC is offered to suitable women after individualised counselling about benefits and risks. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth After Caesarean)
VBAC should be conducted in a centre with continuous CTG and immediate access to theatre; home water birth is not appropriate due to rupture risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth After Caesarean)

Prostaglandins for cervical ripening are contraindicated in VBAC due to a fivefold higher rupture risk; induction of VBAC, if any, is by mechanical methods or oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth After Caesarean)

VBAC is offered with quoted success rate around 72-75% and rupture risk of 0.5%, with continuous CTG and immediate theatre access; this is shared-decision counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth After Caesarean)

Elective repeat caesarean is timed at 39 plus 0 weeks; earlier delivery exposes the neonate to respiratory morbidity and antenatal corticosteroids are not standard at term. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth After Caesarean)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia (BP at or above 160/110 with end-organ involvement) at 34 weeks gestation is managed with maternal stabilisation followed by planned delivery within 24-48 hours. Magnesium sulfate is the agent of choice for seizure prophylaxis (4 g IV loading dose over 15 minutes followed by 1 g/hour infusion), with monitoring of reflexes and urine output. IV labetalol bolus (or hydralazine, or immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg orally) is used for acute severe hypertension targeting BP below 160/110 mmHg. The Magpie and Eclampsia trials demonstrated MgSO4 superiority over phenytoin and diazepam.
key_points: MgSO4 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour (Magpie trial)
IV labetalol or hydralazine for acute severe BP, target below 160/110
Plan delivery within 24-48 hours after maternal stabilisation
explanation.pearls: MgSO4 toxicity is monitored clinically: loss of patellar reflex is the earliest sign and requires infusion cessation; calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote for severe respiratory or cardiac toxicity.

options.rationale: Slow-release nifedipine is not for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy; IV labetalol or hydralazine (or immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg oral) are the appropriate agents. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy)
Maternal stabilisation with MgSO4 and antihypertensive must precede delivery in severe pre-eclampsia unless there is an immediate threat to life. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy)
Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia (Magpie and Eclampsia Trial); MgSO4 is the agent of choice. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy)
Benzodiazepines are not for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia; MgSO4 plus antihypertensive plus delivery planning is correct. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy)

Severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks is managed with MgSO4 seizure prophylaxis (4 g load then 1 g/hour), IV antihypertensive (labetalol or hydralazine), HDU admission, and planned delivery within 24-48 hours. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Clinically suspected endometriosis based on cyclical pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia is managed empirically with first-line hormonal suppression of ovarian cycling: continuous combined oral contraceptive pill or progestogen-only options including a levonorgestrel-releasing IUD, desogestrel, or dienogest. Diagnostic laparoscopy is reserved for women with symptoms failing first-line therapy, suspected deep infiltrating disease, endometrioma, or fertility concerns. Pelvic MRI is added when deep infiltrating endometriosis is suspected on examination or ultrasound. GnRH analogues with add-back are reserved for resistant cases.
key_points: Continuous COCP or progestogen is first-line empirical therapy
Diagnostic laparoscopy reserved for failed medical therapy or fertility concern
Levonorgestrel IUD and dienogest are progestogen alternatives
explanation.pearls: Cyclical pelvic pain that fails escalating hormonal suppression should prompt referral to a gynaecology multidisciplinary endometriosis service for laparoscopic mapping and consideration of excisional surgery and pain medicine input.

options.rationale: Empirical hormonal therapy with continuous COCP is first-line for suspected endometriosis; diagnostic laparoscopy is reserved for symptoms failing medical therapy or fertility concerns. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
Empirical medical therapy is first-line; laparoscopy is offered if medical therapy fails, fertility is a concern, or there are red flags such as endometrioma. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
Pelvic MRI is not routine initial imaging for suspected endometriosis without deep infiltrating disease on TVUS; it does not change first-line empirical management. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
GnRH analogues with add-back are second or third-line due to cost, side effects and need for add-back; not first-line empirical therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)
Chronic opioid therapy for suspected endometriosis without medical therapy or diagnosis is inappropriate; first-line is hormonal suppression. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

explanation.summary: Selective intrauterine growth restriction in monochorionic diamniotic twins is classified by the umbilical artery Doppler pattern of the smaller twin: type I (positive end-diastolic flow), type II (persistent absent or reversed end-diastolic flow), and type III (intermittent absent or reversed end-diastolic flow). Type II from 32 weeks onwards typically prompts delivery; type III is more unpredictable but generally delivered by 34 weeks. Caesarean is preferred for monochorionic discordant twin delivery due to risks of intrapartum hypoxia. Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is given for preterm delivery below 30 weeks routinely.
key_points: Type II selective IUGR (persistent absent/reversed flow) usually delivered from 32 weeks
Type III (intermittent reversed flow) typically delivered by 34 weeks
Caesarean preferred for monochorionic discordant twin delivery
explanation.pearls: Intrauterine demise of one monochorionic twin carries 18-25% risk of co-twin neurological injury due to acute fetal-fetal haemorrhage through placental anastomoses, regardless of how rapidly delivery occurs after demise.

options.rationale: Type II selective IUGR with intermittent or persistent absent or reversed end-diastolic flow at 32 weeks or beyond is an indication for delivery with neonatal team standby; caesarean is preferred for monochorionic discordant twins. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)
Continued expectant management beyond 34 weeks with reversed end-diastolic flow risks demise of twin B and co-twin injury; delivery is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)
Laser ablation is used in twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (Quintero stage II or above) at earlier gestations, not for selective IUGR at 34 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)
Reversed end-diastolic flow reflects placental insufficiency, not anaemia; MCA Doppler is normal here, so intrauterine transfusion is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)
Rescue betamethasone alone does not address the fetal indication for delivery; reversed end-diastolic flow at 34 weeks mandates timely delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: The Australian first-line approach to heavy menstrual bleeding without structural pathology is the 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, which reduces blood loss by approximately 90% and provides contraception. Tranexamic acid and combined oral contraceptive are reasonable medical alternatives if an IUS is declined. Endometrial ablation and hysterectomy are reserved for failed or declined medical management. Concomitant iron deficiency is treated alongside the underlying bleeding control.
key_points: 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing IUS reduces menstrual loss by approximately 90%
Tranexamic acid and COCP reduce loss by approximately 40 to 50%
Endometrial ablation and hysterectomy are second-line after failed or declined medical management
Iron deficiency anaemia is treated alongside the underlying cause
explanation.pearls: The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system is licensed for 8 years for contraception in Australia and 5 years for heavy menstrual bleeding indication, with maximal blood-loss reduction reached around 6 months after insertion.

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive but reserved for women in whom medical and minimally invasive options have failed or are unacceptable. Surgical morbidity and recovery time mean it is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG - Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

The combined oral contraceptive reduces menstrual blood loss by approximately 40 to 50%, less than the levonorgestrel IUS, and is contraindicated in women over 35 with additional cardiovascular risk factors. It is a reasonable second choice when an IUS is declined. (Source: RANZCOG - Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by approximately 40 to 50% and is appropriate for women who decline hormonal therapy or seek symptom relief on heavy days only. It is less effective than a levonorgestrel IUS and does not provide contraception. (Source: RANZCOG - Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Endometrial ablation is appropriate when medical options have failed, are contraindicated, or the woman has firmly declined long-acting reversible contraception. It is not first-line when medical options have not yet been trialled. (Source: RANZCOG - Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

For women with heavy menstrual bleeding without structural cause who do not wish to conceive, the 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system is first-line in Australia. It reduces menstrual blood loss by approximately 90% at 6 months and treats coexistent iron deficiency anaemia by reducing ongoing losses. (Source: RANZCOG - Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (systolic 160 or more, or diastolic 110 or more) requires urgent control to reduce maternal stroke risk while maintaining placental perfusion. The Australian first-line options are oral labetalol, oral immediate-release nifedipine, or intravenous hydralazine. Targets are systolic 140 to 160 and diastolic 90 to 100, not full normotension. Magnesium sulfate is also administered for severe pre-eclampsia regardless of seizure occurrence to reduce eclampsia risk by approximately 50%.
key_points: First-line antihypertensives in severe pre-eclampsia: labetalol, oral nifedipine immediate release, IV hydralazine
Targets: systolic 140 to 160, diastolic 90 to 100, not normotension
Magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/h for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, nitroprusside, and sublingual nifedipine are contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: In severe pre-eclampsia, magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis regardless of whether seizures have occurred, with a 4 g loading dose over 15 to 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for 24 hours after birth or last seizure.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Hypertension in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Severe hypertension persisting after oral labetalol requires intravenous treatment. Hydralazine 5 mg IV bolus repeated at 20 minutes is the SOMANZ first-line intravenous antihypertensive for severe hypertension in pregnancy where oral therapy has been inadequate. The target is systolic 140 to 160 and diastolic 90 to 100, not normotension. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

Sublingual short-acting nifedipine causes rapid uncontrolled hypotension and is not recommended in pregnancy. Immediate-release oral nifedipine 10 mg is acceptable but never sublingual. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

Nitroprusside accumulates cyanide and thiocyanate metabolites in the fetus and is contraindicated in pregnancy except in life-threatening hypertensive emergency where no alternative is available. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

ACE inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal renal injury and oligohydramnios. They have no role in acute antenatal blood pressure control. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

Pre-eclampsia is characterised by intravascular volume contraction despite oedema. Loop diuretics worsen placental perfusion and are reserved for pulmonary oedema, not antihypertensive therapy. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency requiring a structured manoeuvre sequence. HELPERR captures the order: call for Help, evaluate Episiotomy need, Legs (McRoberts), suprapubic Pressure, Enter (internal manoeuvres), Remove the posterior arm, and Roll the patient (all fours). Internal rotational manoeuvres include Rubin II, Wood's screw, and reverse Wood's screw. Brachial plexus injury, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, and humeral fracture are recognised neonatal complications, while postpartum haemorrhage and perineal trauma affect the mother.
key_points: Fundal pressure is contraindicated; suprapubic pressure is the correct external manoeuvre
Internal manoeuvres follow McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure when those fail
Excess downward traction is the main modifiable cause of brachial plexus injury
Zavanelli replacement of the head is the last-resort manoeuvre
explanation.pearls: In shoulder dystocia, the next manoeuvre after McRoberts and suprapubic pressure is internal rotation or posterior arm delivery, not stronger traction - excess axial traction is the main modifiable risk for permanent brachial plexus injury.

options.rationale: Caesarean is not feasible once the head has delivered and the trunk is impacted. The Zavanelli manoeuvre (replacement of the head) is last resort, performed only after all other manoeuvres fail. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia Statement)

Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction by driving the shoulder further onto the symphysis and increases uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury rates. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia Statement)

Symphysiotomy is a last-resort procedure carrying significant maternal morbidity and is not appropriate before internal manoeuvres and all-fours position have been attempted. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia Statement)

Increased traction force is the principal modifiable risk factor for neonatal brachial plexus injury. Routine axial traction is acceptable, but increased downward traction is harmful. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia Statement)

After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure have failed, the next step is an internal manoeuvre: either delivery of the posterior arm or internal rotation. Both are considered first-line second-tier in the RANZCOG shoulder dystocia algorithm with comparable success rates. The HELPERR mnemonic places internal manoeuvres before all-fours and final-resort measures. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia Statement)

explanation.summary: Vaginal birth after one prior lower-segment caesarean is offered as a reasonable choice in Australia, with informed consent covering the success rate (around 60 to 80% achieve vaginal birth) and the rupture risk of approximately 0.5%. Risk modifiers include short inter-pregnancy interval under 18 months, no prior vaginal birth, induction of labour (particularly prostaglandins which roughly triple risk), and labour augmentation. VBAC should occur in a setting with 24-hour obstetric, anaesthetic, and neonatal cover and immediate theatre access.
key_points: Symptomatic uterine rupture with one prior LSCS: approximately 0.5% (1 in 200)
Prostaglandin induction roughly triples rupture risk; oxytocin augmentation roughly doubles it
Classical (vertical upper-segment) scar contraindicates trial of labour (approximately 10% rupture risk)
Continuous CTG monitoring is recommended during VBAC labour
explanation.pearls: Induction of VBAC labour with prostaglandins approximately triples the baseline rupture risk from around 0.5% to 1.5% - mechanical methods or oxytocin alone are preferred when induction is needed.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section
RCOG Green-top Guideline 45 - Birth after Previous Caesarean

options.rationale: A 5% risk overstates uterine rupture by a factor of 10 and would inappropriately drive women away from VBAC. The actual figure is around 0.5%. (Source: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: The risk of symptomatic uterine rupture during trial of labour after one prior lower-segment caesarean is approximately 0.2 to 0.7% in Australian and international datasets. RANZCOG quotes 1 in 200 (approximately 0.5%) as the headline figure for counselling, with augmentation of labour roughly doubling this risk. (Source: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: 0.01% underestimates rupture risk by 50-fold and falsely reassures. The risk is real and requires informed consent with appropriate intrapartum monitoring. (Source: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: 10% is the rough rate for women with a prior classical (upper segment) caesarean undergoing trial of labour and is the basis for the contraindication. With a low-transverse scar the risk is approximately 0.5%. (Source: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section

options.rationale: 2% overestimates rupture by approximately 4-fold and conflates symptomatic rupture with combined uterine-scar dehiscence rates seen on imaging. (Source: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Birth after Previous Caesarean Section

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy presents in the third trimester with nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, mild jaundice, and progressive multi-organ dysfunction. Hallmarks are hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy out of proportion to thrombocytopaenia, hyperammonaemia, hyperuricaemia, and modest transaminase rise (typically 300 to 500). Differentials are severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP and viral hepatitis; the Swansea criteria support the diagnosis. Delivery is the only definitive treatment. Maternal mortality is up to 18% and perinatal mortality 20 to 30% without timely delivery.
key_points: AFLP triad: hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy without HELLP-pattern thrombocytopaenia, hyperammonaemia
Transaminases typically 300 to 500 (lower than viral hepatitis)
Delivery is the only definitive treatment; coagulopathy and glucose corrected before operating
Swansea criteria support clinical diagnosis - liver biopsy is not required
explanation.pearls: Hypoglycaemia in a third-trimester woman with right upper quadrant pain and modestly elevated transaminases (300 to 500) suggests acute fatty liver of pregnancy until proven otherwise - delivery is the only definitive treatment.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy
BMJ Best Practice - Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy

options.rationale: While there is overlap with pre-eclampsia, the dominant features (hypoglycaemia, marked coagulopathy without low platelets, hyperammonaemia, ketonuria) point to acute fatty liver of pregnancy which requires delivery, not magnesium prophylaxis alone. (Source: SOMANZ - Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is suggested by hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy without HELLP-pattern thrombocytopaenia, hyperammonaemia, and modestly raised transaminases in the third trimester. Delivery is definitive and time-critical to halt progressive hepatic and renal failure. Coagulopathy and hypoglycaemia are corrected pre-operatively and tertiary care offers liver and renal support. (Source: SOMANZ - Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

Viral hepatitis typically presents with transaminases in the thousands rather than the hundreds and rarely produces the severe hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy pattern seen here. Awaiting serology delays delivery and worsens outcome in AFLP. (Source: SOMANZ - Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritus and elevated bile acids without hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, or encephalopathy. The clinical picture here is incompatible with cholestasis. (Source: SOMANZ - Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

Biopsy may show microvesicular steatosis but is not required for diagnosis or treatment. Coagulopathy makes biopsy hazardous and delivery is the priority. (Source: SOMANZ - Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Significant bacteriuria with group B streptococcus is a marker of dense genital tract colonisation, and Australian guidance treats it as an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis in its own right, regardless of any later swab. Such a woman therefore does not need the 35 to 37 week vagino-rectal swab, because a negative result would not change the plan and might wrongly reassure the team looking after her in labour. The bacteriuria itself is treated when found, since it carries a maternal risk of pyelonephritis and an association with preterm birth, but that treatment is separate from the newborn indication. In context, the two other standing indications that override the swab are a previous infant with invasive group B streptococcal disease and, on a risk basis, preterm labour or prolonged rupture when carriage status is not known.
key_points: Significant bacteriuria this pregnancy is a standing indication for prophylaxis in labour.
No 35 to 37 week swab is needed once that indication exists.
Treating the bacteriuria does not cancel the intrapartum indication.
A previous infant with invasive disease is the other standing indication.
explanation.pearls: Record standing indications on the front of the antenatal record rather than only in a result, because the team in labour reads the plan and not the microbiology history.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Significant bacteriuria with this organism at any point in the pregnancy indicates heavy colonisation and commits her to intrapartum prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: A swab decides the matter for a woman with no other indication, which is not this woman. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Repeat urine culture is worthwhile for persisting symptoms or a treatment failure, not to revisit a settled indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Retreatment is appropriate if she has symptoms or a fresh significant growth, but it does not replace cover in labour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Treating the bacteriuria protects the mother from pyelonephritis; it does not remove the newborn indication. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

explanation.summary: Anovulatory amenorrhoea in PCOS produces unopposed oestrogen exposure of the endometrium and a higher long-term endometrial hyperplasia and cancer risk. Endometrial protection options include LNG-IUS (5 years, no daily burden), cyclical or continuous progestogens, or a combined hormonal contraceptive. The International PCOS Guideline 2023 supports patient-centred choice based on contraceptive needs, adherence preferences, BMI and metabolic risk. Lifestyle modification remains a first-line non-pharmacological strategy.
key_points: PCOS amenorrhoea requires endometrial protection; bleeding at least every 3 months is the goal
LNG-IUS, COCP, cyclical or continuous progestogen are all valid options
Choice is patient-centred: contraceptive needs, adherence, BMI, metabolic risk
explanation.pearls: The International PCOS Guideline 2023 specifically endorses the LNG-IUS as a low-adherence-burden first-line option for endometrial protection in women who do not want pregnancy and find daily medication difficult.

options.rationale: Cyclical progestogens give adequate endometrial protection but rely on daily oral dosing, which the patient has identified as burdensome and at risk of non-adherence. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

The LNG-IUS provides effective endometrial protection in PCOS-related anovulatory amenorrhoea and avoids the daily-medication burden the patient describes, with a 5-year duration. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)
Metformin improves ovulatory function modestly but does not reliably restore menses or provide endometrial protection in established oligomenorrhoea. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)
A COCP is first-line in many PCOS women, but requires daily adherence which the patient has flagged as a barrier, and her BMI of 31 raises VTE risk. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)
Hysterectomy is disproportionate for a 24-year-old with PCOS-related amenorrhoea, removes future fertility options, and ignores effective reversible strategies. (Source: RANZCOG PCOS)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. The Australian first-line investigation is transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 4 mm or less in non-HRT users has a negative predictive value above 99%. Thicker endometrium or persistent bleeding triggers hysteroscopy and Pipelle biopsy. Risk factors include obesity, diabetes, tamoxifen, unopposed oestrogen, Lynch syndrome and nulliparity. Cervical screening is unrelated to this work-up.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise
TVUS first; endometrial thickness 4 mm or less effectively rules out cancer in non-HRT users
Persistent bleeding or thickness above 4 mm goes to hysteroscopy + Pipelle biopsy
explanation.pearls: In Australian guidance the endometrial thickness threshold for proceeding to biopsy after postmenopausal bleeding is 4 mm in non-HRT users; this rises to around 5 mm in women on cyclical HRT.

options.rationale: Cervical screening is up to date and HPV negative; postmenopausal bleeding is investigated for endometrial pathology, not by repeating cervical screening. (Source: NCSP Australia 2023)

Hysteroscopy with biopsy is the second step after ultrasound shows endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm or persistent bleeding; performing it without prior ultrasound triage misallocates theatre time. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line investigation for postmenopausal bleeding; an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less in a non-HRT user has a very high negative predictive value for endometrial cancer. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Pelvic MRI is reserved for staging confirmed endometrial cancer or for problem-solving complex anatomy; it is not a first-line investigation for postmenopausal bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Any postmenopausal bleeding warrants investigation because endometrial cancer accounts for around 10% of cases and is curable if detected early; reassurance without investigation is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Intrauterine resuscitation addresses reversible causes of fetal compromise: aortocaval compression, hyperstimulation, hypotension and hypoxia. The standard sequence is stop oxytocin, reposition to left lateral, give intravenous fluid bolus, offer maternal oxygen if hypoxic, and review for cord prolapse or abruption. If hyperstimulation persists after oxytocin cessation, subcutaneous terbutaline 250 mcg is the next step. Failure to improve within 5 to 10 minutes triggers escalation to expedited delivery.
key_points: Always stop the oxytocin first when CTG worsens during augmentation
Left-lateral positioning relieves aortocaval compression
Persistent hyperstimulation after stopping oxytocin: terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneously
explanation.pearls: In RANZCOG IFS terminology, tachysystole is more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes, and is the most common driver of repetitive late decelerations during oxytocin augmentation.

options.rationale: Increasing oxytocin will worsen hyperstimulation and exacerbate late decelerations; the contraction interval of 90 seconds already exceeds tachysystole thresholds. (Source: RANZCOG IFS)

Category 1 caesarean is reserved for fetal compromise that fails intrauterine resuscitation or for immediate threats such as cord prolapse, placental abruption or uterine rupture. (Source: RANZCOG IFS)
Terbutaline tocolysis is reserved for tachysystole that persists after stopping oxytocin, not as a first step while oxytocin still runs. (Source: RANZCOG IFS)

Stopping uterine stimulation and left-lateral positioning relieve aortocaval compression and uterine hyperstimulation, the most common reversible causes of repetitive late decelerations during oxytocin augmentation. (Source: RANZCOG IFS)
Fetal scalp sampling can complement decision-making but is not the first step; reversible causes such as hyperstimulation must be corrected first before invasive sampling. (Source: RANZCOG IFS)

explanation.summary: Chorionicity is the single most important determinant of twin pregnancy management because monochorionic pregnancies carry markedly higher rates of twin-twin transfusion, selective growth restriction and perinatal loss. The most reliable first-trimester sign is the lambda (twin peak) sign at the placental insertion of the inter-twin membrane, present in dichorionic pregnancies; the T sign indicates monochorionic. After 14 weeks these signs become less reliable, so chorionicity should be documented and labelled on every dating scan in twin pregnancy.
key_points: Lambda sign at placental insertion of membrane = dichorionic
T sign at placental insertion = monochorionic
Document chorionicity at the dating scan; signs become unreliable after 14 weeks
explanation.pearls: The lambda sign loses sensitivity beyond 14 weeks because chorionic regression renders the placental wedge thin; this is why every Australian twin pregnancy must have chorionicity recorded before 14 weeks.

options.rationale: Apparently separate placentas may still be a single fused dichorionic placenta or even monochorionic with eccentric implantation, and so are not a reliable primary determinant of chorionicity. (Source: ISUOG Twin Practice Guideline)

Two sacs differentiate diamniotic from monoamniotic but do not differentiate monochorionic from dichorionic; both dichorionic-diamniotic and monochorionic-diamniotic show two sacs. (Source: ISUOG Twin Practice Guideline)

Discordant sex confirms dichorionicity, but at 11 to 12 weeks fetal sex is not reliably visible on transabdominal scanning; it cannot be the primary determinant at this gestation. (Source: ISUOG Twin Practice Guideline)
Membrane thickness becomes less reliable as gestation advances and is a poor stand-alone discriminator at 12 weeks compared with the lambda or T sign. (Source: ISUOG Twin Practice Guideline)

At 10 to 14 weeks the lambda (twin peak) sign at the placental insertion of the inter-twin membrane reliably indicates a dichorionic pregnancy with a positive predictive value above 95%; the T sign indicates monochorionic. (Source: ISUOG Twin Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: The 2023 National Cervical Screening Program in Australia stratifies management by HPV genotype and reflex cytology. Oncogenic HPV16 or 18 detection at any cytology grade triggers direct colposcopy referral because of higher cervical cancer risk per infection. Other oncogenic HPV with negative or pLSIL cytology enters 12-month surveillance; with HSIL or higher it also goes to colposcopy. Definitive treatment (LLETZ, cone biopsy, hysterectomy) follows histological confirmation. The copper IUD does not affect the screening pathway.
key_points: HPV16/18 at any cytology grade -> colposcopy referral
Other oncogenic HPV + pLSIL/negative cytology -> 12-month repeat HPV
Other oncogenic HPV + HSIL or higher -> colposcopy referral
explanation.pearls: HPV16 alone carries an absolute 10-year cumulative cervical cancer risk above 10% if untreated, which is why the 2023 NCSP pathway sends HPV16-positive women to colposcopy regardless of cytology grade.

options.rationale: Repeat HPV testing at 12 months is the surveillance pathway for non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with normal or low-grade cytology, not for HPV16 with high-grade cytology. (Source: NCSP Australia 2023)
Oncogenic HPV16 with possible HSIL on reflex cytology is a direct referral to colposcopy under the NCSP 2023 pathway, regardless of previous result history. (Source: NCSP Australia 2023)

LLETZ is performed only after histological confirmation by colposcopy-directed biopsy or when see-and-treat is appropriate at colposcopy with senior judgement, not as a first community step. (Source: NCSP Australia 2023)
Pelvic MRI is reserved for staging biopsy-confirmed invasive cervical cancer; it is not an initial screening abnormality work-up step. (Source: NCSP Australia 2023)
The copper IUD does not need to be removed before colposcopy and removing it adds nothing to evaluation of HPV-related cytological abnormality. (Source: NCSP Australia 2023)

explanation.summary: Antepartum haemorrhage with suspected or known placenta praevia requires admission, IV access, group and hold (consider cross-match if heavy), continuous CTG, no digital vaginal examination, and transabdominal ultrasound to confirm placental location. Sterile speculum is permitted after imaging to assess for local causes. Corticosteroids are given at 24+0 to 34+6 weeks for fetal lung maturation. Two prior caesareans plus praevia raises the risk of placenta accreta spectrum and warrants tertiary review. Bleeding that persists, escalates or compromises mother or fetus mandates expedited delivery by caesarean.
key_points: No digital vaginal examination in suspected praevia
Speculum after ultrasound confirms placental location
Antenatal corticosteroids at 24+0 to 34+6 weeks when delivery is possible within 7 days
explanation.pearls: Placenta praevia plus two or more previous caesareans confers an accreta spectrum risk of around 40%; these women need tertiary multidisciplinary planning, including consideration of caesarean hysterectomy and interventional radiology standby.

options.rationale: In suspected placenta praevia, digital vaginal examination is contraindicated; sterile speculum is permitted after ultrasound confirmation of placental location to assess for local causes. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia)
Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated in suspected placenta praevia because it can precipitate catastrophic haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia)
Uterotonics are not used in antepartum haemorrhage from placenta praevia; they have no role until after delivery and can precipitate maternal hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia)

At 32 weeks, with bleeding now slowing and a stable mother and fetus, conservative inpatient management with corticosteroids is preferred to immediate delivery, which would commit a preterm infant to NICU. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia)

Active or recent antepartum haemorrhage at 32 weeks with previous caesareans and praevia requires inpatient observation, intravenous access, group and hold, and consideration of corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia)

explanation.summary: The Bishop's score combines cervical dilation, effacement, station, position and consistency. A score of 6 or less is unfavourable and benefits from cervical ripening before oxytocin and ARM. Options include mechanical ripening (Cook or Foley balloon) and pharmacological agents (dinoprostone gel or pessary, misoprostol where protocols allow). Mechanical methods have a lower hyperstimulation rate. A favourable cervix (7 or more) is managed with ARM and oxytocin. IOL after 41+0 reduces stillbirth risk in prolonged pregnancy.
key_points: Bishop's score 6 or less = unfavourable cervix, ripen first
Balloon catheter is a low-hyperstimulation Australian first-line ripening option
ARM and oxytocin follow ripening or are used when cervix is already favourable
explanation.pearls: Transcervical balloon catheters are typically inflated to 40 to 60 mL and left in place for up to 12 hours or until they fall out, achieving a mean Bishop's score increase of around 3 points.

options.rationale: ARM followed by oxytocin is appropriate when the cervix is favourable (Bishop's score 7 or more) or after successful ripening; with Bishop's 3 it is likely to fail and the woman has declined ARM. (Source: RANZCOG IOL)

For an unfavourable cervix (Bishop's score 6 or less) in a woman preferring a less pharmacological approach, mechanical ripening with a balloon catheter is an Australian first-line option with low hyperstimulation risk. (Source: RANZCOG IOL)

Vaginal misoprostol is effective for ripening but carries a higher hyperstimulation risk and is restricted in Australian protocols to specific scenarios; balloon catheter is a lower-risk first step in many AU units. (Source: RANZCOG IOL)
Membrane sweeping is offered antenatally to reduce IOL likelihood, not as an in-hospital induction method when admission has already occurred for IOL. (Source: RANZCOG IOL)
Caesarean is not first-line for prolonged pregnancy without obstetric indication; the woman is a candidate for induction and has not requested caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG IOL)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage with bleeding, closed cervix and a confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy is managed expectantly with safety-net advice and outpatient GP follow-up. Vaginal progesterone has only modest benefit in women with previous miscarriage and bleeding; routine use is not recommended. Anti-D is not required in Rh-positive women. Misoprostol and surgical management are reserved for confirmed pregnancy loss.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage with viable IUP and closed cervix is managed expectantly
Anti-D is not required in Rh-positive women
Vaginal progesterone is reserved for bleeding plus previous miscarriage
explanation.pearls: Subchorionic haematoma greater than 25% of gestational sac volume is associated with a slightly higher miscarriage rate but does not change initial expectant management.

options.rationale: Misoprostol is used for confirmed miscarriage, not threatened miscarriage with a viable fetus; offering it here would terminate a viable pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)

Vaginal progesterone has a modest benefit only in women with bleeding and a previous miscarriage; routine use for first-episode threatened miscarriage is not recommended in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)
She is Rh D positive so anti-D is not required; routine first-trimester anti-D is not indicated in Rh-positive women. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

Bed rest does not improve outcomes in threatened miscarriage and admission with serial hCG adds no value when a viable intrauterine pregnancy has already been confirmed. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)

Threatened miscarriage with confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy, closed cervix and stable observations is managed expectantly with outpatient follow-up and safety-net advice; no progesterone or admission is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Early Pregnancy Loss)

explanation.summary: A postmenopausal woman with an intact uterus and disabling vasomotor symptoms is offered systemic menopausal hormone therapy. Once 12 months past the final menstrual period, continuous combined oestrogen with progestogen is preferred to avoid bleeds and provide endometrial protection. Unopposed oestrogen is contraindicated with an intact uterus.
key_points: Continuous combined MHT is preferred more than 12 months post final menses
Progestogen is mandatory with oestrogen for women with an intact uterus
Vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary symptoms only and is not systemic therapy
explanation.pearls: Micronised progesterone (Prometrium) has a more favourable breast and venous safety profile than older synthetic progestins and is widely used in Australia.

options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary symptoms only and does not control systemic vasomotor symptoms. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Unopposed oestrogen in women with an intact uterus increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer regardless of menopausal status; a progestogen is required. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Sequential regimens are used in perimenopausal women still having spontaneous cycles; once she is more than a year post final menses, continuous combined therapy is preferred. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Tibolone is an alternative when standard MHT is unsuitable; it is not preferred first-line over continuous combined therapy in women without specific contraindications. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Women with an intact uterus who are more than 12 months post final menstrual period are offered continuous combined oestradiol with progestogen to protect the endometrium and avoid scheduled withdrawal bleeds. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

explanation.summary: Postnatal contraception at the 6-week check is an opportunity to provide effective long-acting reversible contraception. The LNG-IUD is safe during breastfeeding, can be inserted from 4 weeks postpartum, and is more than 99% effective. Oestrogen-containing methods are avoided within 6 weeks postpartum due to VTE risk and during breastfeeding due to lactation effects.
key_points: LNG-IUD is safe from 4 weeks postpartum and during breastfeeding
Oestrogen-containing combined methods are avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum
Lactational amenorrhoea method requires full breastfeeding plus amenorrhoea under 6 months
explanation.pearls: Copper IUD and the etonogestrel implant are equally suitable LARC options in lactating women and follow the same insertion timing rules.

options.rationale: Combined oestrogen-containing methods are avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum due to VTE risk, and can reduce breast milk supply; they are not first-line in lactating women. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception)
LNG-IUD is a first-line long-acting reversible contraceptive that is safe in breastfeeding, can be inserted from 4 weeks postpartum, and is more than 99% effective. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception)

LAM is reliable only when the woman is fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic and less than 6 months postpartum; she has reached 6 weeks but a long-acting method better suits her family-complete goal. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception)
The combined hormonal ring contains oestrogen and is avoided during breastfeeding and within 6 weeks postpartum because of VTE and lactation impact. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception)
Condoms have higher typical-use failure than LARC and she wants effective long-term contraception without surgery; LNG-IUD better meets her stated preference. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception)

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis with fever and a tender wedge of breast erythema is treated with oral flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5 to 7 days, with continued breastfeeding from the affected breast to maintain drainage. Symptomatic management alone is insufficient when constitutional symptoms are present. Ultrasound is reserved for failed antibiotic response or fluctuance suggesting abscess.
key_points: Flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5 to 7 days is the AU first-line for lactational mastitis
Continue breastfeeding from the affected side; do not suppress lactation
Ultrasound is for failure to respond at 48 hours or fluctuance suggesting abscess
explanation.pearls: If a deep breast abscess is found on ultrasound, image-guided needle aspiration is preferred over open incision and drainage to preserve future lactation.

options.rationale: Amoxicillin lacks reliable Staphylococcus aureus cover and stopping breastfeeding worsens stasis; continued feeding is encouraged. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Mastitis)

Australian guidelines recommend oral flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5 to 7 days for lactational mastitis with constitutional symptoms, plus ongoing breastfeeding from the affected side to drain the duct. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Mastitis)
Constitutional fever with breast erythema warrants antibiotic therapy at presentation; symptomatic management alone risks progression to abscess. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Mastitis)

Without fluctuance or failure to improve, ultrasound is not required at presentation; antibiotics are started empirically and imaging reserved for failure or fluctuance. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Mastitis)
Suppressing lactation worsens stasis and prolongs mastitis; cabergoline has no role and 14 days is longer than required. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Mastitis)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia at or beyond 34 weeks with end-organ involvement is an indication for delivery during the index admission. Magnesium sulfate is continued through labour and for 24 hours postpartum to prevent seizures, and blood pressure is controlled with labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine. Mode of delivery is decided on standard obstetric grounds; an unfavourable cervix is not alone an indication for caesarean.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks or beyond mandates delivery
Magnesium sulfate is continued through delivery and 24 hours postpartum
Mode of delivery follows standard obstetric criteria; cervix score is not the driver
explanation.pearls: Platelet count under 100 x10^9/L combined with transaminitis and epigastric pain define HELLP; the diagnosis adds urgency but the management is still timely delivery with magnesium cover.

options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia is never managed as outpatient; ongoing inpatient observation is required regardless of immediate delivery plan. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Antenatal steroids are not given beyond 35+6 weeks routinely; severe pre-eclampsia at 36+0 mandates delivery rather than further conservative management. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Unfavourable cervix is not in itself an indication for caesarean section; induction with cervical ripening is appropriate unless other obstetric contraindications are present. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Severe pre-eclampsia at 36+0 with end-organ involvement (HELLP-spectrum thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases) is an indication for delivery regardless of cervical status; magnesium sulfate is continued through delivery and for 24 hours postpartum. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Plasma exchange is not part of pre-eclampsia or HELLP management; delivery is the definitive treatment. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Major placental abruption with fetal distress, maternal coagulopathy and active bleeding mandates immediate delivery. Caesarean section is the fastest safe route at 32 weeks with an unfavourable cervix. The massive transfusion protocol is activated for ongoing blood loss and coagulopathy; tocolysis and corticosteroids are not appropriate when delivery cannot be delayed.
key_points: Major abruption with fetal distress requires emergency delivery, usually caesarean
Tocolysis is contraindicated when active abruption causes fetal compromise
Activate MTP for coagulopathic obstetric haemorrhage; aim fibrinogen above 2 g/L
explanation.pearls: Concealed abruption can present with disproportionate maternal shock relative to visible blood loss; couvelaire uterus and DIC are recognised complications and reinforce the need for early delivery and product replacement.

options.rationale: With pathological CTG and active abruption, delay for vaginal birth risks fetal demise; expedited delivery by caesarean is required unless birth is imminent. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)
Tocolysis is contraindicated in significant abruption with fetal distress and maternal compromise; delivery cannot be safely delayed for steroid effect. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

Suspected placental abruption with maternal compromise, fetal distress on CTG and coagulopathy is an indication for immediate delivery; the fastest safe route at 32 weeks with a 2 cm cervix is caesarean section. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)
Transfer for cordocentesis is not appropriate when the woman is unstable and the fetus is compromised; on-site delivery is needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)
Conservative management is not appropriate with fetal distress, maternal coagulopathy and ongoing bleeding; delivery cannot be deferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Antepartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Recurrent first-trimester miscarriage in Australia is investigated with parental karyotyping, pelvic imaging and antiphospholipid antibody screen. Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most common treatable cause and is diagnosed when lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein 1 are persistently abnormal on two samples 12 weeks apart. Inherited thrombophilia panels, NK cell tests and ovarian reserve testing are not recommended.
key_points: APS is the major treatable cause and requires positive tests on two occasions 12 weeks apart
Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended in first-trimester recurrent loss
NK cell testing and immune therapies are not supported by Australian guidelines
explanation.pearls: Confirmed APS in subsequent pregnancy is treated with low-dose aspirin and prophylactic enoxaparin from a positive pregnancy test until 6 weeks postpartum, which roughly doubles live birth rates.

options.rationale: Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended in recurrent first-trimester miscarriage; the evidence base does not support routine investigation or anticoagulation for this group. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)

Antiphospholipid syndrome is a treatable cause of recurrent miscarriage; Australian guidelines recommend lupus anticoagulant and anti-cardiolipin (and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein 1) tested 12 weeks apart in women with three first-trimester losses. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)
Hysteroscopy is reserved for abnormal ultrasound or saline sonohysterography findings; a normal 3D ultrasound makes it unlikely to add diagnostic information. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)
NK cell testing and immunological treatments are not supported by Australian guidelines for recurrent miscarriage; they are not part of routine investigation. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)
Ovarian reserve testing does not investigate recurrent miscarriage; AMH does not predict miscarriage rates and is not part of the work-up. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)

explanation.summary: A recurrent eclamptic seizure on a magnesium sulfate regimen with sub-therapeutic serum level is managed with a further 2 to 4 g IV bolus and increased infusion rate to achieve serum levels of 1.7 to 3.5 mmol/L. Phenytoin and benzodiazepines are reserved for true refractory eclampsia after maximal magnesium. Calcium gluconate is for magnesium toxicity, not failure. Imaging is performed after stabilisation when focal features warrant.
key_points: Recurrent seizure on magnesium with sub-therapeutic level is rebolused with 2 to 4 g IV
Target serum magnesium is 1.7 to 3.5 mmol/L during maintenance infusion
Calcium gluconate is for toxicity (areflexia, respiratory depression), not seizure recurrence
explanation.pearls: Magnesium prophylaxis is continued for 24 hours after delivery OR last seizure (whichever is later); a postnatal eclamptic seizure resets this 24-hour clock.

options.rationale: Phenytoin is not first-line for eclamptic recurrence; magnesium is more effective at a higher dose. Phenytoin is reserved for refractory seizures unresponsive to repeated magnesium boluses. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

A recurrent eclamptic seizure on magnesium with a serum magnesium below the therapeutic range warrants a further 2 to 4 g bolus and increased infusion to reach 1.7 to 3.5 mmol/L target. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Magnesium level is sub-therapeutic; calcium gluconate is reserved for magnesium toxicity (areflexia, respiratory depression). Benzodiazepines are not first-line for eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Imaging is appropriate for atypical features or focal signs but should not delay magnesium bolus for ongoing eclampsia; treat the seizure first, image after stabilisation. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Blood pressure control is essential but does not treat the active seizure; magnesium must be re-bolused in addition to antihypertensive therapy. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy is treated with oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days. Intravaginal clindamycin cream is avoided in later pregnancy due to possible association with membrane rupture. Observation is inappropriate when symptomatic; fluconazole and antibiotics with no vaginal coverage are not relevant.
key_points: Oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 7 days is first-line for symptomatic BV in pregnancy
Intravaginal clindamycin cream is avoided in the second half of pregnancy
Amsel criteria diagnose BV: thin discharge, pH greater than 4.5, clue cells, positive whiff
explanation.pearls: There is no role for routine screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacterial vaginosis in low-risk pregnancies; screening and treatment is reserved for symptomatic women.

options.rationale: Fluconazole treats vulvovaginal candidiasis; the clinical picture and Amsel criteria are diagnostic of bacterial vaginosis rather than candida. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial vaginosis)
