Intravaginal clindamycin cream has been associated with later membrane rupture and is generally avoided in the second half of pregnancy in Australian guidance. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial vaginosis)

Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy is treated to relieve symptoms and may reduce upper genital tract infection; observation alone is inappropriate when symptomatic. (Source: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment)

Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days is the Australian Therapeutic Guidelines first-line regimen for symptomatic bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy at any gestation. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial vaginosis)

Topical metronidazole gel is less preferred than oral therapy in symptomatic pregnant women in Australian guidance; oral therapy treats potential subclinical upper tract carriage. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Bacterial vaginosis)

explanation.summary: Initial management of newly diagnosed gestational diabetes is medical nutrition therapy with exercise and home glucose monitoring, with review in 1 to 2 weeks. Pharmacotherapy with metformin or insulin is added when glycaemic targets are not met. A single abnormal value on the diagnostic OGTT establishes the diagnosis and treatment should not be deferred.
key_points: GDM is diagnosed on a single abnormal OGTT value per ADIPS
Initial therapy is lifestyle with home glucose monitoring and 1-2 week review
Pharmacotherapy starts if fasting or postprandial targets are not met
explanation.pearls: Australian targets are fasting capillary glucose less than 5.0 mmol/L and 1 hour postprandial less than 7.4 mmol/L; persistently exceeding either prompts the addition of metformin or insulin.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

options.rationale: Metformin is added if glucose targets are not met on lifestyle measures alone over 1 to 2 weeks; initial therapy is medical nutrition therapy with monitoring. (Source: ADIPS: Gestational diabetes consensus)

Insulin initiation at diagnosis is reserved for marked hyperglycaemia or maternal factors; mild OGTT abnormalities warrant a trial of lifestyle first per ADIPS. (Source: ADIPS: Gestational diabetes consensus)
A single abnormal value on the diagnostic OGTT establishes gestational diabetes; repeating the test delays appropriate care. (Source: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

options.rationale: Earlier intervention reduces macrosomia and shoulder dystocia; deferring treatment is not appropriate once GDM is diagnosed. (Source: ADIPS: Gestational diabetes consensus)

ADIPS recommends initial management of GDM with medical nutrition therapy, exercise advice and self monitoring of blood glucose; pharmacotherapy is added when targets are not achieved within 1 to 2 weeks. (Source: ADIPS: Gestational diabetes consensus)

explanation.summary: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception with a failure rate under 0.1% and remains effective up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse, with the added benefit of ongoing long-acting reversible contraception. Levonorgestrel efficacy falls beyond 72 hours; ulipristal extends to 120 hours but is less effective than the copper IUD.
key_points: Copper IUD is the most effective EC, working up to 5 days after UPSI
Levonorgestrel is recommended within 72 hours; ulipristal up to 120 hours
Yuzpe combined oral contraceptive regimen is now obsolete
explanation.pearls: Insert the copper IUD at the same visit when feasible; if delayed, use ulipristal acetate as a bridge and recheck pregnancy testing before later IUD insertion.

options.rationale: The copper IUD is effective up to 5 days after unprotected intercourse and is the most effective emergency contraception with a failure rate under 0.1%; it also provides ongoing long-acting reversible contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Emergency contraception)

Oral levonorgestrel is licensed within 72 hours of intercourse and efficacy falls off thereafter; at 96 hours it is outside the recommended window. (Source: eTG Sexual health: Emergency contraception)
Ulipristal acetate is effective up to 120 hours but is less effective than the copper IUD and does not provide ongoing contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Emergency contraception)

The Yuzpe regimen is now obsolete in Australian practice and has higher failure rates and more nausea than levonorgestrel, ulipristal or the copper IUD. (Source: eTG Sexual health: Emergency contraception)

Conception remains possible after a single act of unprotected intercourse, and the copper IUD remains effective up to 5 days; reassurance alone is inappropriate. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Emergency contraception)

explanation.summary: Infants of HBsAg positive mothers are given hepatitis B immunoglobulin 100 IU and the birth-dose monovalent vaccine within 12 hours of birth, followed by the routine vaccine schedule and post-vaccination serology at 9 to 12 months. Caesarean section is not used to reduce vertical transmission. Cord blood testing does not guide prophylaxis.
key_points: HBIG plus birth-dose vaccine within 12 hours for infants of HBsAg+ mothers
Routine schedule completes the series with serology at 9-12 months
Caesarean section does not reduce vertical hepatitis B transmission
explanation.pearls: If the mother has HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL in the third trimester, antiviral therapy with tenofovir reduces vertical transmission further and is recommended per Australian liver society guidance.

sources.label: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants

options.rationale: Routine 6-week vaccination alone is inadequate for an infant of an HBsAg positive mother; birth-dose vaccine plus HBIG is required to prevent vertical transmission. (Source: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants)
source_refs: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants

options.rationale: Infants born to HBsAg positive mothers receive HBIG 100 IU plus birth-dose monovalent hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth, then complete the routine schedule, with post-vaccination serology at 9 to 12 months. (Source: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants)
source_refs: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants

options.rationale: Maternal HBsAg positivity at booking is sufficient indication for neonatal HBIG and vaccine within 12 hours; deferring risks vertical transmission. (Source: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants)
source_refs: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants

options.rationale: Elective caesarean is not recommended to prevent vertical HBV transmission; appropriate neonatal immunoprophylaxis is the proven intervention. (Source: RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment)

Cord blood HBsAg testing is not used to direct prophylaxis; the high stakes of perinatal HBV mandate empiric HBIG and birth dose vaccine in all exposed infants. (Source: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants)
source_refs: NCIRS: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin in pregnancy and infants

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome at or beyond 34 weeks is managed by delivery after maternal stabilisation with antihypertensives and IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis. Expectant management risks hepatic rupture, DIC and eclampsia. Steroids may be given but should not delay delivery when maternal status is deteriorating.
key_points: HELLP at or beyond 34 weeks is an indication for delivery after stabilisation
IV labetalol controls severe hypertension; IV magnesium sulfate prevents eclampsia
Expectant management risks hepatic rupture and DIC in established HELLP
explanation.pearls: Platelet count below 50, marked transaminitis, deteriorating renal function or any neurological symptoms mandate urgent delivery regardless of gestational age in HELLP.

sources.label: SOMANZ: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Expectant management is not appropriate in HELLP at 34 weeks given maternal risks of seizure, hepatic rupture and DIC; delivery is indicated after stabilisation. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Magnesium is given for seizure prophylaxis but observation alone is inadequate; HELLP at this gestation mandates delivery after stabilisation. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: HELLP at or beyond 34 weeks is an indication for delivery after BP control with IV labetalol and IV magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis; mode of delivery is individualised. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

TTP is suggested by MAHA with neurological symptoms and renal injury and very low ADAMTS13; HELLP fits the clinical picture and is treated by delivery. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Delaying delivery for a full steroid course is inappropriate when maternal HELLP is established and worsening; a single dose may be given but delivery should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks is managed with admission, antenatal corticosteroids, a 10-day latency antibiotic such as erythromycin, magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if delivery is imminent before 30 weeks, and expectant management to 34 weeks. Delivery is hastened if there is chorioamnionitis, abruption or fetal compromise.
key_points: Expectant management of PPROM 24-34 weeks if no infection or fetal compromise
Latency antibiotics with erythromycin for 10 days reduce chorioamnionitis
Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection if delivery is imminent before 30 weeks
explanation.pearls: Daily temperature, fetal heart rate auscultation, weekly CRP and twice weekly CTG with weekly biometry guide ongoing monitoring; delivery is advised by 34 weeks given the rising risk of chorioamnionitis.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RWH Melbourne: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes guideline

options.rationale: At 28 weeks lung maturity is incomplete and immediate induction is not appropriate; expectant management to 34 weeks is standard unless infection or fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: PPROM before 34 weeks requires admission for monitoring of infection, fetal wellbeing and labour onset; outpatient management is not standard in Australia. (Source: RWH Melbourne: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes guideline)
source_refs: RWH Melbourne: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes guideline

options.rationale: Tocolysis is not routinely indicated in PPROM without active labour and there is no need to plan delivery at 30 weeks in the absence of infection or fetal distress. (Source: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Standard PPROM care between 24 and 34 weeks includes admission, betamethasone, latency antibiotic with erythromycin for 10 days, magnesium sulfate neuroprotection if delivery imminent before 30 weeks, and expectant management to 34 weeks unless infection or fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Caesarean section is not indicated without infection, labour or fetal compromise; prematurity carries greater immediate risk than expectant management with monitoring. (Source: RWH Melbourne: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes guideline)
source_refs: RWH Melbourne: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes guideline

explanation.summary: Intrapartum GBS chemoprophylaxis is indicated for previous infant with GBS disease, GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy, positive screening swab, or unknown status with risk factors. The Australian first-line regimen is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g four-hourly until delivery. Cefazolin is used for non-severe penicillin allergy; vancomycin for severe allergy or resistant strains.
key_points: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g q4h is first-line GBS prophylaxis
Previous GBS-affected infant is an automatic indication for prophylaxis
Cefazolin substitutes for non-severe allergy; vancomycin for severe allergy
explanation.pearls: Effective prophylaxis requires at least 4 hours of IV antibiotic before birth; consider early antibiotic if labour is progressing rapidly with a previous affected infant.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy
RWH Melbourne: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis guideline

options.rationale: Oral cefalexin does not provide adequate intrapartum tissue and fetal levels for GBS prophylaxis; IV therapy is required. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: IV vancomycin is reserved for confirmed severe penicillin allergy and resistant isolates; it is not first-line in penicillin-tolerant women. (Source: RWH Melbourne: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis guideline)
source_refs: RWH Melbourne: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis guideline

options.rationale: Antibiotics are commenced at presentation in established labour when an indication is present, not deferred for membrane rupture duration. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: IV cefazolin is the option for non-severe penicillin allergy; in penicillin-tolerant women IV benzylpenicillin is first-line. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Previous infant with early-onset GBS sepsis is an indication for intrapartum chemoprophylaxis; IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g four-hourly until delivery is the Australian first-line regimen. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden cardiopulmonary collapse with DIC during labour or delivery. Management is supportive resuscitation with airway protection and vasopressors, massive transfusion protocol with balanced blood products and cryoprecipitate, expedited delivery to assist maternal resuscitation, and intensive care support. Heparin is contraindicated during active haemorrhage with DIC.
key_points: AFE requires massive transfusion protocol with balanced blood products
Expedited delivery is part of maternal resuscitation in AFE collapse
Heparin is contraindicated; product replacement treats DIC
explanation.pearls: Cryoprecipitate and fibrinogen concentrate target fibrinogen above 2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage; consider early activation of the obstetric massive transfusion pathway with named haematology cover.

sources.label: NBA Patient Blood Management: Critical bleeding and massive transfusion

options.rationale: Amniotic fluid embolism causes cardiopulmonary collapse with DIC; treatment is supportive resuscitation with balanced blood products via the massive transfusion protocol, immediate delivery to relieve aortocaval compression and assist resuscitation, cryoprecipitate for hypofibrinogenaemia, and intensive care support. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management: Critical bleeding and massive transfusion)
source_refs: NBA Patient Blood Management: Critical bleeding and massive transfusion

options.rationale: Heparin is contraindicated in active haemorrhage with DIC; AFE coagulopathy is treated with product replacement rather than systemic anticoagulation. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management: Critical bleeding and massive transfusion)
source_refs: NBA Patient Blood Management: Critical bleeding and massive transfusion

options.rationale: TXA and uterotonics treat uterine atony PPH but are inadequate for AFE with DIC; balanced blood product resuscitation and delivery are the primary actions. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse statement)

Delaying delivery worsens maternal resuscitation efforts and fetal outcome; expedited delivery is part of the resuscitation in AFE with maternal collapse. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse statement)
Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in AFE and do not replace the priorities of resuscitation, product replacement and delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse statement)

explanation.summary: Australian-endorsed PCOS care begins with lifestyle change for any woman with elevated BMI, layered with a COCP when fertility is not currently desired to regulate cycles, oppose unopposed oestrogen and reduce androgenic symptoms. Anti-androgens such as spironolactone require reliable contraception because of teratogenicity. Metformin is an adjunct for metabolic or cycle goals not met with lifestyle alone. Ovulation induction agents are deferred until fertility is actively pursued.
key_points: Lifestyle and weight reduction of 5 to 10 percent improves cycle regularity and androgen profile in PCOS
COCP is first-line for cycle regulation and hyperandrogenism when pregnancy is not desired
Spironolactone must be co-prescribed with reliable contraception because of teratogenic risk
explanation.pearls: A combined oral contraceptive plus 5 to 10 percent weight loss over 6 months reduces free testosterone and re-establishes withdrawal bleeds in most women with PCOS without metabolic comorbidity.

sources.label: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG

options.rationale: AU PCOS guidance recommends lifestyle as first line, with a COCP added for menstrual regulation and hyperandrogenism when fertility is not currently desired and there is no contraindication. (Source: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG

options.rationale: Ovulation induction is reserved for women actively trying to conceive; clomifene does not address androgenic symptoms and is not appropriate when pregnancy is not desired. (Source: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG

options.rationale: Anti-androgens are teratogenic and must always be combined with reliable contraception in women of reproductive age. (Source: AMH: spironolactone)

Ovarian drilling is a second-line ovulation induction technique reserved for clomifene-resistant women seeking pregnancy, not primary care management of PCOS. (Source: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG

options.rationale: Metformin is an adjunct that may be added if cycle, weight or metabolic targets are not met with lifestyle; isolated metformin is not first-line and does not provide contraception or androgen control. (Source: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International evidence-based PCOS guideline 2023, endorsed by RANZCOG

explanation.summary: HELLP at or beyond 34 weeks crosses the threshold where delivery improves both maternal and neonatal outcomes versus expectant care. Concurrent magnesium sulfate reduces eclampsia risk and intravenous antihypertensive therapy (labetalol or hydralazine) targets sustained BP below 160/110. Mode of delivery follows obstetric indications. Steroids are reasonable if time permits but must not delay delivery for severe features.
key_points: HELLP at >= 34 weeks is an indication for delivery, not expectant care
Magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/hour for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia
IV labetalol or hydralazine is first-line for crisis-range BP in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: A platelet count below 100 with elevated transaminases above twice the upper limit and LDH above 600 confirms HELLP and prompts delivery at any gestation beyond 34 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG statement on intrapartum hypertensive emergencies

options.rationale: Oral nifedipine alone is inadequate for this BP and omits magnesium; severe pre-eclampsia at 34+5 with HELLP features mandates delivery rather than expectant care for steroid completion. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline)

Severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP at or beyond 34 weeks is an indication for delivery alongside magnesium for seizure prophylaxis and IV antihypertensive control. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline)
Expectant care to 37 weeks is unsafe with HELLP features and platelets below 100; steroids do not change the delivery decision at this gestation. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline)
Loop diuretics are not first-line for severe pre-eclampsia BP control; methyldopa onset is too slow for crisis-range hypertension. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline)

HELLP-related thrombocytopenia rarely requires platelet transfusion above 50, INR is normal so vitamin K adds nothing, and delivery should not be delayed overnight. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: Refractory atonic PPH after first-line oxytocin escalates to second-line ergometrine and carboprost, with tranexamic acid given within 3 hours of bleed onset. Mechanical measures continue alongside drugs: bimanual compression then balloon tamponade if pharmacology fails. Massive transfusion protocol activates if losses exceed 1500 mL or there is haemodynamic instability despite resuscitation. Ergometrine is avoided in hypertensive disease; carboprost is avoided in asthma.
key_points: Ergometrine and carboprost are the second-line uterotonics after oxytocin fails
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV reduces death from bleeding when given within 3 hours
Balloon tamponade follows failed pharmacological control, not before
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of bleed onset reduces death due to bleeding by about a third in PPH per the WOMAN trial.

options.rationale: Oxytocin has reached effective receptor saturation; repeating the same agent will not reverse atony and delays definitive second-line therapy. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)
Tranexamic acid is given within 3 hours alongside escalating uterotonics, not as a substitute for a second-line uterotonic in ongoing atony. (Source: WOMAN trial; RANZCOG PPH statement)

Second-line uterotonics (ergometrine and carboprost) are added when oxytocin fails, in a woman with no hypertension or asthma history; TXA within 3 hours reduces death from bleeding. Continued bimanual compression is essential alongside. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)
Balloon tamponade is the next step only after pharmacological uterotonics have failed; sequencing matters in the PPH algorithm. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)
MTP activation is reserved for ongoing bleeding above 1500 mL or haemodynamic instability not responding to crystalloid and uterotonics. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse with sustained fetal bradycardia is a category 1 obstetric emergency. The immediate steps are to lift the presenting part off the cord manually, position the mother in knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg to offload the cord, and transfer to theatre for a category 1 caesarean with a 30-minute decision-to-delivery interval. Tocolysis is an option only when transfer delays are unavoidable. Avoid handling the cord itself.
key_points: Cord prolapse mandates category 1 caesarean with decision-to-delivery within 30 minutes
Manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord is the first hands-on step
Tocolysis is reserved for transfer delays, not as a definitive measure
explanation.pearls: Manual elevation of the presenting part with the examining hand in the vagina while transferring to theatre maintains cord perfusion until delivery.

options.rationale: Operative vaginal delivery requires full dilatation and engaged head; with the cervix at 4 cm and a high head this is not feasible. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum care guideline)
Manual cord reduction risks vasospasm and is not recommended; ongoing oxytocin and labour worsens cord compression. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum care guideline)
Cord prolapse with sustained fetal bradycardia is a category 1 emergency; observation delays a definitive decision-to-delivery interval. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum care guideline)

Manual elevation of the presenting part and category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes is the AU pathway; positioning offloads the cord while theatre is prepared. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum care guideline)
Tocolysis is an adjunct only when delivery will be delayed during transfer; it is not a substitute for emergent caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum care guideline)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is a bony obstruction. The HELPERR algorithm starts with Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts) and Pressure (suprapubic) before progressing to internal manoeuvres (Rubin II, Woods screw, posterior arm). Fundal pressure is contraindicated. Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are reserved as salvage. Documentation of manoeuvre order and time intervals is mandated for medico-legal review.
key_points: McRoberts position plus suprapubic pressure resolves about half of shoulder dystocias
Fundal pressure is contraindicated as it worsens impaction
Internal rotational manoeuvres follow if McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail
explanation.pearls: McRoberts hyperflexion alone resolves around a third of dystocias; adding suprapubic pressure over the posterior aspect of the anterior shoulder raises that to 50 to 60 percent.

options.rationale: Fundal pressure worsens shoulder impaction and increases brachial plexus and uterine injury risk; it is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)
Symphysiotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre after first and second-line manoeuvres fail; it is not a first step in shoulder dystocia. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)
Zavanelli is a salvage manoeuvre after exhaustion of internal manoeuvres, not a first-line approach. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

Shoulder dystocia is a bony, not soft tissue, obstruction; episiotomy alone does not relieve impaction and is reserved to facilitate internal manoeuvres when needed. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)
McRoberts position plus suprapubic pressure resolves 50 to 60 percent of dystocias and is the first step in the HELPERR algorithm. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis is treated by continued effective milk removal plus narrow-spectrum oral antistaphylococcal cover (dicloxacillin or flucloxacillin) for 5 days when systemic features are present beyond 24 hours. Bedside ultrasound is useful to exclude an abscess that would need drainage. Suppressing lactation worsens stasis. Severe systemic illness, sepsis or no response by 48 hours prompts admission and IV therapy.
key_points: Continue breastfeeding through mastitis to maintain drainage
Dicloxacillin or flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days is first-line
Persistent symptoms beyond 48 hours of antibiotics warrant ultrasound for abscess
explanation.pearls: Mastitis improves within 48 hours of effective drainage plus dicloxacillin; failure to improve should trigger breast ultrasound to exclude an organised abscess.

options.rationale: AU first-line for non-severe lactational mastitis is continued breastfeeding plus oral dicloxacillin or flucloxacillin, with attention to attachment and drainage. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: mastitis)
Stopping feeds and suppressing lactation worsens engorgement and obstructs milk drainage, which is core to resolving mastitis. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: mastitis)
I&D is indicated only for an established abscess; bedside ultrasound here has excluded a collection. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: mastitis)
Symptoms beyond 24 hours with fever and a fissure warrant immediate antibiotics; delay risks abscess formation. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: mastitis)
Augmentin is broader than needed for non-severe mastitis; 5 days of narrow-spectrum cover is preferred to minimise infant gut and resistance impact. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: mastitis)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum with significant ketonuria, dehydration and electrolyte derangement requires admission for IV rehydration. Thiamine 100 mg IV is given before glucose-containing fluids to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Stepwise antiemetics include pyridoxine plus doxylamine, metoclopramide, ondansetron and second-line therapies such as steroids if refractory. Ondansetron is regarded as safe from the first trimester onwards.
key_points: Thiamine 100 mg IV precedes glucose-containing fluids in prolonged vomiting
Ondansetron is now considered safe from the first trimester for hyperemesis
Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after stepwise failure
explanation.pearls: Always give thiamine 100 mg IV before dextrose-containing fluids in any patient with more than 5 days of poor oral intake, including hyperemesis gravidarum, to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

sources.label: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Severe hyperemesis with 3+ ketonuria and hypokalaemia mandates admission and IV therapy, not outpatient oral antiemetics. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Thiamine prophylaxis before glucose-containing fluids prevents Wernicke encephalopathy in prolonged hyperemesis; IV rehydration with potassium replacement is first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Giving dextrose before thiamine in a prolonged starvation state can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must come first. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis after multiple antiemetics have failed, not as first-line outpatient therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Severe dehydration with electrolyte derangement is not safely managed in the community; admission is required. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy guideline

explanation.summary: Medical management of ectopic pregnancy with single-dose methotrexate is appropriate when hCG is below 5000, the ectopic mass is under 35 mm without fetal cardiac activity, the woman is stable with no peritonism, follow-up is reliable, and there is no contraindication on LFT, FBC or renal function. Day 4 and day 7 hCG are used to assess success: a >= 15 percent fall between day 4 and 7 predicts resolution. Surgical management is reserved for instability, rupture or methotrexate failure.
key_points: Methotrexate eligibility: hCG below 5000, no FHB, ectopic mass under 35 mm, stable patient, normal LFT/FBC/renal
Day 4 to day 7 hCG drop of >= 15 percent confirms response, otherwise consider repeat dose or surgery
Surgical salpingectomy or salpingostomy is for instability, rupture, contraindications or failed medical therapy
explanation.pearls: After single-dose methotrexate the hCG often rises between day 1 and 4; the meaningful drop is between day 4 and day 7, and a fall of less than 15 percent triggers a second dose or surgery.

sources.label: AMH: methotrexate dosing in ectopic pregnancy

options.rationale: Expectant care is reserved for hCG below about 1000 with falling trend; at 2400 with a visible adnexal mass the spontaneous resolution rate is too low. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)
Surgery is indicated for haemodynamic instability, rupture, contraindication to methotrexate or failed medical therapy; this patient meets none of those. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

She meets AU criteria for medical management: hCG below 5000, no FHB, mass under 35 mm, stable, no peritonism, normal LFT/FBC/creatinine and reliable follow-up. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

When TVS already shows an adnexal mass with empty uterus and hCG above the discriminatory zone, dilatation and curettage adds no information and delays treatment. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)
A non-tubal pregnancy of unknown location requires repeat assessment; here a definitive adnexal ectopic is already demonstrated, mandating treatment now. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: Planned VBAC is supported after one prior lower segment caesarean for a non-recurrent indication, in a cephalic singleton pregnancy, in a hospital with continuous CTG and immediate theatre access. Quoted risks are uterine rupture about 0.5 percent and overall VBAC success of 60 to 80 percent. Prostaglandins are avoided for induction in scarred uteri because they roughly double rupture risk. Counselling must be balanced, documented, and offered alongside elective repeat caesarean.
key_points: VBAC is offered after one LSCS with non-recurrent indication and a cephalic singleton
Uterine rupture risk is around 0.5 percent during planned VBAC
Prostaglandin induction in a scarred uterus roughly doubles rupture risk and is usually avoided
explanation.pearls: Planned VBAC success after one prior LSCS for a non-recurrent indication is around 70 percent, with uterine rupture about 1 in 200, in an Australian tertiary unit with continuous CTG.

sources.label: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement

options.rationale: VBAC is broadly supported after one prior lower segment scar with cephalic singleton; routine elective caesarean is not mandated. (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement

options.rationale: Prostaglandins double uterine rupture risk in scarred uteri and are generally avoided; mechanical or oxytocin-based methods are preferred when induction is needed. (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement

options.rationale: Trial of labour after caesarean requires intrapartum CTG and ready access to theatre for category 1 caesarean; home birth is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement

options.rationale: She meets criteria for VBAC: one prior LSCS with non-recurrent indication, cephalic singleton, no contraindication; hospital-based monitoring with theatre access is standard. (Source: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG birth after previous caesarean statement

options.rationale: The fetus is already cephalic; ECV is not indicated and the question is mode of birth, not presentation correction. (Source: RANZCOG external cephalic version statement)

explanation.summary: Intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin (3 g load, 1.8 g every 4 hours) is the AU regimen for GBS-colonised women in labour to prevent early-onset neonatal disease. Two or more doses before delivery achieve adequate fetal serum levels. Severe penicillin allergy prompts clindamycin if susceptibilities permit, or vancomycin otherwise. GBS positivity is not an indication for caesarean. The cefazolin alternative is used for non-severe penicillin allergy.
key_points: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g then 1.8 g every 4 hours is the AU intrapartum GBS regimen
Two or more doses before birth achieve adequate fetal serum levels
Severe penicillin allergy with clindamycin resistance prompts vancomycin
explanation.pearls: Two doses of intrapartum benzylpenicillin given at least 4 hours apart before delivery achieves around 95 percent reduction in early-onset neonatal GBS disease.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS

options.rationale: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is started in active labour, not delayed until ROM, to ensure two doses are completed before birth where possible. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)
AU first-line intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in a non-allergic woman is IV benzylpenicillin: 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)
Vancomycin is reserved for severe penicillin allergy with clindamycin resistance; it is not preferred in non-allergic women. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)
Oral antibiotics do not achieve reliable amniotic fluid levels in labour; IV therapy is required. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)
GBS colonisation alone is not an indication for caesarean; AU practice is intrapartum IV prophylaxis with planned vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG GBS guideline)

explanation.summary: Lower UTI in pregnancy is treated empirically to reduce pyelonephritis and preterm birth risk. Cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days is the AU first-line option across all trimesters, with culture-guided adjustment. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonism, NTD risk) and nitrofurantoin is generally avoided at term (neonatal haemolysis risk). Fluoroquinolones are avoided throughout pregnancy.
key_points: Cefalexin is AU first-line empirical therapy for lower UTI in pregnancy
Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester because of NTD risk
Nitrofurantoin is avoided near term to minimise neonatal haemolysis risk
explanation.pearls: Always send a midstream urine culture in pregnancy UTI before starting empirical cefalexin; rescript on culture results within 48 hours if resistance is identified.

options.rationale: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist and is avoided in the first trimester because of neural tube defect risk. (Source: AMH: trimethoprim in pregnancy)

Nitrofurantoin is acceptable in mid-pregnancy but generally avoided near term (G6PD haemolysis risk in neonate); cefalexin is preferred for first-trimester empirical use. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: UTI in pregnancy)
Cefalexin is the AU first-line empirical agent for lower UTI in pregnancy across all trimesters in a non-allergic woman. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: UTI in pregnancy)
Fluoroquinolones are avoided in pregnancy because of fetal cartilage toxicity in animal data and equivalence of safer agents in humans. (Source: AMH: ciprofloxacin in pregnancy)
Symptomatic UTI in pregnancy must be treated to reduce pyelonephritis and preterm birth risk; symptomatic-only management is inadequate. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: UTI in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: When heavy menstrual bleeding persists despite a correctly sited LNG-IUS, the next step is to add tranexamic acid (1 g three times daily during heavy bleeding days) and treat iron deficiency. NSAIDs can also be added cyclically. If bleeding still fails to settle, second-line options include endometrial ablation, uterine artery embolisation (for fibroids), myomectomy or hysterectomy depending on fertility wishes. GnRH agonists are short-term pre-operative bridges.
key_points: Cyclical tranexamic acid adds about 30 to 50 percent further reduction in menstrual blood loss on top of an LNG-IUS
GnRH agonists are short-term bridges (3 to 6 months) before surgery, with add-back HRT after 6 months
Treat iron deficiency aggressively alongside any haemorrhage-control measure
explanation.pearls: Cyclical tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during the heaviest 4 days reduces measured menstrual blood loss by around 40 percent and is taken only on bleeding days.

sources.label: AMH: tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding

options.rationale: Surgical options remain valid, but a stepwise medical option comes before considering hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG heavy menstrual bleeding statement)
Stacking progestogens does not reliably reduce bleeding further and adds bone density and adherence concerns; not a first-step option here. (Source: RANZCOG heavy menstrual bleeding statement)

Combined oral contraceptives may be considered but the LNG-IUS plus tranexamic acid combination is the simpler evidence-based next step for refractory bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG heavy menstrual bleeding statement)

Adding cyclical tranexamic acid to a correctly sited LNG-IUS reduces measured menstrual blood loss by an additional 30 to 50 percent and is appropriate before surgical referral. (Source: RANZCOG heavy menstrual bleeding statement)
GnRH agonists are short-term bridges (3 to 6 months) before surgery and require add-back HRT after 6 months to limit bone loss. (Source: RANZCOG heavy menstrual bleeding statement)

explanation.summary: Australian cervical screening detects oncogenic HPV by PCR with reflex cytology when HPV is positive. HPV 16 or 18 detection prompts direct colposcopy referral regardless of cytology grade. Non-16/18 oncogenic types with negative or low-grade cytology repeat at 12 months. Persistent infection at 12 months or any high-grade cytology triggers colposcopy. Immunocompromised women have a tighter algorithm.
key_points: HPV 16 or 18 detection on CST means direct colposcopy regardless of cytology
Non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with negative or LSIL cytology returns in 12 months
Vaccination does not treat established HPV infection
explanation.pearls: HPV 16 alone causes around half of invasive cervical cancers worldwide, justifying the direct-to-colposcopy pathway whenever it is detected on a screening test.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: cervical cancer screening

options.rationale: HPV 16 or 18 mandates direct colposcopy referral regardless of cytology grade; 12-month repeat is for non-16/18 oncogenic types with negative or low-grade cytology. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines)
Direct colposcopy referral is the AU pathway for HPV 16 or 18 detection on the CST irrespective of cytology grade. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines)

Hysterectomy is not indicated based on an HPV-positive screen with LSIL cytology; colposcopy and targeted treatment of any high-grade lesion is appropriate. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines)
Vaccination does not treat existing infection; it does not replace colposcopy after HPV 16 detection. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines)
Routine 5-year recall applies only to HPV-negative screens; HPV 16 detection alters management. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program guidelines)

explanation.summary: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis in RhD-negative non-sensitised women in Australia comprises 625 IU intramuscular at 28 and 34 weeks, plus a postpartum dose if the cord blood is RhD positive. Sensitising events (bleeding, trauma, procedures, ECV) below 12 weeks use 250 IU; above 12 weeks use 625 IU plus Kleihauer-Betke to estimate fetomaternal haemorrhage and any top-up. Cell-free fetal DNA RhD typing is increasingly available but not yet universal.
key_points: Routine antenatal anti-D in Australia is 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks
Sensitising events under 12 weeks use 250 IU; over 12 weeks use 625 IU plus Kleihauer-Betke
Postpartum dose follows cord blood RhD status of the baby
explanation.pearls: Anti-D 625 IU intramuscular within 72 hours of a sensitising event in a RhD-negative woman reduces alloimmunisation risk from around 16 percent to under 1 percent per pregnancy.

sources.label: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Routine antenatal anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks is standard AU practice in RhD-negative non-sensitised women. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: AU practice uses 625 IU at both 28 and 34 weeks, not a single late-pregnancy dose. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: AU NBA-funded antenatal prophylaxis is two doses of 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks plus postpartum based on cord RhD typing. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: The AU antenatal dose is 625 IU, not 250 IU; 250 IU is the early-pregnancy sensitising-event dose under 12 weeks. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Kleihauer-Betke is used after a sensitising event to estimate the dose; it is not used to decide on routine antenatal prophylaxis. (Source: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage workup after three first-trimester losses prioritises antiphospholipid antibody testing (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I) twice 12 weeks apart, parental karyotyping when indicated by products of conception, and uterine cavity assessment for structural anomaly. Inherited thrombophilia panels and immunological workup are not routinely recommended. APS treatment with low-dose aspirin plus LMWH from a positive pregnancy test improves live-birth rate.
key_points: APS testing (LAC, ACL, anti-beta2-GP1) is the single most actionable workup in recurrent miscarriage
Inherited thrombophilia testing without VTE history is not routinely recommended
APS-positive women receive low-dose aspirin plus LMWH from positive pregnancy test
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid antibodies must be persistently positive 12 weeks apart to meet APS criteria; treatment of confirmed APS with aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH improves live-birth rate from around 40 to 70 percent.

options.rationale: Tubal patency assessment does not explain recurrent miscarriage; it is a fertility investigation, not a miscarriage workup. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)
IVF and PGT-A do not improve live-birth rates over expectant management in idiopathic recurrent miscarriage and are reserved for specific scenarios. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)
Aspirin without an APS diagnosis does not improve outcomes in unexplained recurrent miscarriage; targeted investigation should precede therapy. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

APS testing is the single most actionable workup; APS detection enables aspirin plus LMWH which improves live-birth rate. Parental karyotyping is targeted by POC findings. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

Routine inherited thrombophilia testing in early-pregnancy loss without VTE history is no longer recommended; treatment does not improve live-birth rate. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

explanation.summary: Long-acting reversible contraception is first-line postpartum: progestogen-only methods do not affect lactation and can be commenced from immediate postpartum (implant or IUD post-placental insertion) or at the 6-week visit. Combined hormonal contraceptives are avoided while exclusively breastfeeding because of breast milk volume reduction and VTE risk. Lactational amenorrhoea has efficacy only under 6 months in exclusive breastfeeding with amenorrhoea.
key_points: Progestogen-only LARC (implant, hormonal IUD) does not affect breastfeeding
Combined hormonal contraceptives are avoided while exclusively breastfeeding
Lactational amenorrhoea has time-limited efficacy under 6 months with exclusive feeding
explanation.pearls: Etonogestrel implants and the LNG-IUS have typical-use failure rates under 1 per 100 woman-years and do not affect lactation when started postpartum.

options.rationale: LAM has time-limited efficacy (under 6 months, exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea); it is not first-line for 3-year horizons. (Source: RANZCOG postnatal contraception statement)

LARC methods are first-line postpartum: progestogen-only options do not affect breastfeeding and the implant or IUD can be placed at the 6-week visit. (Source: RANZCOG postnatal contraception statement)

Combined hormonal contraceptives are avoided while exclusively breastfeeding because they reduce milk volume; progestogen-only methods are preferred. (Source: RANZCOG postnatal contraception statement)
Permanent sterilisation is not indicated in a woman who wants further pregnancies in the future. (Source: RANZCOG postnatal contraception statement)
Condoms are typical-use 18 percent failure; not first-line when LARC is acceptable. (Source: RANZCOG postnatal contraception statement)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage with a live intrauterine pregnancy is managed expectantly with safety-net advice (urgent review for heavy bleeding, severe pain, or febrile illness), RhD typing and anti-D for any sensitising bleed (above 12 weeks; under 12 weeks only for high-volume events) and a follow-up scan within 1 to 2 weeks if symptoms persist. Bed rest does not influence outcomes. Progesterone supplementation is considered only for women with recurrent miscarriage and current bleeding.
key_points: Bed rest does not change the natural history of threatened miscarriage
RhD typing and anti-D should be considered for sensitising bleeding events
Progesterone supplementation is reserved for recurrent miscarriage with current bleeding
explanation.pearls: Subchorionic haematomas under 25 percent of the gestational sac volume have a similar live birth rate to women without a haematoma; reassurance with follow-up is appropriate.

options.rationale: Misoprostol is used for missed or incomplete miscarriage, not for threatened miscarriage with a live fetus; this is iatrogenic pregnancy loss. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy loss guideline)
Bed rest does not reduce miscarriage risk; routine progesterone is reserved for women with prior recurrent miscarriage and current bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy loss guideline)
Threatened miscarriage with a viable pregnancy is managed expectantly with safety-net advice, RhD typing and follow-up scan. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy loss guideline)
Surgical evacuation of a viable pregnancy is termination, not management of threatened miscarriage. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy loss guideline)
Methotrexate is used for ectopic pregnancy or termination; using it for a viable pregnancy with bleeding is iatrogenic loss. (Source: AMH: methotrexate)

explanation.summary: Valproate in pregnancy causes up to 10 percent major malformation and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental disorders, mandating switch before conception in any woman of reproductive potential when alternatives are available. Levetiracetam and lamotrigine are preferred substitutes for generalised epilepsy. The plan is cross-taper under neurology, confirm seizure freedom on monotherapy, add folic acid 5 mg daily, and only then deprescribe contraception. Monotherapy is preferred over polytherapy throughout pregnancy.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy whenever an alternative exists
Levetiracetam and lamotrigine are preferred substitutes for generalised epilepsy
Confirm seizure freedom on monotherapy before stopping contraception
explanation.pearls: Folic acid 5 mg daily (not 0.5 mg) is indicated for at least 3 months preconception in women on antiepileptics to reduce neural tube defect risk.

options.rationale: Valproate carries up to 10 percent major malformation and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental disorder risk; continuation through pregnancy is contraindicated unless no alternative. (Source: AMH: valproate; AES preconception guidance)
Abrupt cessation risks seizure recurrence, including status; switching, not stopping, is the safer approach. (Source: AES preconception guidance)
Topiramate is associated with oral clefts and is not the preferred switch; lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred. (Source: AES preconception guidance)
Cross-taper to levetiracetam (or lamotrigine), confirm seizure freedom on monotherapy, add high-dose folate, and only then attempt conception. (Source: AES preconception guidance)
Polytherapy in pregnancy carries higher malformation risk than monotherapy; the goal is monotherapy with the safest agent. (Source: AES preconception guidance)

explanation.summary: Endometriosis is managed in steps: NSAIDs and continuous COCP or progestogens first; if these fail after 6 to 12 months, see-and-treat laparoscopy with excision or ablation of lesions, followed by postoperative hormonal suppression to reduce recurrence. The LNG-IUS, GnRH antagonists (with add-back HRT after 6 months) and GnRH agonists are second-line medical options. Fertility-preserving conservative surgery is preferred over hysterectomy in younger women.
key_points: See-and-treat laparoscopy follows failure of first-line medical therapy
Postoperative hormonal suppression reduces symptom recurrence
Hysterectomy is reserved for refractory disease after fertility decisions are complete
explanation.pearls: Postoperative LNG-IUS or continuous progestogen after laparoscopic excision of endometriosis reduces 5-year symptom recurrence by around half compared with no maintenance therapy.

options.rationale: Switching from COCP to POP is unlikely to add symptom benefit after a year of failed continuous COCP; other progestogenic options or laparoscopy are preferred. (Source: RANZCOG endometriosis statement)
Hysterectomy with BSO is not appropriate for a 30-year-old nulliparous woman without fertility decision made and without confirmed advanced disease. (Source: RANZCOG endometriosis statement)
Danazol has significant androgenic side effects and is rarely used now; LNG-IUS, GnRH antagonists or laparoscopy are preferred. (Source: RANZCOG endometriosis statement)

LNG-IUS is a reasonable progestogenic option but a see-and-treat laparoscopy after failed first-line medical therapy is the AU stepwise approach in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG endometriosis statement)
After failed first-line continuous COCP plus NSAIDs, see-and-treat laparoscopy with postop hormonal suppression is the AU stepwise approach. (Source: RANZCOG endometriosis statement)

explanation.summary: Women 45 or older with abnormal uterine bleeding, and women younger than 45 with persistent symptoms or risk factors (obesity, anovulation, diabetes, PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome, unopposed oestrogen), require imaging (TVUS) and endometrial sampling (pipelle biopsy in outpatients). Hysteroscopy and dilatation and curettage are reserved for inadequate or non-diagnostic outpatient sampling. Management depends on histology: hyperplasia without atypia responds to progestogen (LNG-IUS), atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma is managed surgically.
key_points: AUB in women 45 or older mandates TVUS plus endometrial biopsy
Younger women with obesity, diabetes or anovulation also need sampling
Hysteroscopy and D&C are reserved for inadequate or non-diagnostic pipelle
explanation.pearls: A pipelle biopsy in the outpatient setting is the AU first-line endometrial sampling method; sensitivity for endometrial cancer in a peri-menopausal woman is around 90 to 95 percent with adequate sampling.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: endometrial cancer guideline

options.rationale: Endometrial assessment is mandatory in women 45 or older with abnormal uterine bleeding and obesity given hyperplasia risk; empirical hormonal therapy without histology is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG abnormal uterine bleeding statement)

TVUS alone is insufficient in pre-menopausal women: the negative predictive value of a thin endometrium is uncertain; histology is required given the risk profile. (Source: RANZCOG abnormal uterine bleeding statement)

Women 45 or older with abnormal uterine bleeding, plus those younger with persistent symptoms or risk factors (obesity, anovulation, diabetes, tamoxifen, Lynch), require imaging and endometrial sampling. (Source: RANZCOG abnormal uterine bleeding statement)
Pipelle sampling in outpatients is first-line; D&C is reserved for inadequate pipelle or persistent bleeding after pipelle. (Source: RANZCOG abnormal uterine bleeding statement)
Empirical hormonal therapy without histology risks masking endometrial pathology in a high-risk profile. (Source: RANZCOG abnormal uterine bleeding statement)

explanation.summary: Preconception care in pregestational type 2 diabetes targets HbA1c under 6.5 percent (without significant hypoglycaemia), switches to pregnancy-compatible agents (insulin, metformin), ceases teratogens (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, statins, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists), and starts folic acid 5 mg daily for at least 1 month before conception until 12 weeks gestation. Microvascular complication screening (retinal, renal, neuropathy) is undertaken pre-pregnancy and during pregnancy. Contraception is maintained until glycaemic and medication targets are met.
key_points: Preconception HbA1c target under 6.5 percent without significant hypoglycaemia
Cease ACE inhibitors, ARBs, statins, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists pre-conception
Folic acid 5 mg daily for at least 1 month before conception in pregestational diabetes
explanation.pearls: ADIPS recommends folic acid 5 mg daily (not 0.5 mg) for at least 1 month before conception in pregestational diabetes given elevated neural tube defect risk.

options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and statins are contraindicated in pregnancy; HbA1c targets pre-pregnancy aim for less than 6.5 percent where safe; folate at 5 mg daily is needed. (Source: ADIPS consensus guidelines for pregestational diabetes; RANZCOG preconception care)
HbA1c 8.4 percent is above the preconception target and ACE inhibitors and statins are contraindicated in pregnancy. (Source: ADIPS guidelines for pregestational diabetes)
Diabetes therapy intensifies to optimise control pre-pregnancy, not stop entirely; metformin and insulin are pregnancy-compatible. (Source: ADIPS guidelines for pregestational diabetes)

Australian preconception care for pregestational diabetes targets HbA1c under 6.5 percent (without significant hypoglycaemia), substitutes pregnancy-compatible agents, ceases teratogens, and adds 5 mg folate. (Source: ADIPS guidelines for pregestational diabetes; RANZCOG preconception care)

An HbA1c under 5 percent is below the population mean and unachievable safely; ADIPS target is under 6.5 percent without significant hypoglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS guidelines for pregestational diabetes)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding without structural pathology in a woman who has completed her family is managed first with the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system, which reduces blood loss by around 90% and provides effective contraception. Alternatives include tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily on bleeding days, NSAIDs, combined hormonal contraceptives, and progestogen regimens; each suits specific clinical settings. Surgical options (endometrial ablation, hysterectomy) follow failure of medical therapy. Investigation of heavy menstrual bleeding includes full blood count, ferritin, TSH, coagulation if indicated, and pelvic ultrasound to exclude structural causes.
key_points: 52 mg LNG-IUS is first-line medical therapy for ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding without structural cause
Tranexamic acid is a useful non-hormonal short-course option but less effective than LNG-IUS
Surgical options follow failure of medical therapy
explanation.pearls: The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss by approximately 90% over 12 months and remains effective for 8 years for contraception and 5 to 7 years for heavy menstrual bleeding.

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is a definitive option after medical therapy has been tried, not first-line for a woman who has not yet tried the LNG-IUS. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
Tranexamic acid is effective but second to the 52 mg LNG-IUS as first-line in suitable women and does not provide contraception. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
Endometrial ablation is reserved for women in whom medical therapy has failed and who do not desire fertility, and requires effective contraception. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

AU and international guidance recommends the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system as the first-line medical therapy for ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding without structural cause. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
Combined oral contraceptives reduce menstrual loss less effectively than the LNG-IUS and have contraindications that limit use. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Differentiation of common vaginal discharge causes is by history, vaginal pH and microscopy. Vulvovaginal candidiasis gives curdy white discharge with pH under 4.5, vulval itch and burning, and yeasts and pseudohyphae on microscopy; treatment is oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose or topical imidazole for 1 to 7 days. Bacterial vaginosis is a thin grey discharge with fishy odour, pH above 4.5, and clue cells, treated with metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days or topical clindamycin. Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection causing frothy yellow-green discharge with strawberry cervix and high pH, treated with tinidazole 2 g or metronidazole 2 g single dose plus partner treatment.
key_points: Vaginal pH and discharge character separate candidiasis, BV, and trichomoniasis
Oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose treats uncomplicated candidiasis
Recurrent candidiasis (4 or more episodes per year) prompts longer induction maintenance and trigger review
explanation.pearls: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined as 4 or more episodes in 12 months and is treated with induction oral fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses then weekly for 6 months.

options.rationale: Bacterial vaginosis presents with thin grey discharge, fishy odour, and pH above 4.5, not curdy discharge with pH 4.2. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: bacterial vaginosis)

Uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis in a non-pregnant woman is treated with a single oral 150 mg fluconazole dose or a short topical imidazole course. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: vulvovaginal candidiasis)
Trichomoniasis gives a frothy yellow-green discharge with strawberry cervix and high pH, not the picture here. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: trichomoniasis)
Topical steroids alone do not treat candidiasis and may worsen if used without antifungal cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: vulvovaginal candidiasis)
Oral cephalosporins do not treat vulvovaginal candidiasis and may worsen by altering bacterial flora. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: vulvovaginal candidiasis)

explanation.summary: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, topiramate above 200 mg daily, oxcarbazepine, rufinamide) accelerate metabolism of oestrogens and progestogens and reduce the efficacy of combined hormonal methods, progestogen-only pills, and the etonogestrel implant. AU recommendations favour the copper or 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine systems because intrauterine levels are unaffected. Depot medroxyprogesterone is acceptable but carries other long-term considerations. Valproate, lamotrigine alone, and most newer anticonvulsants do not significantly induce contraceptive metabolism but lamotrigine levels fall with combined hormonal contraceptives, which can worsen seizure control.
key_points: Enzyme inducing antiepileptics reduce efficacy of pills and the etonogestrel implant
Copper IUD and 52 mg LNG-IUS retain efficacy because of local action
Lamotrigine levels fall with combined hormonal contraception and may need monitoring
explanation.pearls: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, topiramate over 200 mg, phenobarbital and primidone are the enzyme inducers to memorise; lamotrigine is not an inducer but its own levels drop with combined hormonal contraception.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception with antiepileptics

options.rationale: Depot medroxyprogesterone has the disadvantage of bone density loss with long-term use and offers no advantage over the copper IUD in this patient. (Source: RANZCOG: Long-acting reversible contraception)

Enzyme inducers reduce combined hormonal contraceptive efficacy unpredictably; higher dose ethinylestradiol is not recommended in current AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG: Long-acting reversible contraception)
Etonogestrel implant is reduced in efficacy by enzyme inducers like carbamazepine and is not recommended. (Source: RANZCOG: Long-acting reversible contraception)
Enzyme inducers also reduce progestogen-only pill efficacy and dose-doubling is not licensed. (Source: RANZCOG: Long-acting reversible contraception)

Non-hormonal copper IUD is not affected by enzyme-inducing antiepileptic medication and is recommended as a first-line long-acting contraceptive in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG: Long-acting reversible contraception)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe nausea and vomiting in pregnancy with weight loss greater than 5%, dehydration, ketonuria, and electrolyte disturbance. Initial admission management is intravenous Hartmann or normal saline rehydration with potassium replacement and thiamine 100 mg intravenously to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy before any glucose-containing fluids. First-line antiemetic in AU practice is oral or rectal pyridoxine doxylamine, with metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, ondansetron, and corticosteroids in escalation. Recurrent presentations prompt screening for molar pregnancy, multiple pregnancy, and thyroid dysfunction.
key_points: IV rehydration with thiamine and first-line pyridoxine doxylamine address dehydration and ketonuria
Outpatient management fails when oral intake cannot be maintained or significant ketonuria is present
Recurrent admissions trigger ultrasound and thyroid function review to exclude molar or multiple pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Thiamine 100 mg IV is given before any glucose containing fluid in hyperemesis to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, which is reported and avoidable in modern practice.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy
SOMANZ: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: Discharge home does not address dehydration and electrolyte derangement requiring intravenous fluids and inpatient assessment. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: Ketonuria, electrolyte derangement and inability to tolerate oral fluids exceed outpatient management. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: Hyperemesis with ketonuria, electrolyte derangement and dehydration requires IV rehydration with thiamine cover plus first-line antiemetic pyridoxine doxylamine. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: Outpatient oral antiemetic therapy is inadequate when oral intake cannot be maintained and dehydration is significant. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: Termination is not the first-line response to inadequate ambulatory care of nausea and vomiting; admission and escalation of antiemetic therapy precede this discussion. (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria affects 2 to 10% of pregnant women and increases the risk of pyelonephritis, preterm birth, and low birth weight. AU practice screens all women at their antenatal booking with MSU culture and treats positive cultures with a 5 to 7 day antibiotic course (nitrofurantoin first or second trimester, cefalexin throughout) followed by test of cure 1 to 2 weeks after completion. Nitrofurantoin is avoided in the third trimester because of neonatal haemolysis risk; trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester. Recurrent infection prompts consideration of low dose prophylaxis for the remainder of pregnancy.
key_points: Antenatal MSU screening detects asymptomatic bacteriuria and treatment reduces pyelonephritis and preterm birth
Nitrofurantoin and cefalexin are common AU first-line options with trimester restrictions
Test of cure 1 to 2 weeks after treatment is routine
explanation.pearls: Nitrofurantoin is avoided after 36 weeks gestation because of neonatal G6PD-related haemolysis risk; cefalexin or amoxicillin clavulanate is preferred at term.

sources.label: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

options.rationale: Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester because of folate antagonism and theoretical teratogenic risk. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

options.rationale: Delaying treatment increases the risk of progression to pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

options.rationale: Single dose fosfomycin is less effective in pregnancy than a longer course and test of cure is routinely recommended. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated with a 5 to 7 day antibiotic course because of pyelonephritis and preterm birth risk, with test of cure. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

options.rationale: Continuous prophylaxis is reserved for recurrent UTI in pregnancy after treatment, not a single positive booking culture. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Antibiotic: asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding warrants exclusion of endometrial cancer. Transvaginal ultrasound measures endometrial thickness; a threshold of 4 mm or less reliably excludes cancer in women on no hormone therapy. Above this threshold, or in the presence of a focal lesion such as an endometrial polyp, hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and polypectomy is the AU standard of care. Most polyps are benign, but 5 to 10% in postmenopausal women harbour atypia or carcinoma. Asymptomatic polyps under 1 cm in premenopausal women may be observed.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrium over 4 mm or a focal lesion requires histology
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and polypectomy beats blind Pipelle for focal lesions
Polyps in postmenopausal women carry a 5 to 10% risk of malignancy
explanation.pearls: Endometrial thickness under 4 mm on TVUS in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding has a negative predictive value of around 99% for endometrial cancer when there is no focal lesion.

options.rationale: Hysterectomy without histology over treats benign polyps which account for most postmenopausal bleeding lesions. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal bleeding)
Repeat imaging without histology in a woman with postmenopausal bleeding and a focal lesion delays diagnosis of malignancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal bleeding)
Blind Pipelle biopsy misses focal lesions and is inadequate when a polyp is identified on ultrasound. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal bleeding)
Hormone therapy does not address postmenopausal bleeding with a focal lesion and may worsen by masking pathology. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal bleeding)

Postmenopausal bleeding with a focal endometrial lesion is investigated with hysteroscopic resection and directed endometrial sampling to exclude malignancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Postmenopausal bleeding)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage is bleeding in early pregnancy with a closed cervix and confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy. Most viable pregnancies (around 85 to 90%) continue to a live birth. Management is supportive: reassurance, pelvic rest, paracetamol for cramping, and review with repeat ultrasound at 1 to 2 weeks. Anti-D is given to Rh-negative women with significant bleeding. Vaginal progesterone has a modest benefit only in women with a history of one or more previous miscarriages presenting with current bleeding.
key_points: Confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy with threatened miscarriage usually continues; manage supportively
Anti-D is given to Rh negative women with bleeding
Vaginal progesterone is selective for women with previous miscarriage history per AU practice
explanation.pearls: The PRISM trial demonstrated vaginal progesterone reduces miscarriage in women with current bleeding AND at least one prior miscarriage, with no benefit in women with no prior loss.

options.rationale: Threatened miscarriage with confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy is managed with reassurance and planned follow up imaging; most viable pregnancies continue. (Source: RANZCOG: Early pregnancy bleeding)
Dilatation and curettage is for retained products of conception or completed miscarriage, not a viable intrauterine pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Early pregnancy bleeding)
Vaginal progesterone is only supported by AU practice for women with previous miscarriages presenting with bleeding, not all women. (Source: RANZCOG: Early pregnancy bleeding)
Anti-D is only indicated in Rh-negative women at risk of sensitising events. (Source: RANZCOG: Anti-D)
Methotrexate is reserved for confirmed ectopic pregnancy without contraindications, not an intrauterine pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Postpartum contraception in breastfeeding women favours progestogen-only methods because they do not affect milk supply. The etonogestrel subdermal implant can be inserted from any time postpartum (including the early postnatal hospital stay), and intrauterine systems are usually placed at 4 weeks or more after delivery. Combined hormonal contraception is delayed until at least 6 weeks postpartum and considered cautiously in breastfeeding because of possible reduction in milk supply and VTE risk. The lactational amenorrhoea method offers about 98% effectiveness only when all three criteria are met: full breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, and infant under 6 months.
key_points: Progestogen-only methods are safe in breastfeeding from any time postpartum
Combined hormonal contraception is delayed until at least 6 weeks postpartum and considered cautiously in breastfeeding
LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, and infant under 6 months for efficacy
explanation.pearls: Etonogestrel implant can be inserted any time postpartum including before hospital discharge and provides 3 years of effective contraception without affecting milk supply.

options.rationale: Although LNG-IUS is appropriate after 4 weeks postpartum, it is not contraindicated and is a reasonable alternative if patient prefers an IUS over an implant. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception postpartum)
Combined hormonal contraception is avoided until at least 6 weeks postpartum and longer in breastfeeding because of VTE and possible milk supply effects. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception postpartum)
Lactational amenorrhoea provides about 98% protection only with exclusive breastfeeding and amenorrhoea in the first 6 months, and is unreliable beyond. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception postpartum)
Progestogen-only methods are safe in breastfeeding from any time postpartum and are first-line LARC for breastfeeding mothers without contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception postpartum)
Diaphragm efficacy is lower than LARC and fitting may need adjustment after pregnancy; not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception postpartum)

explanation.summary: Carriage of group B streptococcus is intermittent, and a result from a previous pregnancy has poor predictive value for the current one, so screening is repeated in every pregnancy and the current result governs the plan. A negative vagino-rectal swab taken within the 35 to 37 week window, in a woman with no bacteriuria this pregnancy and no previous infant with invasive disease, means no intrapartum prophylaxis even though she was positive last time. The important distinction is between previous maternal carriage, which does not carry forward, and a previous infant with invasive disease, which does and obliges prophylaxis in every subsequent labour. In context, over-treating on a historical swab is common and exposes women to unnecessary antibiotics, cannulation and restricted mobility in labour for no reduction in neonatal risk.
key_points: Carriage is intermittent and is reassessed each pregnancy.
A negative current swab within the window means no prophylaxis when no other indication exists.
A previous infant with invasive disease does carry forward and always indicates prophylaxis.
Swab results older than five weeks or outside the window are treated as unknown.
explanation.pearls: The swab window matters: a result from before 35 weeks or more than five weeks old is treated as unknown status, and risk factors then decide.

options.rationale: Colonisation is intermittent and is assessed afresh each pregnancy, so a negative current swab with no other indication means no prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)

Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: This is the plan when the current swab is positive, or when an earlier baby had invasive disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)

options.rationale: Cefazolin is the substitute for an indicated woman whose penicillin reaction was not severe, not a first-line agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)

options.rationale: A newborn blood culture belongs to a baby with clinical signs or a genuinely high risk exposure. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses 5 yearly HPV primary screening with reflex liquid-based cytology if higher risk types are detected. HPV 16 or 18 positive plus HSIL or worse on cytology is a higher risk result and is referred for colposcopy within 2 weeks. HPV non-16/18 positive with low-grade cytology is intermediate risk with 12 month repeat HPV test. Self-collection is approved for women aged 25 to 74 and gives equivalent sensitivity for high-risk HPV.
