Treatment of biopsy-proven HSIL is by excisional therapy (LLETZ) or ablative therapy, with surveillance HPV test at 12 months post-treatment.
key_points: Higher risk HPV with HSIL cytology requires colposcopy within 2 weeks
Intermediate risk (HPV non-16/18 with low-grade cytology) is rechecked at 12 months
Self-collected HPV testing is approved for women aged 25 to 74 with equivalent sensitivity
explanation.pearls: Self-collection cervical screening returns the same higher risk pathway as clinician-collected; reflex cytology is performed on the same sample when HPV 16 or 18 positive.

options.rationale: Higher risk results require direct referral to colposcopy, not deferred repeat testing. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
12 month repeat applies to intermediate risk results, not higher risk with HSIL cytology. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
Copper IUD does not interfere with colposcopy or cervical biopsy and need not be removed. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
Treatment without colposcopic assessment can over-treat and is not supported by AU guidelines. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)
Higher risk HPV with HSIL cytology mandates colposcopy within 2 weeks per AU NCSP pathways. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Recurrent pregnancy loss is defined as three or more consecutive miscarriages, with workup also reasonable after two losses with concerning history. Established causes include antiphospholipid syndrome (treated with low-dose aspirin and prophylactic LMWH), uterine anomalies, parental balanced translocations, untreated thyroid disease, and uncontrolled diabetes. Standard initial workup includes antiphospholipid antibodies on two occasions 12 weeks apart, pelvic imaging (3D ultrasound, saline infusion sonohysterography, or MRI), parental karyotype, thyroid function, and HbA1c. Around 50% of recurrent miscarriages have no identified cause, and expectant pregnancy management has a 60 to 70% live birth rate.
key_points: Antiphospholipid antibody screen is a priority because treatment alters outcome
Uterine cavity assessment (3D ultrasound, SIS, or MRI) identifies treatable anomalies
Parental karyotype is selective in women under 39 without family history but standard after three losses
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid syndrome diagnosis requires two positive antibody results 12 weeks apart; a single positive result is not enough to label and treat.

options.rationale: AU and international guidance for recurrent pregnancy loss screens for antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine anomalies and parental karyotype as the priority initial workup. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
Empirical heparin without diagnosed antiphospholipid syndrome lacks evidence in unexplained recurrent miscarriage. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
Inherited thrombophilia screening is no longer part of the routine recurrent miscarriage workup outside specific situations. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
PGT-A may be considered after structural and parental karyotype workup, not as the sole initial step. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)
Chronic endometritis testing is selective and does not replace the standard antiphospholipid plus structural plus karyotype workup. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Operative vaginal delivery is indicated for fetal compromise, maternal exhaustion, or prolonged second stage. Pre-requisites include full cervical dilation, ruptured membranes, identified fetal position, head at or below the ischial spines, adequate analgesia, empty bladder, consent, and ability to convert to caesarean section. Vacuum is generally preferred for outlet and low-cavity deliveries because of lower maternal trauma and equivalent fetal outcomes when used appropriately. Forceps are favoured for mid-cavity rotation, prematurity under 34 weeks, face presentation, or after-coming head. A failed vacuum should not be followed by sequential forceps in the absence of compelling reasons because of compounded neonatal injury risk.
key_points: Vacuum extraction has lower maternal trauma than forceps for outlet delivery
Pre-requisites include full dilation, identified position, station at or below spines, analgesia, empty bladder, consent, and theatre access
Sequential vacuum then forceps increases neonatal injury and is avoided where possible
explanation.pearls: Vacuum should not be used below 34 weeks gestation because of increased neonatal subgaleal haemorrhage and intraventricular haemorrhage risk.

options.rationale: Category 1 caesarean is reserved when vaginal delivery is not safely achievable; outlet vacuum delivery is preferable when feasible. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)
Outlet operative vaginal delivery with vacuum is appropriate at +2 OA station with non-reassuring CTG and adequate analgesia. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)
Continued pushing in the face of category 2 fetal heart rate trace at +2 station with prolonged second stage delays definitive intervention. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)
Increasing oxytocin in the face of late decelerations and fetal compromise risks worsening fetal acidosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)
Rotational forceps are reserved for malposition or operator preference; OA position at +2 favours vacuum first in AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia is hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ involvement after 20 weeks gestation. Severe disease is defined by blood pressure 160/110 mmHg or higher, proteinuria, or end-organ features (thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, renal impairment, pulmonary oedema, cerebral or visual disturbance, severe epigastric pain). Antihypertensive control to systolic 140 to 155 mmHg and diastolic 90 to 105 mmHg, intravenous magnesium sulfate for severe disease and to prevent eclampsia, and corticosteroids if under 34 weeks are key. Delivery is indicated immediately for severe disease 34 to 37 weeks, eclampsia, abruption, deteriorating end-organ function, or non-reassuring fetal status.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia at or beyond 34 to 37 weeks is an indication for delivery
BP target is 140 to 155 / 90 to 105 mmHg in pregnancy
Magnesium sulfate prevents progression to eclampsia and is loaded then run as infusion
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate loading is 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion, continued for 24 hours after delivery or last seizure with monitoring of reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output.

options.rationale: Continued expectant management with multi-organ involvement risks maternal eclampsia, abruption, and fetal compromise. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)
Severe pre-eclampsia at or beyond 34 to 37 weeks with end-organ features (thrombocytopenia, transaminitis) is an indication for delivery. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)
Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis around delivery, not as a means to delay it. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)
Repeat steroid courses at this gestation are not indicated and delivery should not be delayed for further steroids at 36 weeks. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)
Outpatient management is inadequate for severe pre-eclampsia at 36 weeks with thrombocytopenia and transaminitis. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis is common in the first 3 months postpartum and typically presents with focal breast erythema, swelling, and systemic symptoms responsive to milk drainage and 24 to 48 hours of oral flucloxacillin or cefalexin if not improving. Failure to respond to antibiotics, persistent or diffuse erythema, peau d orange, skin tethering, or a discrete mass should prompt urgent breast clinic referral to exclude inflammatory breast cancer or other malignancy. Inflammatory breast cancer is rare but rapidly progressive, often mimics infection, and requires triple assessment (clinical examination, imaging, and core biopsy). Continuing breastfeeding during mastitis is encouraged because it aids resolution.
key_points: Lactational mastitis is managed with milk drainage and flucloxacillin or cefalexin if not improving
Persistent peau d orange or non-response to antibiotics prompts triple assessment to exclude inflammatory breast cancer
Continuing breastfeeding usually helps resolve mastitis
explanation.pearls: Inflammatory breast cancer presents with diffuse erythema, peau d orange and no discrete mass; it accounts for under 5% of breast cancers but has the worst prognosis if missed.

options.rationale: Skin changes (peau d orange, persistent erythema) that fail to respond to antibiotic therapy require breast clinic referral to exclude inflammatory breast cancer. (Source: RACGP: Breast cancer red flags)
Antibiotic monotherapy of persistent peau d orange without trial of response and no clear infection delays evaluation for inflammatory carcinoma. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: lactational mastitis)
Cessation of breastfeeding is not first-line and does not address inflammatory cancer if present. (Source: RANZCOG: Breastfeeding and lactation)
Bedside ultrasound is negative for abscess; surgical drainage without collection risks needless intervention. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: lactational mastitis)
Persistent peau d orange beyond a normal mastitis course is a red flag and warrants urgent breast clinic referral. (Source: RACGP: Breast cancer red flags)

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injuries (OASIS) include third degree tears (3a less than 50% external sphincter, 3b more than 50% external sphincter, 3c involving internal sphincter) and fourth degree tears (involving rectal mucosa). Repair is performed in theatre by a trained operator under regional or general anaesthesia with broad spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis, end-to-end or overlap technique for external sphincter, mattress sutures for internal sphincter, and continuous closure of rectal mucosa with absorbable sutures. Postoperative management includes laxatives, pelvic floor physiotherapy, and follow up with perineal clinic at 6 to 12 weeks. Future deliveries are discussed in a perineal clinic with reference to symptoms and anal manometry.
key_points: OASIS includes 3a, 3b, 3c (internal sphincter), and 4th degree (rectal mucosa) tears
Repair occurs in theatre with antibiotic prophylaxis and postoperative laxatives
Future delivery planning depends on symptoms, anal manometry, and ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic prophylaxis for OASIS uses intravenous cefazolin and metronidazole at induction, with at least 5 days of oral cefalexin and metronidazole after repair to reduce wound infection and breakdown.

sources.label: RCOG GTG 29: Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Incomplete repair of internal sphincter and rectal mucosa leads to fistula and incontinence; full theatre repair is required. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS guideline)
Bedside repair under local infiltration does not provide adequate visualisation or sphincter approximation for OASIS. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS guideline)
Unrepaired sphincter injury leads to incontinence and infection; theatre repair is the standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS guideline)
Defunctioning colostomy is reserved for complex or breakdown injuries, not primary OASIS repair. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS guideline)
OASIS injury (3c or 4th degree tears) is repaired in theatre by a trained operator with antibiotic prophylaxis and laxatives to optimise functional outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: OASIS guideline)

explanation.summary: Maternal sepsis carries high maternal and fetal mortality and is recognised early using maternal early warning systems. SOMANZ guidance applies the hour-1 bundle in obstetric settings: serum lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics where possible, broad spectrum empirical antibiotics within 1 hour (piperacillin-tazobactam with consideration of clindamycin for streptococcal toxic shock), 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation, source control assessment, and noradrenaline for fluid-refractory hypotension. Source control for chorioamnionitis is delivery; for septic abortion is uterine evacuation. Multidisciplinary involvement of obstetrics, intensive care, neonatology, and microbiology is essential.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle (cultures, antibiotics, fluids, source control assessment) applies in pregnancy
Piperacillin-tazobactam with clindamycin if streptococcal toxic shock suspected
Source control for chorioamnionitis is delivery rather than continued conservative management
explanation.pearls: Add intravenous clindamycin to broad spectrum cover in suspected streptococcal toxic shock syndrome to reduce toxin production; continue until clinical response is established.

sources.label: RCOG GTG 64: Bacterial sepsis in pregnancy

options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in maternal sepsis and may worsen haemodynamic instability. (Source: SOMANZ: Maternal sepsis)
Delivery considerations follow resuscitation and antibiotic administration; antibiotics within 1 hour reduce maternal and fetal mortality. (Source: SOMANZ: Maternal sepsis)
Maternal sepsis is managed with sepsis hour-1 bundle including blood cultures, broad spectrum antibiotics, IV fluids 30 mL/kg, and source control planning. (Source: SOMANZ: Maternal sepsis)
Delaying antibiotics until cultures grow increases mortality in sepsis; empirical broad spectrum cover is given within 1 hour. (Source: SOMANZ: Maternal sepsis)
Corticosteroids are part of the obstetric management plan once mother is stabilising, not the first priority over resuscitation. (Source: SOMANZ: Maternal sepsis)

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is diagnosed by the Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3: oligo or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology) after exclusion of other causes. The international evidence-based PCOS guideline (with significant AU input) recommends letrozole as the first-line ovulation induction agent in anovulatory PCOS infertility because of higher live birth rates and lower multiple pregnancy rates compared to clomifene. Clomifene or metformin remain alternatives, and combined letrozole-metformin is considered in higher BMI. Gonadotropins or IVF are second and third line. Pre-conception screening for diabetes and lifestyle measures including weight loss of 5 to 10% improve ovulation and pregnancy outcomes.
key_points: Letrozole is first-line ovulation induction in PCOS-related infertility per current guidelines
Pre-conception screening (OGTT, BP, thyroid) is part of PCOS workup
Pre-conception weight loss of 5 to 10% improves ovulation and live birth
explanation.pearls: Letrozole 2.5 to 7.5 mg daily for 5 days starting day 2 to 5 of cycle achieves ovulation in around 75% of PCOS women with higher live birth rates than clomifene.

options.rationale: Metformin alone produces lower ovulation and pregnancy rates than letrozole in PCOS-related infertility. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS)
Clomifene remains effective but is now positioned behind letrozole in current AU and international guidance. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS)

AU and international PCOS guidance prefers letrozole over clomifene for first-line ovulation induction in anovulatory PCOS infertility because of higher live birth rates. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS)
Gonadotropins are second-line after failure of oral agents because of higher multiple pregnancy and OHSS risk. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS)
IVF is reserved for failure of ovulation induction, tubal disease, or other infertility indications. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for PCOS)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding requires investigation because the population risk of endometrial cancer is approximately 10%, rising with obesity, diabetes, and unopposed oestrogen exposure. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line investigation; an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less in a woman not on tamoxifen has very high negative predictive value. Persistent bleeding or thickness above 4 mm leads to endometrial sampling, usually outpatient pipelle, with hysteroscopy if sampling is inadequate or focal lesions are suspected. Tamoxifen users follow a different pathway because they may have a thickened sub-endometrial complex.
key_points: All postmenopausal bleeding requires investigation regardless of how minor it appears
First-line is transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness
Endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less has high negative predictive value in non-tamoxifen users
explanation.pearls: Obesity, diabetes, and chronic anovulation drive unopposed oestrogen exposure and lift endometrial cancer risk markedly even in non-bleeding women.

options.rationale: Cervical screening does not investigate endometrial pathology, which is the priority concern in postmenopausal bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)
Operative hysteroscopy is escalation after non-diagnostic outpatient imaging or sampling, not the initial step. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Transvaginal ultrasound measuring endometrial thickness is the first-line investigation; less than 4 mm has a high negative predictive value for endometrial cancer in postmenopausal women. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)
CA-125 and computed tomography are not first-line in postmenopausal bleeding; transvaginal ultrasound directs further workup. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)
All postmenopausal bleeding warrants investigation; endometrial cancer risk is approximately 10% across the population. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome causes anovulatory subfertility through chronic anovulation. International evidence-based guidance now recommends letrozole as the first-line ovulation induction agent because of higher cumulative live-birth rates compared with clomifene citrate. Clomifene remains an alternative if letrozole is contraindicated or unavailable. Metformin is adjunctive for insulin resistance and may improve ovulation rates when combined with letrozole, particularly in higher body mass index. Lifestyle weight loss of 5-10% restores ovulation in many women and should accompany pharmacological induction.
key_points: Letrozole is first-line ovulation induction in PCOS
Lifestyle and 5-10% weight loss adjuncts restore ovulation in many women
Gonadotrophins or ovarian drilling are second-line
explanation.pearls: Letrozole carries no increased risk of congenital anomaly compared with clomifene despite earlier safety concerns from short courses.

options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception suppresses ovulation and is not used to induce conception. (Source: RANZCOG: PCOS Guideline)
Gonadotrophin injections require intensive monitoring and are reserved for those failing oral ovulation induction. (Source: RANZCOG: PCOS Guideline)
Metformin alone has lower live-birth rates than letrozole; it is adjunctive rather than first-line for anovulatory subfertility. (Source: RANZCOG: PCOS Guideline)
Ovarian drilling is second-line surgery reserved for women who do not ovulate on oral therapy or those needing laparoscopy for another reason. (Source: RANZCOG: PCOS Guideline)
Letrozole is now the recommended first-line ovulation induction agent in polycystic ovary syndrome with higher live-birth rates than clomifene. (Source: RANZCOG: PCOS Guideline)

explanation.summary: RhD-negative women without preformed anti-D require anti-D prophylaxis after sensitising events including abdominal trauma in pregnancy. Dosing is 250 IU before 13 weeks and 625 IU at or after 13 weeks, given within 72 hours of the event. Routine antenatal prophylaxis is still offered at 28 and 34 weeks unless a 625 IU dose was given within the preceding 3 weeks. Kleihauer-Betke is used to detect feto-maternal haemorrhage exceeding 6 mL of fetal cells, which requires additional anti-D.
key_points: 250 IU before 13 weeks, 625 IU from 13 weeks for sensitising events
Give anti-D within 72 hours of any sensitising event
Continue routine 28-week and 34-week prophylaxis unless within 3 weeks of an event dose
explanation.pearls: Falls in pregnancy without bleeding still count as sensitising events from 20 weeks; treat by default and use Kleihauer to detect larger feto-maternal haemorrhage.

options.rationale: The 250 IU dose is for sensitising events before 12 weeks; from 13 weeks the dose is 625 IU, and routine antenatal prophylaxis is still offered at 28 and 34 weeks. (Source: NBA: Anti-D Use Guideline)
For sensitising events at or after 13 weeks the dose is 625 IU within 72 hours; routine prophylaxis continues unless given within the preceding 3 weeks. (Source: NBA: Anti-D Use Guideline)

Standard intramuscular dosing covers the Kleihauer-Betke estimate here; daily Kleihauer titration is not standard and intravenous use is restricted to specific clotting risk scenarios. (Source: NBA: Anti-D Use Guideline)
Anti-D after a sensitising event is time-critical; delay beyond 72 hours reduces effectiveness, with sensitisation rates rising sharply thereafter. (Source: NBA: Anti-D Use Guideline)
Any clinically significant sensitising event after 13 weeks warrants 625 IU within 72 hours regardless of Kleihauer estimate within standard volume ranges. (Source: NBA: Anti-D Use Guideline)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency requiring same-day laparoscopy. The classic triad of sudden pelvic pain, palpable mass, and reduced or absent ovarian Doppler flow has high specificity but absent flow is not required for diagnosis as venous compromise often precedes arterial loss. Detorsion with preservation of the ovary is preferred over oophorectomy even when the ovary appears dusky, because viable cortex often recovers. Cyst aspiration is not therapeutic and risks chemical peritonitis.
key_points: Acute pelvic pain with adnexal mass and reduced Doppler flow needs same-day laparoscopy
Detorsion with ovarian conservation is preferred over oophorectomy
Doppler flow can be preserved early due to dual ovarian blood supply
explanation.pearls: Even a black ischaemic-appearing ovary often recovers function after detorsion; never assume non-viability based on intraoperative colour alone.

options.rationale: Delaying intervention in suspected ovarian torsion risks irreversible ischaemic loss of ovarian tissue. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

Tubo-ovarian abscess typically has fever, leucocytosis, and inflammatory adnexal fluid; ultrasound here shows compromised flow rather than abscess. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: pelvic inflammatory disease)
Outpatient pathway is inappropriate when ultrasound and clinical features support torsion; this risks ovarian loss within hours. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)
Suspected ovarian torsion is a surgical diagnosis warranting same-day laparoscopy; detorsion with ovarian conservation is preferred over oophorectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)
Cyst aspiration does not address torsion and may cause cyst rupture and chemical peritonitis. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes from 24 to 36+6 weeks is managed expectantly with antenatal corticosteroids, regular infection surveillance, and prophylactic antibiotics if labour starts or chorioamnionitis is suspected. Australian guidance now favours planned delivery at 37+0 weeks rather than immediate delivery at 34 weeks because respiratory morbidity outweighs neonatal infection risk in this range. Inpatient surveillance with serial maternal observations and fetal monitoring is standard. Magnesium neuroprotection applies for births before 30 weeks.
key_points: Expectant management with steroids and surveillance from 24 to 36+6 weeks
Plan delivery at 37+0 weeks in stable cases
Tocolysis is not indicated without active preterm labour
explanation.pearls: Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis is required in labour regardless of negative screen if rupture exceeds 18 hours; protocols vary by health service.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: From 24 to 36+6 weeks expectant management with steroids and infection surveillance is recommended; planned delivery by 37+0 weeks balances respiratory and infection risks. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Steroids are given before birth to be effective; immediate caesarean without indication does not improve outcomes at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal Corticosteroids)
Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes requires inpatient surveillance; outpatient management is not standard given chorioamnionitis risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Magnesium neuroprotection is for delivery under 30 weeks; immediate induction at 34 weeks without other indication carries higher respiratory morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection)

Tocolysis is not indicated without active preterm labour; antibiotics and steroids are routine adjuncts in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is associated with prior caesarean and placenta praevia. Antenatal imaging features include loss of the retroplacental clear space, intraplacental lacunae, and bridging vessels at the uterus-bladder interface. Tertiary multidisciplinary care including blood bank, urology, interventional radiology, and intensive care reduces maternal morbidity. The default plan is elective lower-segment caesarean delivery with caesarean hysterectomy at 35 to 36+6 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids. Magnetic resonance imaging is adjunctive in posterior placentation or where ultrasound is equivocal.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum demands tertiary multidisciplinary care
Plan elective delivery at 35 to 36+6 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids
Caesarean hysterectomy is the default; conservative management is highly selective
explanation.pearls: Three or more previous caesareans with anterior praevia carries up to a 60% risk of placenta accreta spectrum; have a high pre-test probability.

options.rationale: Placenta accreta spectrum requires delivery at a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary expertise; local elective caesarean risks catastrophic haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)
Magnetic resonance imaging is adjunctive in posterior or equivocal cases but referral is based on clinical suspicion, not awaiting imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in placenta accreta spectrum because of catastrophic haemorrhage risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

Conservative leave-in-situ is selective; the default plan at multidisciplinary centres remains planned caesarean hysterectomy unless future fertility is a priority. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

Tertiary multidisciplinary care with planned 35 to 36 week elective caesarean hysterectomy under cell salvage and major haemorrhage protocols halves maternal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

explanation.summary: The T-sign with a single placental disc indicates a monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancy. These pregnancies require fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to detect twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome which classically presents between 16 and 26 weeks. Elective delivery at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks balances stillbirth and prematurity risks. Dichorionic twins have a lambda sign and surveillance starts at 20 weeks with growth scans every 4 weeks.
key_points: T-sign means monochorionic; lambda sign means dichorionic
Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks in monochorionic-diamniotic twins
Aim delivery at 36 to 37 weeks for monochorionic-diamniotic, 37 to 38 weeks for dichorionic
explanation.pearls: Chorionicity is most accurate in the first trimester; never defer determination beyond 14 weeks because membranes thin progressively.

options.rationale: Monochorionic twins require fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome surveillance regardless of low first trimester screen risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin Pregnancy)
Surveillance starts at 16 weeks for monochorionic twins because twin-to-twin transfusion typically presents between 16 and 26 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin Pregnancy)

The T-sign indicates monochorionic-diamniotic pregnancy requiring fortnightly surveillance from 16 weeks and delivery at 36 to 37 weeks; later delivery raises stillbirth risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin Pregnancy)
Selective reduction is not routine in uncomplicated monochorionic-diamniotic twins; it is reserved for complications such as severe selective growth restriction. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin Pregnancy)
Elective preterm delivery at 32 weeks exposes both twins to significant prematurity morbidity without proportional benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Twin Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome is defined by persistent antiphospholipid antibody positivity 12 weeks apart together with pregnancy morbidity such as three or more consecutive first trimester losses or fetal death after 10 weeks. Management is combined low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic enoxaparin from confirmation of pregnancy through to 6 weeks postpartum to reduce venous thromboembolism and improve live-birth rates. Therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for prior venous thromboembolism. Hydroxychloroquine and prednisolone are adjunctive in lupus-associated cases.
key_points: Aspirin plus prophylactic enoxaparin for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome
Continue anticoagulation for 6 weeks postpartum
Therapeutic dosing reserved for prior venous thromboembolism
explanation.pearls: Confirm antibody persistence at least 12 weeks apart before labelling antiphospholipid syndrome; transient positivity post-infection is common.

options.rationale: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome with prior late pregnancy loss requires both low-dose aspirin and prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)

Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome is treated with combined low-dose aspirin and prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin antenatally and for 6 weeks postpartum. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)
Warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic; it is not used antenatally for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome. (Source: AMH: Anticoagulants in Pregnancy)
Hydroxychloroquine is adjunctive in lupus-associated antiphospholipid syndrome but not a substitute for aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)
Therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for those with prior venous thromboembolism; prednisolone is not first-line for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent Miscarriage)

explanation.summary: The modified World Health Organization classification stratifies maternal cardiovascular risk. Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with syncope or limited exercise tolerance is class IV with maternal mortality of up to 10%. Pregnancy is contraindicated and women should be advised effective contraception, ideally progestogen-only, while valve intervention is planned. Reassessment of class after valve intervention guides safe future conception. Mechanical valves complicate pregnancy because warfarin is teratogenic and dose-dependent, while bioprostheses degrade faster but allow heparin-based regimens.
key_points: Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with syncope is modified World Health Organization class IV
Pregnancy is contraindicated until valve gradient and symptoms are reduced
Avoid oestrogen-containing contraception in significant valvular heart disease
explanation.pearls: Mean gradient over 50 mmHg, valve area under 1.0 cm2, or symptoms define severe aortic stenosis; symptomatic disease in young women always merits valve intervention discussion before pregnancy.

options.rationale: Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with prior syncope is modified World Health Organization class IV with extreme maternal morbidity and mortality risk. (Source: ESC: Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy)
Recommending conception in severe symptomatic aortic stenosis without first addressing the valve violates contemporary preconception care standards. (Source: ESC: Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy)
Oestrogen-containing contraception is contraindicated due to thrombotic risk in severe valvular heart disease; progestogen-only methods are preferred. (Source: RANZCOG: Contraception)

Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with syncope is a modified World Health Organization class IV lesion; pregnancy is contraindicated until valve intervention reduces gradient and symptoms. (Source: ESC: Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy)
Valve choice in young women must consider warfarin teratogenicity and pregnancy plans; bioprosthetic or transcatheter options are often discussed. (Source: ESC: Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia complicates 15 to 25 percent of Australian pregnancies. RANZCOG endorses parenteral iron when oral iron has failed (no Hb rise after 2 to 4 weeks of adherent therapy), when there is malabsorption or intolerance, or when there is insufficient time to delivery to correct anaemia orally. Ferric carboxymaltose can deliver 1000 mg in a single infusion and is the AU first-line parenteral preparation. Antenatal correction reduces postpartum transfusion risk and improves neonatal iron stores.
key_points: Treat antenatal Hb under 110 g/L (first trimester) or under 105 g/L (second/third) plus ferritin under 30 mcg/L.
Oral iron failure = no Hb rise over 2 to 4 weeks of adherent dosing.
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg single-dose IV is AU first-line parenteral.
Transfusion threshold in stable antenatal anaemia is Hb under 70 g/L.
Aim for Hb >= 110 g/L by term to reduce postpartum transfusion risk.
explanation.pearls: Ferric carboxymaltose causes transient hypophosphataemia in up to 50 percent of recipients; check serum phosphate at 2 weeks if symptoms of bone pain or fatigue persist.

options.rationale: She has had over 12 weeks of oral iron without an adequate Hb response and ferritin remains low; continuing the same agent risks an unprepared third trimester. (Source: RANZCOG iron in pregnancy 2023)

An oral switch is reasonable earlier in pregnancy but with Hb 92 g/L at 28 weeks and documented oral failure, the gain in Hb over 6 to 8 weeks is unlikely to reach target before delivery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pregnancy)

Hb under 100 g/L after second trimester with failed oral iron and 12 weeks to term meets RANZCOG criteria for parenteral iron; ferric carboxymaltose is the preferred AU agent. (Source: RANZCOG iron in pregnancy 2023; AMH ferric carboxymaltose)

Transfusion in stable antenatal anaemia is reserved for Hb under 70 g/L or symptomatic instability; this patient is haemodynamically stable with a treatable cause. (Source: NBA patient blood management module 5)
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are not first-line for uncomplicated iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy; iron replacement alone restores erythropoiesis. (Source: AMH erythropoietins)

explanation.summary: Risk-based prophylaxis in preterm labour covers the woman whose carriage status is unknown and who is actually labouring before 37 weeks, because that baby is both more likely to be exposed and less able to withstand invasive disease. Threatened preterm labour that settles, with a closed unchanged cervix and intact membranes, no longer meets the indication, and the infusion is stopped rather than run on until discharge. The reasoning has two steps: first recognise that the original prescription was appropriate at the time, and second recognise that the indication is a state rather than an event, so it is reviewed when the state changes. Taking a vagino-rectal swab before discharge is sensible so that the result is available if she returns. In context, most women admitted with threatened preterm labour do not deliver within a week, which is exactly why these prescriptions need reviewing rather than continuing by default.
key_points: Risk-based prophylaxis requires established preterm labour or ruptured membranes.
Settled contractions with a closed cervix and intact membranes means the indication has lapsed.
Swab before discharge so a result exists if she represents.
The ten day erythromycin course is specific to preterm prelabour rupture of membranes.
explanation.pearls: Fewer than half of women admitted with threatened preterm labour give birth before 37 weeks, so every antibiotic and tocolytic started on admission deserves an explicit review point.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis
Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: The risk-based indication is established preterm labour or ruptured membranes, neither of which is now present, so continuing adds exposure without benefit. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Four hourly dosing is continued to birth once she is genuinely labouring preterm with unknown status. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

options.rationale: Swabbing and waiting is reasonable when birth is not imminent, but it does not justify an infusion in the meantime. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: The ten day erythromycin course belongs to preterm prelabour rupture of the membranes, which she does not have. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Preterm labour and birth

options.rationale: A single extra dose has no role; either the indication stands and dosing continues to birth, or it does not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis

explanation.summary: Term prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM, after 37 weeks) occurs in about 8 percent of pregnancies. The TERMPROM trial and subsequent AU guidance show that immediate induction (within 24 hours) reduces chorioamnionitis and early neonatal sepsis without increasing caesarean rates compared with expectant management. Oxytocin is the AU first-line agent when the cervix is favourable; prostaglandins are reserved for unfavourable cervix and carry a higher infection risk after ROM. GBS prophylaxis is needed only for positive carriers, prior GBS-affected infant, or chorioamnionitis features.
key_points: Term PROM = ROM after 37 weeks before labour; speculum + amnisure or pooling for diagnosis.
Offer induction within 24 hours of ROM to reduce infection.
Oxytocin first-line if favourable cervix; PG agents increase infection risk post-ROM.
GBS-negative women do not need prophylactic antibiotics in absence of clinical chorioamnionitis.
Maternal fever, fetal tachycardia, foul liquor, or uterine tenderness = treat as chorioamnionitis.
explanation.pearls: After term PROM, neonatal early-onset sepsis risk rises sharply after 18 hours of ruptured membranes; document the rupture time precisely as it triggers neonatal observation pathways.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Induction of labour

options.rationale: Australian practice is inpatient observation or expedited induction after term PROM; 96 hours of expectant management increases chorioamnionitis risk without clear benefit. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2023)
GBS-negative women do not need empirical antibiotics in the absence of chorioamnionitis features; antibiotics do not reduce neonatal sepsis without infection. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy 2024)
PGE2 in the presence of ruptured membranes increases chorioamnionitis risk and oxytocin is preferred when the cervix is favourable. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Induction of labour)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Induction of labour

options.rationale: TERMPROM and AU guidance favour induction within 24 hours of term PROM to reduce maternal and neonatal infection; oxytocin is first-line with a favourable cervix and no contraindication. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2023)
Term PROM is not an indication for caesarean; vaginal birth is associated with better maternal and neonatal outcomes when there is no obstetric contraindication. (Source: RANZCOG term PROM 2023)

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis spans an inflammatory continuum from ductal narrowing through bacterial infection (most commonly Staphylococcus aureus) to abscess. The 2022 ABM and 2023 ABA updates emphasise that effective milk removal, anti-inflammatories and cool compresses are first-line; antibiotics are added when systemic features persist beyond 24 hours, nipple trauma is present, or the patient is septic. Flucloxacillin is AU first-line antibiotic. Cessation of feeding on the affected side worsens engorgement and increases abscess risk.
key_points: Continue feeding from the affected breast; effective drainage is therapeutic.
Add antibiotics if systemic features beyond 24 hours or nipple trauma.
Flucloxacillin 500 mg QID PO is AU first-line.
Cefalexin is an alternative for non-severe penicillin allergy.
Persistent symptoms after 48 hours of antibiotics warrant ultrasound to exclude abscess.
explanation.pearls: An unresolving 'mastitis' in a non-lactating or peri-weaning woman over 35 warrants ultrasound and biopsy to exclude inflammatory breast cancer, regardless of antibiotic response.

sources.label: Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine Protocol 36: Mastitis Spectrum 2022

options.rationale: Continued effective milk removal from the affected breast accelerates resolution; abrupt cessation worsens engorgement and abscess risk. (Source: ABA mastitis 2023)
There is no fluctuance on examination; imaging-drainage is reserved for suspected or confirmed abscess. (Source: eTG)
Cefalexin is a reasonable alternative only in non-severe penicillin allergy; with no allergy flucloxacillin gives narrower S. aureus cover. (Source: eTG)
Conservative measures are appropriate within the first 24 hours; persistent systemic features beyond 24 hours indicate bacterial mastitis requiring antibiotics. (Source: ABA mastitis 2023)

Inflammatory mastitis with systemic features after 24 hours warrants empirical anti-staphylococcal therapy; flucloxacillin is AU first-line and breastfeeding should continue. (Source: eTG; ABA mastitis 2023)

explanation.summary: ADIPS 2014 criteria diagnose GDM on a 75 g OGTT if any of fasting >= 5.1, 1 hour >= 10.0 or 2 hour >= 8.5 mmol/L. A single elevated value is diagnostic; repeat testing is not required. Initial management is diabetes-educator-led, with dietitian input and home BSL monitoring (fasting plus 1 or 2 hour postprandial). Pharmacotherapy is added after 1 to 2 weeks of lifestyle measures fail to keep fasting <= 5.0 and postprandial <= 6.7 (1 hour) or <= 6.0 (2 hour). Metformin is AU first-line for women without contraindications; insulin is added or substituted for failure.
key_points: ADIPS cut-offs: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L (any one is diagnostic).
Single elevated value is diagnostic - do not repeat.
Initial Tx: educator + dietitian + home BSL monitoring.
Targets: fasting <= 5.0, 1 hr postprandial <= 7.4, 2 hr postprandial <= 6.7.
Pharmacotherapy if targets unmet at 1 to 2 weeks: metformin first, insulin as needed.
explanation.pearls: Women diagnosed with GDM have a 50 percent risk of developing type 2 diabetes within 10 years; book a postpartum 75 g OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks and annual fasting glucose or HbA1c thereafter.

options.rationale: Fasting glucose of 5.4 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS 2014 cut-off of 5.1 mmol/L, so she meets criteria for GDM. (Source: ADIPS 2014)
A single OGTT meeting ADIPS criteria is diagnostic; repeating delays treatment and increases macrosomia risk. (Source: ADIPS 2014)
Pharmacotherapy is only added after a 1 to 2 week trial of lifestyle measures fails to achieve targets; immediate metformin is not first-line. (Source: NDSS GDM management 2023)

Insulin is reserved for failure of lifestyle and metformin; with no maternal hyperglycaemic symptoms and modestly elevated values, insulin first-up is inappropriate. (Source: NDSS GDM management 2023)

Fasting at or above 5.1 mmol/L meets ADIPS GDM criteria; first-line management is dietitian, education and four-times-daily BSL monitoring before considering pharmacotherapy. (Source: ADIPS 2014; NDSS GDM management)

explanation.summary: Quick-start COCP means commencing the pill the day the prescription is given, after excluding pregnancy. If started within the first 5 days of a normal menstrual cycle no back-up is theoretically required, but Australian guidance now standardises a 7-day condom back-up message to simplify counselling and reduce error. Migraine without aura is UKMEC 2 (benefits outweigh risk) for the COCP; migraine with aura, age over 35 with smoking, BP over 160/100, or prior VTE are absolute contraindications.
key_points: Quick-start COCP after excluding pregnancy; back-up condoms for 7 days.
Migraine WITHOUT aura: UKMEC 2 for COCP.
Migraine WITH aura: UKMEC 4 - do not use COCP.
BP >= 160/100, age >= 35 + smoking, or prior VTE = UKMEC 4.
LARC (IUD, implant) remains more effective than COCP and warrants discussion.
explanation.pearls: A new-onset focal aura in a woman on the COCP is a stop-now indication; switch to progesterone-only and arrange neurology review to exclude TIA.

options.rationale: Quick-start is safe and reduces unplanned pregnancy versus deferral; waiting is no longer routinely recommended. (Source: RACGP contraception 2024)
Migraine without aura is UKMEC 2 for the combined pill; only migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 (an absolute contraindication). (Source: FSRH UKMEC 2023)
Regular cycles are already documented; further tracking delays effective contraception without clinical benefit. (Source: RACGP contraception 2024)
Copper IUD is highly effective but is not what the patient is requesting and is a separate decision-making conversation. (Source: RACGP contraception 2024)

Quick-start within 5 days of period onset gives immediate cover; many AU guidelines recommend a 7-day back-up to harmonise advice and protect against ovulation if any pills are missed. (Source: RACGP contraception 2024; FSRH UKMEC quick start)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage (vaginal bleeding before 20 weeks with a viable intrauterine pregnancy and closed os) occurs in around 1 in 5 pregnancies; about 50 percent continue without complication. Once a fetal heart is detected by transvaginal ultrasound at 8 to 9 weeks the subsequent miscarriage risk falls to under 5 percent in low-risk women. Subchorionic haematoma confers a modest increase in miscarriage risk but a small haematoma in a viable pregnancy is reassuring. Bed rest, progesterone (except per PRISM in recurrent miscarriage), and surgical intervention have no general benefit.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage = bleeding + closed os + viable IUP before 20 weeks.
After fetal heart on TVUS, ongoing miscarriage risk under 5 percent.
Vaginal progesterone benefit is restricted (PRISM): prior miscarriage AND current bleeding.
Bed rest does not reduce miscarriage rate.
Rh-negative women with bleeding require Anti-D from 12 weeks onwards.
explanation.pearls: Subchorionic haematoma over 50 percent of the sac diameter raises the miscarriage risk substantially; document the haematoma size as a fraction of the sac, not just in millimetres.

options.rationale: Strict bed rest does not reduce miscarriage and progesterone benefit is restricted to women with prior miscarriages on a different protocol. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy bleeding 2023)
Tranexamic acid is not standard in threatened miscarriage with light bleeding and stable vitals; admission is not required. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy bleeding 2023)
Surgical intervention is not indicated for a small subchorionic haematoma with a viable fetus; it does not improve outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy bleeding 2023)

Vaginal progesterone has a small benefit in women with prior miscarriage AND current bleeding (PRISM trial); this patient's prior loss was 2 years ago and the benefit is modest with NNT around 13. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy bleeding 2023)

Viable intrauterine pregnancy at 8 weeks with light bleeding and a small subchorionic haematoma has a good prognosis; expectant management with safety-netting is AU first-line. (Source: RANZCOG early pregnancy bleeding 2023)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG VBAC counselling after one previous low-transverse LSCS quotes a 60 to 75 percent vaginal birth success (around 70 percent average), uterine rupture risk around 0.5 percent (rising with induction or augmentation), and increased need for blood transfusion or hysterectomy compared with planned repeat caesarean. Continuous intrapartum CTG and rapid access to caesarean are non-negotiable safety requirements. Two or more prior caesareans, a classical incision, or a previous uterine rupture are usual contraindications to VBAC.
key_points: VBAC after one LSCS: 60 to 75 percent vaginal birth success.
Uterine rupture risk around 0.5 percent (higher with induction/augmentation).
Continuous CTG and immediate-access caesarean theatre required.
Classical incision, previous rupture, two or more prior LSCS = generally contraindicated.
Counsel re emergency hysterectomy and transfusion risks.
explanation.pearls: Induction with prostaglandins after a previous caesarean roughly doubles the rupture risk to about 1 percent; balloon catheter mechanical induction does not carry this excess risk and is the preferred AU method when induction is needed.

options.rationale: AU data show VBAC success around 70 percent after one prior LSCS with low transverse incision and uterine rupture risk around 0.5 percent; both are core consent points. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC 2019)
VBAC success rates with one prior LSCS sit around 60 to 75 percent in AU centres; 90 percent overstates the chance. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC 2019)
Both figures are too pessimistic; the actual success and rupture rates after one prior LSCS are more favourable. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC 2019)
Success rate is correct but rupture risk after a single low-transverse LSCS is around 0.5 percent, not 4 percent. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC 2019)
Both rates underestimate AU outcomes; 50 percent under-counsels success and 0.05 percent under-counsels rupture risk. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC 2019)

explanation.summary: Induction at 41+0 to 41+3 weeks is recommended in AU to reduce stillbirth without increasing caesarean rates; balloon catheter ripening for an unfavourable cervix (Bishop under 6) is at least as effective as PGE2 with a lower hyperstimulation rate, making it the preferred outpatient or low-risk option. PGE2 (dinoprostone gel or pessary) remains acceptable, particularly in inpatient settings. Oxytocin alone is reserved for favourable cervix or after successful ripening; ARM is added once the cervix admits a finger.
key_points: Bishop under 6 = ripen first; balloon or PGE2.
Balloon has lower hyperstimulation rate than PGE2 with equivalent vaginal-birth success.
Avoid PGE2 in women with previous caesarean (rupture risk).
AU induce by 41+3 to 42+0 weeks to reduce stillbirth.
Oxytocin once cervix favourable or membranes ruptured.
explanation.pearls: Balloon ripening can be performed safely in selected day-stay outpatients; reattend in 12 hours or earlier for contractions, ROM or balloon expulsion, which alone usually achieves Bishop over 6.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Induction of labour

options.rationale: Oxytocin alone is rarely effective with Bishop under 6; cervical ripening is required first. (Source: RANZCOG induction of labour 2024)
ARM is technically very difficult with a closed posterior cervix and Bishop 2; ripening is needed before ARM is feasible. (Source: RANZCOG IOL 2024)

Dinoprostone is an acceptable ripening option but carries higher hyperstimulation and CTG-abnormality rates than balloon and is therefore not the gentlest first-line option. (Source: RANZCOG IOL 2024)
Post-term induction by 41+3 to 42+0 weeks reduces perinatal mortality compared with ongoing expectant management (SWEPIS, ARRIVE-postdates); further waiting is not advised. (Source: RANZCOG IOL 2024)

With Bishop under 6 and an intact unscarred uterus, mechanical balloon ripening is at least equivalent to PGE2 with lower hyperstimulation risk; AU first-line for unfavourable cervix in many centres. (Source: RANZCOG induction of labour 2024; Queensland IOL guideline)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Induction of labour

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage (three or more consecutive losses before 20 weeks) affects around 1 percent of couples. AU guidance prioritises antiphospholipid syndrome screening (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I IgG/IgM) on two occasions 12 weeks apart, pelvic anatomy assessment, and thyroid and diabetes screening. Inherited thrombophilia screening is not routinely advised. Treatment with aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH improves live-birth rates in confirmed APS by around 40 percent.
key_points: Recurrent miscarriage = three or more consecutive losses before 20 weeks.
First-line screen: APS, pelvic anatomy, TSH, diabetes.
Confirm APS antibodies on two occasions 12 weeks apart at qualifying titres.
Inherited thrombophilia screen NOT recommended for recurrent miscarriage.
APS treatment: aspirin 100 mg from conception + LMWH from positive UPT.
explanation.pearls: Beta2-glycoprotein-I IgG titre above 99th centile predicts the highest pregnancy-loss risk in APS; couples with triple-positive serology have around 30 percent live-birth rate even with aspirin plus LMWH and warrant tertiary referral.

options.rationale: Chronic endometritis is a contested cause; biopsy is not first-line and yields modest evidence in AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage 2023)

Parental karyotype yields 2 to 5 percent positivity; product-of-conception karyotype on a future loss is higher-yield and lower-cost as first investigation. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage 2023)
Pelvic ultrasound has already excluded a Mullerian anomaly; HSG adds little when sonohysterography or 3D ultrasound is normal. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage 2023)

Antiphospholipid syndrome causes 15 percent of recurrent miscarriage; her two unprovoked DVTs further raise pre-test probability and treatment with aspirin plus LMWH improves live-birth rates. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage 2023; ASTH 2023)

Inherited thrombophilias have a weak association with first-trimester recurrent miscarriage and treatment does not improve live birth; routine screening is not recommended. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage 2023)

explanation.summary: SOMANZ 2024 recognises atypical pre-eclampsia where end-organ damage (thrombocytopenia, doubling of creatinine, hepatic transaminitis, neurological symptoms, pulmonary oedema, or fetal growth restriction) develops without sustained BP 140/90. HELLP-spectrum (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe variant. Definitive management at 34+ weeks is delivery (vaginal if feasible) with magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, BP control to under 160/110 and high-dependency monitoring. Steroids for fetal lung maturity remain indicated under 34+6 weeks; corticosteroids do not delay delivery.
key_points: Atypical pre-eclampsia = end-organ damage without classical BP >= 140/90.
HELLP spectrum: any of platelets under 100, transaminases doubled, microangiopathy.
Delivery at 34+ weeks for severe PE / HELLP.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/h for 24 hours post-delivery.
Antihypertensive target under 160/110 acutely with labetalol/hydralazine.
explanation.pearls: Recurrence risk of severe pre-eclampsia in a future pregnancy is around 15 percent; prophylactic aspirin 150 mg from 12 weeks reduces recurrence by 60 percent if started before 16 weeks.

options.rationale: Multi-system involvement (thrombocytopenia, doubled creatinine, transaminitis, proteinuria) plus BP rising establishes pre-eclampsia even without sustained 140/90 readings. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy 2024)

Atypical pre-eclampsia is recognised on multi-system features without classical BP 140/90; doubled creatinine, platelets dropping under 100, transaminitis and epigastric pain meet HELLP-spectrum criteria mandating delivery preparation at 35 weeks. (Source: SOMANZ 2024)
AFLP typically shows much higher transaminases, hypoglycaemia, raised ammonia and coagulopathy; this picture is HELLP-spectrum not AFLP. (Source: SOMANZ 2024)
TTP would show much lower platelets, schistocytes, neurological signs and very high LDH; this constellation is far more consistent with HELLP. (Source: SOMANZ 2024)

No prior hypertension and a previously normal platelet count and creatinine make superimposed PE on chronic hypertension less likely; an isolated UTI does not explain transaminitis. (Source: SOMANZ 2024)

explanation.summary: Anti-D prophylaxis prevents Rh-D sensitisation in Rh-negative women carrying an Rh-positive fetus. AU NBA dose schedule: 250 IU IM within 72 hours of a potentially sensitising event before 12 weeks, 625 IU after 12 weeks, plus routine antenatal 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks (since 2023 a single 1500 IU dose at 28 weeks is an accepted alternative in some centres). Kleihauer-Betke quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage and is required for sensitising events at 20 weeks or later, after delivery, or after significant trauma to guide whether additional Anti-D is needed beyond the standard dose.
key_points: Anti-D before 12 weeks: 250 IU IM within 72 hours.
Anti-D after 12 weeks: 625 IU IM within 72 hours.
Routine antenatal doses at 28 and 34 weeks (or 1500 IU once at 28 weeks).
Kleihauer-Betke required from 20 weeks and at delivery.
Maternal antibody screen at booking and 28 weeks.
explanation.pearls: If anti-D administration is delayed beyond 72 hours after a sensitising event, give it as soon as possible up to 10 days later - efficacy decreases progressively but partial protection is better than none.

options.rationale: Bleeding at or after 12 weeks of gestation in an Rh-negative woman is a potentially sensitising event regardless of volume; Anti-D is required. (Source: NBA Anti-D guidelines 2021)
250 IU is the standard dose only before 12 weeks; after 12 weeks the dose is 625 IU and Kleihauer is required if at 20+ weeks. (Source: NBA Anti-D 2021)
1500 IU is the routine antenatal prophylaxis dose at 28 and 34 weeks; for a first-trimester sensitising event 625 IU suffices. (Source: NBA Anti-D 2021)

Sensitising event after 12 weeks requires Anti-D 625 IU within 72 hours plus continuation of routine 28 and 34 week prophylaxis; Kleihauer becomes mandatory only after 20 weeks. (Source: NBA Anti-D 2021)
AU practice does not delay Anti-D for paternal genotyping; cffDNA fetal Rh typing is available in some centres but does not delay administration. (Source: NBA Anti-D 2021)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is the presence of unprotected fetal vessels traversing the membranes within 2 cm of the internal cervical os. It is classified as type I (velamentous cord insertion) or type II (vessels between placental lobes). Antenatal diagnosis at morphology with transvaginal confirmation is essential because intrapartum rupture causes rapid fetal exsanguination. AU guidance recommends elective caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after a course of corticosteroids. Antenatal admission is reserved for women with short cervix, preterm contractions or any bleeding.
key_points: Vasa praevia = unprotected fetal vessels within 2 cm of internal os.
Mortality with vaginal birth approaches 60 percent.
Risk factors: IVF, velamentous cord, succenturiate lobe, multiple pregnancy.
Plan LSCS at 34 to 36 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids.
Admit if short cervix, preterm labour or any antepartum haemorrhage.
explanation.pearls: If amniotomy is inadvertently performed in undiagnosed vasa praevia, expect bright-red bleeding immediately followed by sinusoidal CTG - this is fetal not maternal blood and demands immediate caesarean delivery.

options.rationale: Confirmed vasa praevia is delivered by elective LSCS at 34 to 36 weeks with prior antenatal corticosteroids; balance is fetal exsanguination risk against prematurity. (Source: RANZCOG vasa praevia 2023; Queensland Clinical Guideline)
Vasa praevia carries up to 60 percent fetal mortality with vaginal birth due to fetal exsanguination on ROM; vaginal trial is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG vasa praevia 2023)

Late preterm delivery (34 to 36 weeks) balances ROM-related fetal death risk against prematurity; waiting to 39 weeks increases the risk of spontaneous ROM and fetal exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG vasa praevia 2023)
Routine inpatient admission is not required when there is no bleeding or cervical change; admission is reserved for short cervix or threatened preterm labour. (Source: RANZCOG 2023)
Vasa praevia type I (velamentous cord) does not migrate like a low-lying placenta; deferring decisions risks spontaneous ROM. (Source: RANZCOG 2023)

explanation.summary: First-trimester chorionicity determination (11 to 14 weeks) is critical because it dictates scan frequency, complications profile, and timing of delivery. The lambda (twin peak) sign denotes dichorionic (separate placentas meeting); the T-sign denotes monochorionic (single placenta with a thin membrane). Monochorionic twins carry risks of twin-twin transfusion syndrome, twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence, and selective growth restriction, mandating 2-weekly ultrasound from 16 weeks. DCDA twins need 4-weekly growth scans from 24 weeks and are delivered from 37 weeks.
key_points: Determine chorionicity at 11 to 14 weeks for accuracy.
Lambda sign = DCDA; T-sign = monochorionic.
MCDA: 2-weekly scans from 16 weeks; delivery 36 to 37 weeks.
DCDA: 4-weekly scans from 24 weeks; delivery 37 to 38 weeks.
MCMA: rare, weekly scans from 16 to 18 weeks, delivery by caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks.
explanation.pearls: Unequal CRL discordance of more than 10 percent at 11 to 14 weeks is a strong predictor of TTTS in monochorionic twins and warrants tertiary maternal-fetal medicine referral, regardless of subsequent absolute growth measurements.

options.rationale: MCMA twins share a single placenta with no dividing membrane; the visible lambda sign and thick membrane exclude MCMA. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy 2024)
MCDA twins show a T-sign and thin membrane; the lambda sign and thick membrane here exclude monochorionic. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy 2024)
Conjoined twins show shared body parts on ultrasound; separate sacs with a thick dividing membrane exclude this. (Source: RANZCOG 2024)
Lambda sign, thick membrane and two placental masses confirm DCDA; AU growth scans are 4-weekly from 24 weeks with delivery offered from 37 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy 2024)
Chorionicity is most accurately assigned at 11 to 14 weeks; deferring decreases accuracy. (Source: RANZCOG 2024)

explanation.summary: OHSS results from gonadotrophin- or hCG-driven vascular leak after assisted reproduction. Severity ranges from mild (bloating) to severe/critical (third-spacing, intravascular depletion, renal failure, pleural effusions, VTE, ARDS). The pathognomonic biochemistry is haemoconcentration with paradoxical hyponatraemia. AU first-line is admission, isotonic crystalloid (around 1000 mL initially then titrate), strict fluid balance, LMWH thromboprophylaxis and paracentesis only if tense ascites fails to respond. Cabergoline is preventive; diuretics are contraindicated.
key_points: Severe OHSS = haemoconcentration, oligoanuria, ascites, dyspnoea.
Treat with IV crystalloid resuscitation and LMWH thromboprophylaxis.
Paracentesis only if tense ascites unresponsive to fluids or respiratory compromise.
Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion and are avoided.
Pregnancy worsens course - elevated beta-hCG sustains the syndrome.
explanation.pearls: The single biggest risk factor for severe OHSS is PCOS combined with high antral follicle count - prevent it with GnRH agonist trigger and freeze-all strategy in any cycle with more than 18 follicles or oestradiol over 18,000 pmol/L on trigger day.

sources.label: Fertility Society of Australia OHSS guideline

options.rationale: Severe OHSS with intravascular depletion (Hct 0.52, oligoanuria, creatinine 142) demands inpatient IV fluid resuscitation and pharmacological thromboprophylaxis with LMWH due to high VTE risk. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS 2022; FSA OHSS guideline)
source_refs: Fertility Society of Australia OHSS guideline

options.rationale: Cabergoline is preventive (started at trigger) and adjunctive; in severe OHSS with intravascular depletion it does not replace IV resuscitation and admission. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS 2022)
Paracentesis is reserved for tense ascites failing IV fluids or causing respiratory compromise after volume resuscitation, not the first step. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS 2022)
Diuretics in OHSS worsen intravascular depletion and renal injury and are contraindicated in initial management. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS 2022)
Severe OHSS is a medical emergency; outpatient review is inappropriate and risks deterioration or VTE. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS 2022)

explanation.summary: Post-molar surveillance uses weekly beta-hCG to detect gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) - which occurs in around 15 percent after complete moles and 1 percent after partial moles. FIGO 2021 criteria diagnose GTN if hCG plateaus (within 10 percent) for 4 values over 3 weeks, rises 10 percent or more for 3 values over 2 weeks, persists for 6 months post-evacuation, or metastatic disease is identified. Low-risk disease (FIGO score under 7) is treated with single-agent methotrexate (or actinomycin-D for methotrexate resistance); high-risk disease (>= 7) requires multi-agent EMA-CO. Treatment is centralised through national GTD registries.
key_points: Post-mole monitoring: weekly hCG until 3 consecutive normal, then monthly for 6 months.
Diagnose GTN on plateau, rise, persistence over 6 months, or metastases.
FIGO score under 7 = low risk, single-agent methotrexate.
FIGO score >= 7 = high risk, multi-agent EMA-CO.
Avoid pregnancy for at least 6 months after hCG normalisation.
explanation.pearls: Choriocarcinoma can present years after a normal pregnancy as haemoptysis, neurological signs, or amenorrhoea with a positive pregnancy test - check beta-hCG in any reproductive-age woman with unexplained metastatic disease.

options.rationale: FIGO criteria for GTN are met (plateau over 3 weeks); FIGO score 4 (low risk) is treated with single-agent methotrexate or actinomycin-D via a national GTD centre. (Source: RANZCOG GTD 2023; eviQ GTN)

Four consecutive plateaued values (within 10 percent) over 3 weeks meets FIGO 2021 criteria for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia and mandates treatment now, not further surveillance. (Source: RANZCOG GTD 2023)
Repeat evacuation does not improve outcomes and risks uterine perforation; chemotherapy is the AU first-line for GTN. (Source: RANZCOG GTD 2023)
Multi-agent EMA-CO is reserved for high-risk GTN (FIGO score >= 7); this patient scores 4 and warrants single-agent therapy. (Source: eviQ GTN)

Hysterectomy is reserved for placental site trophoblastic tumour, drug-resistant disease, or patient choice with completed family; first-line for low-risk GTN remains chemotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG GTD 2023)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency with maternal mortality of 20 to 60%. The classical triad is sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, and disseminated intravascular coagulation occurring peripartum, often with seizures. Management is supportive: high-quality CPR if arrest, advanced airway, vasopressors, and aggressive correction of coagulopathy via massive transfusion protocol. Uterotonics treat coexistent atony. ECMO has been used in refractory cases at tertiary centres. Early multidisciplinary involvement (obstetrics, anaesthesia, ICU, haematology) is essential.
key_points: Classical triad: cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, DIC in the peripartum window
Activate massive transfusion protocol urgently; do not wait for lab confirmation
Uterotonics for coexistent atony; coagulation correction with FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets
ECMO at tertiary centres in refractory cardiopulmonary failure
explanation.pearls: In suspected amniotic fluid embolism, fibrinogen should be replaced aggressively if less than 2 g/L using cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate - hypofibrinogenaemia is the strongest early predictor of ongoing haemorrhage and maternal death.

sources.label: National Blood Authority - Patient Blood Management Module 5: Obstetrics

options.rationale: Eclampsia is unlikely given the absence of antecedent hypertension or proteinuria and the dominant cardiovascular collapse and DIC. Magnesium will not treat the embolism, hypotension, or coagulopathy. (Source: ANZICS Statement - Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

Although AFE has been described as anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy, intramuscular adrenaline alone is insufficient for the cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, and DIC pattern seen. The priority is full ABCD resuscitation and MTP activation. (Source: ANZICS Statement - Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

Amniotic fluid embolism presents with cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, coagulopathy, and seizures in the peripartum period. Activation of the massive transfusion protocol with packed cells, FFP, cryoprecipitate, and platelets is the critical early intervention along with ABC support and uterotonics for uterine atony. Definitive treatment is supportive while DIC and hypovolaemia are corrected. (Source: ANZICS Statement - Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

Thrombolysis in a woman with massive ongoing haemorrhage and severe DIC is contraindicated. Even if pulmonary embolism were considered, the bleeding contraindicates lysis. (Source: ANZICS Statement - Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

Waiting for laboratory confirmation in a woman who is exsanguinating with point-of-care INR over 4 will be fatal. MTP activates blood-bank delivery of empirical balanced products immediately. (Source: ANZICS Statement - Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

explanation.summary: ADIPS criteria for GDM diagnosis on 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks: fasting at least 5.1, 1 hour at least 10.0, 2 hour at least 8.5 mmol/L. Any single elevated value diagnoses GDM. First-line management is medical nutrition therapy plus daily monitoring (fasting target under 5.0 and 2 hour postprandial under 6.7). Metformin or insulin is added if targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks of lifestyle change.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5 mmol/L are the AU diagnostic criteria
Diet and monitoring first; pharmacotherapy if targets not reached in 1 to 2 weeks
Insulin is first-line pharmacotherapy in AU; metformin is acceptable alternative
explanation.pearls: ADIPS recommends repeat OGTT 6 to 12 weeks postpartum and lifetime annual diabetes screening because lifetime T2DM risk is around 50% after GDM.

options.rationale: HbA1c is useful at booking to detect overt diabetes but is not the diagnostic test at 26 weeks; OGTT thresholds apply. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)
The fasting value of 5.4 exceeds the 5.1 mmol/L threshold and the 2 hour exceeds 8.5; the test is positive. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)
First-line is diet and exercise with capillary monitoring; pharmacotherapy follows if targets are not met. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)
GDM is diagnosed on a single OGTT meeting ADIPS thresholds; repeating delays care. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)
ADIPS thresholds (fasting 5.1, 1h 10.0, 2h 8.5) are met by fasting and 2 hour values; diagnosis of GDM follows with diet first and monitoring. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines)

explanation.summary: PPH management follows the 4Ts framework: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin. Tone (atony) is by far the most common cause. Initial actions include bladder emptying, uterine massage and bimanual compression, additional uterotonics (oxytocin infusion, ergometrine if BP allows, syntometrine, carboprost, misoprostol), TXA 1 g IV, fluid resuscitation, and senior call. Persistent bleeding triggers theatre for EUA, balloon tamponade, and surgical control.
key_points: Bladder emptying is a high-yield often-missed first step
Uterotonic sequence: oxytocin then ergometrine (avoid in HTN) then carboprost or misoprostol
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces mortality (WOMAN trial)
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG PPH bundle: massage, empty bladder, second uterotonic, TXA, IV access x2, group and crossmatch, senior call, theatre activation if not responding.

options.rationale: Theatre is appropriate if first-line medical and mechanical measures fail; immediate transfer skips simpler effective steps. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)
Carboprost is third-line after oxytocin and ergometrine; mechanical measures and second uterotonic come first. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

Uterine atony with full bladder is the leading cause of PPH; bladder emptying, bimanual compression, and additional uterotonic combined with senior call form the immediate response. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)
TXA is given alongside uterotonics, not in place of them; sole TXA without addressing atony is insufficient. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)
PPH is defined as 500 mL or more after vaginal birth; 900 mL with ongoing bleeding requires escalation. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Painless bright red bleeding with a soft uterus and known praevia is classic for placenta praevia. Digital examination is contraindicated. Management is admission, IV access, group and crossmatch, antenatal corticosteroids if under 35 weeks, anti-D if Rh negative, CTG monitoring, and ultrasound to confirm position and exclude accreta. Definitive delivery is by elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks for stable cases.
key_points: Painless bleeding + known praevia = no digital exam
Anti-D 625 IU within 72 hours if Rh negative for sensitising event
Antenatal steroids if 24+0 to 34+6 weeks
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG places the elective caesarean window for major praevia at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks unless prior bleeds or accreta concerns prompt earlier delivery.

options.rationale: In suspected praevia, digital examination risks catastrophic haemorrhage; admission, monitoring, and ultrasound assessment are first-line. (Source: RANZCOG APH Statement)
Digital examination is contraindicated when praevia is suspected as it may precipitate massive haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG APH Statement)
Antepartum haemorrhage from praevia requires inpatient observation and steroid administration; outpatient deferral is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG APH Statement)
Category one caesarean is reserved for ongoing massive haemorrhage or fetal compromise; assessment first is appropriate when stable. (Source: RANZCOG APH Statement)
Tocolysis is not first-line for praevia bleeding and may mask deterioration; admission and monitoring are required. (Source: RANZCOG APH Statement)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms, hepatic involvement, and platelet drop requires magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, BP control with labetalol or hydralazine targeting 140 to 150 systolic, antenatal corticosteroids if under 35 weeks, and planning for delivery. Magpie trial showed magnesium halves eclampsia risk and reduces maternal death. Magnesium toxicity is monitored by reflexes and respiratory rate; calcium gluconate is the antidote.
key_points: Magnesium sulfate loading 4 g IV over 20 min, then 1 g/hr; halves eclampsia risk
BP target around 140 to 150 systolic; not lower
Calcium gluconate is the magnesium toxicity antidote
explanation.pearls: HELLP variant (haemolysis, raised LFTs, low platelets) overlaps with severe pre-eclampsia; LDH over 600 plus haptoglobin reduction confirms haemolysis.

options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is superior to phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis in eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Statement)
BP target is around 140 to 150 systolic to avoid hypoperfusion; aiming under 130 risks placental compromise. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Statement)

Magnesium sulfate halves the risk of eclampsia in severe pre-eclampsia (Magpie trial) and is the strongest evidence-based maternal intervention pending delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Statement)
Furosemide is not standard in pre-eclampsia without pulmonary oedema; volume restriction is the focus. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Statement)
Aspirin is for prevention before disease, not treatment once severe features are present. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Statement)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is an impaction of the anterior shoulder behind the pubic symphysis, a bony obstruction, so cutting the perineum does not of itself relieve it and episiotomy is not a routine step in the sequence. Its place is functional: when the operator needs to get a hand into the sacral hollow for internal rotation or to deliver the posterior arm, a tight perineum can prevent that, and an episiotomy is then performed to create access. Where one is cut, a mediolateral incision is used in Australia because midline incisions extend into the anal sphincter. The manoeuvre sequence itself proceeds without delay, and increasing traction on the head is never an answer. In context, shoulder dystocia complicates roughly one in 200 vaginal births, is largely unpredictable, and outcomes depend on a rehearsed drill rather than on any single manoeuvre.
key_points: The obstruction is bony, so episiotomy does not relieve it.
Episiotomy is used to gain access for internal manoeuvres when the perineum is tight.
Mediolateral rather than midline is used in Australian practice.
Increased traction on the head causes brachial plexus injury and is never indicated.
explanation.pearls: Routine episiotomy does not prevent or relieve shoulder dystocia; the decision to cut is about whether your hand can reach the sacral hollow, not about the shoulder itself.

options.rationale: The obstruction is bony, so an episiotomy adds nothing on its own and is used to create room for internal manoeuvres. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder dystocia)
Cutting to release the shoulder would make sense if soft tissue were the obstruction, which it is not here. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder dystocia)
