Midline incisions are avoided in Australian practice because of the risk of extension into the anal sphincter. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Shoulder dystocia)
Increasing traction is the main cause of brachial plexus injury and is never the answer to a failed manoeuvre. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder dystocia)
That is right for the impaction itself, but ignores the access an episiotomy can give for internal manoeuvres. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: PPROM at 24 to 34 weeks is managed expectantly with antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, prophylactic antibiotics (erythromycin 250 mg QID for 10 days), magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if delivery is imminent under 30 weeks, and surveillance for chorioamnionitis. Delivery is planned around 34 to 36 weeks balancing infection versus prematurity. Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided due to NEC risk in the ORACLE trial.
key_points: Erythromycin (not amoxicillin with clavulanic acid) is the antibiotic of choice in PPROM
Antenatal corticosteroids under 35 weeks; magnesium for neuroprotection under 30 weeks if delivery imminent
Deliver around 34 to 36 weeks balancing prematurity vs chorioamnionitis
explanation.pearls: ORACLE trial demonstrated amoxicillin with clavulanic acid increases necrotising enterocolitis in preterm neonates; erythromycin alone is the standard antibiotic in PPROM.

options.rationale: Cerclage after membrane rupture is contraindicated due to infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)
Immediate induction is not first-line at 33 weeks; expectant management with steroids and antibiotics gives better neonatal outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)
PPROM requires inpatient monitoring for chorioamnionitis; outpatient management is not standard at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)
Tocolysis is not recommended in PPROM without active preterm labour; it may delay delivery without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

PPROM at 33 weeks requires admission, steroids, prophylactic antibiotics (erythromycin), and expectant management with delivery planned around 34 to 36 weeks balancing infection versus prematurity risks. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a rare third-trimester emergency with maternal mortality 7 to 18%. Swansea criteria help diagnosis (vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia, encephalopathy, raised bilirubin, hypoglycaemia, raised urate, leucocytosis, ascites, raised transaminases, raised ammonia, renal impairment, coagulopathy, microvesicular steatosis on biopsy). Treatment is delivery (regardless of gestation) with supportive care including dextrose for hypoglycaemia, FFP for coagulopathy, and ICU monitoring.
key_points: Hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy out of proportion to platelets, and encephalopathy point to AFLP
LCHAD fetal deficiency is associated; screen newborn after delivery
Definitive treatment is expedited delivery regardless of gestation
explanation.pearls: AFLP fetal LCHAD deficiency (long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) is identifiable on newborn screening; maternal heterozygosity for LCHAD predisposes to AFLP in affected pregnancies.

sources.label: RCOG Obstetric Cholestasis and Liver Disease in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Both AFLP and HELLP present in the third trimester with RUQ pain and transaminitis. (Source: SOMANZ Liver Disease in Pregnancy)
Mild hypertension and RUQ pain occur in both conditions and do not discriminate. (Source: SOMANZ Liver Disease in Pregnancy)
Mild proteinuria and modest thrombocytopenia overlap with HELLP and do not specifically favour AFLP. (Source: SOMANZ Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

AFLP characteristically has hypoglycaemia, marked coagulopathy out of proportion to thrombocytopenia, encephalopathy, and raised ammonia, distinguishing it from HELLP where the platelet drop dominates. (Source: SOMANZ Liver Disease in Pregnancy)
Family history may suggest LCHAD deficiency in the fetus but is supportive rather than the strongest discriminator. (Source: SOMANZ Liver Disease in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is suspected with prior mid-trimester painless loss. Singleton pregnancies with one or more prior preterm births and a short cervix on transvaginal ultrasound (under 25 mm before 24 weeks) benefit from ultrasound-indicated cerclage. History-indicated cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks is an alternative for three or more prior losses. Vaginal progesterone is often added. Bed rest is not recommended.
key_points: Ultrasound-indicated cerclage for short cervix + prior preterm birth halves recurrent preterm birth
Transabdominal cerclage reserved for failed transvaginal or anatomic abnormality
Vaginal progesterone is often combined; bed rest is not effective
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG distinguishes history-indicated (3 prior mid-trimester losses), ultrasound-indicated (1 to 2 prior preterm + cervix under 25 mm), and rescue cerclage (asymptomatic dilatation without infection); each has different evidence and timing.

options.rationale: Transabdominal cerclage is reserved for failed transvaginal cerclage or anatomical abnormalities; not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)
Progesterone alone is insufficient with this clear history plus short cervix; cerclage has stronger evidence. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

Singleton pregnancy with prior mid-trimester loss and short cervix (under 25 mm) before 24 weeks has clear evidence for ultrasound-indicated cerclage which halves preterm birth; vaginal progesterone is a reasonable adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)
Prophylactic tocolytics and bed rest do not prevent preterm birth in cervical insufficiency and may cause harm. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)
Cervical pessary evidence is mixed and inferior to cerclage in singletons with prior mid-trimester loss. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

explanation.summary: SOMANZ defines severe hypertension in pregnancy as systolic >=160 or diastolic >=110 mmHg, requiring urgent pharmacological control. Acute first-line oral options are labetalol or nifedipine PA; methyldopa has slow onset and is reserved for ongoing control. IV options include hydralazine and labetalol. Target acute reduction is to <160/110 within 30 minutes, then ongoing target <140/90. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy. Magnesium sulfate (loading 4 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour) is indicated for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia and for eclampsia treatment. Delivery is the only definitive treatment and is timed by gestation, maternal stability, and fetal wellbeing.
key_points: Severe pregnancy HTN >=160/110: urgent treatment within 30 min
Oral labetalol, oral nifedipine PA = first-line
IV labetalol or hydralazine if oral not feasible
Avoid ACEi/ARBs in pregnancy (fetal renal injury)
Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in severe PE; not for BP control
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate loading is 4 g IV over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour maintenance; serum levels are not routinely required if reflexes are monitored 2 hourly.

options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is unpredictable and unsafe in pregnancy; oral nifedipine PA tablets or labetalol are preferred. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)

SOMANZ recommends oral labetalol as a first-line antihypertensive in severe pregnancy hypertension when oral therapy is feasible; target BP <160/110 acutely, then <140/90 ongoing. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)
ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal renal injury and oligohydramnios; never used in pre-eclampsia management. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)

Magnesium is indicated for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia or for eclampsia treatment, but is not an antihypertensive; antihypertensive control is the priority. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)
Methyldopa has slow onset (3-6 hours) and is used for ongoing rather than acute severe hypertension control. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023)

explanation.summary: Australian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society (ADIPS) recommends universal screening for GDM with a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks. The diagnostic thresholds are fasting >=5.1, 1 hour >=10.0, or 2 hour >=8.5 mmol/L. Any single value meeting the threshold confirms GDM. Early-pregnancy screening at booking with fasting glucose or HbA1c targets women at high risk (prior GDM, BMI >=35, polycystic ovary syndrome, family history, ethnic risk groups). HbA1c >=6.5% at booking suggests overt diabetes rather than GDM. Initial management is diet and exercise with self-monitoring of blood glucose; metformin and/or insulin are added if targets not met. Fetal growth scans at 28 to 32 weeks and aspirin for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis as appropriate.
key_points: ADIPS: universal 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24-28 weeks
Diagnostic thresholds: fasting >=5.1, 1h >=10.0, 2h >=8.5 mmol/L
Any single value meeting threshold = GDM
Booking HbA1c >=6.5% suggests overt diabetes
Initial management: diet + exercise + SMBG; escalate to metformin/insulin
explanation.pearls: Australian GDM treatment targets are fasting <5.0 mmol/L and 2 hour post-meal <6.7 mmol/L, tighter than non-pregnant diabetes targets and based on the HAPI study.

options.rationale: HbA1c is unreliable in pregnancy due to increased red cell turnover and is not the OGTT-equivalent diagnostic test for GDM in Australia. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guideline)
Fasting glucose alone misses post-prandial GDM phenotype; the OGTT detects all three diagnostic time points. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guideline)

ADIPS recommends 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks for all pregnant women, with fasting, 1 hour and 2 hour samples; diagnostic thresholds are 5.1, 10.0 and 8.5 mmol/L respectively. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guideline)
The two-step 50 g GCT then 100 g OGTT is a US protocol; Australia uses the one-step 75 g 2-hour OGTT. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guideline)
Random capillary glucose is not the screening test for GDM in Australian guidelines. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guideline)

explanation.summary: Routine antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis reduces D-antigen sensitisation in Rh-negative women from approximately 1.5% to less than 0.2%. The Australian National Blood Authority regimen is 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks for women with negative antibody screen. Additional doses (250 IU first trimester, 625 IU second/third trimester) are required for potentially sensitising events including miscarriage, antepartum haemorrhage, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, external cephalic version, and abdominal trauma. Postpartum anti-D 625 IU is given within 72 hours of delivery if the baby is confirmed Rh positive. Kleihauer testing quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage and guides additional anti-D dosing when feto-maternal haemorrhage exceeds 4 mL.
key_points: Australian routine antenatal anti-D: 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks
Sensitising events <12 weeks: 250 IU; >=12 weeks: 625 IU within 72 hours
Postpartum 625 IU within 72 hours if baby Rh positive
Kleihauer test quantifies FMH; additional anti-D if FMH >4 mL
cffDNA Rh typing is emerging but not universal in Australia yet
explanation.pearls: 625 IU of Rh(D) immunoglobulin neutralises approximately 6 mL of D-positive fetal red cells; Kleihauer test estimates FMH and dictates whether additional doses are required.

options.rationale: Routine antenatal anti-D prevents silent sensitisation by fetomaternal haemorrhage which can occur without overt bleeding; deferral risks anti-D sensitisation. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guideline)
The Australian dose is 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks (total 1250 IU); a single 1500 IU dose is the UK regimen and not Australian standard. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guideline)
250 IU is the dose for first-trimester sensitising events, not routine antenatal prophylaxis. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guideline)

NBA guidelines recommend routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks for Rh negative women with negative antibody screen, with 625 IU IM each dose; this regimen reduces sensitisation from 1.5% to <0.2%. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guideline)
Cell-free fetal DNA Rh typing is available in some Australian centres but is not yet universal; in standard NBA pathway, all Rh negative women receive routine anti-D. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guideline)

explanation.summary: PPROM at 24 to 34 weeks is managed expectantly with inpatient monitoring, antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM 24 hours apart x 2), and latency antibiotics (oral erythromycin 250 mg QID for 10 days). Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is contraindicated due to increased neonatal NEC risk (ORACLE I). Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection is given if delivery anticipated within 24 hours and gestation <30 weeks. Tocolysis is not recommended in PPROM. Monitoring includes maternal observations 4-hourly, FBC and CRP twice weekly, CTG daily and biophysical profile twice weekly. Delivery is recommended at 34 weeks or if chorioamnionitis, placental abruption, non-reassuring fetal status, or labour develops. Group B Strep prophylaxis in labour is mandatory unless screening negative within preceding 5 weeks.
key_points: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM 24 hours apart x 2 doses
Erythromycin 250 mg QID PO x 10 days (NOT amoxicillin with clavulanic acid)
Magnesium neuroprotection if delivery <24 hours and <30 weeks
Avoid tocolysis in PPROM
Plan delivery at 34 weeks unless complications
explanation.pearls: ORACLE I showed amoxicillin with clavulanic acid in PPROM increased neonatal NEC by absolute 1.5%, which has made erythromycin the only recommended latency antibiotic.

options.rationale: Tocolysis is not recommended in PPROM as it does not improve outcomes and may delay recognition of chorioamnionitis; inpatient management is standard. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)

Empirical IV ampicillin + gentamicin is for clinical chorioamnionitis (fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness); in stable PPROM, oral erythromycin is the evidence-based latency antibiotic. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)

Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid in PPROM is associated with increased risk of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis (ORACLE I) and is contraindicated as latency antibiotic. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)

Magnesium neuroprotection is indicated when delivery is imminent (within 24 hours) <30 weeks but is not the sole intervention here; corticosteroid and antibiotic latency are also indicated. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)

RANZCOG and SOMANZ recommend antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM at 0 and 24 hours) and 10 days of erythromycin in PPROM <34 weeks to reduce respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and chorioamnionitis. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline)

explanation.summary: PPH management follows the four T's: Tone (uterotonics, bimanual compression), Trauma (inspect for genital tract injury), Tissue (retained placenta), Thrombin (coagulopathy). First-line uterotonic is oxytocin; second-line options are ergometrine (contraindicated in HTN), carboprost (contraindicated in asthma), or misoprostol (broad safety profile). Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is recommended early as adjunct (WOMAN trial). Escalation includes intrauterine balloon tamponade (Bakri), uterine artery embolisation, and surgical options (B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, hysterectomy). Massive transfusion protocol should be activated for ongoing bleeding >1500 mL. Maternal vitals, urine output and ongoing loss must be monitored continuously.
key_points: First-line uterotonic: oxytocin (IM/IV)
Ergometrine: avoid in HTN/pre-eclampsia
Carboprost: avoid in asthma
Misoprostol: safest when others contraindicated (800 mcg SL or 1000 mcg PR)
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV early (WOMAN trial)
explanation.pearls: TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours of PPH onset reduces death from bleeding by about 30% (WOMAN trial); efficacy falls sharply after 3 hours.

options.rationale: Misoprostol is the safest second-line uterotonic when ergometrine (HTN) and carboprost (asthma) are contraindicated; 800 mcg sublingual or 1000 mcg rectal is the recommended dose. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

Carboprost is contraindicated in active asthma; while her asthma is well controlled, the alternative misoprostol is safer in this combined asthma + pre-eclampsia profile. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia due to severe vasoconstriction; her BP is 154/96 with active pre-eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

Tranexamic acid is recommended adjunctively in PPH and should be given (WOMAN trial), but uterotonic for ongoing atony is still required; TXA is adjunct, not replacement. (Source: WOMAN trial; RANZCOG PPH Guideline)
She has already received maximal first-line oxytocin without effect; escalation to second-line uterotonic is required, not repeat first-line. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is a true obstetric emergency requiring rapid systematic intervention to prevent neonatal brachial plexus injury, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and maternal trauma. The HELPERR mnemonic structures intervention: H - call for Help; E - Evaluate for Episiotomy; L - Legs hyperflexed (McRoberts); P - suprapubic Pressure; E - Enter and rotate (internal rotation manoeuvres including Woods corkscrew, Rubin); R - Remove posterior arm; R - Roll over to all-fours. Fundal pressure is contraindicated as it worsens impaction. Symphysiotomy is essentially obsolete. The Zavanelli manoeuvre (cephalic replacement and caesarean delivery) is reserved as the last option after all others have failed. Time is critical - 5 minutes from head delivery is a soft upper limit before significant hypoxic injury risk.
key_points: HELPERR: Help, Episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure, Enter & rotate, Remove posterior arm, Roll
McRoberts + suprapubic pressure resolves ~50% of cases
Avoid fundal pressure (worsens dystocia)
Zavanelli = last resort with high maternal morbidity
Brachial plexus injury occurs in ~10% of shoulder dystocias
explanation.pearls: Delivery of the posterior arm has the highest success rate of any single manoeuvre (about 85% release) and should be attempted before internal rotation manoeuvres when McRoberts + suprapubic pressure fails.

options.rationale: Zavanelli is last resort after multiple manoeuvres have failed and carries high maternal morbidity; not a first step. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline)

McRoberts (hyperflexion of maternal hips) combined with suprapubic pressure resolves about 50% of shoulder dystocias and is the first step in HELPERR after Help is called. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline)
Fundal pressure worsens shoulder dystocia by impacting the shoulder against the symphysis and risks uterine rupture; contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline)
Internal rotation manoeuvres are part of HELPERR but come after McRoberts + suprapubic pressure; not the first step. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline)
Symphysiotomy is essentially obsolete in Australian practice with severe maternal morbidity; not a recommended manoeuvre. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline)

explanation.summary: SOMANZ defines gestational hypertension as new-onset BP >=140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ involvement. Pre-eclampsia adds proteinuria (PCR >=30 mg/mmol or ACR >=8) or end-organ dysfunction (renal, liver, neurological, haematological, uteroplacental). Severe hypertension is >=160/110 and requires admission and acute lowering with IV labetalol, oral nifedipine, or IV hydralazine. Non-severe hypertension (140 to 159/90 to 109) is treated with oral labetalol (Australian first-line), oral nifedipine, or methyldopa; target BP is 110 to 140 systolic and 80 to 95 diastolic. Twice-weekly DAU monitoring includes BP, urinalysis, FBC, EUC, LFTs, PCR, CTG, and growth scans every 2 to 4 weeks. Aspirin (started before 16 weeks) prevents 60% of pre-eclampsia in high-risk women. Delivery timing depends on severity: 37 weeks for gestational hypertension or non-severe pre-eclampsia, earlier for severe disease.
key_points: Gestational HTN: BP >=140/90, no proteinuria, no end-organ involvement
Pre-eclampsia: + proteinuria (PCR >=30) OR end-organ dysfunction
Severe HTN >=160/110: admit + acute lowering
Non-severe HTN: oral labetalol first-line + DAU surveillance twice weekly
explanation.pearls: About 25% of women with gestational hypertension progress to pre-eclampsia within 2 to 4 weeks, which is why twice-weekly surveillance with urinalysis and bloods is mandatory until delivery.

options.rationale: Severe-range hypertension (>=160/110) is an admission threshold but 148-152/94-98 (non-severe) still warrants careful evaluation; community monitoring alone misses progression to pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Magnesium prophylaxis and expedited delivery are reserved for severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia; gestational hypertension without proteinuria or features does not meet either threshold. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

New non-severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP 140 to 159/90 to 109) without proteinuria or end-organ involvement is gestational hypertension; labetalol is the Australian first-line, with day-stay or DAU monitoring twice weekly for progression to pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Methyldopa is acceptable but labetalol is preferred first-line per SOMANZ; the major error is the 4-week interval which is far too long for new hypertension. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)
Repeated readings on contralateral arms in clinical setting confirm true hypertension; home monitoring alone misses end-organ involvement evolution. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Australian RANZCOG guidelines recommend universal antenatal vaginal-rectal GBS screening at 35 to 37 weeks with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) for: positive swab within 5 weeks, GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy, previous GBS-infected infant, preterm labour <37 weeks (regardless of swab status), or intrapartum fever >=38 (regardless of swab status). First-line IAP is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g 4-hourly; cefazolin for low-risk penicillin allergy; clindamycin (if sensitive) or vancomycin for high-risk allergy. Optimum coverage requires at least 4 hours before delivery, but partial cover is still given. PROM at term is not in itself an indication for IAP if GBS swab is negative within 5 weeks. Newborn observation is required for at least 24 to 48 hours in IAP exposure; full sepsis workup for unwell neonates.
key_points: Universal screening at 35-37 weeks (RANZCOG approach)
IAP indications: positive swab, GBS bacteriuria, prior GBS-infected infant, preterm, intrapartum fever
First-line: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g 4 hourly
Optimum coverage requires >=4 hours before delivery
Negative swab + low risk = NO antibiotic needed
explanation.pearls: Intrapartum benzylpenicillin given >=4 hours before delivery reduces early-onset neonatal GBS disease by approximately 86%; partial coverage (less than 4 hours) still provides about 47% reduction.

options.rationale: Negative GBS swab at 36 weeks (within 5 weeks of delivery), no GBS bacteriuria, no previous GBS-infected infant, term and afebrile means no GBS prophylaxis is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in Pregnancy)
Repeating swab in labour does not change immediate decisions and starting prophylaxis pending unnecessary results is overtreatment. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in Pregnancy)

Duration of ROM <18 hours at term with negative GBS swab is not an indication for prophylaxis; cefazolin would be reserved for penicillin allergy with low anaphylaxis risk. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in Pregnancy)

Negative GBS swab within 5 weeks of delivery in low-risk labour (afebrile, term, no prior GBS infant, no GBS bacteriuria) excludes need for prophylaxis under universal-screening RANZCOG/SOMANZ pathway. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in Pregnancy)
Clindamycin is for penicillin-allergic women with high anaphylaxis risk AND positive GBS or risk factors; no indication here. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage is defined as PV bleeding before 20 weeks with a viable intrauterine pregnancy and closed cervical os. Over 90% of viable pregnancies with first-trimester bleeding continue to live birth. Investigation is transvaginal ultrasound (fetal heart confirms viability) and beta hCG only if scan is non-diagnostic (PUL). Anti-D immunoglobulin is NOT required in Australia for spontaneous bleeding in viable pregnancy under 12 weeks; it IS required for surgical termination, ectopic pregnancy, or any sensitising event from 13 weeks onwards (250 IU under 20 weeks, 625 IU from 20 weeks). Vaginal progesterone has weak evidence for women with prior miscarriage AND current bleeding (PRISM/ALIFE subgroups), and is not routine. Patient counselling, EPAS follow-up, and clear written safety net (heavy bleeding, severe pain, dizziness, fever) are essential.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage: PV bleed + viable IUP + closed os
>90% continue to live birth if viable on scan
Anti-D NOT required for spontaneous bleed <12 weeks viable IUP
Anti-D required for surgical termination, ectopic, or >=13 weeks
Progesterone benefit only in prior-miscarriage + current bleeding subgroup
explanation.pearls: Australian anti-D dosing: 250 IU for sensitising events from 13 to 20 weeks, 625 IU from 20 weeks onwards including routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks; spontaneous bleed before 12 weeks does NOT require anti-D.

options.rationale: Threatened miscarriage with viable IUP at <12 weeks: reassure (over 90% continue to live birth); anti-D is NOT required for sensitising events under 12 weeks unless the pregnancy is terminated surgically or in ectopic; follow-up with usual antenatal pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline; RANZCOG First Trimester Bleeding)
Anti-D is NOT indicated for spontaneous bleeding in viable pregnancy under 12 weeks in Australia; routine administration before 12 weeks is overtreatment. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline)

PRISM showed progesterone benefit only in women with prior miscarriage AND current bleeding (subgroup); this is her second pregnancy with no prior miscarriage, so progesterone is not first-line. (Source: PRISM trial; RANZCOG)
Viable IUP confirmed on TVUS does not require serial hCG; serial hCG is for pregnancy of unknown location. (Source: RANZCOG First Trimester Bleeding)
Surgical evacuation is for incomplete or missed miscarriage; this is a viable pregnancy and evacuation would terminate it. (Source: RANZCOG First Trimester Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Australian Menopause Society (AMS) recommends menopausal hormone therapy (MHT, formerly HRT) as first-line for moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms in women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause without contraindication (oestrogen-sensitive cancer, undiagnosed PV bleeding, active VTE, severe liver disease, uncontrolled hypertension, recent ACS). Transdermal oestradiol is preferred over oral for VTE risk reduction (avoids hepatic first-pass) and is the choice in overweight, migraine with aura, or VTE risk. Progestogen is mandatory if uterus present: cyclical for perimenopausal (LMP <12 months) to mimic menstrual cycle, continuous for postmenopausal. Micronised progesterone (Prometrium 100 mg daily continuous or 200 mg for 12 days cyclical) has more favourable breast and VTE profile than synthetic progestins. Review symptoms and risks annually. Vaginal oestrogen is for GSM only (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms) and has no systemic effects.
key_points: MHT first-line for vasomotor symptoms <60 yo or <10 yr from menopause
Transdermal oestradiol preferred (no first-pass VTE risk)
Progestogen mandatory if uterus: cyclical (perimeno) or continuous (postmeno)
Micronised progesterone preferred over synthetic progestins
Vaginal oestrogen = GSM only, no systemic effects
explanation.pearls: WHI sub-analysis shows transdermal oestradiol carries no excess VTE risk compared with oral oestrogen which doubles VTE risk; this is the basis for preferring patches/gels in overweight women or VTE risk factors.

options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with intact uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma; progestogen is mandatory for endometrial protection. (Source: AMS Menopausal Hormone Therapy)

Continuous combined regimen is for women >12 months amenorrhoeic (postmenopausal); she is perimenopausal with LMP 8 months ago and would need cyclical progesterone to avoid breakthrough bleeding. (Source: AMS Menopausal Hormone Therapy)

Perimenopausal women (LMP <12 months ago) need cyclical progesterone to mimic menstrual cycle and avoid breakthrough bleeding; transdermal oestradiol avoids first-pass hepatic VTE risk; micronised progesterone has more favourable breast and VTE profile than synthetic progestins. (Source: AMS Menopausal Hormone Therapy; RANZCOG)

Tibolone is licensed for postmenopausal women (>12 months amenorrhoeic) and is unsuitable for perimenopause; her current pattern needs cyclical bleed-replicating therapy. (Source: AMS Menopausal Hormone Therapy)

Local vaginal oestrogen treats GSM not vasomotor symptoms; SSRI/SNRI is second-line for vasomotor symptoms when HRT contraindicated, not as first-line in absence of contraindication. (Source: AMS Menopausal Hormone Therapy)

explanation.summary: Chorionicity determination in twin pregnancy is most accurate at 10 to 14 weeks and determines surveillance intensity, complication risk, and timing of delivery. Lambda sign (thick triangular projection of placental tissue into the membrane base) indicates dichorionic placentation; T-sign (perpendicular membrane meeting placenta without projection) indicates monochorionic. Dichorionic-diamniotic (DCDA, 70% of twins): two placentas (may appear fused), lambda sign, thick (3-layer) membrane; growth scans 4-weekly from 24 weeks; deliver 37 to 38 weeks. Monochorionic-diamniotic (MCDA, 25% to 30%): single placenta, T-sign, thin (2-layer) membrane; fortnightly scans from 16 weeks for TTTS (Quintero staging), TAPS, sIUGR; deliver 36 to 37 weeks. Monochorionic-monoamniotic (MCMA, <1%): single placenta, no inter-twin membrane, high cord entanglement risk; inpatient surveillance from 24 to 28 weeks; deliver by caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks. Selective fetoscopic laser is treatment for severe TTTS (Quintero stage II or higher).
key_points: Chorionicity best at 10-14 weeks: lambda (DC) vs T-sign (MC)
DCDA (70%): 4-weekly scans from 24 weeks, deliver 37-38 weeks
MCDA (25-30%): fortnightly from 16 weeks for TTTS, deliver 36-37 weeks
MCMA (<1%): inpatient from 24-28 weeks, caesarean 32-34 weeks
TTTS severe (Quintero II+): fetoscopic laser at tertiary centre
explanation.pearls: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome affects 10 to 15% of monochorionic-diamniotic twins, peaks at 16 to 26 weeks, and untreated severe disease (Quintero stage III or higher) carries mortality of about 90% for both twins.

options.rationale: Lambda sign would be expected in DCDA; T-sign and absent lambda indicate monochorionic placentation requiring more intensive surveillance than DCDA. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline)
Dichorionic-monoamniotic does not occur biologically (each chorion develops its own amniotic sac); this is an impossible combination. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline)
MCMA shows absent inter-twin membrane (single amniotic cavity); presence of a thin membrane excludes MCMA. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline)

T-sign and absent lambda with 2 amniotic cavities = monochorionic-diamniotic; RANZCOG recommends fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), TAPS, and growth discordance surveillance with delivery at 36 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline)
Conjoined twins are visible on ultrasound as shared body parts; the scan shows 2 separate fetuses in separate amniotic cavities. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Rhesus negative women without anti-D antibodies receive routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis (RAADP) at 28 weeks (625 IU IM, covers FMH up to about 6 mL) and 34 weeks (625 IU IM), plus 625 IU IM postpartum if neonate is Rh-positive. Sensitising events (PV bleed >=13 weeks, abdominal trauma, external cephalic version, invasive procedures, intrauterine death, antepartum haemorrhage) require additional anti-D within 72 hours, dosed by Kleihauer-Betke test (100 IU per 1 mL fetal RBC). Doses over 1500 IU IM should be given IV. Repeat Kleihauer at 48 hours confirms clearance; if fetal cells remain, repeat anti-D and arrange MCA Doppler for fetal anaemia surveillance. Sensitised women (anti-D titre >=1:16 or rising) require tertiary surveillance with MCA Doppler PSV from 18 weeks for fetal anaemia detection (PSV >1.5 multiples of median triggers cordocentesis and IUT).
key_points: RAADP: 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks + postpartum if neonate Rh+
Sensitising event: additional anti-D within 72 hours Kleihauer-guided
Dose: 100 IU per 1 mL fetal RBC; >1500 IU give IV
Repeat Kleihauer at 48 hours to confirm clearance
Sensitised: MCA Doppler PSV from 18 weeks; IUT if PSV >1.5 MoM
explanation.pearls: Standard 625 IU anti-D dose covers approximately 6 mL of fetal red cells (about 12 mL of fetal whole blood); above this, Kleihauer-guided dosing at 100 IU per 1 mL fetal RBC is mandatory.

options.rationale: Routine prophylaxis covers feto-maternal haemorrhage of about 6 mL or less; 35 mL exceeds the routine dose capacity and requires additional anti-D. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline; NBA Anti-D)
Fetal red cells clear from maternal circulation over days; awaiting clearance loses the window for sensitisation prevention which is critical in the first 72 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline)
Dose is Kleihauer-guided: 100 IU per 1 mL fetal RBC; 35 mL requires about 3500 IU additional (much more than 625 IU); single 625 IU is insufficient. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline)

Kleihauer-guided dosing: 100 IU anti-D per 1 mL of fetal red cells in maternal circulation; 35 mL requires 3500 IU; given within 72 hours of sensitising event; follow-up Kleihauer at 48 hours confirms clearance. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline; NBA)
IVIG is reserved for established alloimmunisation with severe fetal anaemia; it is not the preventive agent. (Source: RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency presents as painless cervical dilation and second-trimester pregnancy loss without preceding labour, infection, or bleeding. Cerclage is indicated in three scenarios: history-indicated (>=3 prior mid-trimester losses or preterm births, placed at 12 to 14 weeks); ultrasound-indicated (history of 1 to 2 prior preterm births or losses AND TVUS cervical length <25 mm before 24 weeks); physical examination-indicated rescue cerclage (cervix dilated with visible membranes before 24 weeks, no infection, no labour). McDonald cerclage (transvaginal purse-string at cervicovaginal junction) is the standard technique; Shirodkar is alternative; abdominal cerclage is reserved for prior failed transvaginal cerclage. Vaginal progesterone (200 mg nightly) is first-line for incidental short cervix without prior history. Cerclage is removed at 36 to 37 weeks or earlier if labour begins. Tocolysis is not given prophylactically.
key_points: Cervical insufficiency: painless dilation, mid-trimester loss
History-indicated cerclage: >=3 prior mid-trimester losses, place at 12-14 weeks
Ultrasound-indicated: 1-2 prior + CL <25 mm before 24 weeks
Rescue cerclage: dilated cervix with membranes, no infection or labour
Vaginal progesterone first-line for incidental short cervix, no prior history
explanation.pearls: TVUS cervical length under 15 mm at 16 to 24 weeks in a woman with prior preterm birth carries about 50% risk of recurrent preterm delivery before 32 weeks without intervention, and is a strong driver of cerclage placement.

options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone is first-line for incidental short cervix without prior history; with history of 2 painless mid-trimester losses, cerclage is the indicated intervention (history-indicated). (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Birth Prevention)
Bed rest has no evidence for preterm birth prevention; surveillance alone misses the window for cerclage which works best at 12 to 14 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Birth Prevention)

Combination of history of >=2 prior mid-trimester losses + TVUS cervical length under 25 mm at <24 weeks is ultrasound-indicated cerclage; insertion before 24 weeks reduces preterm birth before 35 weeks by about 30%. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Birth Prevention; RCOG Cerclage)

Arabin pessary evidence is mixed and is not first-line in Australian practice when classical history-indicated or ultrasound-indicated cerclage criteria are met. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Birth Prevention)
17-OHPC was the older standard but the PROLONG trial showed no benefit, and FDA withdrew approval in 2023; not first-line for cervical insufficiency. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Birth Prevention)
